The launched `git-upload-pack` of a delivery keeps the server's `$HOME` (the server's own fetch reads `$HOME/.gitconfig`, so the agent's home must not stand in for it), so it prints a harmless `unable to access '/home/node/.config/git/attributes'` warning. `stripUngovernedRepoCatalog` still removes a checkout's `.claude` with the server's `rmSync` (not git, so not this ruling's rule), and a new checkout is renamed into a directory an agent could have replaced with a symlink; neither executes anything, and both are left for a later ruling. *Dated note 2026-09-25 (ruling 485, F40-62):* the first is closed, and it was not harmless: the server's recursive remove of a supporting checkout died half-way on a wrangler `mkdtemp` directory (0700 as the agent's uid) and left a tree with no `.git` that every later review tripped over. Every removal or replacement of a tree an agent can write (the strip's `.claude` among them) now runs as its person through the launcher (`removeAgentTree`, ruling 485). The rename into a workspace still stands as written.

    **(k) Dated note 2026-09-25 (pass 40 review, R-seams-1, high): the server never executes git with an agent-writable repository as its working repository under its own uid.** (c) said git clone, fetch, merge and push stayed `node`. The review measured what that meant in `viberr-app-1`: a workspace's `.git/hooks` and `.git/config` are group-writable to every agent uid (they have to be: agents commit there), and the server then ran its own git in it as `node` with `process.env` (`VIBERR_SECRET_ENCRYPTION_KEY`, `VIBERR_SESSION_SECRET`) — the pre-run refresh's `status` (which runs `core.fsmonitor`) and `checkout`/`merge` (hooks), ruling 468's unborn check, the delivery's `add -A` (filter drivers), `commit` (hooks) and `push` (`pre-push`, plus the PAT in the askpass env, where a planted `insteadOf`/`pushInsteadOf` or credential helper would carry it to a host of the agent's choosing). The verifier reproduced a `reference-transaction` hook on fetch, fsmonitor on status and `post-checkout` on checkout against git 2.47.3. So an agent could have the server run its code with the server's authority, which defeats everything above. The rule, in two halves. *Local git inside a workspace runs as the person the work bills* — the task's owner (ruling 127) — through the launcher like their runs, with the agent's `$HOME` and no credential in its environment: `taskWorkspaceGit` (`workspace-git.server.ts`) over `agentGitLaunchFor` (the runtime root and agent `$HOME` prepared, no vendor home to hand back). Moved there: the refresh's fetch-from-mirror, status, checkout, merge and every read (`workspace-refresh.server.ts`); the unborn check (`unborn-checkout.server.ts`); the supporting `clone --no-local` of the delivering checkout, the origin rewrite, the identity, the review pin (`specialist-run.server.ts`); the `.claude` strip's `ls-files`/`update-index` (`skill-mount.server.ts`, and its operator call); every workspace read, the auto-commit, the lease/store-layout/workflow gates' reads, the discard's reads and delete (`push-workspace.server.ts`); the branch update's reads, merge, conflict listing, abort and reset (`update-branch.server.ts`); the reconcile's reads (`workspace-delivery.server.ts`); the operator's `origin` read and its clone-time fallback `git show` (`operator-repo-read.server.ts`). With no launcher (dev, the test harness) the same git runs as the server, as before; with isolation on and nobody to name (no task, no owner) it refuses — the refresh degrades, the delivery reports it — and never falls back (460(h)). *Anything that needs the PAT runs as the server in a repository the server owns*: the mirror, or a per-operation bare **stage** (`withServerStage`, `projects/<slug>/.repo-stage/`, 0755, removed afterwards and swept after six hours) that borrows the mirror's objects through `objects/info/alternates` under the mirror's lock, so a rebuild cannot pull them out from under it. `ls-remote` and the push, the branch update's fetches of the base and of origin's copy of the task branch, the refresh's no-mirror fallback, all run there against `https://github.com/<repo>.git` from the project file — never the `origin` a checkout's config names; the workspace then fetches GitHub's refs from the stage (or the mirror) as the person. A branch leaves a workspace by the server's `git fetch --no-tags` into the stage over git's transport (never `--local`) with `--upload-pack=<launcher>` and `VIBERR_LAUNCH_EXEC=git-upload-pack` (`workspaceUploadPack`): git runs the launcher with the workspace path as its one argument, so the workspace's repository — its config, alternates, a `.git` that is a gitfile — is read only by the person, and the server's side parses a pack stream, as it does from any remote. The push publishes `<sha>:refs/heads/<branch>`, the head the delivery read for its origin compare (ruling 134), so a branch moved after that read cannot slip a different head into the push (a failed hand-off is a `push_failed` that says the branch "could not be read out of the workspace"). A new checkout is cloned by the server into a stage of its own, its origin rewritten there, handed to the agent group and renamed into place (`cloneThroughStage`), so no server git ever runs in a directory an agent can write mid-clone; the hardlinks from the mirror are kept (the agent's own uid could not make them under `fs.protected_hardlinks`). The `gh` of the reconcile runs as the server but in the task's directory, never the checkout, on the credential-free base plus `gh`'s own sign-in names. *Defense in depth for every git the server spawns*, as itself or as a person: an environment built on `filteredSpawnEnv()` (`serverGitEnv`, and `createGitHubAskpassEnv`/`createGitHubClonePlan` now build on it too — they used to spread `process.env`) with `core.hooksPath=/dev/null` and `core.fsmonitor=false` at command-line precedence through `GIT_CONFIG_COUNT`/`_KEY_n`/`_VALUE_n` (after the credentialed git's `credential.helper` reset). They ride only the child's environment, never `process.env` or `filteredSpawnEnv()`, so an agent's own git keeps its hooks (asserted in the image). `filteredSpawnEnv` moved to a leaf module, `spawn-env.server.ts`, that `runtime-registry.server.ts` re-exports. Found on the way and fixed with it: boot's pre-460 hand-over added group write to every server-owned file in a checkout, including object files HARDLINKED from the mirror, which widened the mirror's own inode to every agent. A file with a second link is never widened now (`shareTreeWithAgents`, and `shareTreeBuiltForAgents` for a staged checkout), and boot takes group and other write off every server-owned file under `projects/*/.repo-mirror/` (`revokeMirrorWrites`, `mirrorWritesRevoked` in the layout report). Where the full rule is not applied: nowhere that runs git. `rmSync` of a checkout's `.claude` and the rename into a workspace are server file operations in an agent-writable directory, recorded in (j). Tests: `workspace-git.server.test.ts` (real git and a GitHub stand-in on disk: a checkout carrying planted hooks in `.git/hooks` and in a `core.hooksPath`, a `core.fsmonitor`, a credential helper and `insteadOf`/`pushInsteadOf` to an agent's repository is refreshed, delivered with an auto-commit, updated from its base and reconciled, and nothing planted runs while the push reaches the project's repository and the agent's stays empty; `gh` runs in the task directory; with a stand-in launcher, every workspace git and the transport's `git-upload-pack` run as the owner's uid with the overrides and without the server's secret or the PAT, the push and `ls-remote` are never launched, and a refresh with nobody to name refuses; the server git's environment carries no secret, the overrides are not in `process.env` or an agent's base), `agent-isolation.server.test.ts` (a linked object is never widened, a widened mirror file is revoked, a staged tree is shared), and the updated `push-workspace`, `update-branch`, `delivery-decision` T3 and `task-governance` discard tests (the push, `ls-remote` and the base fetch from the stage, against the project's URL). Canaried: `SERVER_GIT_CONFIG` emptied (the refresh, delivery, update and env tests fail on planted hooks and fsmonitor), the push from the workspace again (the planted `pushInsteadOf` takes it), `workspaceSpawn` ignoring the launch and `workspaceUploadPack` returning no `--upload-pack` (the shape tests find no launched line), `serverGitEnv` on `process.env` (the secret is seen), `gh` back in the checkout, the `nlink` skip dropped and `revokeMirrorWrites` a no-op. In the image (`viberr-app:review-iso-seams`, a throwaway named volume, 2026-09-25): `scripts/check-agent-isolation.sh` passed every check, including four new ones — an agent's own git runs the hooks it planted, a workspace git launched as a person with the overrides runs nothing planted, the server's own git cannot read a checkout only its agent can read, and the server fetches a branch out of that checkout with `git-upload-pack` launched as its person; and the real refresh, staged clone, delivery push, branch update and reconcile, driven against a checkout an agent uid committed in and planted into, with the real launcher, ran nothing planted, pushed the project's repository and left the agent's empty.

    **(l) Dated note 2026-09-25 (pass 40 review, R-launcher-1, medium): the model-catalog probe runs as the viewer.** `fetchLiveClaudeModels` spawned the vendored Claude CLI as `node` with `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` = the viewer's own `claude-home`; a CLI with an expired OAuth token refreshes it and rewrites `.credentials.json` there 0600, which left a `node:node` sign-in the viewer's agent uid could not read, so their next launched run failed as signed out (the launcher's post-run hand-back then repaired it). Chosen: route the probe through the launcher as the viewer (`claudeProbeOptions(credential, launch)` sets `spawnClaudeCodeProcess` to `spawnClaudeCli` with `agentLaunchFor`'s launch and `$HOME` to their agent home; the launcher hands `claude-home` back when the probe exits), exactly like their runs. Rejected: a throwaway `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` the server may write — the CLI ROTATES the refresh token when it refreshes, so a refresh in a copy would spend the one in the real home and sign the person out for good. The route passes the viewer's id (`userId`); where this server launches agents and there is no viewer or the launch cannot be prepared, the curated catalog is served and nothing is spawned as `node` (460(h)). Tests: `model-catalog.server.test.ts` "R-launcher-1" (with a stand-in launcher the CLI is spawned through it as the viewer's uid, `VIBERR_LAUNCH_HOME` = their `claude-home`, `$HOME` = their agent home; no viewer → curated and no query; isolation off → the probe spawns as before). Canaried: `spawnClaudeCodeProcess` dropped, the `launchesAgents()` guard skipped. In the image: a 0600 `.credentials.json` rewritten by the probe's spawned command is owned by the viewer's uid and group-readable once it exits.

    It narrows ruling 127 (a person's runtime home is owned by their agent uid, not created 0o700 by the server), narrows ruling 174 (a launched Claude run's group is led by the launcher and its hard kill is SIGUSR2; the sweep reaches agent processes through `--reap`; the Codex SDK is given a `codexPathOverride` after all, the launcher, whose override is not D1's wrapper and prepends the helper `PATH` itself) and narrows ruling 181 (the run home's copies are handed to the person's uid, and the settle hands them over before it reads them). Tests: `agent-isolation.server.test.ts` (the uid map: from the floor, stable, never reused after the account is deleted, refused past the range; the Dockerfile ARGs pinned to the constants; the boot layout on a temp root; health `off`, `on`, `degraded` from a probe that reads and from a probe that fails, and the key order; `agentLaunchFor` off, on, and refused with the launcher's words), `claude-runtime.server.test.ts` "ruling 460" (the spawn shape: the launcher detached, the absolute binary, the uid, argv untouched, no server secret in the env, the person's key kept; SIGKILL → SIGUSR2; a bare `node` resolved on PATH; the compaction launched too), `codex-runtime.server.test.ts` "ruling 460" (`codexPathOverride` = the launcher, the env carries the vendored binary and its PATH helpers, the run home and the written-back sign-in handed to the uid), `run-processes.server.test.ts` "ruling 460" (the launcher's TERM then KILL, SIGUSR2 for a launched group), `run-service.server.test.ts` "ruling 460" (the spec carries the uid, launcher and `$HOME`; a launch that cannot be prepared refuses the run with `run·unavailable` and spawns nothing), and `backend-login.server.test.ts` "ruling 460" (the sign-in and its confirmation through the launcher as the person). Every new test was canaried: the source broken, the test seen failing, the source restored. The kernel's side is `scripts/check-agent-isolation.sh`, which `npm run e2e` runs in the e2e stack's app container after requiring `agentIsolation` to be `on`.

    **(z) A test that read the host's `./docker-data`.** `update-branch-operator.server.test.ts` compared the shipped operator asset with `docker-data/agents/definitions/operator.md` on the developer's machine, on the premise that the host folder WAS the live store. After the move it is at most the pre-move fallback, so the check is retired: the store's copy is upgraded at boot from the asset by its shipped hash (`PRIOR_SHIPPED_HASHES`), which the seed tests already pin.

461. **A credentialed MCP connection is served through Viberr's loopback gateway: the credential stays in the server, a run holds a run-scoped token** (owner, 2026-09-24, pass 40, findings F40-2, F40-3 and F40-4; spec `planning/discovery-2026-09-24-pass40-akinozer-site/SPEC-461-mcp-credential-proxy.md`; "breaking changes welcome"). Measured: `resolveSpecialistMcpServersDetailed` decrypted an org MCP server's sealed credential into the run's own config (`headers.Authorization` on HTTP, `env.MCP_CREDENTIAL` on stdio), and the Claude SDK serializes `mcpServers` onto the CLI's argv (`--mcp-config`), so the agent's own shell could read the bearer with `ps` and a stdio server's environment at `/proc/<pid>/environ` (F40-2); `codexMcpServers` dropped the credential for that very reason, so a credentialed server connected anonymously on Codex (F40-3); and the owner's Cloudflare provisioning, done by agents with a Cloudflare API token that only Viberr holds, had nowhere to live (F40-4). Decided: (a) *The gateway.* `app/server/mcp-proxy/gateway.server.ts` is an HTTP listener bound to `127.0.0.1` only, on `VIBERR_MCP_PROXY_PORT` (default `0`: a free port picked at boot and read back), started in boot before anything can start a run and torn down by `runProcessShutdown`, synchronously enough that every stdio process it spawned is killed before the signal is re-raised. It is not a React Router route and nothing outside the host reaches it; its state lives on `globalThis`, as the run service's does, so a dev reload keeps the listener and the live tokens; the SDK's DNS-rebinding guard pins the `Host` header to the loopback address. A bind failure is logged and boot carries on: a credentialed server then resolves to nothing, and the run's prompt names that reason ("Viberr's MCP gateway … is not running"). (b) *Run-scoped tokens.* A credentialed org server resolves, on either transport and for every backend, to `{ type: "http", url: "http://127.0.0.1:<port>/mcp/<name>" }`; that URL is the only marker, so no second channel has to carry "this one is proxied" through the specialist, operator, controller and resume paths in between. `startRun`, the funnel all of them take, mints ONE random 256-bit token per run after its refusal checks (`bindRunToMcpGateway`), bound to the run id, the exact server names the run mounts and the ruling-176 write tools it withholds on each, and puts `Authorization: Bearer <token>` on each gateway mount (the config is rebuilt from the parsed mount, so nothing but the URL, the run's token and ruling 176's per-tool denies reaches the run). The marker is the gateway's exact URL, its own port included, so an uncredentialed org server that merely lives on the loopback at a `/mcp/<name>` path is left alone, and a gateway that is not listening marks nothing. Only the token's SHA-256 is kept. It is revoked on every path that ends the run: in `settleRun` (success and failure alike — from its first line the token calls nothing, and it is revoked once a completion compaction is done, or at once when there is none, because that compaction replays the session with the run's own servers; R-gateway-4 below), in `stopRunProcess` on both arms (an interrupt with a live process, and one with none — a queued or reserved run, which holds its token from `startRun`), when the drain drops a queued run that stopped waiting, and when an adapter's `start` throws; it dies with the process. Beside those, the gateway refuses a token whose run row is no longer `running` or `queued` (and revokes it), so a path that forgot would still fail closed. An unknown, revoked or wrong-server token is answered 401 with a JSON-RPC error whose sentence says a 401 means the run ended, and nothing is forwarded. (c) *What a run is handed.* The same gateway mount on both backends: the Claude adapter passes it verbatim, the Codex translation carries `headers` as the server's `http_headers` (ruling 176's `disabled_tools` still ride beside it), so a Codex run authenticates exactly as a Claude run does and the "credential dropped on Codex" limitation, its docstring, the persona's "MCP credentials on this Codex run" section (F27-P2), the Settings row's "Claude runs only · Codex mounts it unauthenticated" caveat (F-P3), the capability matrix's line and the Codex-only credential-less pre-flight (B-4) with its shared-health re-probe (P9) are gone. The stdio pre-flight now runs WITH the credential on every backend, because the gateway spawns the command with it for every backend. An uncredentialed server mounts directly, as before. The run token is nobody's secret: it opens only that run's grants, only through the gateway, only while the run lives. (d) *Upstream.* The gateway speaks MCP to the run over Streamable HTTP (the SDK's server transport; `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk` moves to `dependencies`) with one session per `initialize`, and MCP to the real server through the ONE client Viberr now speaks to an org server with (`upstream.server.ts`): Streamable HTTP with `Authorization: Bearer <credential>` attached in the server process, falling back to the legacy HTTP+SSE transport when the POST is answered with a 4xx other than 401/403 (an authentication refusal is reported as itself, "authentication rejected", not retried as something else); a stdio server is a command the SERVER spawns (`upstream-stdio.server.ts`, over `spawnMcpProcess`, the discovery probe's own spawn: the server's uid, the secret-filtered environment plus `MCP_CREDENTIAL`, a process group of its own torn down with `killMcpProcessTree`), one upstream per (run, server), closed at revoke. The SDK's own stdio transport was not used: it spawns through `cross-spawn` with its own environment and signals only the direct child, orphaning an `npx` tree. The upstream client declares the capability set the probe always declared (roots, sampling, elicitation, P13-LV-19, so a run sees every tool) and answers each honestly: no roots, elicitation declined, sampling refused with a sentence. Forwarded: `tools/list` with the withheld write tools removed, `tools/call` with a withheld one refused as a tool error in `bashDenyReason`'s shape (`mcpWriteToolDenyReason`: the capability by label and id, the tool and server, "say what you needed in your report instead" — a direct mount never lists such a tool, so this is what a run reads only if it calls the name anyway), resources and prompts when the upstream declares them, the three `list_changed` notifications, and progress (which also resets the call timeout). A call slower than five minutes, a listing slower than one, an upstream that cannot be reached (a 502 on `initialize`) and an upstream's own error all come back as JSON-RPC errors naming the server, never a hang. (e) *Record.* Every forwarded call is logged at info (run id, server, tool, duration, outcome — `ok`, `tool_error`, `withheld` or `error`; never arguments or results). A call to a tool the admin marked as a write tool is audited `task.agent.mcp_write_call` (run id, server, tool, outcome, duration), a refused one too, under the run's own actor: the agent's ref on a specialist run, `operator` on an operator run, and on a controller turn the asker as the controller's instrument, which is the actor the turn already starts under; one action name for all three, since the actor says whose call it was. (f) *Health and probes.* The HTTP health probe (`saveMcpServer`'s probe and `testMcpServer`, which the controller's `test_mcp_server` calls) runs through `connectHttpUpstream` and `listAllTools` for every HTTP server, so a credentialed server's "up" means up with its credential over the transport the run's calls will take; the raw handshake it replaced called a legacy SSE server "endpoint answered 405". The stdio probe keeps its own handshake (its install heuristics are the probe's) over the same spawn. `healthSnapshot` appends `mcpProxy: { listening, port, liveTokens }` after `toolchain` (key order is the contract), so `/resources/health` and `instance_health` report it; it never degrades health — restarting the rest of the instance would not bind the port, and the runs say what they are missing. (g) *The prompt tells the truth.* `gatewayMcpSection` is one sentence shared by the three prompts ("<names> is/are mounted through Viberr's MCP gateway: the credential is held by Viberr, and you never need it or see it; a 401 from the gateway means this run has ended"): in a specialist's static block (the proxied set follows the profile's grants, not the task), in the operator's dynamic tail beside its other MCP notes, and in the controller's static block after its runtime block. Deliberate residuals: the run token sits in the CLI's argv on both backends (the Claude SDK's `--mcp-config`, Codex's `--config`), so another process on the host that can list processes can read a LIVE run's token and use that run's grants through the gateway until the run settles — the spec accepts this as "not a secret of any person"; carrying it in the CLI's environment instead (Codex's `bearer_token_env_var`, and whatever the Claude CLI expands) would close it and is left for a later ruling, since the Claude half is unverified. A stdio server behind the gateway runs under the server's uid, as the discovery probe always has, so an admin-registered command is trusted to that level. Not a numbered-ruling change: the code comment that called F7-MCP1 "ruling 8" was a citation collision (decisions.md's ruling 8 is the tweaks panel; recorded by the 2026-09-01 doc validation), so F7-MCP1's "credential attached at spawn" is replaced in `specialist-mcp.server.ts`'s docstring, not here; ruling 116's aside about the credential-less Codex mount carries a dated note. Tests: `gateway.server.test.ts` (against a real in-test Streamable HTTP server that REQUIRES its bearer: list and call through with every upstream request carrying the credential and the run config never containing it; ruling 176's filter, refusal and audit; a marked tool called through by a run holding the grant; a wrong token, another server's name and a revoked token all 401 with nothing forwarded, the live session dead with the token; a run no longer live refused; an upstream error and a timeout named; an unreachable upstream a 502; a refused credential "authentication rejected"; the SSE fallback against a real legacy server; a stdio command the server spawns reading `MCP_CREDENTIAL` from its environment while the run config holds neither the value nor the name, and killed at revoke; a stopped gateway leaving a credentialed server unmounted with its reason; a loopback server at `/mcp/<name>` on another port left unbound), `gateway-runs.server.test.ts` (through `startRun` on Claude and Codex: one token on the HTTP and stdio mounts, the whole spec free of the credential, the token live while the run is; the settle after success and after failure, an interrupt, and an interrupt of a queued run with no live handle all revoke it), `specialist-mcp.server.test.ts` (resolution: gateway URLs for HTTP and stdio, the JSON free of the credential, an uncredentialed server direct, a marked tool's per-tool deny kept, rotation), `codex-runtime.server.test.ts` (`http_headers`), `claude-runtime.server.test.ts`, `controller-run.server.test.ts` (a turn mounts a granted credentialed server through the gateway with its own token, the prompt says so, the token dies with the turn), `resources.server.test.ts` (a credentialed legacy-SSE server probed up with every request carrying the credential; a refused credential reads "authentication rejected"; the HTTP fake now answers the real handshake), `health-snapshot.server.test.ts`, `audit-coverage.server.test.ts`, `operator-kb-injection.server.test.ts`, `specialist-run.server.test.ts`. Canaries, each run by breaking the source, watching the named tests fail and restoring the file byte for byte: the resolver attaching the credential again; Codex dropping `http_headers`; the gateway listing a withheld tool, and forwarding a call to one; a token opening any server; the settle not revoking; the no-handle interrupt not revoking; the stdio upstream spawned without `MCP_CREDENTIAL`; `mcpProxy` dropped from health; the upstream client sending no credential; no SSE fallback; each of the three prompts dropping its sentence; a write call not audited; a mount recognized by its loopback shape instead of the gateway's own URL. Smoke against real servers (2026-09-24): through the gateway, `https://docs.mcp.cloudflare.com/mcp` answered `initialize`, `tools/list` (`search_cloudflare_documentation`, `migrate_pages_to_workers_guide`) and a `tools/call`, with and without a bearer attached upstream; the Cloudflare API MCP server (`https://mcp.cloudflare.com/mcp`) answers a bogus token 401, which the upstream client reports as "authentication rejected" without falling back. *Pre-merge review (2026-09-25), confirmed findings and what changed:* **R-gateway-1 (high).** A stdio upstream that printed one JSON-RPC line over 10 MiB (a large query result, a `read_file` of a big log) made the SDK's `ReadBuffer` throw inside `McpChildTransport`'s stdout listener; in the server process that is an uncaughtException, and the crash handler exits the whole instance — where before this ruling the same line hurt only the CLI that spawned the server. Now nothing a child prints can throw out of the listener: a line over the SDK's 10 MiB limit (`MCP_STDIO_MAX_LINE_BYTES`, the limit the CLI's own stdio transport applied) stops that process, as the SDK's transport does, and its calls fail as "stopped: it sent one message over the 10 MiB stdio limit"; a throw from the message handler is reported, not raised. **R-gateway-2 (low).** When a stdio process died mid-call the gateway closed the run's sessions from the upstream's `onclose`, which the SDK runs BEFORE it rejects the calls still waiting, so the session's handlers were aborted and the call was never answered (the CLI's own watchdog ended it 1.5–5 minutes later with a generic error) — contrary to (d)'s "never a hang". A session on an upstream that closed now stops routing at once (the run's next request is a 404, and it re-initializes onto a fresh upstream) and closes one macrotask later, after the calls in flight have been answered; a call on a connection that closed reads the upstream's own account ("exited (exit code 3): <stderr>") instead of "Connection closed". Tests: `gateway.server.test.ts` "R-gateway-1" (an 11 MiB answer through a real spawned stdio server: the call fails by name, the process is gone, the next run gets a fresh one) and "R-gateway-2" (a stdio server that exits 3 mid-call: the call rejects naming its exit, the session then 404s). Canaries, each seen red and restored byte for byte: the append unguarded (vitest reports the uncaught `ReadBuffer exceeded maximum size` and the call only times out); the sessions closed in `onclose` (both calls hang to the client's timeout). **R-gateway-5 (low).** (a)'s promise that every stdio process the gateway spawned dies before the signal is re-raised did not hold for one still in its handshake (a cold `npx -y` holds `initialize` for up to the 30 s connect timeout): its entry had no `ready` upstream yet, so the close was deferred to `pending.then(close)`, which never runs once the signal kills Node, and the process — the leader of its own group — outlived the server on a bare host (compose's `init: true` reaps it in the container). Each upstream entry now carries an `AbortController` that every close aborts; the connect's abort listener closes the client at once, which reaches the stdio transport's process-group kill before `abort()` returns, and `ready` is set in the same synchronous stretch that builds the upstream, so no window leaves a live process unreachable. Test: `gateway.server.test.ts` "R-gateway-5" (a stdio server that never answers `initialize`, a 20 s handshake clock, `void stopMcpGateway()` as the shutdown hook calls it: the process is gone within a second). Canary: the close not aborting the entry (the process lives on to the handshake timeout). **R-gateway-3 (medium).** An HTTP upstream that lost its session mid-run (a restart, a redeploy, an idle expiry of a server that keeps sessions in memory) answered every later request 404 on the stale `Mcp-Session-Id`; the SDK's client transport throws on that but never closes, so the gateway kept the dead upstream, every call failed as "Error POSTing to endpoint" for the rest of the run, and a run that re-initialized was handed the same dead client. The MCP spec asks a client that meets that 404 to open a new session, and the gateway is the upstream's client: a POST refused 404 — or 400, which servers built from the SDK's examples answer — while it carried a session (on the legacy transport, any POST to its per-session message URL) now throws `UpstreamSessionLost` from the transport's own `fetch`; the request was not processed, so `forward` opens a new connection to the server as its row reads now (single-flight per upstream, so the calls that met one loss share one reconnect), swaps it in, closes the old one quietly and sends the request again once. A reconnect that fails names both reasons. The run's own session never notices. Tests: `gateway.server.test.ts` "R-gateway-3" (a stateful Streamable HTTP server that forgets its sessions, answering 404 and then 400: the next call goes through on a second session and the refused request was never processed; two concurrent listings after a second loss open one session; a legacy SSE server that forgot its session the same). Canaries: the lost session reported instead of reconnected (all three red); the reconnect not single-flight (4 sessions where 3 are expected); the legacy transport's POSTs not treated as on a session (the SSE test red). **R-gateway-4 (low).** (b) revoked the token first thing in `settleRun`, "before a completion compaction, which needs no org server" — but ruling 376's compaction is built from the same spec (`assembleClaudeOptions`: the run's token and gateway URLs), whose docstring says it must carry the run's tools and servers or its prefix misses the cache it was meant to read. With the token gone the compaction's CLI met a 401 on every gateway server, marked it failed, and rewrote the history's references to its tools, so a run that used a credentialed server paid full input price for its compaction. `settleRun` now calls `closeRunMcpGatewayCalls` first — the grant keeps opening `initialize` and the listings on the upstreams the run already holds, and refuses `tools/call`, `resources/read` and `prompts/get` ("the run has ended…"), since nothing acts for a run that is over — and revokes the token once `adapter.compact` returns (in its `finally`), or right away when there is no compaction, before the finalize and on the settle's error path; the isLive belt still refuses the token once the row is terminal. Test: `gateway-runs.server.test.ts` "R-gateway-4" (a finished Claude run over the threshold with a credentialed HTTP mount: during its compaction a client holding the spec's mount lists the server's four tools and has its call refused, nothing reaches the upstream, and after the settle the token is dead — 0 live tokens, 401). Canaries: the revoke back at the top of `settleRun` (the compaction's listing is a 401); calls left open during the compaction (the call goes through).

462. **Creating a project can create its GitHub repository** (owner, 2026-09-24, pass 40, F40-5: the owner asked the controller to "create everything: the repo and project" and had to make `akin-ozer/website` by hand first; extends ruling 99's `create_project` and the repo-bound creation rule of 2026-07-17). No product path created a repository. `createProjectImpl` probed an existing one and warned "Check the name, or create it before agents start delivering", and `create_project` took an owner and a name and nothing else. Decided: **(a)** `CreateProjectInput.createRepository` is `{ private, description? }`. When it is set and the probe answers 404, the server creates the repository with the connection's PAT BEFORE `project.md` is written: `POST /user/repos` when the connection's owner is the token's own login as its stored validation recorded it (compared without case), else `POST /orgs/{owner}/repos`, with `auto_init: true` so the default branch exists. It then re-probes, and `repoAccess` and the default branch come from that probe. A repository that already exists makes the flag a no-op, and the reply says the existing one was used. **(b)** A refusal writes no project. A 401 or 403 says "The <owner> connection's token cannot create repositories. A fine-grained token needs Administration: Read and write for All repositories (a classic token needs `repo`). Create <owner>/<name> on GitHub, or widen the token, and ask again."; a 422 relays GitHub's own message with its field errors ("Repository creation failed (name already exists on this account)"); a 404 on the organization endpoint says the token can create nothing under that owner; a dropped connection or a 5xx is first read back (the dated note below: when the repository is there now it was made, and the project uses it), and when it is not there, that and any other status say no project was written without claiming that no repository was, because GitHub may have made it before failing. Three details the spec left open, each decided the simplest way that keeps the rule true: a probe that cannot tell whether the repository exists (the token refused, GitHub unreachable) refuses too, because a project created without its repository could only answer "already exists" when asked again; a name outside GitHub's alphabet (`[A-Za-z0-9._-]`) is refused before any call, because GitHub rewrites it on creation and the project would be bound to a name that does not exist; and a connection with no stored login takes the organization endpoint, whose refusal then says so, rather than spending a `GET /user` on a case a validated connection never reaches. **(c)** Audit `project.repository.created { repo, private }` under the acting person, recorded the moment GitHub is known to have made it (its 201, or the read-back after an answer that said nothing), so a project write that fails after it still leaves the repository on the record. The controller's row carries `<email> · via controller` as every controller write does, and the project's Activity panel reads it as "created the private GitHub repository **owner/name**". **(d)** Both doors reach the one server function. `create_project` takes `createRepository`, whose description says when to pass it, and its `[done]` reply adds what became of the repository. The New project modal's repository field carries "Create this repository on GitHub if it does not exist", off by default so a typo never becomes a repository, and once it is checked "Create it as a private repository", checked by default; the form sends `createRepository=private|public`, and the success toast adds the same sentence the controller reply carries. The checkbox line is `.check-line`, the branch-cleanup switch's rule under a name both can share. **(e)** The spec said the controller's doctrine told the model a repository must pre-exist. Neither seeded asset said so: the model followed the probe's warning and a tool description that named only the connection. The controller playbook (`controller-guide`, "Bringing up a new project") gains a bullet naming `createRepository`, and its outgoing hash joins `PRIOR_SHIPPED_HASHES` so an unedited store copy upgrades in place. Tests: `project-create.server.test.ts` "ruling 462" (against a fake GitHub handed in as `fetchImpl`: 404, 201, 200 gives the POST body `{name, private, auto_init}`, the order probe, create, re-probe, the project written and the audit row; a 403 and a 422 write nothing and say the sentences above; an existing repository sends no POST and says it was used; an organization owner reaches `/orgs/{owner}/repos` with `private: false` and the description; an unreachable probe and a name GitHub would rewrite refuse), `controller-toolkit.server.test.ts` (the published schema carries the flag, the handler forwards it, the audit row names the instrument), `workspace-routes.server.test.ts` (the intent's `createRepository=public`), `new-project-modal.test.tsx` (off by default, private unless cleared, the toast), `audit-coverage.server.test.ts`, `activity-feed-phase10.server.test.ts` and `default-assets.server.test.ts`. Canaries, each seen red and restored: skip the creation call; map only 401; drop the 422 arm; POST whatever the probe said; always `/user/repos`; rename the audit action; let an unreachable probe or a rewritten name through; stop forwarding the flag in the tool, or drop it from the schema; stop reading it in the route; stop sending it from the modal, or default it on; drop the note from the toast; drop the action from the Activity whitelist; drop the outgoing hash.

*(Corrected 2026-09-25 by the pre-merge review of the pass-40 branch, finding R-repo-1. **A create the client retried could say "Nothing was created" about a repository Viberr had made.** The GitHub client retries every request once on a 5xx, the create POST included: a create GitHub made and then answered 502 (a slow `auto_init` create past the gateway) was sent again, refused 422 "name already exists", and (b)'s 422 sentence then said nothing was created, no `project.repository.created` row was written, and asking again adopted the repository as one that "already exists", so no record ever said Viberr made it. `GithubRequestOptions.retryServerError: false` sends a write once; the create uses it, and a 5xx or a dropped connection is read back with the same probe: a repository there now is recorded as created and the project uses it ("Created <repo> on GitHub (private): GitHub answered 502, but the repository is there now."); one that is not refuses as before, without claiming nothing was made. The 422 sentence now answers the only attempt. Ruling 468's bootstrap PUT had the same shape and is corrected in its own note. The client's retry of other writes is unchanged (other callers were not reviewed here). Tests: `github-client.server.test.ts` (a `retryServerError: false` POST goes out once and hands its 502 back), `project-create.server.test.ts` "ruling 462" (a create made then answered 502 is sent once, recorded and used; a dropped connection is read back the same way; a 502 that made nothing refuses without "Nothing was created", one POST). Canaries, each seen red and restored: ignore `retryServerError` in the client; skip the read-back after an unanswered create.)*

463. **A GitHub connection says which repositories its token reaches, to the controller and on its card** (owner, 2026-09-24, pass 40, F40-6: the controller's `create_project` refuses without "a GitHub connection for the repo owner" while none of its 52 tools listed connections, and live it wrote "Creating it also needs a GitHub connection for `akin-ozer` in Instance settings, and I can't see whether that exists from here"; the connection card read "PAT ····k3ui · 3 public repos", the ACCOUNT's `public_repos` from `GET /users/{owner}`, while the fine-grained token behind it had been granted a set of repositories that included the PRIVATE `akin-ozer/website`). Decided: **(a)** Every validation of a connection's token (a save, a replaced token, the 24-hour re-proof `ensureConnectionFresh`, and the card's new Re-check) also reads `GET /user/repos?per_page=100&affiliation=owner,collaborator,organization_member` (`app/server/org/connection-reach.server.ts`), paged up to `REACH_CAP` (300) and recorded as `capped` when the last page is full, storing each repository's `fullName`, `private` and `canPush` (GitHub's `permissions` block for this token, read through `repoWritable`, null when no block came) in a new `github_connections.reach_json` column. The column is in `0001_baseline.sql` and in `BASELINE_COLUMNS`, so an existing root gains it at boot; it takes no backfill, because NULL ("not read yet") is exactly true of every connection saved before the read. A failed read (any page: a 403, an unreachable GitHub, a page whose rows lack a name or a privacy flag) is stored as `unknown` with GitHub's reason, never as zero and never as a partial count, and never refuses the save; a token whose validation just failed gets an `unknown` reach naming the verdict, with no read spent. **(b)** The card's row says what the token reaches: a `<details>` whose summary is "Reaches 3 repositories · 1 private" ("300+" past the cap) and whose body lists every repository, private ones with a quiet pill and "read only" where the token cannot push; an `unknown` reach says "could not be read" with the reason; a connection not yet read says Re-check reads it. The account's public-repo count is gone from the card, the record (`ConnectionRecord.repos`) and the baseline (`repos_count`): it described the account, not the token, and nothing else read it. `GET /users/{owner}` stays as the owner-existence check. A save's toast adds what the token reaches. **(c)** Re-check is the one detail the spec left open that needed a new door: the spec's "revalidated" had no manual path (the 24-hour re-proof runs only where a token is used), so the owner's existing connection would have read "not read yet" until a token use or a re-pasted token. `connection-recheck` (`recheckConnection`) validates the STORED token again under the same per-actor throttle as a save, records GitHub's verdict and the reach either way (a refusal included, which is what a re-check is for), changes nothing when GitHub is unreachable, and audits `org.connection.rechecked {owner, status, reach}`. The button carries ruling 368's in-flight state ("Checking…", the loader in `refresh`'s place). **(d)** The controller gets `list_github_connections`, open to any signed-in person because the New project dialog already shows every signed-in person these connections: per connection `owner`, `default`, the token's kind, the validation state with the validator's own reason when it failed and `lastValidatedAt`, expiry and `daysLeft`, `missingScopes`, `boundProjects`, and `reach` (`read` with a summary, counts and the list; `unknown` with the reason; `not_read` with how it gets read). It carries no token material, not the masked suffix and not the PAT id. The reach names private repositories to every signed-in person; that is the spec's decision, recorded here. `create_project`'s description sends the model to it first, and the shipped controller playbook (`controller-guide`, "Bringing up a new project") gains a bullet saying the same, with its outgoing hash in `PRIOR_SHIPPED_HASHES` so an unedited store copy upgrades in place. Tests: `connections.server.test.ts` "ruling 463" (a save records the list with private and push through a fake GitHub handed in as `fetchImpl`, a 403 and an unreachable read are `unknown` with the reason and the save still lands, paging stops at three full pages and at a short one, a replaced token and the re-proof replace the reach, a refused re-proof spends no read, Re-check reads an unread connection and audits, and refuses out loud when GitHub is down or refuses the token), `sqlite.server.test.ts` (the column added to an older root, unread, twice), `org-settings-page.test.tsx` (the row's summary, list, pills and unread line; an unknown reach's reason; Re-check's intent), `controller-toolkit.server.test.ts` (a non-member org member reads the reach, the serialized reply carries neither the token, its suffix nor the PAT id; the create description), `default-assets.server.test.ts`, `audit-coverage.server.test.ts` and `app.css.test.ts` (the fifth disclosure and the new GlyphSwap). Canaries, each seen red and restored: skip the reach read on save; store a failed read as zero; one page, or four; keep the old reach on a replace or a re-proof; read the reach of a refused token; drop or rename the Re-check audit; drop the row's reach line; post another intent from Re-check; drop the `BASELINE_COLUMNS` entry; unregister the tool; spread the whole record into its reply; drop the reach from it; drop the sentence from `create_project`; drop the playbook bullet or its outgoing hash.

*(Extended 2026-09-25 by the pre-merge review of the pass-40 branch, finding R-seams-4. **A repository Viberr created through the token was missing from its reach.** Ruling 462 creates a repository with the connection's token, and nothing re-read (a)'s stored reach: until a Re-check or the 24-hour re-proof, `list_github_connections` listed a `read` reach without it, and its own description says a repository missing from a `read` reach is one the token cannot see, so the controller could tell the owner the token cannot reach the repository it had just made; the card's count was one short. A creation GitHub is known to have made (its 201, or ruling 462's read-back) now adds `{ fullName, private, canPush }` to the connection's stored `read` reach (`recordCreatedRepositoryInReach`; `canPush` from the re-probe's permissions block), with no GitHub call and `readAt` kept, since the rest of the list is still that read. A reach not read, or read as `unknown`, is left alone: one entry is not a count. Tests: `project-create.server.test.ts` "ruling 462" (a created repository joins a `read` reach, counts updated; an `unknown` reach stays unknown). Canaries, each seen red and restored: drop the reach update; let an unknown reach become a one-repository list.)*

464. **A controller-built project gets the roster it asked for, and the controller can take an agent off a project** (owner, 2026-09-24, pass 40, F40-7: measured 20:27 UTC, `create_project` wrote the base roster, operator plus the generic Developer on Sonnet with `open-review-pr` on plus the Reviewer on Sonnet, before the controller deployed the six specialists it had designed; with no tool that removes a deployment it moved the two generic agents to Opus "so they follow your model rule" and asked the owner to delete them on the Agents page, and until then the operator could engage the generic Developer, which opens its own PR). This narrows ruling 99(c)'s "No tool deletes anything, in either scope" by one tool, and extends ruling 280. Decided: **(a)** `create_project` takes an optional `agents` list, `[{ profileId, model?, effort? }]` with `profileId` a global template's store key as `deploy_agent` takes it, and an optional `operator: { model?, effort? }`. Given, the project is written with the operator plus exactly those deployments and no base Developer or Reviewer; absent, today's base roster, so the New project dialog, which never sends it, is unchanged. Each entry is the deployment `deploy_agent` would write: `deployAgentProfileFromLibrary` is split into `readLibraryTemplate` (the id is a store segment, the template exists, it is a specialist, each refused by name) and the pure `buildLibraryDeployment` (the template's grants copied, its model and effort unless overridden, an override judged by `assertModelForBackend` / `assertEffortForBackend` against the template's backend), and both the Agents page's deploy and `createProject` call them. `resolveRoster` runs right after the custom blueprint, before the repository probe and ruling 462's creation, so a refused roster leaves nothing on GitHub or on disk. Two refusals the spec left open, each the simplest that keeps the rule true: an entry listed twice, and an EMPTY list, because `ensureBaseAgentsDeployed` backfills the base specialists into a project with no specialist at the next boot, which would silently undo the roster. The operator's overrides are judged against the operator's own primary backend (`deploymentRuntimeIdentity`) and written as a partial `definition`, which the per-field view merges and the `auto` policy preset (`presetAgents`) still spreads. The reply lists every deployment written with its name, model and effort (`CreateProjectResult.agents`, read off the write through `effectiveProfileView`), and `project.created` records the roster's profile ids. **(b)** `remove_agent_deployment { projectSlug?, profileId, reason }` is the Agents page's Delete from the controller: `requireVisible` (the not-visible posture for a non-member), then `deleteAgentProfile` itself, so the gate is its `manage-agents`, the audit row is its `project.agent_profile.deleted`, and the global template is never touched. `reason` is required (empty or blank refused, nothing removed) and recorded in the audit details. The Operator is refused by the page's own sentence ("The Operator is a system profile and can't be deleted.", a `[denied]`). A profile that is the delivering or an engaged agent on an open task is refused with the tasks named ("Developer is the delivering agent on VIB-142, …"), "open" being the population the Agents page lists under a profile's active deployments (`listAgentDeployments`: not archived, not in the final stage). That refusal is an option of `deleteAgentProfile` (`refuseOpenEngagements`) which only the controller's door sets: the spec asked it of the tool, and the page keeps its confirm and its toast that says what the engagements lose. A removal that leaves no specialist says the base Developer and Reviewer return at the next restart. **(c)** The toolkit's "no tool deletes an entity" invariant is amended by this ruling and only by it: taking a deployment off a project's roster edits that roster, as `update_stages op: remove` edits a board's stages; no tool deletes a project, task, user, template or resource. The toolkit's instructions and header comment say so, the invariant test pins `remove_agent_deployment` as the only `remove_*` tool, and `deploy_agent`'s description names it beside the Agents page (ruling 280's rule, kept). `controller-and-goals.md` counts 54 tools. **(d)** The shipped controller playbook tells the model to pass the designed roster as `agents` (and the operator's model and effort as `operator`), and its "No deletes" line names the one removal it holds; the outgoing hash (ruling 463's version) joins `PRIOR_SHIPPED_HASHES`. Tests: `project-create.server.test.ts` "ruling 464" (the designed roster written with its models and efforts and no Developer or Reviewer, the operator's overrides, the reply's list, the audit ids; the base roster without `agents`; seven refusals by name, an unknown template, the operator as an entry, a bad effort, a foreign model, a bad operator effort, a duplicate and an empty list, each with no project on disk, no `project.created` row and no GitHub call), `controller-toolkit.server.test.ts` (`agents` published and forwarded and the reply's list; a removal audited with the instrument and the reason and the template left; the Operator, an engaged developer naming its tasks, a maintainer and a non-member refused; the one `remove_*` tool; `deploy_agent` naming it), `audit-coverage.server.test.ts` and `default-assets.server.test.ts`. Canaries, each seen red and restored: ignore `agents`; drop the entry overrides; resolve the roster after the probe; write no base roster without `agents`; accept an empty list or a duplicate; ignore the operator's overrides or skip its effort check; skip an entry's effort check; make the removal write nothing; drop the reason from the audit; call without `refuseOpenEngagements`; drop the operator check; drop the `manage-agents` gate; rename the tool; restore "This toolkit does not remove a deployment"; drop `EXACTLY` from the published description or stop forwarding `agents`; drop either playbook sentence or the outgoing hash; rename the deletion's audit action. *(Amended 2026-09-28 by ruling 545: `operator` also takes `backend`.)*

465. **The controller's queue is visible, and a turn reads only the conversation up to the message it answers** (owner, 2026-09-24, pass 40, F40-8 and F40-10; extends rulings 99 and 448). Measured live 2026-09-24 20:39–20:47 UTC: a message sent while a turn worked was queued in memory (`MAX_QUEUED_MESSAGES` 8), but the transcript rendered it as the newest message with "Controller is working…" under it, and nothing in `app/features/controller/` said a message was queued or where it sat. A user message takes its `seq` when it is recorded, which for a message sent mid-turn is when it is QUEUED, so once the replies landed the transcript read part 1, part 2, part 3, reply, correction, reply, reply, with nothing tying a reply to its message. And `buildTurnPrompt`'s digest was the newest 30 rows with no bound at the answered message, so a message queued behind the running turn reached it as a 600-character stub; the model told the owner "The 04 correction never reached me … Please resend it" about a message that was simply next in the queue. Decided: **(a)** `controller_messages.reply_to` records, on a controller row, the user message it answers. Every writer sets it: the settle's reply and U39-30's early post, the refusals (no Claude, a full queue, a turn that could not start, and, since the dated note below, a note of its own under each message queued behind a first turn whose start failed), the queued-start failure (under the message it tried) and a note of its own under each message it dropped (the old single note spoke for them, and a message no reply names would now read as unanswered), and the restart notes; only a released project's note answers nothing. The column is in the baseline and added to an older root by the healer with a backfill, as ruling 448 added `seen_seq`, except that the meaning is not one statement: `BASELINE_COLUMNS` gains `backfillWith`, and `backfillControllerReplyLinks` replays the writers' order per conversation and links only what that order PROVES (the dated note below: the first version linked by FIFO past lost messages). A reply that carries a run answers the OLDEST waiting message (turns ran in FIFO order); a run-less refusal answers the message directly before it (every one was written right after the message it refused); both start failures answer the head of the queue and each "I dropped this message" note after them the next one behind; a restart note answers the dead turn's message or the one directly before it; a released project's note, recognised by its text like the failure and restart notes because all predate this ruling, answers nothing. What the order cannot place is marked `unlinked_history`: earlier history, not linked. Without the backfill, (d) below would write a restart note under every old message on the first boot. **(b)** The lease records the message the current turn answers, and `conversationTurnState` exposes `answering` and `queued: [{ messageId, ahead }]` (ahead counts the turns before that message's own, the answering one included, so the first waiting message is "1 ahead") on the page's and the dock's views; joining the queue publishes `controller.updated`, because the append that recorded the message published before it joined. **(c)** Both transcripts render in reply order (`inReplyOrder`, `app/shared/controller-thread.ts`, one home for the page, the dock and the digest): each controller row that names its message sits directly under it; user messages and unlinked notes keep their `seq` order, so an older transcript whose backfill could not link a row reads as it always did. A user message with no reply yet says "answering now" or "queued · N ahead" (`MessageState` in `turn-step.tsx`, shared by both), read off the server's lease and never from what the page sent, so there is no optimistic state; after a restart its reply is the restart note. "… is working" sits under the answered message and any reply already posted to it (U39-30 posts before the compaction ends), never under a later one. **(d)** Boot recovery notes every user message no reply names and the backfill did not mark earlier history, in a conversation no live turn holds: the dead turn's note carries its run id (which settles the run, as before) and answers the oldest waiting message, and each remaining one gets its own. The old order-based arms missed the messages still in the lost queue: the dead turn's note made the newest message a controller one, so they were never noted at all. **(e)** The digest (`messagesUpTo`) is the conversation up to the answered message in reply order, not raw `seq`, and this is the one place the spec's "by `seq` of that message" is refined: every user message up to and including it, every reply to one of those (a reply to an earlier message can land after the answered one was queued, and a turn must see it), and every unlinked note written before it; a later message and a refusal a later message got are out. When messages wait behind the answered one, the prompt says so in one line, before the message: "N more messages from <person> are queued behind this one; each is answered in its own turn, in order — do not treat them as lost". A queued turn's run-input disclosure now counts its own message's characters, not the first turn's. Tests: `controller-run.server.test.ts` "ruling 465" (a queued message and a later message's refusal are absent from the prompt, a reply to an earlier message is in it under that message, the queue line is present, and absent with nothing queued); `controller-conversations.server.test.ts` "ruling 465" (three sends: the view's `answering` and `queued` with positions on the lease and on the page's view; the FIFO drains with the stop note and both replies naming their messages; turn two's prompt has no third message and counts it; turn three's has no queue line; a turn that cannot start names its message), plus `replyTo` on the no-Claude and full-queue refusals, the stop note and U39-30's early post, the dropped-message notes and the restart notes (the dead run answers the oldest waiting message; the lost queued one gets its own); `sqlite.server.test.ts` (the backfill links each old reply as its writer wrote it); `controller-page.test.tsx` and `controller-dock.test.tsx` "ruling 465" (reply order, the working row under the answered message, "answering now" and "queued · 1 ahead", an unlinked older transcript unchanged). Canaries, each seen red and restored: an unbounded digest; the queue line dropped; `queued` emptied in the turn state; `replyTo` dropped from the settle, the early post, the start-failure note, the full-queue refusal and the no-Claude refusal; the per-message dropped notes skipped; the recovery's unanswered-message arm skipped; the backfill dropped, or a run's reply given the newest message; the page and the dock in `seq` order; `MessageState` dropped from either header; the working row put at the end.

*(Corrected 2026-09-25 by the pre-merge review of the pass-40 branch, findings R-controller-1, R-controller-2 and R-seams-3. **The backfill linked past lost messages.** It kept one FIFO per conversation and emptied it only after the queued-start failure note, but before this ruling two paths lost a queued message without a row: a restart while messages waited (the old recovery noted only the dead turn) and a first turn whose start failed while a message queued behind it (its note went to the NEWEST waiting message). After either, every later reply was linked to the message before its own, for good (the backfill runs once), and the same boot's recovery wrote a false restart note under the last answered message and under each message an old queued-start failure had dropped. `backfillControllerReplyLinks` now links only what the order proves: a run's reply takes the oldest waiting message only while the walk is in step and that message was recorded before the run started (`agent_runs.created_at`); a run-less refusal takes the message directly before it; a start failure takes the head, and a queued-start failure only when its count of dropped messages matches the walk's; a restart note takes its dead turn's message (one dead turn per group, checked the same way), a message its stored link names that was still waiting, or the message directly before the group. Every event that empties the real queue resets the walk: a start failure, a group of restart notes, and a boot any other conversation's restart note dates. What was still waiting then, and everything waiting while the walk is out of step, is marked with the new column `controller_messages.unlinked_history` (baseline and `BASELINE_COLUMNS`): earlier history with no linked answer, which (d)'s recovery skips. The messages still waiting after the last dated boot are the ones the current boot interrupted, and recovery notes them. `reply_to` lost its own backfill; `unlinked_history`'s runs the walk, which writes both, so a root the first backfill already linked (the owner's, deployed 2026-09-24 21:50 UTC) gains the column and is walked once more: its shifted links are replaced, and a restart note the first boot wrote under a message the walk shows answered or lost is left in the transcript unlinked, never moved or deleted. The walk is idempotent. **A first turn that could not start dropped the queue silently.** A message sent from another surface while `startTurnRun` awaited (the stdio MCP pre-flight, a continuity reset) joined the lease's queue, and the catch deleted the lease with only the first message noted. It now drains the queue and writes "I dropped this message: the turn before it could not start. Say it again to retry." under each, as the queued-start failure does. The note texts have one home, `controller-reply-links.server.ts`, which the writers and the walk share. Tests: `controller-reply-links.server.test.ts` (the lost-queue restart, the first-turn failure with a queued message, the old dropped-message note, a boot dated by another conversation, a reply the walk cannot place, a message the current boot interrupted, each run through recovery on the same root, and a root the first backfill linked, walked twice), `sqlite.server.test.ts` (the dropped message marked; a root with `reply_to` walked again when `unlinked_history` arrives), `controller-conversations.server.test.ts` (two sends in one tick into a start that throws: the second gets its note). Canaries, each seen red and restored: no reset after a restart group; the newest message for a start failure; no cross-conversation boot reset; a restart note's stored link trusted without checking it waits; no run-start check; recovery without the `unlinked_history` filter; nothing marked at a reset; no drain in the first turn's catch; no `backfillWith` on `unlinked_history`.)* *(Narrowed 2026-09-27 by ruling 527: a message that steered a turn sits in that turn, under its message and above its reply, not in `seq` order; (d)'s recovery writes no note under it, and (e)'s digest includes it whatever its `seq`.)*

466. **A store write reports UTF-8 bytes, and an append adds exactly what was sent** (owner, 2026-09-24, pass 40, F40-9 and F40-13; extends rulings 257 and F39-1). `writeStoreDoc` returned and audited `bytes: body.length`, UTF-16 code units: live, an 8,220-byte document (byte-identical to its source) was reported and audited as "8,170 bytes", and ruling 257's "how many bytes a replace destroyed" rested on the same measure (it read the editor's capped text, so a replaced document past the cap was under-reported too). Decided: **(a)** every size a store, KB or skill write reports or audits is `Buffer.byteLength(…, "utf8")`: `org.store.doc_written`'s `bytes`, the result's `bytes`, the new `previousBytes` (the replaced or appended-to file's size measured on disk before the write, which is now the figure "its previous N bytes are gone" names), `read_knowledge_base_doc`'s `bytes`, the operator's `task.operator.ruling_proposed` audit and the single-file restore's report. The grep for other `bytes: …length` found those three besides the writer; the run-log budget's SQL `length()` measures a console window, not a write, and stays. The editor's reader (`readStoreDoc`) caps in bytes as its `maxBytes` says: it sliced characters, so a non-ASCII document could come back whole while `truncated` said it was cut. **(b)** F40-13: `save_knowledge_base` with `doc.append: true` built `before.text.replace(/\s+$/, "") + "\n\n" + content.trim() + "\n"`, trimming the part and forcing a blank line between parts, so a part boundary inside a markdown table, list or fenced block broke it (live, a table split in two until the controller rewrote the whole file), and it rebuilt the file from the editor's 256 KB read, so a document past the cap would have lost its tail. An append now goes through `writeStoreDoc(…, { append: true })`, which reads the existing file whole from disk and concatenates EXACTLY the bytes sent, with no trim and no separator; the audit row carries `appended` beside the new total. The tool's description says the caller owns separators and newlines ("end a part with a newline when the next part starts a new line"), and the reply's "Appended N bytes … it is now M bytes" counts UTF-8 bytes. Tests: `store-files.server.test.ts` "ruling 466" (a non-ASCII body's result and audit row equal the file's size on disk; a replace names the bytes it destroyed; two appends that split a table concatenate byte for byte and audit `appended`; the read cap is in bytes), `controller-toolkit.server.test.ts` "ruling 466" (the same table split through the tool, the replies' byte counts, `read_knowledge_base_doc`'s `bytes`, the REPLACED sentence) and `operator-actions.server.test.ts` "ruling 466". Canaries, each seen red and restored: report `body.length` in the audit row, and in the result; trim the part and put the separator back, in the writer and in the tool; count `content.length` in the reply; slice characters in the reader; audit the ruling proposal's `entry.length`.

467. **The controller can bring a deployed agent's persona in line** (owner, 2026-09-24, pass 40, F40-11; extends rulings 156 and 277). A deployment snapshots its template's persona (P13-AP-07), `update_agent_deployment` took no persona, and `save_global_agent`'s `propagate` rewrote only grants, so a deployment kept persona text its owner had overturned. Live, the deployed Content Writer and Fact Checker still carried "no email until the rulings name one" and "the colophon's AI-built line waits for Akin's wording" an hour after the owner overturned both, the rulings KB contradicted the persona every run of them read, and the controller had to ask the owner to edit the two copies by hand. Decided: **(a)** `update_agent_deployment` takes `persona`, the deployment's WHOLE persona (its system prompt). It goes through the same form writer the Agents page uses (`updateAgentProfile`), so the `manage-agents` gate and the B5 fingerprint check are the ones every other field of the tool already rides. An empty (or all-whitespace) persona is refused before anything is read, because the writer reads "" as "keep" and the call would answer `[done]` for nothing. The reply adds a `persona` entry to the old → new list, built from the record the write left, never the request: `describePersonaChange` (`app/server/agents/persona-change.server.ts`) names the length before and after in characters and the first and last changed lines, old and new, comparing lines from both ends so an inserted paragraph reads as one range; a quoted line over 120 characters is cut with "…" and the sentence then says the whole persona was written, so the reply never shortens anything silently. **(b)** `save_global_agent` with `propagate: true` on a call that CHANGED the template's persona also rewrites the persona of every copy ruling 277's `listTemplateTextDrift` names for `persona` (`propagateTemplatePersona`, beside the grants writer), and the reply says per project what it rewrote ("Persona rewritten on 1 project copy: web (412 → 398 characters; line 3 of 9 changed: first … → …)"). A call that leaves the persona alone rewrites no persona, so a project's own persona edit survives a grants propagation, and a summary is never propagated. The rule lives in the server function, so the org modal's "copy these grants" box does the same, and its hint says so; the Agents page's own editor stays the per-copy human door. The "still runs the older persona" sentence now names the doors that exist (propagate on a persona change, `update_agent_deployment`'s `persona`, the Agents page); a summary-only drift keeps its old sentence. **(c)** Audit as the human surface audits a persona edit: `project.agent_profile.updated`, which now carries `personaChanged` and `personaChars` whenever a save changed the stored persona (the Agents page and the tool through the one writer), and the propagation writes the same row per copy with `source: "org-template"` and `templateId`; `org.agent_profile.updated` gains `personaPropagated`. Tests: `controller-toolkit.server.test.ts` "ruling 467" (the persona written whole, the reply's before/after, the audit row with the instrument, a form composed before the write refused by the fingerprint, a contributor refused, an empty persona refused with nothing written; propagate on a persona change rewrites the copy and names it, a repeat save with the same persona leaves a project's own text alone), `template-propagation.server.test.ts` "ruling 467" (the org door's toast, audit rows, and the no-propagate and unchanged-persona arms) and `persona-change.server.test.ts`. Canaries, each seen red and restored: drop `persona` from the tool's form; drop the empty check; skip `propagateTemplatePersona`; propagate on every save; drop `personaChanged` from the writer's audit; make the propagation write nothing; compare lines from the front only; drop the clipping note.

468. **Viberr initializes an empty repository instead of asking a person to push a commit** (owner, 2026-09-24, pass 40, F40-12; extends ruling 128). Live: `akin-ozer/website` existed with no commits, project creation accepted it (`probeRemoteRepo` answered `ok` with `default_branch: main`), `get_github_state` read "no branches", and WEB-1's first operator run found an unborn `main` in its checkout and opened a packet asking the owner to "push one initial commit (a README)", recommending "I pushed an initial commit to main". Two things the spec asked for were already true or not possible, and both are said here rather than built twice. Ruling 128 already makes the default branch's first commit before a task's first branch (`ensureDefaultBranch` from `ensureTaskBranch`, the branch preparation `ensureTaskBranchBestEffort` runs) and audits it as `github.repo.bootstrapped { repo, defaultBranch, how, sha }` with a `github` timeline event; a second audit action (the spec's `github.repository.initialized`) for the same act would split one fact across two names, so the existing one stands. And the spec's empty-tree commit through the Git Data API cannot be the first commit: GitHub answers every Git Database endpoint (blobs, trees, commits, refs) 409 "Git Repository is empty." until a first commit exists, and its own guide names `PUT /repos/{r}/contents/{path}` as the way to initialize an empty repository. Ruling 128 already uses it, and the Contents API cannot write an empty tree, so the first commit carries one file, the `README.md` naming the project (the file ruling 462's `auto_init` writes too). What was missing, decided: **(a)** an empty repository is recognised and named. `size: 0` on `GET /repos/{r}` is the cue (GitHub computes it lazily, so it is not proof) and `GET /repos/{r}/commits` answering 409 is the proof (`repositoryIsEmpty` in `repo-access-check.server.ts`); only a size-0 repository pays the second read. Project creation's probe and the GitHub page's access check both run it and record `empty: true` on the connected `RepoAccessResult` (the stored row's schema mirrors it, optional so older rows parse). Creation's reply and toast say "<repo> is empty: Viberr will create its first commit on <branch> before the first task branch, so nobody needs to push one"; the GitHub page's Repository panel carries a Contents row saying the same; `get_github_state` answers `contents: "empty: viberr will create the first commit on <branch> before the first task branch"` (null otherwise). All three say otherwise when the token can only read the repository (the second dated note below). **(b)** The operator's checkout is the other path that needs the base, and the one that failed live: the operator runs before any branch is prepared. `ensureOperatorRepoCheckout` now asks `initializeUnbornCheckout` (`app/server/tasks/unborn-checkout.server.ts`) after a fresh clone and for an existing checkout: a HEAD with no commit runs ruling 128's bootstrap under `system:delivery`, whose timeline line names the operator's first checkout, then ruling 129's refresh moves the unborn checkout onto the new commit (it refuses a checkout with staged changes or files the move would overwrite). Every other checkout pays one `git rev-parse`; nothing throws, and a checkout that could not be initialized is used as it stands. The existing-checkout arm is what reaches the live WEB-1 workspace, cloned unborn before this ruling. **(c)** Idempotent under a race: with two paths bootstrapping, a PUT GitHub refuses because another call already made the branch (the file exists, or the branch moved) re-reads the ref and answers `exists`, writing no audit row and no timeline line. A token that cannot write still gets ruling 128's `repo` scope violation, the refusal delivery gives. **(d)** The operator doctrine (`operator.definition.md`) says an empty repository is never a person's chore: Viberr makes the first commit before the operator's checkout and before the first task branch, the operator never asks anyone to push an initial commit or a README and never opens a packet for one, and an unborn checkout means handing the work to the delivering agent as usual. No shipped asset had told the operator to ask for one; the packet was the model's own inference from an unborn `main` and silence, so the fix is the sentence plus the server acting first. The outgoing hash joins `PRIOR_SHIPPED_HASHES` so an unedited store copy upgrades in place at the next deploy; the live store copy was not edited. Tests: `project-create.server.test.ts` "ruling 468" (an empty repository recorded and named at creation against a fake GitHub; a size-0 repository with commits says nothing), `repo-access-check.server.test.ts` "ruling 468" (empty, lazily sized with commits, and a sized repository that never pays the commits read), `repo-bootstrap.server.test.ts` "ruling 468" (a refused create that finds the branch answers `exists` with no audit and no timeline line), `unborn-checkout.server.test.ts` (against a local bare origin and a fake GitHub whose Contents write lands a real commit: the first clone of an empty repository gets the commit, the checkout stands on it, the timeline and audit say so, and a second run asks GitHub nothing; a checkout left unborn by a refused write is initialized on the next run), `github-view.test.tsx` "ruling 468", `controller-access.server.test.ts` "ruling 468" (through `primeRepoAccessForTests`, the tool reading GitHub with the global fetch) and `default-assets.server.test.ts` "ruling 468". Canaries, each seen red and restored: drop `empty` from the creation probe, the access check's empty read, or its size cue; drop the re-read after a refused create; drop the initializer after the clone, or from the existing-checkout arm; skip the fast-forward; drop the GitHub page's Contents row, or the tool's `contents`; drop the doctrine sentence, or the outgoing hash.

*(Corrected 2026-09-25 by the pre-merge review of the pass-40 branch, finding R-repo-1's bootstrap half. **(c)'s race arm could file Viberr's own first commit as another call's.** The Contents PUT went through the client's one 5xx retry: a PUT that landed and answered 502 was sent again, refused 422 ("sha wasn't supplied"), and the race re-read found the branch and answered `exists`, so the first commit Viberr made got no `github.repo.bootstrapped` row and no timeline line. The PUT is now sent once (`retryServerError: false`, ruling 462's note), and when its answer said nothing (a 5xx, a dropped connection, an undecodable 2xx) and the branch exists, its head is read (`GET /repos/{r}/git/commits/{sha}`): a root commit carrying this PUT's own message is recorded as the bootstrap; any other head is `exists`, as before. A second Viberr path that lost the same race to a 502-answered PUT would also see its message on a root commit, so that double record is possible, and was judged better than a first commit on no record. Tests: `repo-bootstrap.server.test.ts` (a PUT that landed and answered 502 goes out once and is recorded, audit and timeline; after a 502, a head that is not this write's root commit is `exists` with no audit). Canaries, each seen red and restored: retry the PUT; skip the head read; accept any head commit.)*

*(Corrected 2026-09-25 by the same review, finding R-repo-2. **An empty repository behind a token that can only read was promised a first commit.** Creation's probe proves `read_only` (GitHub's permissions block says `push: false`) and still copied `empty` onto the connected result, so the note said "Viberr will create its first commit … so nobody needs to push one" beside the warning that the token cannot push; the GitHub page's Contents row and `get_github_state.contents` said the same, and `checkRepoAccess` never read the block. That commit is a Contents PUT, which GitHub refuses such a token, so (c)'s `repo` scope violation opens and the checkout stays unborn until the token changes. The connected `RepoAccessResult` now carries `readOnly: true` when `repoWritable` says the token cannot push (creation's read-only arm and `checkRepoAccess`, which now reads the block; the stored row's schema mirrors it, optional), and all three surfaces name the token instead: creation says "<repo> is empty, and this connection's token can only read it, so Viberr cannot create its first commit on <branch> yet.
