Once the token can push, Viberr makes that commit before the first task branch."; the Contents row "empty, and the token can only read it: Viberr cannot create the first commit on <branch> until the token can push"; `contents` "empty, and this token can only read it: viberr cannot create the first commit on <branch> until the token is granted write access (the fix is the token, not a pushed commit)". Tests: `project-create.server.test.ts` "ruling 468" (read-only and empty: the record, the warning and the note), `repo-access-check.server.test.ts` (`push: false` is read-only; `push: true` and no block are not), `github-view.test.tsx` (the row), `controller-access.server.test.ts` (the tool's line). Canaries, each seen red and restored: drop the read-only arm from the note, the row or the tool; skip the permissions read in the access check; drop `readOnly` from the stored schema.)*

469. **An HTTP MCP connection can sign in with OAuth; the tokens live only in the server and reach upstream only through the gateway** (owner, 2026-09-24, pass 40, F40-14; spec `planning/discovery-2026-09-24-pass40-akinozer-site/SPEC-469-mcp-oauth.md`; builds on ruling 461; "breaking changes welcome"). Measured: the registry held one pasted credential per connection and had no sign-in door, while `https://mcp.cloudflare.com/mcp` answers 401 with `WWW-Authenticate: Bearer realm="OAuth", resource_metadata=".../.well-known/oauth-protected-resource/mcp"`, so the owner had to mint a seven-group Cloudflare API token and paste it where Claude Code would open Cloudflare's consent page. Decided: **(a)** *Sign in.* The MCP editor in Instance settings → Agent resources carries an "OAuth sign-in" section beside the credential field, for a saved HTTP server. **Sign in** (`mcp-oauth-start`, org admin) runs `startMcpOAuthSignIn` (`app/server/org/mcp-oauth.server.ts`): discovery through the SDK's client helpers (`app/server/mcp-proxy/oauth-client.server.ts`) — the protected-resource metadata at the URL the server's own challenge named (kept from the probe) or the well-known locations, then the authorization server's RFC 8414 metadata — dynamic registration (RFC 7591) as "Viberr" with the redirect URI `<origin>/resources/mcp-oauth/callback`, and the authorization-code request with PKCE (S256), a random 256-bit `state` and the RFC 8707 `resource`. The origin is `BETTER_AUTH_URL` when set, else the request's own, which is how better-auth derives its own OAuth callbacks (behind a reverse proxy the request's origin is the proxy's upstream). The editor renders the URL as a link that opens a new tab ("Continue at <host>"), not a script-opened window, so no popup blocker stands in the way. **(b)** *The callback.* `GET /resources/mcp-oauth/callback` (org admin; a signed-out admin goes through `/login` and back with the query) runs `completeMcpOAuthSignIn`: the state is looked up by its SHA-256, deleted on first sight whatever follows (a replay, and a second tab, find nothing), refused unless the callback arrived in the same user AND session that started it, and refused after 10 minutes; an `error` the authorization server returned (the person declined) is reported in its words. The code is exchanged with the verifier and the tokens SEALED: `org_mcp_servers.oauth_ref` is a secret-box (the same AES-256-GCM box as `cred_ref`, lazily re-sealed under a rotated key and registered as its own `SEALED_STORES` entry, `org_mcp_oauth`, so `keys -- reseal` and the convergence count reach it) around the endpoints, the registered client (with its secret when one was issued), the endpoint it is for and the tokens with their expiry; `oauth_json` is the public half every surface reads without opening a box (status `needs_sign_in` | `signed_in` | `expired`, expiry, whether it renews, the issuer's host, the challenge's metadata URL, an expiry's reason). Both are new baseline columns with the idempotent boot heal (no backfill: NULL is the truth for every older row). The page it answers is plain HTML (screen label `MCP sign-in`, `no-store`, no referrer, no token, code or state in it): "Signed in to <name>", the connection check it then ran, and "You can close this tab". The callback publishes the resource event, so the Settings tab that started it updates by itself. Audit `org.mcp.oauth_connected` {name, issuer, scope, expiresAt, renews, replacedStaticCredential} and `org.mcp.oauth_failed` {name, stage (`discovery`, `registration`, `authorization`, `state`, `token`, `refresh`), reason}, each reason scrubbed by value of every code, verifier, token and client secret the flow holds before it is stored or logged. **(c)** *The gateway uses and renews it.* A signed-in connection resolves to a gateway mount exactly as a pasted credential does (ruling 461(b)); the gateway, and the health probe, hand `connectHttpUpstream` a token source (`mcpOAuthTokenSource`) instead of a token. Every upstream request asks it for the access token (read from the row each time, so a sign-out or a renewal by another run takes effect on the next request); within 60 s of its expiry it is renewed with the refresh token first, and an upstream 401 renews it once and retries the request (a body is a string, so it replays), a second 401 ending the sign-in rather than looping. Renewal is single-flight per connection, so two runs that meet an expired token spend a rotating refresh token once, and the new pair is re-sealed only if the sign-in it renewed is still the stored one. A renewal the authorization server REFUSES (any OAuth error but `server_error`, `temporarily_unavailable` and `too_many_requests`) or a missing refresh token ends the sign-in — compare-and-set like the success path: only while the stored tokens are still the ones refused, else what was stored meanwhile is used (R-oauth-3 below): the tokens are dropped (the registration kept for the next sign-in — unless the server refused the client itself, `invalid_client` or `unauthorized_client`, when the registration goes too; R-oauth-4 below), the row reads "sign-in expired: an admin must sign in again" with the server's words, `org.mcp.oauth_failed` {stage: "refresh"} is audited under `system`, and the run's call fails with that sentence as a JSON-RPC error naming the server. A renewal that fails for now (unreachable, slow, a 5xx) says "could not renew the OAuth sign-in: …" and keeps the sign-in. The run still holds only its run-scoped gateway token; no token is ever in its config, argv or environment. **(d)** *Health.* A probe that sent no credential of any kind and met a 401 carrying `resource_metadata` (the MCP authorization challenge; `UpstreamSignInNeeded`) records `needs_sign_in` and reads "needs sign-in: this server asks for an OAuth sign-in, which an org admin does from its editor in Instance settings → Agent resources"; a bare probe that gets in clears it. A pasted credential's 401 stays "authentication rejected" (ruling 461(d)). `test_mcp_server`, Save & re-test and the editor say "needs sign-in", "healthy: N tools · …ms · signed in (expires in 52 minutes, renews itself)" or "sign-in expired: …" as themselves, never "unreachable"; the Settings row shows a red dot with "needs sign-in · checked …" or "sign-in expired: an admin must sign in again", or "auth: OAuth, signed in (…); held by Viberr, runs connect through its gateway" (one home for the words, `app/shared/mcp-oauth.ts`). A connection that needs a sign-in it does not have, or whose sign-in expired, is not mounted on any run; the run's prompt names it with that reason (ruling 310's `unavailableMcpSection`) instead of a server that answers every call 401. The controller's `list_mcp_servers` carries `signIn` {status, expiresAt, renews, issuer, reason} and `signInNote`, never a token; `save_mcp_server`'s description says an OAuth server is signed in by an org admin in Instance settings, which the controller cannot do, and a save that met the challenge replies with that instead of "add a secret". There is no per-server MCP health in `/resources/health`; "the health check" of the spec is the probe the Settings row and `test_mcp_server` run. **(e)** *One credential per connection; static tokens unchanged.* A pasted credential works exactly as before and wins when present. A sign-in that lands drops a pasted credential (the audit row says so); pasting one over a live sign-in is refused ("Sign it out first"), and the editor replaces the field with a sentence meanwhile; pasting one over a sign-in that is not live ("needs sign-in", "expired") clears what is left of it (R-oauth-2 below). Re-pointing the row's endpoint or transport drops the sign-in (its tokens were issued for the old resource and are sent to no other), audited on `org.mcp.updated` as `oauthDropped`, and the editor warns before the save; a connection a run still holds to the old endpoint is handed no token after that, the next sign-in's included, and reconnects to the new one (R-oauth-1 below). **(f)** *Sign out.* `mcp-oauth-sign-out` revokes the refresh token, then the access token, at the server's RFC 7009 endpoint when it offers one, authenticating as the client registered; revocation failing still drops the tokens here and the toast says which happened. The sealed half is deleted and the row reads "needs sign-in". Audited `org.mcp.oauth_signed_out` {name, revocation: `revoked` | `not offered` | `failed` | `nothing to revoke`, reason}. Details the spec left open, each decided the simplest way that keeps the rule true: sign-ins in flight live in memory for 10 minutes (on `globalThis`, like the gateway's state), so a restart forgets them and the admin starts again, rather than persisting a verifier; starting a sign-in writes nothing, so an abandoned one leaves the connection as it was and a live sign-in keeps working until the new one lands; the client registration is reused while the endpoint, the authorization server and the redirect URI are unchanged and its secret has not lapsed (RFC 7591's `client_secret_expires_at`, now kept with it), else Viberr registers again; the editor offers Sign in on every saved HTTP server, not only one whose probe saw the challenge, because discovery also finds a server that only answers the older spec's origin fallback; a server that advertises no PKCE S256, publishes no registration endpoint (no manual client id is taken), names another resource in its metadata, or has a non-`https:` endpoint (a loopback `http:` one excepted, as RFC 8252 does for redirects) is refused before the browser leaves, audited as a `discovery` or `registration` failure; the scope asked for is the resource's advertised `scopes_supported`, or none (Cloudflare advertises none); and the callback is a resource route answering plain HTML rather than a page in the app shell, because it renders nothing of the app and must not re-run on a revalidation (its state is spent). Deliberate residuals: tokens dropped by a re-point are not revoked at the old server; a sign-in in flight does not survive a restart; the editor's MCP modal does not refresh a token itself (the gateway and the probe do). Found on the way: the MCP editor's credential note still said a Codex run mounts the server unauthenticated, which ruling 461 made false; it now says the gateway sends the credential on either backend. Real-metadata check (2026-09-24, the one network read allowed): `discoverMcpOAuth("https://mcp.cloudflare.com/mcp")` made exactly two GETs (`/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource/mcp`, `/.well-known/oauth-authorization-server`) and parsed resource `https://mcp.cloudflare.com/mcp`, authorization server `https://mcp.cloudflare.com`, `/authorize`, `/token`, `/register`, revocation at `/token`, PKCE `S256`, client auth `client_secret_basic`/`client_secret_post`/`none`, no scopes; nothing was registered or authorized. Tests: `test-support/mcp-oauth-server.ts` (an in-test authorization server and protected resource: the challenge, both metadata documents, registration, an authorization endpoint that consents or declines, a token endpoint that verifies client auth, PKCE, the redirect URI and the resource and rotates refresh tokens, revocation, and switches for TTL, refusals and missing features), `mcp-oauth.server.test.ts` (the authorization request's PKCE, state, redirect URI and resource; PKCE-less and registration-less servers refused and audited; the exchange sealing tokens as a secret-box with a pasted credential dropped; a wrong state, a replayed state and another session refused with nothing sealed; a declined consent; the token upstream; renewal on expiry, on a 401, single-flight; a refused renewal ending the sign-in and a 503 keeping it; the probe's "needs sign-in", the signed-in probe's toast, the resolver dropping an unsigned server with its reason and mounting a signed one through the gateway; an expired sign-in probed and reported; sign-out revoking both tokens; a pasted credential refused and a re-point dropping the sign-in; and every issued code, token and client secret searched for, and absent, in the audit rows, the captured log lines and the views across the whole life), `gateway-oauth.server.test.ts` (a run through the gateway: the access token upstream and no token in the run config; a mid-run 401 renewed; a refused renewal reaching the run as "sign-in expired"; a sign-out effective on the next call), `resources.mcp-oauth.callback.test.ts` (through `/org/settings` and the callback with real sessions: the redirect URI; a member refused without spending the state; the admin's page and its headers, no secret in it; a replay; another session of the same admin), `mcp-sign-in.test.tsx` (the row's and the editor's needs sign-in / signed in / expired, Sign in posting the start and rendering the link, Sign out, the credential field hidden while signed in, the warning before a re-point drops a live sign-in, no section on stdio), `controller-toolkit.server.test.ts`, `audit-coverage.server.test.ts`, `sqlite.server.test.ts` and `key-rotation.server.test.ts`. Canaries, each seen red and restored byte for byte: drop the state from the authorization request; stop spending a state; bind it to the user only; store the tokens unsealed; exchange with a wrong verifier; the gateway attaching no OAuth token; no renewal on expiry; no retry after a 401; a refused renewal never ending the sign-in; sign-out keeping the tokens; log the renewed token; put a token in the connected audit row; the resolver mounting a signed-out server; the challenge not recognized; the editor without its section; the row calling a signed-out server unreachable; `list_mcp_servers` without `signIn`; the callback admitting a member; renewal not single-flight; a pasted credential allowed over a sign-in; a re-point keeping the sign-in; the editor never warning before a re-point; the column heal and the sealed-store entry removed. *Pre-merge review (2026-09-25), confirmed findings and what changed:* **R-oauth-1 (medium).** (e)'s "sent to no other" did not hold for a connection a run already held: `saveMcpServer` never closes gateway upstreams, the connection's URL is fixed when it opens, and the token source (built from the row id alone) re-read the row on every request, so after a re-point and a new sign-in the run's old connection sent the NEW tokens to the OLD endpoint, whose 401 then spent the new refresh token and ended the new sign-in. `mcpOAuthTokenSource(db, id, target)` is now bound to the endpoint its connection was opened against (the gateway's, the save probe's and `testMcpServer`'s), and once the row points anywhere else (or is no longer HTTP) it hands over nothing: it throws `UpstreamEndpointChanged` before a request is sent, and the gateway — on the machinery ruling 461's R-gateway-3 note describes — opens a new connection to where the row points and sends the request again, with that endpoint's own sign-in (or fails naming why, "needs sign-in" until an admin signs in). Test: `gateway-oauth.server.test.ts` "R-oauth-1" (a run holds its connection, the admin re-points the row to a second in-test OAuth server: the next call reads "needs sign-in"; after signing in there the call goes through to the new server, the old one heard nothing more and none of the new tokens, and the sign-in stays signed in). Canary: the token source not checking the row's endpoint against its own (the new sign-in reads "sign-in expired"). **R-oauth-2 (medium).** A credential pasted on a row that read "needs sign-in" (a bare probe met the challenge — or the admin signed out, as the editor's "Sign out below to paste one instead" says) or "sign-in expired" left `oauth_json` as it was for good: the save probes WITH the credential, so neither `recordMcpOAuthChallenge` nor `clearMcpOAuthChallenge` ran, and nothing else writes it. The resolver mounted the pasted credential (it wins), while the Settings row showed a red "needs sign-in", the editor "Needs sign-in", and the controller's `signInNote` and `save_mcp_server` reply said runs do not mount it and advised a sign-in — which drops the working credential. Both ends are fixed: `saveMcpServer` clears both OAuth columns when the saved row holds a credential and its sign-in is not live (audited `oauthDropped` on `org.mcp.updated`, as a re-point's is), and `mapMcp` reports `oauth: null` for any row holding a pasted credential, so every surface agrees with the resolver even for a row written before this. Tests: `mcp-oauth.server.test.ts` "R-oauth-2" (a paste over "needs sign-in", then over "sign-in expired": both columns cleared, the view has no sign-in status, the audit says `oauthDropped`; a row holding a credential beside a stale "needs sign-in" reads `oauth: null`). Canaries, each alone: the save not clearing the columns (the first test red on the raw row); the view mapping the public half regardless (the second red). **R-oauth-3 (low).** Two writes skipped the compare-and-set (c) promised. (1) A refused renewal read the row, awaited the refresh (up to 15 s) and then ended "the sign-in" it had read: a new sign-in that landed meanwhile — the admin's "Sign in again", whose re-consent is exactly what makes some servers refuse the old refresh token — was overwritten with the old registration and no tokens, and a `refresh` failure audited; `refusedAfterRenewal` likewise expired whatever the row held, not the token that was refused. (2) `completeMcpOAuthSignIn` checked the row's endpoint before the code exchange and wrote after it, so a re-pointing save that landed meanwhile got a sign-in sealed for the OLD endpoint and lost the credential it had just pasted (`cred_ref = NULL`). Now the token source ends a sign-in through `expireIf`, which re-reads the row and writes in one synchronous stretch only while the stored tokens are still the refused ones (the renewal's pair; for `refusedAfterRenewal(rejected)` — the interface now carries the refused token — that access token), keeping the freshly read sealed half; otherwise the renewal answers with what was stored meanwhile and the refused request fails without ending anything. The callback reads the row again after the exchange and refuses ("its endpoint changed during the sign-in") unless the endpoint and transport still match, writing in the same stretch; the tokens it got are dropped unrevoked, as a re-point's are. Tests: `mcp-oauth.server.test.ts` "R-oauth-3" (a refresh refused while a new sign-in lands through the injected `fetch`: the renewal answers with the new token, the row stays signed in, nothing audited; `refusedAfterRenewal` with a stale token ends nothing and with the stored one ends the sign-in; a re-pointing save with a pasted credential landing during the code exchange: the callback refuses, the credential and the new endpoint stay, no OAuth columns written). Canaries, each alone: the renewal's refusal ending whatever is stored; `refusedAfterRenewal` ignoring which token was refused; the callback writing the row it read before the exchange. **R-oauth-4 (low).** A renewal refused with `invalid_client` (the authorization server forgot Viberr's dynamically registered client, or its secret lapsed) ended the sign-in but kept the client, and the next Sign in reused it: the consent screen refused the unknown id (usually without redirecting back, so nothing was audited) or the exchange failed `invalid_client`, which wrote nothing — every retry failed the same way until someone happened to sign out. `McpOAuthError` now carries `clientRejected` (`isClientRefusal`: `InvalidClientError` or `UnauthorizedClientError`, the two the SDK's own `auth()` drops client credentials on); a renewal refused that way drops the whole sealed half, and a code exchange refused that way drops the stored sealed half when it holds the client that exchange reused (`forgetRefusedClient`, the row then reading "sign-in expired" with the server's words), so the next sign-in registers again. The registration now keeps `client_secret_expires_at`, and a lapsed secret is registered again rather than reused. Tests: `mcp-oauth.server.test.ts` "R-oauth-4" (the in-test server forgets its clients: the renewal ends the sign-in and drops the client, and the next sign-in registers a new one and works; the server changes the client's secret: the refused exchange drops the stored client and the next sign-in registers again; a secret whose `client_secret_expires_at` has passed is registered again while one that never lapses is reused). Canaries, each alone: the renewal keeping the client on a client refusal; the refused exchange leaving the stored client; the lapse check dropped from the reuse. *Dated note (2026-09-25, ruling 486, F40-63):* the public half (b) now also carries the scope the server granted, and every surface that says "signed in" says what the sign-in may do ("read-only · 194 scopes"). "The scope asked for is the resource's advertised `scopes_supported`, or none" no longer holds alone: an admin's Requested scopes (`oauth_requested_scope`), when set, are asked for instead. A gateway-relayed authorization refusal on a read-only grant names the grant and the remedy. See ruling 486. *Dated note (2026-09-27, ruling 514):* (e)'s sentence in place of the field now also drops what the field held. A key typed, or filled in by the browser, before the sign-in landed stayed in the editor and rode every save, which the server refused as a pasted credential over the live sign-in, so Save & re-test of a signed-in server failed. A refusal about the credential now reads at the credential field, and `appErrorResponse` answers the form field a refusal names. See ruling 514.

470. **A packet observation's key is the agent's own label, shown as written** (owner, 2026-09-24, pass 40, F40-15: the owner asked for every finding fixed). `observationLabel` (`app/features/task-detail/decision-packet.tsx`) replaced any key containing `/` or `\\` with the word "detail", on the theory (pass 20, C7) that a path-shaped key is a value the operator put in the wrong slot. Live on WEB-1's first packet the operator keyed a row `origin/main`, the git ref it had just read, and the card said "DETAIL fatal: invalid object name 'main'…": the one word telling the reader what the row was about was gone. `origin/main`, `CI/CD` and `src/pages` are ordinary labels, and a key that really is a mis-slotted value is still the operator's words, which the reader is better served seeing than a generic stand-in. So a path-shaped key is shown verbatim (no camelCase split, no underscore rewrite, which would damage a path), capped at 40 characters like every key; the humanising of ordinary keys is unchanged. The pass-20 test that required "detail" is replaced by one that requires the key (`task-detail-components.test.tsx`, "ruling 470"), red against the old code.

471. **A person's acceptance answers the open decision that offers it** (owner, 2026-09-25, pass 40, F40-16; spec `planning/discovery-2026-09-24-pass40-akinozer-site/SPEC-471-accept-answers-decision.md`; amends F32-11). Measured live 2026-09-24 22:55 UTC on WEB-1: the operator's decision "WEB-1 ready to accept: both reviewers approved PR #1 at a95c337" recommended `accept_completion` ("Accept WEB-1 and merge PR #1"), and the owner pressed the task page's Accept, the same ceremony and the same merge. The dialog said the decision "closes unanswered with the task", the timeline "Withdrew the open decision … so the decision was never answered", and the audit row was `task.packet.withdrawn`. The owner had answered it, with its own recommended option; rulings 164 and F19-7 already make the PACKET door record that as an answer, so the record depended on which of two identical buttons was pressed. Decided: **(a)** *Which option.* One predicate, `acceptanceAnswerOf` (`app/shared/packet-acceptance-answer.ts`), read by the server's write and by the loader. A plain acceptance performs `accept_completion`; that covers every door into `acceptCompletion`: Accept, a board or stage-menu move into the terminal stage, an applied acceptance card. A forced acceptance performs `force_accept`, and `accept_completion` when the decision offers no `force_accept`: the person accepted the completion, which is that option's answer, and the override keeps its own `task.acceptance.forced` row. A plain acceptance never answers `force_accept`, whose title promises an override that a plain acceptance did not make. Among options of the kind the recommended one wins, then the first. A decision already decided (`awaiting`, an `edit_goal` waiting for its goal) takes no second answer, the refusal the packet door makes too. **(b)** *The record is the packet door's.* `applyAcceptanceWrite` takes `answerer`, the person, set by `acceptCompletion` alone. Inside the file lock it reads the packet actually there, and when the predicate answers it the packet is cleared with no withdrawal note and no `task.packet.withdrawn` row; after the write it records `task.packet.resolved` under that person with the packet door's own fields (`optionKind`, `optionTitle`, `packetKind`) plus `via: "accept" | "force-accept"`, and marks the task's packet and approval notifications read, as the packet door does for a settled decision. The marker is named `via` with the vocabulary of the withdrawal row's `by`, not the spec's example `accept-button`, because four doors reach the one function. There is no operator hand-off: the packet door queues none for either kind (`NO_REQUEUE`, the task is Done), and this path never makes one, so nothing fires twice. The packet door's `accept_completion` answer IS its completion event, so here the answer rides the completion event as one clause, "This acceptance answers the open decision "<title>" with "<option>".". The forced completion's "Bypassed: …" list now ends its sentence with a period, so the clause after it starts a new one. The operator's own full-autonomy acceptance (`operatorAcceptCompletion`) passes no person: it answers a question put to nobody, and withdraws as before. **(c)** *Everything else is F32-11.* A decision offering neither option is withdrawn exactly as before, note and row. When a forced acceptance answers the decision, `forceAcceptDisclosure.withdrawnPacket` is null, so neither the forced completion event nor `task.acceptance.forced` calls it withdrawn. **(d)** *The dialog says which before the click, from the loader.* `mapPacket` sets `acceptAnswersWith` and `forceAnswersWith` on the packet render (the title of the option each door answers with, absent when that door withdraws) from the same predicate; the board card carries `acceptAnswersWith`; the task page passes the pressed door's field to `AcceptConfirm` as `answersWith` (none for the packet mode, which is the answer itself). The row then reads "Answers the open decision "<title>" with "<option>". The answer is recorded on the timeline and in the audit trail."; without an answer it keeps F32-11's "Withdraws" row. Not changed, and named so nobody reads it as covered: the acceptance gates. An open `blocked` packet still refuses a plain acceptance (`blockedPacket`) even when it offers `accept_completion`, and a forced acceptance that answers such a packet still lists that gate among the ones it bypassed. Ruling 319's fan-out is not applied, because the packets that share a cause (a backend's quota or credential) never offer either kind. Budgets (ruling 457), each raised to the measured value with the reason beside it: the task loader's two console payloads by 79 bytes (VIB-142's packet carries both answer fields, "Accept completion"), the board-40 revalidation and card payloads by 160 bytes (four cards cloned from VIB-142 carry `acceptAnswersWith`), and the gzip closures of `routes/project.board` by 67 B and `routes/project.task` by 74 B (the dialog's Answers arm and the page's per-door choice). Tests: `accept-answers-decision.server.test.ts` "ruling 471" (a plain acceptance: the row and its fields, no withdrawal row or note, Done with no packet in the file and the projection, the clause, the notification read, no operator run with an operator deployed; a plain acceptance withdraws a `force_accept`-only decision; a decision with neither option is withdrawn as before; the operator's own acceptance withdraws; Force accept answers `force_accept` over `accept_completion`, with `withdrawnPacket` null and the bypass sentence closed; force falls back to `accept_completion`; the packet door's `force_accept` still writes ONE row), `task.server.test.ts`, `board-card.test.ts`, `accept-confirm.test.tsx`, `task-disposition.test.tsx` and `board-page.test.tsx` "ruling 471". F32-11's force test in `task-governance.server.test.ts` now uses a decision without `accept_completion`, which that force would answer. The seven answer tests are red against the pre-ruling source. Canaries, each seen red and restored: drop `answerer` from `acceptCompletion`; drop the notification read; fire a `packet-resolved` hand-off from the answer; give the plain door `force_accept`; answer any recommended option, and any first option; put `accept_completion` before `force_accept` on the force door, and drop it; ignore `answerer` inside the lock; restore the old `withdrawnPacket`; drop the bypass list's period; keep the packet on the packet door's `force_accept` arm; drop the render's derivation; drop the dialog's Answers arm; swap the page's per-door fields; slice the board card back to type and title; stop the board passing `answersWith`.

472. **A decision packet's body is markdown and renders as markdown** (owner, 2026-09-25, pass 40, F40-17: the owner asked for every finding fixed). The asking agent writes the body, and agents write markdown: WEB-3's Platform Engineer raised a 3,500-character Cloudflare Workers Builds Connect guide with a bold lead-in, a `## (a)` / `## (b)` heading per part and numbered dashboard steps with bold field names. `DecisionPacket` (`app/features/task-detail/decision-packet.tsx`) rendered the body through `renderInlineCode` alone, inside a `<p>` with `white-space: normal`, so the owner was handed one run-on paragraph with literal `**` and `##` and the step numbers run together, for the one step only the owner can do. The body now renders through the app's GFM renderer (`~/ui/markdown.tsx`, the same one the timeline's comments and the goal use, raw HTML escaped) in a `<div class="packet-lede md-body">` (a list cannot sit inside a `<p>`), on both the open and the decided card; a heading inside the body is set at the body's size (`app/app.css`) so it never outranks the packet's own title. The option titles and descriptions keep the inline-code pass: they are one line each. Test `task-detail-components.test.tsx` "ruling 472", red against the inline-code body.

473. **The store volume is external: Compose never owns it** (owner, 2026-09-25, pass 40, F40-18: the owner asked for every finding fixed). Ruling 460 put the store on the named volume `viberr-data` and declared it in `compose.yml` without `external`. On the owner's host the volume came from `npm run store:to-volume`, so it carries no Compose labels, and every deploy printed "volume \"viberr-data\" already exists but was not created by Docker Compose". On a fresh host Compose creates it on the first `up`, labelled as its own, and a volume Compose owns is one `docker compose down -v` deletes: the canonical files, the database, every sealed credential and every person's sign-in, in one routine command. Measured 2026-09-25 with a throwaway volume: an unlabelled volume survives `down -v`, so the owner's store was safe only by the accident of how it was made. The volume is now `external: true`. `npm run deploy` (`scripts/deploy.ts`) inspects it and creates it when it is missing, before `up`, and never touches an existing one. The fresh-install steps in `docs/operations/deployment.md` create it by hand. An `up` without it fails with "external volume not found" instead of starting on an empty store. Test `app/server/ops/store-volume-wiring.test.ts`, red by canary on either half (drop `external`; drop the create).
    *(Superseded 2026-09-26 by ruling 504: Compose owns the store volume, so a starter's bare
    `docker compose up` creates it, and `docker compose down -v` deletes it, as that flag
    asks. There is no guard: `-v` is an explicit request to delete volumes, and plain `down`
    keeps them. `npm run deploy` no longer creates the volume.)*

474. **A review PR's body follows the delivery it describes** (owner, 2026-09-25, pass 40, F40-19; spec `planning/discovery-2026-09-24-pass40-akinozer-site/SPEC-474-pr-body-follows-delivery.md`). Measured live 2026-09-25 on akin-ozer/website PR #2 (WEB-4): Viberr opened the PR on the first delivery with "10 file(s) changed (+814/-15)" and "3 commit(s) delivered, revision 7cf1edc"; the reviewers asked for rework, two more commits were pushed and re-delivered to the same PR (head cc9aa30, 5 commits, +823/−15), and the body went on describing 7cf1edc, so a reviewer on GitHub read a revision that was not the one under review. `composePrBody` ran on the create path only, and nothing in `app/server/github/` edited a PR body. Decided: **(a)** *When.* After both reuse arms of `openTaskPr` (the cached live PR, and a PR found on the branch head), `refreshReusedPrBody` (`pr-open.server.ts`) compares the revision the body was written for with the one delivered now. The revision is the delivered revision the Evidence line names (`workRevision.headSha`), else the PR head GitHub reported; the delivered revision is preferred because GitHub's `head.sha` on a pull request can lag the push that just moved it. An unchanged revision sends nothing. **(b)** *What.* The body is recomposed from the current task through `composeTaskPrBody`, which the create path now calls too, so a rewrite carries exactly the inputs a fresh PR would: the live compare's stats (F22-10), the delivered revision, the current goal. It goes out as one `PATCH /repos/{r}/pulls/{n}` with `retryServerError: false` (the option the pass-40 pre-merge review added for writes that must not be sent twice). No other wording changes; the Evidence line already names the revision. **(c)** *Never a person's edit.* The record is `pr.bodyWritten: { sha256, revision, keptRevision? }`, set on create and on every rewrite, not the spec's example `pr.bodySha256`: the revision the body describes is what decides (a) and what the audit's `fromRevision` reports, so it is recorded beside the hash. Before rewriting, the description GitHub holds (read by the reuse path's own `GET`) is hashed with line endings read as LF (`prBodySha256`: GitHub's web editor saves CRLF, so a description opened and saved unchanged is not an edit). A mismatch is a person's edit: nothing is sent, and one `github` timeline note by `system:delivery` per delivered revision (`keptRevision`) says the description was left as the person wrote it, the revision it was written for, and the revision, commits, files and +/− the PR now carries. That note writes nothing to GitHub, so it has no audit row. A PR Viberr never recorded a body for (opened before this ruling, or adopted: a PR an agent opened from its workspace included) counts as Viberr's and is rewritten on its next re-delivery, as the spec rules. A recorded body that GitHub's answer did not include is never assumed unedited: it is handled as a failure (d). **(d)** *A failure never fails the delivery.* A refused or unreachable `PATCH` leaves the delivery `ok`; a `github` note says which revision the description still describes, the revision it could not be updated to, and GitHub's reason, and the next delivery tries again. Audit `github.pr.body_updated` or `github.pr.body_update_failed` with `{prNumber, fromRevision, toRevision}` (the failure adds `reason`); both are in the audit-coverage table. Anything else that throws in the refresh is logged and the reuse stands. A successful rewrite has no timeline note of its own: the "Pushed `<sha>` to **PR #N**" event already says the head moved. **(e)** *Kept by every writer.* The reconciler rebuilds `pr` from scratch each pass, so it now carries `bodyWritten` for the same PR number, and under its write lock keeps a record a delivery wrote during the pass. It also sets the loose `humanApproval` key last, the order a parse gives the file back, so an unchanged PR still compares equal and writes nothing. The field rides the task-file schema every route bundles, so seven ruling-457 bundle ceilings rose by 30 to 38 bytes, each with this reason beside it. Tests: `pr-open.server.test.ts` "ruling 474" (moved head rewritten; unchanged head sends nothing; a person's edit kept with one note; a CRLF save still Viberr's; a failed PATCH sent once with note and row; a legacy PR rewritten; an adopted PR rewritten; an unreadable description not assumed unedited), `github-reconciler.server.test.ts` "ruling 474" (carried every pass with no rewrite churn; a mid-pass record survives), and the audit-coverage rows; each red by canary.

475. **The operator routes a conflict to the delivering agent, a merge re-checks its siblings, and the timeline speaks to people** (owner, 2026-09-25, pass 40, F40-20, F40-55, F40-60; the owner asked for every finding fixed, and decided F40-20 directly). Measured live 2026-09-25 on akinozer-com: the owner accepted WEB-4 at 00:26:20 and Viberr merged PR #2; WEB-2's PR #3 changed the same `package.json`, which Viberr already knew (both `pr.paths`, the review queue's ruling-236 chip, the operator's ruling-413 `collisions`). At 00:27:54 the owner pressed Accept on WEB-2's still-open packet, which still said "the PR is mergeable", and the acceptance-time refresh refused it. The operator ran `update_branch_from_base`, wrote a comment naming the exact fix (keep the new "test" script and main's "check:contrast"), and opened "`web-2` conflicts with `main`": "A person decides how this is resolved." The owner confirmed the packet's own recommendation, "Have Platform Engineer resolve the conflict", at 00:29:10; the deliverer resolved it at 00:38. Thirteen minutes and three owner actions for a conflict Viberr caused a minute earlier. **(a) F40-20, owner decision ("Operator routes it"): the operator hands a merge conflict or push conflict straight to the delivering agent.** When `update_branch_from_base` meets a `conflict` or a `push_conflict` and the task's delivering engagement is deployed with a repo-write grant (ruling 133(b)'s eligibility), the tool itself starts that agent's run (through `operatorDispatchAgent`, so the `dispatch-agents` gate, the owner's credential and the concurrency cap all apply) with ruling 438's directive: merge `origin/<base>` (or origin's copy of the branch) into the task branch in its own workspace, never a rebase or a force-push, resolve the named files keeping both sides' intent, run the gates, commit, and leave delivery to the operator. In the same write a task at or past the review stage returns to it (ruling 163's `returnsToReview`, audited `task.transition {boundary: rework, via: conflict_handoff}`, withdrawing the acceptance offers the move makes moot, ruling 137), and the timeline gets one person-facing line: "The operator sent the `package.json` conflict between `web-2` and `main` to Platform Engineer, which merges `main` into the branch in its own workspace and resolves it. WEB-2 returns from Merge to Review, so the reviewers judge the resolved branch before anyone accepts it." The resolved branch goes through the required reviewers as before (ruling 134(b): the delivery moves the head, ruling 163(c) and the verdict gate hold it until a fresh verdict). The blocking packet is the fallback, and says which of these it is: no deliverer or no repo-write grant (resolving by hand recommended, as ruling 133(b) had it); the deliverer was already sent this same conflict and the branch still conflicts (the same files against the same base commit, `baseSha` on the conflict result, or the same origin head refusing the push, `remoteHeadSha`; resolving by hand recommended, "Have <deliverer> try the conflict again" offered second); an operator whose `dispatch-agents` policy only recommends; or a run that could not start (the dispatch's own refusal quoted). While the deliverer's run on this same conflict is still live the tool sends nothing and opens nothing. Every route writes the `github.branch_update.operator` audit row with `route` (`deliverer`, `packet`, `in_progress`), `handedTo`, `repeat` and `handoffRefused`; the earlier-handoff check reads those rows (`taskAuditDetails`). The operator doctrine (seed asset; the outgoing hash is in `PRIOR_SHIPPED_HASHES`), the tool description and the `pr-conflicting` turn instruction say so, and tell the operator never to open a conflict packet of its own. This supersedes, for this case, the "a person decides how this is resolved" the conflict packet always said, and narrows ruling 133(b) and ruling 438 (both marked). **(b) F40-55: a merge re-checks the project's other open pull requests, and a flip to conflicting is acted on.** (1) `mergeTaskPr`, on a successful merge (the acceptance's and "Complete merge"'s one door), starts `recheckOpenReviewPrs` without awaiting it: every other open review PR of the project (`review` or `accepted`, not archived) is reconciled at once, and one GitHub still answers "unknown" for (its mergeability is computed asynchronously, and the first read after a base move usually starts that computation) is read again after 5 and 20 seconds (`SIBLING_RECHECK_DELAYS_MS`). Every PR that shares a path with the merged one is among them by construction, so nothing is filtered by `prPathOverlaps`: a path list can be capped or unread, and the conflict is GitHub's to name. (2) The reconciler's flip to `conflicting` (ruling 162(d)) now also withdraws an open decision packet that offers `accept_completion` (`withdrawAcceptancePacket`: a "**Packet withdrawn:**" note, audit `task.packet.withdrawn_superseded {reason: pr_conflicting}`, the packet's bell marked read), tells the task's watchers why in a `policy` notification, and wakes the operator with the existing `pr-conflicting` trigger (ruling 332), whose turn instruction now names both origins. The operator's conflict arm withdraws such a packet too before it routes the conflict. (3) The accept dialog names the collision before the click, from both of its doors: a "Collides" row, "Merging this will likely put WEB-2's PR #3 in conflict on `package.json`. Viberr re-checks it right after the merge, and the operator hands a conflict to the delivering agent." (`mergeCollisions` in `app/shared/pr-overlaps.ts`, where ruling 236's `prPathOverlaps` now lives; the task page's loader computes it from the projections, `taskMergeCollisions`, and the board from the cards it holds). **(c) F40-60: the timeline gets the person's sentence, the tool result keeps the model's.** Ruling 134(c) put origin's lag on the record for the humans with the model's words: "call `deliver_for_review` to push it. Do not ask a person to push." before every delivery on WEB-1, WEB-2 and WEB-4, and "That is a person's act, not yours" for a diverged branch. The timeline line is now `remotePersonSentence`: "`web-2` is level with `main`. GitHub's copy of the branch (`9f96fc9`) is 7 commits behind the workspace; the operator's next delivery pushes them." (absent: "The branch is not on GitHub yet; the operator's next delivery pushes it."; diverged: the fact and `DIVERGED_BRANCH_REMEDY`), suppressed when it would repeat the newest `github` line; the tool result is unchanged. This narrows ruling 134(c)'s timeline line. Tests: `update-branch-operator.server.test.ts` "ruling 475 (F40-20)" (the handoff, the return to review, the same conflict never sent twice, a new base commit sent again, the push conflict, a dispatch that throws, the recommend-only policy, the moot accept packet) and "ruling 475 (F40-60)", and the persona test; `github-reconciler.server.test.ts` "ruling 475 (F40-55)"; `accept-confirm.test.tsx`, `board-page.test.tsx`, `pr-overlaps.test.ts`, `pr-collisions.server.test.ts` and `project.task.server.test.ts` for the Collides row. (`routeConflict`, `earlierHandoff`, `recordHandoff` and `remotePersonSentence` in `app/server/github/update-branch-operator.server.ts`; `recheckOpenReviewPrs` and the flip in `app/server/github/github-reconciler.server.ts`; `withdrawAcceptancePacket` in `app/server/tasks/task-mutation.server.ts`; `CollidesRow` in `app/features/task-detail/accept-confirm.tsx`.)

476. **The controller page, its dock and its goals rail say what they hold, where a person reads it** (owner, 2026-09-25, pass 40, F40-21, F40-22, F40-23, F40-24, F40-25, F40-26, F40-56 and F40-61: the owner asked for every finding fixed; extends rulings 419, 425 and 465). Measured live on the owner's akinozer.com instance. **(a) F40-21: a link in a message wraps.** The owner's 16-message instance thread held 228 links whose text is their URL, one unbreakable run: the dock's transcript scrolled 702px in 388 with 142 links past its edge at every desktop width, and `/controller` at 375px 693px in 315, so reading one URL scrolled the whole thread sideways. `.md-body a` now takes `overflow-wrap: anywhere`, as ruling 419(i) gave inline code; a table keeps its own scroller. **(b) F40-22: a link is named by its number.** Every other surface says "goal-1 · link 3", "waiting on goal-1 link 1", "Links 6 and 10", and the rail printed no number, so finding link N meant counting rows; its wait summary "waits on 1" read as "waits on link 1" (live, link 10 said it while it waited on link 9), and a wait entry naming a goal link sent a keyboard user to the chain's summary. Each row now prints its number ("Link 3" to a screen reader) and carries the id `goal-N-link-M` (`goalLinkAnchor`, `app/shared/goal-anchor.ts`); the task page's chain chip and every wait entry naming a goal link (on the rail and on the task hero, `dependencyAnchor`) point at that row; `useTargetedGoal` opens its chain, scrolls only the nearest scroller to the row, focuses it (`tabIndex=-1`) and marks it `data-targeted`; the summary reads "waits on N open · M done" and "waited on N entries, all done". **(c) F40-23: a reply is met at its first line.** Both transcripts set `scrollTop = scrollHeight` on every count or working change, so a reply taller than the box (every one of the thread's eight, at 375px) opened at its tail, and under ruling 465's reply order a reply to a message with queued messages behind it scrolled about 13,000px past the answer to the last queued message. One hook now places both (`useTranscriptFollow`, `app/features/controller/transcript-follow.ts`): an opened transcript (a thread, the dock's panel, its transcript back from the thread list) shows the newest reply from its first line when a reply is the newest message, and its end otherwise; a controller message that lands is scrolled to its first line unless the reader has scrolled above the newest reply they had, when nothing moves; the person's own message, and a turn that starts while they follow the thread, go to the end. **(d) F40-24: a screen reader hears the turn.** The page's only status region was the working row, inserted with its sentence already in it (the one case screen readers skip, `docs/ui/surfaces.md`) and removed when the reply landed in a transcript with no live region; the dock's announcer beside its button leaves the thread on screen out while the panel is open, so a reply there cleared it to "". The page mounts one visually hidden `role="status"` region outside the per-thread subtree (`TurnAnnouncer`) whose text becomes "<name> is working" when a turn starts and "<name> replied: <first sentence>" when the reply lands (`useTurnAnnouncement`, `replyGist`); the open dock panel mounts its own for replies to the thread on screen, the button's region keeps "is working"; both working rows lose `role="status"`. **(e) F40-25: the phone's thread switcher gets a row.** In the one-column head the picker sat beside New and Home at 97px and read "Hi. I'm s", naming nothing, which is what ruling 419(a) put it there to do; `.ctl-head-acts` wraps and `.ctl-picker` takes `flex: 1 1 100%`, New and Home on the row under it. **(f) F40-26: the Goals head counts by status.** "N running · M settled" counted a paused chain and one stopped on a failed link as running; it reads "1 active · 1 paused · 2 need attention · 3 settled", non-zero parts only (`goalsCountLine`). **(g) F40-56: a started link says what its task's board card says.** Live, goal-1 drew WEB-2, WEB-3 and WEB-5 as "active" in the agent-working purple while their cards said "waiting on you" and WEB-3's open packet held five other links, against ruling 425(a)'s "the word and colour the board's card uses for the same task". The project Controller loader now computes each task's card status exactly as the board loader does (`linkTaskStatuses`: `waitingOnViewer` over the workspace read's review queue, `withLiveRun`, `toBoardCard`, `cardStatus`), asked for only when a chain has a started link, and an active link carries it as `taskStatus` (`GoalLinkView`); its pill shows that word in the board's colour (`CARD_PILL`: "waiting on you" in `.pill.info`, the board's blue; "waiting on a human" and "resumes <time>" neutral; "input required"; "agent working"; "blocked" keeps ruling 425(a)'s pill), ruling 425(a)'s held rule standing where no status is carried. The chain's line adds "· N waiting on you" and "· N waiting on a human". **(h) F40-61: a chain links back to where it was planned.** goal-1 was planned in a 16-message instance thread, and the project's Controller page said "No conversations yet" beside it: the goal file named its creator only. The goal frontmatter gains `conversationId` (after `createdByLabel`, null for a chain written before it); a turn's mounts hand the conversation to the toolkit and `create_goal` records it. The page reads it with the chain's history in one read of the file (`readGoalFileFacts`, which took over ruling 419(h)'s `readGoalHistory`; the projection does not carry it) and, for a viewer who may open that conversation (its owner or an org admin, `canAccessConversation`), shows "Planned in <title> · <scope>" first under "About this chain", linking to the conversation on its own scope's page; the Conversations panel lists the planning threads its own list does not hold under "Where this board's chains were planned", each naming the chains it planned, and its empty line says "No conversations on this board yet." when there are some. Tests: `app.css.test.ts` "ruling 476(a)" and "ruling 476(e)"; `controller-page.test.tsx` "ruling 476" ((b), (c), (d), (f), (g), (h)); `controller-dock.test.tsx` "ruling 476" ((c), (d)); `controller-goals-loader.test.ts` ((g), (h) through the route's loader, against the board loader's own card); `controller-run.server.test.ts` "ruling 476(h)" (a turn's own `create_goal` records its conversation); `task-detail-components.test.tsx` "ruling 419(h) and 476(b)".

    **(i) Live verification 2026-09-25 (deploy 4, F40-21): prose wraps a long token too, not only a link.** (a) gave `overflow-wrap: anywhere` to `.md-body a` alone. On the deployed build a plain token with no break opportunity, "Added/Changed/Deprecated/Removed/Fixed/Security." in a list item, still widened `/controller`'s transcript at 375px (scrollWidth 433 in 315) and the dock's (442 in 388). Rendered markdown prose now breaks any such token where it must: `.md-body` paragraphs, list items, blockquotes and headings take `overflow-wrap: anywhere`, and `.md-body pre` and `.md-table-wrap` set it back to `normal`, so a code block and a table (one inside a list item included) keep their own scrollers. None or several leave the key null, with one info line per boot naming those chains; a chain that names a conversation is never touched, so a second boot writes nothing. (g)'s board status per task and (h)'s "Planned in" link moved to the epic's page, and (j)'s backfill is deleted: a converted epic keeps the goal's `conversationId`. (a), (c), (d), (e) and (i) stand.)* *(Extended 2026-09-28 by ruling 572(a): a reply (c) leaves below a reader in history is also said on screen, by the transcript's jump, "New reply", which takes the reader to its first line.)*

477. **The board, the review queue and Activity say what waits, what the chain did, and where a row goes** (owner, 2026-09-25, pass 40, F40-27, F40-28 and F40-29: the owner asked for every finding fixed). **(a)** *F40-27: "Blocked or waiting" selects a task holding an open question.* Measured live on akinozer.com: WEB-3 carried the Platform Engineer's question ("connect Workers Builds"), its card read "waiting on you", and the board loader shipped `readiness: "ready"`, `displayReadiness: "input_required"`, `waiting: "human"`, `packet.type: "input"`; under `?filter=risk` the head read "0 of 4 tasks · 1 waiting on a human in this project" above lanes saying every task was hidden. An input packet sets `waiting` to `human` and leaves the stored readiness where it was (only a `blocked` packet moves it), and `matchesBoardFilter`'s risk arm read the stored enum alone, so ruling 36's defect came back through the packet door and ruling 91's "raising a packet reasserts input required everywhere" did not hold for the filter. The arm now also matches `waiting === "human"` with an open packet of either type, whatever the stored readiness (`board-filters.ts`; `BoardCard.packet` already rode to the board). The finding's first suggestion, `displayReadiness === "input_required"`, would miss the same packet on a task whose stored readiness is not `ready` (an `in_review` task with an input packet, a decided `edit_goal` packet reading "goal edit pending"); the packet is the demand, so the filter reads it. Ruling 91's exclusion holds through `waiting` (an agent carrying the task), and ruling 225's cannot arise (an open packet outranks the clock, so such a task never rests on a schedule). The filter stays project-wide: a member the packet is not addressed to, whose "Waiting on me" chip does not select it, finds it here. A human-next task with no packet open is not selected, because nothing asserted it is stuck. Tests: `board-filters.test.ts` "ruling 477(a)" and `board-page.test.tsx` "keeps a ready card holding an open question visible", both red by canary. **(b)** *F40-28: the goal chain is on the record, as the chain.* Measured: the org audit store held project-scoped `goal.created` and `goal.updated` rows for goal-1 while the project's Audit logs column ("58 of 58 entries") showed neither, because `AUDIT_ACTION_KINDS` (`activity-feed.server.ts`) had no `goal.*` action; and with the stream's Humans filter, six of 13 "human" rows were the chain starting links 2 to 4 in the second WEB-1 was accepted ("Took task ownership by creating the task" and "Waits on other work", credited to the owner). Decided: `goal.created` and `goal.updated` join the whitelist as `change`, `goal.completed` as `audit`, each with a sentence: "<person> created goal **goal-1** (<title>) with 11 links."; one per redirect op ("paused", "resumed", "cancelled ...: <reason>", "skipped link N of ...: <reason>", "retried link N of", "edited link N of", "added link N to", "removed pending link N from", "bound link N of ... to an existing task on" with the adopted task's chip, "renamed goal **goal-1** from **A** to **B**" or "rewrote the description of"); "changed nothing on" for an op that changed nothing (a pause on a paused chain, a resume on an active one, a rename to the same text); and the runner's "Goal **goal-1** (<title>) completed: every link is settled." with no actor, like the policy engine's rows. The actor goes through `auditActorDisplay`, so a controller-driven redirect reads "(via the controller)". The writers record what the sentences read: `goal.updated {op, message, title, index?, reason?, from?, to?, unchanged?}` (the title after the op; an `adopt_task` row carries the adopted task in `task_key`) and `goal.completed {title}`; a row written before this ruling reads with the chain's id alone. A chain-started task's creation is the chain's act (`createTask` when `goalRef` is set): the owner seat's `assign` event and the "Waits on other work" note are signed `system:goal-chain`, rendered "Goal chain", a system actor the Humans filter drops, and the seat reads "Started by **goal-1** as link 2, on <creator>'s authority, with <owner> as owner." before the usual sentence about the owner's accounts; on a retry the authority is the person who retried. The seat itself, the `task.created` audit row and its label (`<creator> · goal chain`) are unchanged, and a task a person creates by hand still reads "Took task ownership by creating the task". The finding's example named a trigger ("when WEB-1 reached Done"); a link starts because its whole declared wait is satisfied (ruling 398 starts links together), which the wait note beside the seat already lists, so the seat names the chain, the link and the authority and no trigger. Tests: `activity-feed.server.test.ts` "ruling 477(b)" (every op's sentence, the instrument, the kinds), `goal-actions.server.test.ts` "ruling 477" (a started task's creation signed by the chain and dropped by Humans; a person's own creation still theirs; a real define, redirect and complete sequence read as sentences; an adoption with its chip), each red by canary. **(c)** *F40-29: what goes to a page is a link.* Measured live: the WEB-4 queue row was `<button type="button" class="rq-row">` with `<div>`s inside, and every Activity task key a `<button class="keybtn">`, each calling `navigate()`, so a person working the queue could not open rows in tabs or copy an address, and a screen reader announced a button for navigation; the board card, the list view and the Goals panel already link to the same pages. The queue row (`review-page.tsx`), the queue's policy chip (the same defect on the same page) and every Activity key (the stream, the audit rows and the rows a compacted run gives back, `activity-page.tsx`) are `<Link>`s with the class names they had, and `.rq-main` is a `div` (a link's content model is its parent's, so the two lines stay blocks; a span inside a button allowed neither). The finding's "app.css is unchanged" was wrong: an anchor takes the UA link colour and underline and is inline, so `a.rq-row` and `a.keybtn` join the anchor-neutralizing rule (`color: inherit` on the row, no underline on either) and `a.keybtn` keeps a button's `inline-block`, without which its press scale would not apply. Tests: `review-page.test.tsx` "rows and the policy chip are links to their pages" and R15-11's case finding the row by role `link`, and `activity-page.test.tsx` "ruling 477(c)", each red by canary. *(Narrowed 2026-09-26 by ruling 503: nothing writes `goal.*` rows any more, and the rows a project holds still read; no chain creates a task any more, and the conversion signs the tasks it makes for unstarted links through the same `signedBy`. (a) and (c) stand.)*

478. **The task page says what an agent's question needs and renders what the record holds** (owner, 2026-09-25, pass 40, F40-30 to F40-35, F40-57, F40-58: the owner asked for every finding fixed). Measured on the live akinozer.com board (WEB-1 to WEB-5) at 375×812 and 840px. Decided: **(a)** *Typed-event text is markdown* (F40-30). The server's own notes put a tool's words in a fenced block (the checkout failure, the push failure, the provider's reply) and separate paragraphs with blank lines, but `TimelineItem` rendered every typed event through the inline-only `RichText`: WEB-1's "Workspace checkout failed" note printed two literal backticks on either side of one run-on `<code>`, collapsed git's two lines into one, and its unbreakable `/data/projects/…` path widened `.detail` to 598px against 365 on a phone. Typed-event text now renders through the GFM renderer comments use (`~/ui/markdown.tsx`, raw HTML escaped, the same known-name mention filter and task links, F20), in `.tl-text.md-body`, so a fence is a `<pre>` that scrolls on its own and inline code breaks (ruling 419(i)). `RichText` keeps its other surfaces. **(b)** *An attachment's name wins its row on a phone* (F40-32). The fixed "by <actor> · <time>" (144px) and the size left the name 48px, so WEB-3's two files both read "WEB-3…". Under the 720px breakpoint a file row wraps: the name takes the line beside its icon, whole (`white-space: normal`, `overflow-wrap: anywhere`), and the by-line (which may now shrink, with its own ellipsis) and the size drop under it. Every name carries `title` with the whole name. **(c)** *The Live run strip's step shrinks to the strip* (F40-33). The phase's text column was a flex item with an automatic minimum, so the step's 44ch (317px) held it wider than a 283px phase: the step ran through the card's border, its ellipsis off screen, and the page scrolled 23px sideways. The column is `.run-phase-text { min-width: 0 }`. **(d)** *The agent log stream picker says whose console is shown, and only a choice switches it* (F40-34). Its trigger's `aria-label` was the fixed "Select agent log stream", replacing the visible "Platform Engineer · delivering" (WCAG 2.5.3), and ArrowUp/ArrowDown on the open trigger swapped the console with focus left on the trigger and nothing announced. The trigger is named "<label>: <what it shows>" ("Agent log stream: Platform Engineer · delivering"; the live strip's is "Running agent: …"), built from the same strings it draws. Opening it (click, ArrowDown or ArrowUp) moves focus into the list onto the stream shown; ArrowUp/ArrowDown/Home/End move focus there; Enter, Space or a click switches the console, closes the list and returns focus to the trigger; Escape closes it the same way unchanged; Tab closes it. The trigger carries `aria-controls` while open. **(e)** *An agent's question asks for what it needs, recommends only what the agent recommends, and preselects nothing* (F40-31, F40-57). On WEB-3 the Platform Engineer's question asked for the Worker name and URL, its recommended option "Connected; the first build succeeded" was preselected, and the only box read "Note for the operator · optional", although `resolvePacket` sends an agent question's answer back to the agent that asked (R15-14), and a note that named the operator, as the label invited, re-routed it (ruling 447). On WEB-5 a question only the owner could answer showed option 1 as "recommended" because `buildAgentQuestionPacket` recommended the first option whenever none was marked, and the agent had to disown the pick in a comment. Now: an agent's option is recommended only when the agent marks it ("(Recommended)" at the end of its title, U39-23); an unmarked list carries no `rec`, and `ask_human` and the Codex envelope say so (`ASK_HUMAN_RECOMMEND_NOTE`). A choice may carry `reply: true` (`ask_human`'s option schema and the envelope's, `ASK_HUMAN_REPLY_NOTE`; the packet option's new `reply` field) when choosing it needs the person to type something back; the options-less fallback ("Answer the question") always does and recommends nothing, and no longer says the operator picks it up. The packet render names `answerTo`, the asking agent, on exactly the packets `resolvePacket` routes to it (kind `Agent question` with `askedBy`). On such a packet the card preselects nothing, whatever the agent recommends (its pill stays), and nothing is preselected on any packet that recommends nothing; the first choice is the group's tab stop. The note box reads "Your answer to <agent>", its hint "optional" or "required · goes back to <agent> with your choice · 4,000 characters max", and the directive's hint "resolves this decision · goes back to <agent>"; an operator's packet keeps "Note for the operator". Confirm stays enabled (ruling 147) and refuses in place: with no choice, "Choose an answer above first." on the radiogroup (`aria-invalid`, described by the alert) with focus on the first choice; with a `reply` choice and an empty box, "Write your answer to <agent> first." on the box, focused. `resolvePacket` refuses a `reply` option with no note for every other door ("… needs your answer … Nothing was recorded."). The `packet.rec_count` diagnostic now fires only on more than one recommendation: none is a legitimate packet. **(f)** *Written headings sit under the page's own* (F40-35). `Markdown` takes `headingBase`: the text's top heading renders at that level and deeper ones follow, relative to the top level the author used (agents open sections with `##` as often as `#`, and a fixed shift skipped a level), capped at h6. Timeline entries (comments and typed events) use 3, under the Timeline's h2 (WEB-4 had twelve agent h2s beside the page's regions); a packet body uses 3, under the packet's h2 title, so WEB-3's "(a) Connect Workers Builds" is part of the question (ruling 472's size rule is unchanged). The GitHub panel's bar carries a visually hidden h2 "GitHub", which only its no-branch state had. **(g)** *An approval says why it has not cleared* (F40-58). The verdict event's last arm titled every approved-but-not-cleared state "Approval noted, rework still needed", including `changed`, where another required reviewer simply had not reported; the title reached the owner's bell on WEB-1, WEB-2 and WEB-4, minutes before "Review passed". Now `failing` keeps "Approval noted, rework still needed" and names who requested changes; `changed` with required reviewers still owed reads "Approval noted, waiting on <names>" and "<names> has not reviewed it yet, and acceptance waits for every required reviewer."; any other state reads "Approval noted". Names come from the project's agent definitions, else the engagement's role. Tests: `task-detail-components.test.tsx` "ruling 478" (a, e, f), `markdown.test.tsx` "ruling 478(f)", `attachments-panel.test.tsx` "ruling 478(b)", `runs-panels.test.tsx` "ruling 478(d)" and the phase test (c), `app.css.test.ts` "ruling 478" (b, c), `agent-outcome.server.test.ts` and `agent-toolkit.server.test.ts` "ruling 478(e)", `task-governance.server.test.ts` "ruling 478(e)" (the server refusal), `task.server.test.ts` (mapping) "ruling 478(e)", `task-file.schema.test.ts` "ruling 478(e)" (the diagnostic), `task-actions.server.test.ts` "ruling 478(g)"; each red by canary.

479. **The Agents page and the global profile editor say what the runtime does** (owner, 2026-09-25, pass 40, F40-36 to F40-42 and F40-46: the owner asked for every finding fixed; extends rulings 31, 156 and 469). Measured live on akinozer.com: the capability matrix and the Policy cards one click apart counted different things, a granted MCP server that no run mounts looked healthy, "Use the template's grants" failed on the Operator and silently dropped a grant on every other profile, the page showed no effort anywhere and no model for the Operator, screen readers could not tell eligible stages from ineligible ones, the profile editor promised a fork that had already happened, and the global profile editor hid a profile's real stage. Decided: **(a)** *The matrix grid holds enforced capabilities only* (F40-36). `CapabilityMatrixModal` put every label outside the agent catalog into an "Other actions" group with mode colours, so both required reviewers read "Approve the review: Off", every builder "Move the task to Review: Acts directly", and the grid's "Acts directly" cells counted 16 per builder where the Policy card said 9. The grid now partitions by `GOVERNED_CAP_LABELS`, the set the Policy counts (D-2) and the profile panel's columns (F15-05) read: the agent editor's groups plus "Operator actions" (the operator's own capabilities). An advisory line (`group: null`, the three verdict outcomes among them, or a bespoke extra) is listed under the grid in a collapsed `<details>` "Advisory only · N lines the runtime does not read", each with the profiles that hold it and its stored mode, the way the panel lists them (ruling 31); a line stored `off` holds nothing and is not listed, as on the panel. The list's sentence points at the `report-validation-verdict` row as what decides whether a review can approve or request changes. **(b)** *A granted MCP server no run gets tools from is marked* (F40-37). `ResGroup` marked a chip only when the store lacked the name, so `cloudflare-api` (needs sign-in, dropped from every run by `resolveSpecialistMcpServersDetailed`) read like its two healthy neighbours, and the remedy was named only in each run's record and on another page. `buildResourceCatalog` now carries `warning: { note, title }` (`ResItemWarning`, `capability-catalog.ts`) on each MCP item, read off the registry row the Settings list renders, in the resolver's order: "credential unreadable", then "needs sign-in" / "sign-in expired" (the public `oauth` status, ruling 469), then "unreachable" for a failed last check (mounted and flagged down). The chip takes the missing chip's class (`.res-chip.missing`, so the stylesheet every page loads does not grow) with its own note, and the title with the remedy (an org admin, Instance settings → Agent resources) is also in its visually hidden text. **(c)** *The operator's template is a propagation source* (F40-38). The page computed the Operator's drift and showed the button to an org admin, and `propagateTemplateResources` refused every press with `notFound("No such agent profile.")` because it took `kind: "specialist"` templates only. The three grant lists have the same shape and an operator run mounts its copy's lists (`resolveOperatorAuthority`), so the writer now refuses only a profile with no template (`readTemplate` still resolves none for the controller, ruling 99). Ruling 467's persona propagation stays specialist-only: the org editor edits no operator template. **(d)** *"Use the template's grants" asks, and the reply says what went* (F40-39). The button submitted at once, and the toast ignored the `removed` list the writer returned, so a press that took `cloudflare-api` off the agent owning the open Cloudflare task read as an addition; ruling 156 says such a grant "is dropped and the reply says so". The button now opens `SyncGrantsConfirm` (the shared `ConfirmDialog`, screen label `Template grants dialog`): "Replace <name>'s grants with the template's?", naming what the press removes and adds from the drift the card already renders (`describeDriftLists`, moved to the client-safe `agent-types.ts` so the confirm, the writer and the controller share one wording), danger-toned when it removes anything. The toast adds "removed …" and "added …" clauses from the writer's `PropagatedCopy`. The label stays. **(e)** *Model and effort for every kind* (F40-40). The runtime row showed only the model, and for the Operator only Autonomy; the Live tab's Backend column printed "orchestration" for every operator row. The row's "Model · effort" cell ("Claude Opus · Maximum", the editor's `effortLabel` words, "default effort" when none is stored) now renders for every kind, with the operator's Autonomy as its own cell (`.runtime-row` fits its cells). The Live roster names the operator's run backend, the operator profile's first backend or Claude, the rule `resolveOperatorAuthority` applies. **(f)** *Stage eligibility is text* (F40-41). The Eligible stages chips differed only in ink and a strike-through (WCAG 1.3.1); each chip now carries ", eligible" or ", not eligible" as visually hidden text. **(g)** *The editor says "forks" only when a save forks* (F40-42). `forksTemplate` was `source === "template"`, true for every profile with a template file, while all seven akinozer.com deployments already held a full definition snapshot. The view carries `tracksTemplate` (`agents-query.server.ts`): a template exists and the deployment's definition is absent or leaves unset a field a save always writes (name, role, icon, backends, model, scope, desc, stages, spanAll, resources); effort and persona are not counted because a save writes each only when it has a value. Only then do the header and the confirm hint say the save forks; otherwise the existing "Update this project's copy. Changes apply from the next run." line. **(h)** *A global profile's stored stage outside the default workflow is shown and removable* (F40-46). The org editor offered chips only for the default template's stages, so a stored `build` (akinozer.com's work stage) had no chip: Content Writer opened with nothing pressed, and every save kept the id. The row printed the bare id. The row now reads "build (not in the default workflow)" (`storedStageLabel`, `resource-helpers.ts`), and the editor adds a pressed chip for each stored id it does not offer, with that note, which toggles off and back on until the save. Tests: `agents-page.test.tsx` "ruling 479" (a) to (g) and the updated LiveRoster and ruling-156 cases, `resource-catalog.server.test.ts` (b), `template-propagation.server.test.ts` (c), `agents-route.server.test.ts` "sync-profile-resources" (d, both clauses), `agents-query.server.test.ts` "ruling 479(g)", `org-settings-page.test.tsx` "ruling 479(h)"; each red by canary. `app.css.test.ts` counts the matrix's `<summary>` among the app's disclosures.

480. **Instance settings and the GitHub credential say what is true** (owner, 2026-09-25, pass 40, F40-43, F40-44, F40-45, F40-47: the owner asked for every finding fixed). **(a) A fine-grained token is proven per repository, and a narrower question never unproves it (F40-43).** Live, akinozer.com's card read "repo unproven (verified on first use)" after three pushes, two pull requests and a merge through its token, and Instance settings read "repo unproven. Verified when attached to a project" beside a reach listing the repository as writable. Attach did prove `repo` (the `permissions` block of `GET /repos/{r}`, `proveAttachedCredential`), but the proof lived only in `github_pats.validation_json`, the token's NEWEST validator run: the connection's Re-check and the 24-hour re-proof ask about no repository, so they overwrote it with `assumed`, and `markWriteScopeProven` upgraded only `pull_request:write`, so no push or merge ever made the card's promise true. Decided: `github_pats.repo_scopes_json` (new column, healed onto older roots by `BASELINE_COLUMNS`) holds, per repository, the last verdict each repository-scoped scope (`REPO_SCOPED_SCOPES`: `repo`, `pull_request:write`) received there, always `probe` with its time and a note (`RepoScopeProof`, `parseRepoScopeProofs`). `recordPatValidation` folds each run into it (`repoScopesAfter`): a run that probed a repository records its probe verdicts there, a refusal as much as a grant; a run that could not see the repository (`repo_not_found`, `org_approval_missing`) ends that repository's proof; `revoked` or `expired` ends every proof; a run that asked about no repository, or never reached GitHub, changes nothing. A write Viberr made proves what it needed, on the repository it went to (`markWriteScopeProven(db, patId, repo, write)`, still on the PAT that made the call, F28-U2b): a branch created (`branch-sync`, and the bootstrap's ref) or pushed (`push-workspace`) or the initial commit (`repo-bootstrap`) proves `repo`; a pull request opened proves `pull_request:write`; a merge proves both. It no longer edits the token's validation. A replaced token starts with no proof (`replacePatToken`). The project card's chip for a repository-scoped scope reads the proof of the PROJECT's repository (names compared without case); a classic token's `header` verdict still answers for every repository, and a verdict the token earned on another repository, or on none, reads `assumed`. A row cached before the column existed still proves the repository its validation probed (`repoScopeProofsOf`), and every write folds that in, so an upgrade loses nothing. The connection card keeps token-wide chips token-wide: a repository's probe in the token's newest validation reads `assumed` there ("proven per repository, not for the token as a whole") and appears instead as a line per repository ("akin-ozer/website: repo, pull_request:write proven", `ConnectionRecord.repoProofs`, omitting what a classic header already proved). Its unproven line now says "… unproven for the token as a whole: each repository proves them", and, while no repository has, how one will. The Update-token modal no longer promises "write dry-runs" (they run only under `VIBERR_GITHUB_WRITE_PROBE`, off by default): a fine-grained PAT is proven when a project attaches it and by the first branch, push or pull request Viberr makes there. The finding's other suggestion, reading the reach's `canPush` as proof, is not adopted: attach already reads the same permission block for the project's repository, and a real write is stronger evidence than a listing. **(b) The Agent resources tab hydrates (F40-44).** Its rows built "re-scanned …", "checked …" and "updated …" as strings with `formatRelative`, which reads now and the host zone ("yesterday" is a local-day fact), so the server's UTC render and the viewer's hydration disagreed around either midnight and on any minute rollover between them: React #418 and the whole tab painted twice. They render through `LocalRelative` (`RelativeStamp`, `UpdatedStamp` in `resource-rows.tsx`; `rel` and `updatedLabel` are gone), so the first pass depends on the row alone, per the hydration contract in `docs/ui/surfaces.md`. Two more clock reads on the same rows wait for hydration too (`useHydrated`): the MCP row's stale mark ("· stale, retest", amber) and a signed-in OAuth token's "expires in 52 minutes" (the first pass says "signed in (renews itself)"). The store browser's footer takes a node for the same stamps. **(c) "Rotate credential" is "Re-attach connection" (F40-45).** It never rotated anything: it binds the connection matching the repository's owner (or the default) again and re-checks it, so on a one-connection instance the token that runs afterwards is the one before, and someone reacting to a leaked token was told "Credential rotated … Sync uses it now". `runSetCredential` now answers `reattached` ("Re-attached akin-ozer's connection and re-checked it. The token is unchanged: replace it with Update token in Instance settings, under GitHub connections") when the bound PAT did not change and `switched` ("Switched to …'s connection. Sync uses its token now") when it did; `attached` is unchanged and nothing says "rotated". The manage row says where a token IS replaced: an instance admin gets **Replace token**, a link to `/org/settings?tab=connections&update=<connection id>` (the health's new optional `connectionId`, absent when no connection holds the token and withheld with the rest of the credential detail from readers without `grant-github-scope`), and the Connections tab opens that connection's Update token from the parameter; everyone else, who cannot open Instance settings, reads "Re-attaching never replaces a token.
