An instance admin replaces it in Instance settings, under GitHub connections." **(d) The controller's grant request says when it was asked, in the viewer's time (F40-47).** "Asked 2026-09-24T20:25:54.327Z by …" printed the stored UTC ISO string; it renders through `LocalDayDotTime` like the audit rows on the same page. Budgets (ruling 457): nothing measured moves. Every bundle `measure-routes.mjs --check` measures is unchanged, and `connectionId` is a key only a bound, connection-held token carries, so the settings revalidation payload stays within 4,261 bytes (always present, even as `null`, it measured 4,281). Tests (each red by canary against its fix): `pat-store.server.test.ts` "ruling 480" (a repo-less Re-check keeps the project's proof; a push, branch and merge prove their repository and no other, names compared without case; a refusal is recorded and a newer write replaces it; replaced, `repo_not_found` and revoked end proof; a pre-column row still proves and survives a Re-check; a classic header answers everywhere; the connection id) and the F27-U2/F28-U2b cases rewritten to the per-repository record; `connections.server.test.ts` "ruling 480" (the live sequence: attach probe, then the connection's Re-check through `recheckConnection`, the project chip still `probe`, the connection card's token-wide `assumed` and its repository line; a classic token has no repository line); `push-workspace.server.test.ts` (an accepted push proves `repo`, a refused one nothing); `github-reconciler.server.test.ts` F28-U2a (a merge proves both from a repo-less state); `sqlite.server.test.ts` (the column heals onto an older root); `github-actions.server.test.ts` "ruling 480" (re-attached and switched); `github-view.test.tsx` "ruling 480" (the link for an instance admin, the sentence for others, neither when unbound); `org-settings-page.test.tsx` "ruling 480" (repository lines; `?update=` opens that connection's modal and an unknown id opens none; the modal names no dry-run); `resources-hydration.test.tsx` (the Agent resources tab rendered in UTC at 23:59:59Z and hydrated in Pacific/Auckland at 00:00:01Z, the task page's pair, with no recoverable error and a server markup free of clock text); `controller-admin-panel.test.tsx` "ruling 480".

481. **Notifications reach a tab nobody is looking at, an agent's question is filed as a question, Profile's Disconnects ask first, and a usage reading ages** (owner, 2026-09-25, pass 40, F40-48, F40-49, F40-50, F40-51: the owner asked for every finding fixed; spec `planning/discovery-2026-09-24-pass40-akinozer-site/FINDINGS-481.md`). Notifications stay in-app (`docs/product/overview.md`: no mailer, no push service, no webhook); the per-user outbound webhook F40-51 left to the owner is not built. Decided: **(a)** *An agent's question is a `question` (F40-48).* Both question doors wrote the owner's notice as kind `approval` (`openAgentQuestionPacket` in `agent-toolkit.server.ts`, the Claude `ask_human`; the Codex outcome envelope in `task-actions.server.ts`), so the owner's "Waiting on you" row wore the stage arrow and the "approval" pill beside operator packets pilled as decisions, and "Approval requests" off, described as "Operator transition requests at boundaries you can approve", silenced every agent question: `createNotification` never wrote the row. `question` is now a `NOTIFICATION_KINDS` member (and the baseline's CHECK), with its own category `questions` ("Agent questions", default on), the `hand` glyph on the `act-policy` palette and an "agent question" input pill (the task page's "Agent question"). The decision kinds are one list, `DECISION_NOTIFICATION_KINDS` (packet, question, approval): "Waiting on you" (`listNotifications`, and the page's split now trusts its `waitingOnYou`), the live reconciliation (a question waits while the task carries a packet), `markTaskPacketApprovalRead`'s default (resolving the packet clears the question row) and (c)'s count read it. Every toggle's description names what its writers send: packets are the operator's (a blocked task, a question about scope, a completion report), approvals are the operator's recommendations and a delivery's recorded next step. A deployed root's CHECK predates the kind, and a refused INSERT would have thrown inside the question door, so boot widens a lagging `notifications.kind` CHECK in place before anything writes (`widenNotificationKindCheck`, `boot.server.ts`): the app-owned table is rebuilt from the shipped baseline's own DDL (read from an in-memory migration), rows copied, indexes recreated, in one transaction; a failure is logged and the drift WARN still names the remedy. Tests: `notification-prefs.test.ts` "each toggle names what its writers send" (writer, kind, the words its toggle must use), `agent-toolkit.server.test.ts` "files an agent's question as a `question`…", `agent-completion.server.test.ts` F37-64 (the Codex door's kind), `notifications-page.test.tsx` "the agent question row", `notifications.server.test.ts` "clears an agent question with the packet", `boot.server.test.ts` "widenNotificationKindCheck"; each red by canary. **(b)** *Profile's two Disconnects ask first (F40-49).* The Agent accounts card's Disconnect ran the vendor's logout and deleted the credential on one tap, and the GitHub identity Disconnect likewise, while every other one-way control confirms (ruling 458(f)). Both now open the shared `ConfirmDialog` (danger tone): "Disconnect Claude?" (or Codex), "Viberr signs this server out of your Claude account and deletes the stored credential. Tasks you own and your controller conversations can't start a Claude run until you connect again.", confirmed by "Disconnect Claude" (screen label `Disconnect agent account dialog`); and "Disconnect GitHub?", naming the audit attribution that falls back to the workspace identity, confirmed by "Disconnect GitHub" (`Disconnect GitHub dialog`). The spec's "runs in flight keep going" is not claimed: a vendor logout may revoke the token a running CLI holds, and nothing here verified otherwise. Tests: `agent-accounts-panel.test.tsx` "connected: … offers Disconnect", `profile-page.test.tsx` "GitHub identity: … behind a confirm"; each red by canary. **(c)** *A tab that is not in front of the person still says a decision waits (F40-51).* A notification was a row and an SSE event, and the one signal outside the page was the bell inside it; on this pass WEB-3's owner-only packet and the five goal links behind it reached the owner through a driver's chat message. `AttentionWatcher` (`features/notifications/attention-watcher.tsx`), mounted once by `root.tsx` for a signed-in tab (a csrf token in root's data, as for the dock), reads `GET /resources/attention` (`attentionSnapshot`: the count of the viewer's unread decision rows that lead somewhere, under the bell's orphan rule, and the newest ten worded for a desktop notification with the bell's own destination; 401 when signed out; no-store). It prefixes the page's title with the count ("(1) WEB-3 · … · Viberr", "99+" past 99; kept through the page's own retitling by a `MutationObserver` on `<head>`, taken off at zero or on unmount). It reads on mount, on a `notification.created` or `notification.read` the tab's live stream hands it (`useLiveUpdates` now passes data events to `onLiveFrame` too, once per id, after the ledger has them), when the tab gains or loses attention, and every 60 s while it is not visible and focused: a hidden tab holds no stream (ruling 301), and a short read holds no connection. **Desktop notifications** on Profile is a per-browser opt-in (the permission it rests on is the browser's, so it lives in that browser's storage, not `user_prefs`): the switch is the ONLY place `Notification.requestPermission()` is called, it turns on once the browser allowed it and showed one notification (a platform that refuses to construct one, such as Android Chrome without a service worker, reads as unsupported), and a denial leaves it off with the site-settings sentence on the row. Opted in, a decision new to every tab of the browser shows a system notification (tag = the row id) while the tab is not attended; a tab's first reading only records what was already waiting, and ids any tab saw, attended or announced, are shared in `localStorage` so no second tab announces them. A click focuses the tab, marks the row read through `/notifications/read` and navigates where the bell would. A tab that polls re-authenticates like any request, so an open tab keeps a rolling session alive. The watcher is its own chunk, which `root.tsx` fetches once the page has hydrated (`React.lazy`), so it rides no route's closure; what the Profile row and the confirms add is measured, and the ceilings are the integrator's. Tests: `root-attention.test.tsx` (root mounts it for a signed-in tab only), `attention-watcher.test.tsx` (the title count through a retitle; a hidden tab's poll announcing a new decision once, the click marking it read and opening it; an attended tab announcing nothing, and no other tab announcing what it saw; no opt-in, no announcement), `profile-page.test.tsx` "the Desktop notifications switch" (permission only on the press; a denial stays off), `notifications.server.test.ts` "attentionSnapshot…", `resources.attention.test.ts`, `use-live-updates.test.tsx` "hands a data event to a frame listener once"; each red by canary. **(d)** *A usage reading ages against its own reset (F40-50).* `latestBackendRateLimits` retired an exhaustion once its `resetsAt` passed and returned a reading untouched, so on an idle instance Profile said "The window resets 03:30" and Insights drew "92% of five hour · resets 03:30" hours after 03:30. The same instant now marks a reading whose window has reset (`readingWindowReset` on the row, the provider's own epoch, no grace), the one home both surfaces read: Profile's pill reads "<window> window reset" (neutral, no percentage) and its note "That window reset <time>, and no Claude run has reported a reading since."; Insights keeps the row with no bar, "<window> · window reset, no reading since", "reset <time>", and drops the old window's warning and overage words. The reading itself is kept as history. Tests: `insights-query.server.test.ts` "marks a reading whose window reset before generatedAt", `profile-route.server.test.ts` "ruling 481: the viewer's reading whose window already reset…", `agent-accounts-panel.test.tsx` "words a reading whose window has reset in the past tense…", `insights-page.test.tsx` "a reading whose window has reset draws no bar…"; each red by canary.

482. **Viberr runs the project's gates itself, on the revision a person accepts, and a failing gate blocks a plain acceptance** (owner, 2026-09-25, pass 40, F40-52: the owner asked for every finding fixed). Measured live 2026-09-24 on akinozer-com: the rulings KB said "Gate commands: not yet settled … the only gate is `pnpm build`", WEB-1's measured set (install, astro check, build, wrangler dry-run) sat unpromoted under "Proposed (not binding)", every directive restated the gates in prose (WEB-4's rework: "re-run the gates from link 1 on the new revision"; WEB-6: "Report each exit code honestly"), and the results came back as agents' sentences ("4 exit 0 · 0 failed"), the deliverer, the Site Reviewer and the Fact Checker each running the same four by hand. The owner accepted PR #1 and PR #2, both production deploys, on those reports, and a skipped or misreported gate could not be told from a real one. `project-file.schema.ts` had no gates field and nothing under `app/server` ran a project-declared command on a checkout; the two validation capabilities are advisory persona guidance and stay so. Decided, all F40-52: **(a)** *Declared in project.md.* `gates: [{name, command, timeoutSeconds?}]` (per row, like every list; absent, never `[]`, on a project that declares none; at most 10; a name one line of at most 40 characters and unique ignoring case; a command at most 2,000 characters; `timeoutSeconds` 1..3600, 600 when absent). Written only by `setProjectGates` (`settings-actions.server.ts`, `edit-policy`, audited `project.gates.updated`, an unchanged list writes nothing), which Settings → Gates (`set-project-gates`) and the controller's new `set_project_gates` both call; `get_project` lists them. The controller guide now sends a measured gate set there instead of into the rulings KB as prose (its old text is in `PRIOR_SHIPPED_HASHES`). The `projects` row carries the list as `gates_json` (baseline and `BASELINE_COLUMNS`), and it is part of the task-context digest, so an edit re-projects every task's acceptance block. **(b)** *When a run is asked for.* A delivery's `delivered` outcome (`performDelivery`); a workspace reconcile that mints a new revision while the task's pull request stands; the reconciler's external revision (ruling 179); a changed gate list (every open task with a delivered revision, so a promoted set is evidence on the tasks already in review); a person's "Run gates" on the GitHub card (`run-gates`, maintainer+ or the owner like a manual delivery, audited `task.gates.requested`); and boot, for a record a restart left `queued` or `running`. The request writes `gateRun: queued` on the task and enqueues, nothing more: one worker runs one task's gates at a time, instance-wide, off every request path. A revision whose run is queued or running in this process, or finished under the declared list, is not run twice; a person's request re-runs a finished one. **(c)** *Where and as whom.* A fresh clone of the delivering checkout (`clone --no-local`, pass 40 review R-seams-2) into `workspace/.gates/<runId>/`, made by the task owner through the ruling-460 launcher (R-seams-1), origin's heads fetched from the mirror when the revision is not in it (an external head), detached at the revision's sha, removed afterwards (as the person first). Each command runs with `sh -c` in order, as the owner's agent uid, with `filteredSpawnEnv()` and the agent's own `$HOME`, in its own process group, stopped at its timeout (SIGTERM, then the group killed 5 s later) and swept by its `VIBERR_RUN_ID` marker. With no launcher (the host dev server, the tests) it runs as the server's own user, the way workspace git does; with isolation on and no owner the run records an error and runs nothing as the server (460(h)). Every gate runs whatever an earlier one returned, so each is its own evidence. **(d)** *What is recorded.* `task.md` `gateRun: {id, revisionId, headSha, status: queued|running|finished|error, reason, requestedAt, startedAt, finishedAt, error, results[]}`, the latest run only, bound to the revision id and sha like a verdict; each result `{name, command, exitCode, timedOut, wallMs, log}` lands as the gate finishes (`exitCode` null when killed at the timeout or never started; a signal reads as 128 + n). The combined output is saved as the task attachment `gate-<sha7>-<NN>-<name>-<stamp>.log` (head 256 KB and tail kept, the middle cut, a header naming the command, the uid and the start, a footer the result), never counted as a file a concurrent run produced (`isGateLogName` in `attachmentNamesSince`). The finished run writes one note from "Project gates" that claims its logs, and audit `task.gates.run` (passed, total, failed, who it ran as). A malformed record reads as absent, which blocks (fail closed); the next run rewrites it. **(e)** *What every surface says.* One pure reading, `projectGatesView` (`app/shared/project-gates.ts`), prints "Gates on `<sha7>`: N/M exit 0 (run by Viberr)" on the PR card (a gates pill in the bar and a Gates row with each gate's outcome, time and log link), in the accept dialog's Gates row, in the operator's snapshot (`gates`) and the controller's `get_task`, and in every agent's canonical anchor, which tells the agent the record is the result and never to re-run the gates to report them. **(f)** *It blocks a plain acceptance.* `projectGatesRefusal`, after the verdict gate in `acceptanceRefusalReasons` and in the projection's `acceptanceBlockReason`: missing, queued or running, stale (the list changed after the run), failed and could-not-run evidence each refuse with its own sentence. A person merging a production deploy is shown a fact about the sha or a refusal, never the absence of a fact. Force accept still bypasses it, and the forced record names it among the bypassed gates. A `verified` (no-change) revision and a files-only delivery have no checkout to gate and owe nothing; a base refresh that keeps the revision (ruling 439) keeps its gate record, as it keeps its verdicts. **(g)** *A failure is the operator's.* A finished run with a gate that did not exit 0 re-invokes the operator with the new `gates-failed` trigger, whose turn names each failing gate, its command and its log, and has it `run_agent` the deliverer with them and deliver the fix; every ordinary turn carries a gate rule while gates are declared (never offer or perform `accept_completion` while `gates.state` is not `passed`, never ask an agent to report the gates). The suggested SDK Stop hook for deliverer runs is not taken: the server's run is what binds a result to the sha, and a second copy of the gates inside the agent's session would be one more claim, not a fact. Tests: `app/server/tasks/project-gates.server.test.ts` (real git and `sh`: the revision's sha checked out, not the checkout's later HEAD; each exit code, log and note; no server secret in a gate's environment; the timeout; a run that could not execute; idempotence and a person's re-run with its tier; nothing owed without gates or a revision; the boot requeue; a gate log not credited to a run; the acceptance block, the projected block, the operator snapshot and force accept's record; the `gates-failed` hand-off; a changed list queuing the open task; the workspace reconcile's and the delivery's requests; a stand-in launcher proving the clone, each gate and the clean-up run as the owner's uid with no secret, and a task with no owner refused), `app/shared/project-gates.test.ts`, `github-reconciler.server.test.ts` (the external head is gated), `canonical-anchor.server.test.ts`, `operator-gates-prompt.server.test.ts`, `controller-toolkit.server.test.ts` (`set_project_gates`), `settings-route.server.test.ts` (`set-project-gates`), `project-file.schema.test.ts`, `task-file.server.test.ts` (the record round-trips; a malformed one reads absent), `task-detail-components.test.tsx` (the PR card), `accept-confirm.test.tsx` (the Gates row) and `settings-page.test.tsx` (the panel). Each was canaried. *(Narrowed 2026-09-25 by ruling 491: "gates passed" and "N checks passing" are green fills, not outlines — the owner read the outline as dry.)* *(Narrowed 2026-09-26 by ruling 493: each gate's outcome, time and log is a row of the one gate table, on the PR card, in the accept dialog and on the run's timeline note, which is drawn from its rows.)* *(Narrowed 2026-09-26 by ruling 511: on the PR card the gates are one status row, their pill's words its title and their line under it, and a pass folds the table behind "Show all".)*

483. **Any agent on a task proposes a correction to a knowledge base it was given, and the proposal comes back to the people who can promote it** (owner, 2026-09-25, pass 40, F40-53 and F40-59: the owner asked for every finding fixed; generalizes ruling 378, keeps its "an agent proposes, a person promotes"). Measured live on the akinozer-com board: at 22:21Z on WEB-1 the Site Engineer found the generated `wrangler.json` differs from akin-dossier T-013 and wrangler at 4.139.0 where T-003 says 4.138.0; at 23:11:31Z on WEB-3 the Platform Engineer re-derived both, wrote "The knowledge-base runbook is read-only to me, so I carried it into the repo", listed T-055 and T-013 under "Discrepancies to reconcile" and noted the runbook's Step 1 is behind `docs/deploy-runbook.md`; at 23:11:51Z the operator answered "Some sources need reconciling, and I'm not changing them myself"; at 00:33Z `akin-dossier/06-platform-facts.md` and `akinozer-deploy-runbook/runbook.md` still held the old facts while directives kept sending agents to those lines. Ruling 378's `propose_ruling` reached the project's rulings KB only. On WEB-1 the operator's two rulings proposals (strike go 1.25.1; replace "Gate commands: not yet settled" with the measured gate set) each rendered "Operator · Review verdict · Ruling contradicted by evidence", the second directly above a real "Review passed", with no link and no control; nothing brought them back, they were never promoted, and at 23:08 UTC the WEB-3 packet asked the owner to type that build command into Cloudflare, noting the rulings "still list [it] under 'Proposed (not binding)'". Decided: **(a)** *The channel (F40-53).* `propose_ruling` becomes `propose_kb_correction {kb?, doc, line?, correction, evidence}` (`app/server/tasks/kb-proposal-actions.server.ts`, `proposeKbCorrection`, one implementation for every filer). The operator may propose against any knowledge base a run on the task was given: its own grants, the project's rulings, and every engaged agent's (`kbsGivenToTaskRuns`); `kb` omitted keeps ruling 378's default, the rulings. On Codex the plan action carries `<kb>/<doc>` in `kbSource` (a bare document is the rulings'; `splitKbSource` reads the first segment as a knowledge base only when the store has one by that name), the line in `reason`, the correction in `text` and the evidence in `repoSource`. A Claude specialist gets the same tool on `viberr_agent`, gated like `read_knowledge_doc` on its knowledge-base grant and mounted after `read_board` so a knowledge base alone widens nothing on U11's gate, against its own knowledge bases only. The suggested fix offered `report_outcome`; a tool was chosen instead because `report_outcome` is built only for a verdict or evidence grant, and a correction is owed by any agent that reads a knowledge base. A Codex specialist mounts no Viberr tools, so its Collaboration note (`KB_CORRECTION_NOTE_CODEX`) asks it to end its report with a `Knowledge-base correction` section, and the operator's `agent-reply` instruction relays any knowledge-base line a report proved wrong that has no proposal on the timeline; the operator skill (`viberr-app-expertise`, outgoing hash recorded) and the tool description say the same. The entry is filed at the end of the document's `## Proposed corrections (not binding)` section (`fileKbProposal`, `app/server/org/kb-proposals.server.ts`; format in `file-formats.md` §7): created at the end of the document with an intro the first time, ruling 378's `## Proposed (not binding)` read as the same section and renamed on the next filing, the stamp `[<task>, <day>, <filer>]`, then `Line:` and `Evidence:`. The quoted line must stand in the settled text (the document without the section, compared loosely), or nothing is written; a document the knowledge base does not hold is refused, never created; the same open correction of the same line is a `noop`; the write goes through `writeStoreDoc` under a per-document lock, built by slicing so `$$` and `$&` stay literal. The document is the record: nothing else lists proposals, so a person who deletes an entry in the editor has closed it, and the index every run is handed names the section. Audit `task.kb_proposal.filed` {id, kb, doc, rulings, bytes (UTF-8, ruling 466), actorRef} under the filer (the operator, or the agent itself). **(b)** *The label, the link, the count and the door (F40-59).* A proposal is a timeline event of a new type, `proposal` (twelve types now), pilled "Proposal" in the info tone with the edit glyph, titled "Proposed ruling change" in the project's rulings and "Proposed knowledge-base correction" elsewhere; its text names the id and the document, and on the task page it links "Open proposals" to `/projects/<slug>/controller#kb-proposals` (a string prop, never a router hook, which re-rendered every memoised row on a send, ruling 457 CS-3). Its notification keeps the `quality` kind under the neutral title: a new kind needs a baseline CHECK and a new preference row, and the title is what the bell reads. The controller learns of it without being asked: a board or task turn's context read lists the project's open proposals (up to 10, by id, with the document, task, filer, line and correction) and says to tell the person they wait; an instance turn counts them per visible project; `get_project` carries `openProposals`. `resolve_kb_proposal {id, action, replaces?, text?, reason}` closes one (org admin, because it edits an org knowledge base; and only when a person asks): `promote` writes `text` into the settled text in place of `replaces`, which must stand there once outside the section, or appends it, and removes the entry in the same write; `dismiss` removes the entry only; the last entry takes the heading with it; audit `org.kb.proposal_promoted` / `org.kb.proposal_dismissed` with the reason. The project Controller page's rail gains the Proposals panel between the conversations and the goal chains: a count, each open proposal with its kind, document, line, correction, evidence, task link, filer, day and id, and for an org admin Promote, Dismiss (confirmed first) and "Open document" (`/org/settings?tab=resources&kb=<dir>&doc=<path>`, which now opens that knowledge base's browser on the document). Promote and Dismiss write nothing: each sends the request to the controller in the open conversation, which carries it out, so promotion stays a person's decision walked by the controller as the pass-39 model has it and ruling 390 is not reopened. The controller guide says all of this (outgoing hash recorded). Not coupled to project gates (ruling 482). Budgets (ruling 457), measured and NOT raised here (the integrator sets the ceilings): gzip closures `root` +165 B (the new `proposal` type in the schema every route bundles, and root.css +156 B for the timeline node, the activity tint and the panel's rules), `routes/login` +168, `routes/_index` +160, `routes/project.board` +154, `routes/profile` +161, `routes/project.task` +290 (plus the link), `routes/controller` +1,127 (the panel lives in the controller page module both controller routes share); unbudgeted, `routes/project.controller` +1,127 and `routes/org.settings` +308. Tests: `kb-proposals.server.test.ts` (the section created, filed in order, read back whole; ruling 378's section read and renamed; a fenced heading ignored; a missing document refused naming what the base holds; a line only the section quotes refused; a nested document; the project filter; promote, an ambiguous passage refused, dismiss), `operator-actions.server.test.ts` "rulings 378 and 483" (the rulings default with the `proposal` event, neutral title, audit and notification; a knowledge base only an engaged agent holds; a base no run holds and an unanchored line refused; UTF-8 bytes; stacking, `$` and the duplicate; no rulings KB and a mistyped document; the missing fields and the denied capability), `agent-toolkit.server.test.ts` "ruling 483" (the specialist files against its own base as itself, and is refused another), `operator-run.server.test.ts` "ruling 483" (the relay sentence; a Codex plan's `<kb>/<doc>`), `specialist-run.server.test.ts` "ruling 483" (each backend's note), `controller-context.server.test.ts`, `controller-toolkit.server.test.ts`, `controller-query.server.test.ts` and `controller-page.test.tsx` "ruling 483", `task-detail-components.test.tsx` (the twelve types; the link), `org-settings-page.test.tsx` "ruling 483" (the deep link), `default-assets.server.test.ts` "ruling 483" (the outgoing hashes). Each red by canary against its source, restored byte for byte. *(2026-09-26, ruling 497: the proposal's notification opens its entry on the Controller page, `#proposal-<id>`, which the page marks, instead of the task it came from; the kind and the title stay.)* *(Reversed in part 2026-09-26 by ruling 498, owner: "No human can approve all of these while inspecting them thoroughly". (a)'s reach, refusals and relay stand, but `propose_kb_correction` became `correct_knowledge_doc`, which writes the correction into the settled text in place of the exact passage, and nothing files a proposal; (b)'s proposal event, its notification and the Proposals panel's queue gave way to a short `kb_correction` event, no notification, and the Knowledge base panel listing the corrections with Undo. The proposals documents still hold keep this ruling's reader, context lines, `openProposals`, `resolve_kb_proposal`, Promote and Dismiss, plus Promote all.)* *(Narrowed 2026-09-26 by ruling 503: the goal chains the Proposals panel sat above are gone; it follows the conversations.)*

484. **A person reads the delivered changes on the task, and review notes reach the agent that delivered them** (owner, 2026-09-25, pass 40, F40-54: the owner asked for every finding fixed). WEB-6's directive and goal 1 link 7 both said "Akin approves each note individually in review", and the task page gave a person `Diff N files · +a −d` and the commit subjects: no file list, no patch (`readPullRequestDiff`, ruling 266, had one consumer, the controller). So the review had to happen on GitHub, where a CHANGES_REQUESTED review became a pill state and nothing read a line comment at all (`deriveReviewState` reduced the reviews to a state; no server code read `pulls/{n}/comments` or a review body). Rejecting one note there never reached the Content Writer; retyping each objection as a task comment naming its file and line was the only door. Decided: **(a)** *The Changes panel (F40-54).* The task page shows a Changes panel while the review PR is open (`pr.state: review`) and a revision is delivered (`task-detail-page.tsx`, `changes-slot.tsx`). It ships as a heading, one sentence and a Show changes button; the reader (`changes-panel.tsx`) is its own chunk, fetched when the button is reached or pressed, and the files are read only when it opens, from a resource route, `GET /projects/:slug/tasks/:key/changes` (`task-changes.ts` → `readTaskChanges`, `app/server/github/task-changes.server.ts`): membership as the task page (`requireVisibleProject`, the unknown-slug 404), a 401 rather than a login redirect because a fetcher loads it, `shouldRevalidate` false, and a `clientLoader` that turns any failed load into the panel's own failure row. The read is `readPullRequestDiff` BOUND to the delivered revision: its new `headSha` option reads the PR's live head first (one extra GET) and answers `liveHeadSha` and no files when the PR is elsewhere, so the panel says why (the revision is not pushed yet, "Push it from the GitHub panel"; or the PR moved past it, "The next status check records the new head as the revision under review") instead of drawing commits nobody delivered under a heading that says they were. 200,000 encoded patch characters per read (the controller keeps its 40,000); a file past that is listed with its counts and a Load this file button that reads it alone by `?path=`, at 1,000,000. Each file is a `<details>` (status, path, +/−, the set's chevron; the first five open) of its hunks, drawn by `diffRows` (`app/shared/diff-rows.ts`) on a three-column grid: the line's number (the new file's for an added or context line, the old file's for a removed one), the mark, the code, which wraps so a phone reads a long line without the page scrolling sideways. Code is the mono face, unhighlighted: the attachment reader's Shiki pass (ruling 363) tokenizes a whole file by its grammar, and a hunk is a window onto one, so it would colour wrongly as often as not. A file GitHub sends no patch for says so ("a binary file, or one too large for GitHub to diff"). The read writes no audit row: it is a member reading their own project's pull request, as the GitHub page is. **(b)** *Line notes are one comment to the deliverer (F40-54).* A line's number is the button that opens a note under it (Escape cancels, focus returns to the number; one note per line, pressing again edits it); unsent notes survive hiding the panel. Send to @<deliverer> posts every note at once through the task route's new `review-notes` intent with the `headSha` the person read. `review-notes.server.ts` validates the notes (1 to 50, each a path, a line, a side, 1 to 4,000 characters), refuses when the delivered revision has moved since the read, when nothing is delivered on a PR, or when no DEPLOYED agent delivers the task (the mention resolver would route the handle to nobody), each with the sentence a person acts on; the notes stay in the panel. The comment is `reviewNotesDirective`: `@<handle> Review notes on \`<sha7>\` (PR #N):`, then one list item per note, `` `path:line` `` (`path:start-end` for a range, "(removed line)" for an old-file line, a bare path for a whole file). The handle is `agentMentionHandle` of the delivering engagement's deployed profile, the one derivation every writer uses (P14-RT-12). It goes through `commentToAgent`, the comment door, so the deliverer resumes on it as it would on the same words typed in the composer, under the same role gate, and the toast is the comment's (`commentToast`, now shared by both intents: "2 notes sent · @Content Writer is picking it up", "… · your role can't trigger agent runs"). Every other `@` in a note is backslash-escaped (markdown renders it as the `@` it was, and the mention grammar reads no mention after a backslash), so the comment has ONE addressee: the resolver routes `@operator` ahead of any agent, and a GitHub body's `@login` names a GitHub account, not a Viberr person. Only the reference is quoted, not the line's content: code carries `@` too, and the agent has the checkout. **(c)** *The reconciler relays GitHub reviews the same way (F40-54).* `findPrForBranch` keeps each submitted review's id and body off the SAME `/reviews` payload the pill reads (`reviewEventsOf`: never a PENDING draft). After its own write, inside the task's reconcile lock, `reconcileTask` calls `relayPrReviews` (`pr-review-relay.server.ts`) for an open PR the task owns. A review is relayed when it is APPROVED, CHANGES_REQUESTED or COMMENTED (a DISMISSED one was withdrawn first), was submitted on the delivered revision's head, is by a project member (the login mapped through `users.github_handle` by R19-B's `resolveGithubHandle`, failing closed on an unlinked or ambiguous handle, a non-member, a disabled account), and is not yet recorded. Only such a review has its line comments listed (`GET …/pulls/{n}/reviews/{id}/comments`, up to three pages), so a quiet pass costs no call. Per reviewer, ONE comment through `commentToAgent`, authored by that member with the audit label `<email> · via GitHub`: the same directive with ", from GitHub (a review by <login>)" in its first line, a CHANGES_REQUESTED body first ("Requested changes"), then each line comment at its line on the commit it was written on (`original_line`, a LEFT side as "removed line"); a comment carried in from another head is skipped; a relayed comment past 4,000 characters is cut and says the rest is on the pull request. Once each: the ids relayed (`review:<id>`, `comment:<id>`, dedupe by comment id as asked) are stamped on the loose `pr.reviewRelay.relayed` key (the `humanApproval` pattern; newest 500 kept) in the SAME locked write that appends the comment (`appendComment`/`commentToAgent` take a server-only `alsoWrite`), so a relay and its record cannot come apart; a review with nothing to relay (an approval with no comments) is stamped alone, then re-projected. The reconciler carries the record for the same PR after `humanApproval`, the order the stamp leaves them in, so a quiet pass writes nothing. A review whose comments GitHub would not list is left for the next pass; with no deployed deliverer nothing is relayed or recorded, so a deliverer engaged on the same head still receives it; a relay failure is logged and never fails the pass. The finding's softest part stands: the board card still shows "changes requested"; now its content reaches the agent too. Not changed: an APPROVED or COMMENTED review's body is not relayed (the brief named CHANGES_REQUESTED bodies; line comments of every relayed review are), nor are the PR's conversation comments (`issues/{n}/comments`), and the reviews list is still read one page of 100, as for the pill and R19-B. Budgets (ruling 457), measured and NOT raised here (the integrator sets them after merging): `bundle:root.css` +568 B gzip (the panel's rules; `app.css` is one stylesheet), so every route closure +568 B, and `routes/project.task` +1,193 B (the same 568 plus 625 for the panel's stub and the page's gate); the reader is a separate 8.8 KB chunk loaded on demand. No loader payload changed. Tests: `pr-diff.server.test.ts`, `task-changes.server.test.ts`, `review-notes.server.test.ts`, `pr-review-relay.server.test.ts` (the real reconciler over a fake GitHub: one @deliverer comment quoting file:line from GitHub with the audit label; non-member, other head, draft and unmapped reviews never listed; once each with no rewrite churn; an approval recorded alone and re-projected; nothing without a deliverer; an unlisted review retried; a maintainer's review resumes the deliverer's session on the fake runtime), `diff-rows.test.ts`, `routes/task-changes.server.test.ts` (401, 404 for a non-member and an unknown task, the reason for a member; the intent's comment, its toast, the stale and malformed refusals), `changes-panel.test.tsx` (closed and unread until opened; the numbers and their note buttons; one post bound to the revision, cleared, toasted; Escape; kept while hidden; a file loaded by path; no note on a stale revision or without a deliverer; the failure alert and its retry) and `task-disposition.test.tsx` "ruling 484" (the page's gate), each red by canary; `app.css.test.ts` counts the new `<summary>` and the four new GlyphSwaps.
*(Amended 2026-09-26 by ruling 509: a note may cover several lines of one hunk, picked by a mouse drag across the numbers or by a shift-click from the open note (Shift+Enter from the keyboard). A line still carries one note, so a range stops before a line that has its own, and pressing any line of a note opens it. The comment quotes such a note as `path:start-end`, "(removed lines)" for the old file's, or by both ends when it runs from a removed line to an added one; the relay reads a GitHub comment's `start_side` for the same reason. Still only the reference is quoted, never the lines.)*

485. **A tree an agent can write is removed as its person, and a local fault is never blamed on a credential** (owner, 2026-09-25, pass 40, F40-62, a residual of ruling 460 and of pass-40 review R-seams-1; spec `planning/discovery-2026-09-24-pass40-akinozer-site/SPEC-485-agent-trees-removed-as-their-person.md`). Measured live at 07:50 UTC on deploy 4 (`ac2e7934`): WEB-5's required Site Reviewer re-review started with no checkout and recorded no verdict. Its supporting checkout (`…/WEB-5/workspace/support/site-reviewer/website`, uid 20001, `viberr-agents`, 2770) held two wrangler `mkdtemp` directories at 0700 as the agent's uid. The next review's replace was the server's `rmSync(dir, {recursive: true, force: true})`: it removed what group permission allowed (`.git` among it), threw EACCES on the rest, and left a tree that no later clone could land in. The throw came before `credential = "not_involved"`, so the log read `credential: absent`, and the operator told the owner to attach a GitHub credential, which ruling 249 says is never the remedy for a local step. It was unblocked by hand at 07:55, by removing the directory as its uid. Decided: **(a)** *The removal* (`app/server/runtimes/agent-trees.server.ts`). `removeAgentTree(target, person)` runs `chmod -R u+rwX -- <tree>` (what a tool left read-only or unenterable becomes its owner's to remove) and then `rm -rf -- <tree>`. Both are absolute binaries on `filteredSpawnEnv()` with `LC_ALL=C`, run through the launcher as the person. The launch is the one `agentGitLaunchFor` makes, reduced to its uid and launcher, because a removal hands no home back. `removeAgentTreeSync` is the same plan, for a caller that must finish before it returns: a Codex run home's settle, boot's reclaim, a plugin at a run's settle, the seed. A `person` of null means the server's own user, and only a server with isolation `off` accepts it (the host dev server, the test harness). There the same two commands run directly, so a read-only directory no longer defeats the server either. With isolation on, a null person is refused with a `run_unavailable` AppError and nothing is removed; nothing falls back (460(h)). A tree still there afterwards is an `AgentTreeRemovalError` that names the path rm stopped at and its errno ("EACCES on …/dev-1wnDsF", read from rm's own refusal). The person is the task's owner for anything in a task's workspace (`taskWorkspaceLaunch`, split out of `taskWorkspaceGit`, which throws when isolation is on and the task has no owner), and the run's own launch (`RunSpec.agent`) for a Codex run home. **(b)** *A tree more than one uid wrote* (a task whose owner changed, so two people's agents wrote it). Chosen: remove as each uid found in the tree. After the person's pass, the server reads the owners it can see in what is left: every entry in a directory it may read (it is in the agents' group), and the owner of each directory it may not. It then runs the same pass as each of them, this time also opening their entries to the group (`u+rwX,g+rwX`), so a layer another uid wrote underneath becomes visible and removable in the next round. There are at most three rounds, and the scan stops at 200,000 entries. The scan is read-only and never follows a link, so a path an agent swaps mid-scan can only change who is asked to remove, and the kernel confines each of them to what its own uid may do. No launcher verb is added: the server can see the owners itself. Rejected: moving the tree aside to a reaped graveyard and cloning into a fresh path. That unblocks the clone but not the removal: the reaper meets the same tree, and until it succeeds the disk keeps every copy. **(c)** *Every agent-writable removal goes through it* (every `rmSync(`, `fs.rm(` and `rm -rf` under `app/server`, classified): the supporting checkout's replace, its unfinished clone and a fresh clone's unfinished tree (`specialist-run.server.ts`); a clone destination that stands in the way (`cloneWorkspaceRepo`'s new `person`, `repo-mirror.server.ts`); the gate checkout (`project-gates.server.ts`, whose rm-as-the-person-then-`rmSync`-as-the-server is gone); a finished task's `workspace/` (`workspace-retention.server.ts`); the stripped `.claude`, the run's skill plugin beside the checkout and a half-copied skill in it (`skill-mount.server.ts`, with `SkillPlugin.person` carrying whom to remove it as to the settle); the operator's unfinished clone (`operator-run.server.ts`); a Codex run home and a predecessor's (`user-homes.server.ts`, through `RunHomePerson.remove` from the adapter and from boot recovery); and the seed's reset, which removes each task's `workspace/`, `attachments/` and `.operator-scratch/` (`TASK_SHARED_DIRS`, now exported) as its owner before the rest of `projects/`. Left as the server's, because no agent writes under them: the askpass temp dir, the mirror with its `.building` sidecar and stale siblings, the stages, knowledge bases, skills, agent profiles, store imports, atomic-write temp files, the database and its backups, the writer lock and the raw run logs. Single-file unlinks in an agent-writable directory also stay the server's, since they never descend: a vendor sign-in on disconnect, the server's own write-back lock, a session transcript past retention, an attachment. **(d)** *A local fault blames no credential.* The supporting arm sets `not_involved` before its first step, because a checkout cloned from the delivering one never reaches GitHub. Every local step, in either arm and in the operator's checkout, runs through `workspaceStep` (`git-clone-auth.server.ts`), and its failure becomes a `WorkspaceFault` naming what failed, the path and the OS error: "`…/website` could not be replaced: EACCES on …/dev-1wnDsF", a node:fs errno and its path, or git's exit for the local clone. `cloneFailureLogDetails` classifies it `reason: "workspace_fault"` with the `fault` (a removal's EACCES is not `clone_failed`, and a mkdir's ENOENT is not a missing git), and the catch sets `credential: not_involved`. `cloneFailureSentence` then says only "The workspace checkout could not be prepared on the Viberr server: <fault>. The fault is in the task's workspace on the server's disk; nothing here reached GitHub." The prompt's failure clause for it asks for no access of any kind (`PromptCloneFailure.workspaceFault`). So the timeline note, the sentence the agent is told to quote, and the operator's own view of a failed operator checkout never say "credential". The operator doctrine and the recovery packets had no clone-failure credential language to change, and ruling 248's no-checkout note already puts the failure on the server. **(e)** *The heal (defence in depth).* In `cloneRepo` and in `ensureOperatorRepoCheckout`, a checkout with no `.git/HEAD` (a clone killed mid-way, or a tree an older build half-removed) is removed as its person before anything reuses it, and then cloned again. The state F40-62 left therefore heals on the next run. Removing an unfinished clone after a failure is logged, and never thrown over the clone's own error. **(f)** `shareDirWithAgentsOrWarn` (`agent-isolation.server.ts`) is the gates' former private best-effort share, now in one place and used by the gates and both clone paths: a directory left unshared makes the person's own step in it fail in its own words. Tests (each red by canary, with the source restored byte for byte afterwards): `agent-trees.server.test.ts`. With a stand-in launcher, a checkout holding a directory the server cannot empty is removed through the launch, chmod then rm as the person's uid with absolute binaries, and the sync form does the same (canaries: the launch ignored; the chmod dropped). Isolation on with no person refuses and removes nothing (canary: the refusal dropped). With isolation off, the server removes it itself (canary: no chmod). A tree that cannot go names "EACCES on <path>", and rm's refusal is read in GNU and BSD form. `specialist-run.server.test.ts` "ruling 485" drives the real reviewer dispatch. With the stand-in launcher, a supporting checkout a tool left an unenterable directory in is replaced as the owner's uid and cloned by them; with isolation off, by the server. A checkout that cannot be replaced logs `credential: not_involved`, `reason: workspace_fault` and the fault, and neither the timeline note nor the prompt's failure lines say "credential" (canaries: `rmSync` back in the supporting arm; the pre-485 order, which logs `absent`; the sentence's arm; the prompt's flag). A delivering checkout with no `.git/HEAD` is removed and cloned again (canary: the heal skipped). `operator-run.server.test.ts` "ruling 485": the operator's checkout heals the same way before its clone, which then lands from the mirror (canary: the heal skipped, and the mirror's clone is refused the occupied path). The ruling-248/249 test now expects a failed local clone to be a workspace fault naming git's exit. `workspace-retention.server.test.ts` "ruling 485": a finished workspace goes through the launch as its owner, and an unowned one stays (canary: `rmSync` back). `git-clone-auth.server.test.ts` "ruling 485": a mkdir's ENOENT and a local clone's exit are classified as workspace faults, with no credential clause whatever the credential state (canary: the `WorkspaceFault` arm dropped). In the image, `scripts/check-agent-isolation.sh` gained three checks. The server's own `rm -rf` dies half-way on an agent's 0700 directory with `.git` gone (F40-62 reproduced). The server's replace (`removeAgentTree` itself, run with the image's `tsx`) removes that tree as its person and then as a second agent uid it found there. A fresh clone into the freed path has `.git/HEAD`. Run in a throwaway image (`viberr-app:r485`) on a throwaway named volume, 2026-09-25: every check held (38 of 38). With the fallback rounds set to 0 it failed naming "EACCES on …/by-another-owner"; with every step spawned as `node`, naming "EACCES on …/dev-1wnDsF". It narrows ruling 249 (dated note there) and closes the `.claude` half of 460(j)'s residual (dated note there). *Dated note 2026-09-26 (ruling 495, F40-71): completed by ruling 495.* What the server itself wrote in such a tree was beyond every pass: a run's skill plugin, whose `cpSync` copy kept the store folder's 0755, and a task's `workspace/` root, the server's own in a task directory only the server writes. The mount now leaves its plugin removable by the person, and when the agent passes leave entries the server opens its own to their group (`chmod -R -P g+rwX`) for the person to remove; when they leave an empty directory the server owns, the server removes it with `rmdir`. The server still never runs `rm` on a tree an agent can write.

486. **An OAuth-signed MCP connection says what its sign-in may do, and a refused write names the grant** (owner, 2026-09-25, pass 40, F40-63; spec `planning/discovery-2026-09-24-pass40-akinozer-site/SPEC-486-mcp-grant-visible.md`; builds on rulings 461 and 469, and amends what 469(a) asks for). Measured live at ~08:38 UTC: after the owner signed `cloudflare-api` in, the Settings row, the editor, `list_mcp_servers` and the run's prompt all said "signed in (expires in …, renews itself)". The grant itself (194 scopes, every one a read: `*.read`, `*.metadata_read`, `teams-connector-cloudflared.monitoring`, `teams.report`, no write) was kept only in the sealed half and the `org.mcp.oauth_connected` audit row. WEB-3's Platform Engineer sent the one approved Builds API write and got `Cloudflare API error: 10000: Authentication error`, and the owner was asked to choose between three remedies without seeing why. Decided: **(a)** *The grant is public.* `oauth_json` carries `scope`, the scope the token reply granted, space-joined as the server returned it. A reply that names none granted what was asked for (RFC 6749 §5.1 on the code exchange; §6 on a refresh, where it is the scope already held). A refresh reply that names one replaces it. A sign-out, a sign-in that expires or whose client is refused, and a "needs sign-in" challenge clear it. It is not a secret (the audit row always carried it), and `McpOAuthView.scope` reads it; a row written before this reads null. **(b)** *One classifier* (`app/shared/mcp-oauth.ts`, tested in `mcp-oauth.test.ts`). `isWriteScope`: a write is any scope whose action, after its last `.` or `:`, is not `read`, `metadata_read`, `monitoring` or `report`, and that is not `offline_access`. That covers `user:read` and `account:read` through their `:read`. The spec named only `.read` and `.metadata_read`, but the live grant it requires to read as read-only also carries `teams-connector-cloudflared.monitoring` and `teams.report`. Cloudflare's own consent screen counts both as read-only (the read-only template, `isReadOnlyScope` in `cloudflare/mcp`'s `src/auth/scopes.ts`), so the classifier does too. A scope with no action word (`repo`) is a write, so "read-only" is only ever claimed when every scope is a known read. `summarizeMcpGrant` counts the scopes once each and names the writes. `mcpGrantPhrase` says "read-only · 194 scopes" or "194 scopes · 12 writes". `mcpReadOnlyRefusal` is (e)'s sentence. **(c)** *Every surface that names the sign-in names the grant, summarized, never all 194 inline.* The Settings row reads "auth: OAuth, signed in (expires in 52 minutes, renews itself), read-only · 194 scopes; held by Viberr, runs connect through its gateway". The editor puts "Granted read-only · 194 scopes. Runs can read through it, and the server refuses any call that writes. To allow writes, add write scopes to Requested scopes above, save, and sign in again." under the sign-in's status line. Below it, a disclosure, "The 194 scopes it granted", lists every scope and marks each write "write"; it is drawn as a GitHub connection's reach list (`.conn-reach`), so the stylesheet does not grow. A server that named no scope reads "The server did not say which scopes it granted." `list_mcp_servers` carries `signIn.grant` {`scopes`, `writes`, `readOnly`, `summary`, `writeScopes`}, null when unknown, and `requestedScopes`. `signInNote` ends with the grant: "Its grant is read-only (194 scopes): the server refuses any call that writes, until an org admin signs it in again with write scopes (Requested scopes in its editor, Instance settings → Agent resources); the controller cannot." `test_mcp_server` and the row's Test end "healthy: N tools · …ms · signed in (…) · read-only · 194 scopes". A save that keeps the sign-in (Save & re-test, `save_mcp_server`) reads "saved: N tools discovered · signed in with OAuth (read-only · 194 scopes)". The run's prompt names it too. `resolveSpecialistMcpServersDetailed` returns `oauthGrants` (each OAuth-signed-in proxied server and its scope), carried to the specialist, resumed, operator and controller prompts. `gatewayMcpSection` adds one line per server, "cloudflare-api: signed in with OAuth, granted read-only · 194 scopes. The server refuses any call that writes, so do not attempt one; if the task needs a write, report that an org admin must sign it in again with write scopes in Instance settings → Agent resources." **(d)** *Requested scopes.* `org_mcp_servers.oauth_requested_scope` is a new baseline column, healed by `BASELINE_COLUMNS` (NULL for every older row). Two places set it: the editor's optional "Requested scopes" field (an HTTP server's, a text area) and `save_mcp_server`'s `requestedScopes`. Scopes are separated by spaces, commas or newlines and kept once each (`parseRequestedScopes`). A token RFC 6749 does not allow is refused at save, before the probe. An absent field keeps what is stored, a blank one clears it, and a stdio row stores none. `org.mcp.added` and `org.mcp.updated` record `requestedScope` when a save changed it. The next sign-in sends it as the authorization request's `scope` (and the registration's); without it the resource's advertised `scopes_supported` goes, as before. The field's hint says the server's own sign-in page decides what it grants, so the editor shows what it granted, and a change applies at the next sign-in. Real-metadata check (2026-09-25, the two read-only GETs allowed): neither `https://mcp.cloudflare.com/.well-known/oauth-authorization-server` nor the protected-resource metadata advertises `scopes_supported`. Nothing was registered or authorized. Cloudflare's consent page picks its read-only template when the request names no scope, and that template is exactly the 194 scopes of the live grant (`test-support/cloudflare-read-only-grant.ts`). **(e)** *A refused write names the grant.* Some calls through the gateway come back as an upstream authorization refusal. That is an HTTP 401 or 403 the transport raised, a JSON-RPC error that says authentication, authorization, forbidden, insufficient scope or permission denied, or a tool result with `isError` whose text says so (Cloudflare's "10000: Authentication error"). When the row is signed in with OAuth on a grant with no write, the run's error gains one sentence: "This connection's sign-in granted read-only scopes (N); an admin must sign it in again with write scopes in Instance settings → Agent resources." It follows the upstream's words, which stay untouched: after a thrown error's message, or as one more text block of the tool result. The grant is read from the row at the refusal, so a sign-in again with write scopes ends it at once. A grant that writes, or one the server did not state, adds nothing. Deliberate residual: a 401 is still renewed and retried, and a second one still ends the sign-in (469(c)), including a 401 that carries `error="insufficient_scope"` (RFC 6750 and the MCP spec say 403 for that). Tests: `mcp-oauth.test.ts` (the 194 live scopes read-only, including the `.monitoring`, `.report`, `:read` and `offline_access` ones; a mixed set counting its writes; the refusal sentence only for a signed-in read-only grant; the controller's note; Requested scopes parsed and refused). `mcp-oauth.server.test.ts` "ruling 486": the scope kept on the callback, replaced by a refresh that names one, kept by one that does not, and cleared on sign-out and on expiry; Requested scopes forwarded as the authorization URL's `scope`, with `scopes_supported` sent when there are none, against the in-test server, which now grants a configurable `scope`, advertises `scopes_supported` and refuses writes; the save and test toasts' grant and the run's grant line. `gateway-oauth.server.test.ts` "ruling 486": an upstream 403 and a Cloudflare-shaped tool error on a read-only grant gain the sentence, and on a grant that writes they do not. `controller-toolkit.server.test.ts` "ruling 486": `signIn.grant`, `requestedScopes` and `test_mcp_server`. `mcp-sign-in.test.tsx` "ruling 486": the row and the editor say "read-only · 194 scopes", the disclosure lists all 194, writes are marked, and "Requested scopes" is present and saved. `sqlite.server.test.ts`: the heal. `app.css.test.ts` counts the new `<summary>`. Canaries, each seen red and restored byte for byte: `monitoring`/`report` dropped from the read actions; every scope classed a read; the callback's public half without `scope`; a refresh keeping the old public scope; sign-out keeping it; expiry keeping it; the sign-in ignoring Requested scopes; the save not storing them; the save toast and the test toast each without the grant; the resolver dropping the grant; the gateway relaying a 403 bare; the gateway relaying the tool error bare; `list_mcp_servers` without `grant`; the row without the grant; the editor without its grant block; the editor not sending Requested scopes; the column heal removed. *(Live verification, 2026-09-25: the owner's cloudflare-api sign-in was made before the public half carried its grant, and the grant was then only in the sealed half's token scope. So every surface would have named no grant until a refresh repeated it. Boot now copies `tokens.scope` into the public half of each signed-in row that lacks one: `backfillMcpGrantScopes` in `app/server/org/mcp-oauth.server.ts`, run from `boot.server.ts` before the watcher. It is idempotent, and a row whose sealed tokens name no scope is left alone, because there is nothing true to copy. Tests: `mcp-oauth.server.test.ts`, "a sign-in stored before ruling 486…" (red by canary: drop the write) and "the grant backfill leaves…".)* *(Live verification 2026-09-25, F40-66: on WEB-8 at 10:42 UTC (deploy 6, which has this ruling) the Platform Engineer asked the owner before a KV namespace create, reasoning from an earlier comment of the owner's instead of the grant. The run's prompt said only "cloudflare-api: signed in with OAuth, granted 384 scopes · 192 writes", nothing a run could reach named the scopes, and the stored grant does hold `workers-kv-storage.write`. Listing every scope in every prompt is bloat, so the gateway answers on demand. On every connection signed in with OAuth that it proxies to a run, ruling 461's gateway adds one tool of its own to that server's `tools/list`, `viberr_connection_grant` (`app/server/mcp-proxy/grant-tool.server.ts`, annotated read-only, non-destructive, idempotent and closed-world), and answers it itself from the registry row's public half as it reads at the call: the sign-in and its expiry (`mcpSignInPhrase`, then the access token's `expiresAt`), then the granted scopes split by `isWriteScope` into "Writes (N):" and "Reads (N):", one per line, in the order the server named them ("Writes: none" on a read-only grant). A sign-in that named no scope answers "The server did not say which scopes it granted", and a connection signed out or expired since the listing answers that it grants nothing until an org admin signs it in again. The public half holds no token, so neither the answer nor its log line (`mcp gateway answered its grant tool`: run, server, status) carries token material. The call is never forwarded upstream; it needs the run's token like every request and is refused like any call once the run's calls close (R-gateway-4); it is answered before ruling 176's withheld check and the write-call audit, so it is never withheld or audited as a write, even when an admin marks its name. It is offered once, on the first page, only while the row is signed in; on such a connection an upstream tool of the same name is left out of the listing, and a connection whose server offers no tools still declares tools so the grant tool reaches the run. A connection with a pasted credential or none offers it nowhere, and a call by that name there is the server's. The prompt's grant line (`grantLine`) adds one sentence for a known grant: "Call its `viberr_connection_grant` tool to see exactly which scopes are granted before you assume a write will be refused or accepted." ("a read" on a read-only grant, whose line already says a write is refused); a grant the server did not name gets none. Tests: `gateway-oauth.server.test.ts` "the connection's grant tool (ruling 486, F40-66)" (the 194 read-only scopes plus `workers-kv-storage.write` and `workers-scripts.write`: the tool is listed after the server's four and answers "Granted 196 scopes: 2 writes and 194 reads", "Writes (2):" with exactly those two, "Reads (194):" and the expiry, while the in-test server hears no request at all; no secret the server issued and not the run's token appear in the serialized answer; no `task.agent.mcp_write_call` although its name is marked; an unnamed grant; a sign-out, then the calls-closed refusal), `gateway.server.test.ts` "ruling 486 (F40-66)…" (a pasted-credential connection, and an uncredentialed one reached through the gateway, list only the server's four tools), `mcp-oauth.server.test.ts` "F40-66…" (the sentence on a grant that writes and on a read-only one, none on an unnamed one, no scope listed). Canaries, each seen red and restored byte for byte: the tool never offered; offered on every gateway connection; offered on an uncredentialed one; the call forwarded upstream; every scope listed as a write; the run's bearer put in the answer's `_meta`; the tool answered before the calls-closed check; the tool audited as a marked write; the sentence dropped from the line.)*

487. **The operator schedules its own task's runs, and a hold a schedule explains is never a packet** (owner, 2026-09-25, pass 40, F40-65; spec `planning/discovery-2026-09-24-pass40-akinozer-site/SPEC-487-operator-schedules.md`; extends ruling 153 to the operator). Measured live on WEB-9 at 10:39–10:40 UTC: the task had to read a deployed cron run at 11:17Z and another at 12:17Z. The operator wrote that it had no scheduling tool and asked the owner to have the controller schedule a Platform Engineer run at 12:25Z or later. It then opened "Build holds for the scheduled 11:25Z Platform Engineer run. Confirm the hold?", a packet whose own body said it existed only so Build "is not left idle with nothing recorded". The owner had to confirm a hold and route a schedule by hand. The controller already held the verbs (ruling 153), the stranded sweep already counted a pending schedule as a reason for quiet (ruling 330), and the operator could already start the same run at once, so scheduling it later adds no authority. Decided: **(a)** *The tools.* The operator gets `schedule_task_action` (`agent`: `"operator"` for its own re-run or a deployed profile id; `delayMinutes` 1..40320 or an ISO `dueAt`; an optional `prompt`, under 4000 characters) and `cancel_task_schedule` (`scheduleId`), on the Claude toolkit and as the Codex plan's fourteenth and fifteenth verbs (the target in `profileId`, the steer in `text`, and three new required nullable fields, `dueAt`, `delayMinutes` and `scheduleId`). Both are bound to the task the run is on. `operatorScheduleRun` writes through `scheduleTaskAction` under `operatorAuthorized`, so it is the same store entry, the same firing path (the profile deployed when it fires, R22) and the same `task.schedule.created` row and "Scheduled:" line, attributed to the operator: the entry reads `createdBy: "operator"` (`OPERATOR_SCHEDULER_ID`) and `createdByLabel: "operator"`, the note's actor is `{kind: "operator"}` and the audit actor is `OPERATOR_AUDIT_ACTOR`. The cancel's note and row are the operator's the same way. The reply names the schedule id and how far out it is; an out-of-range time is refused with the task page's sentence plus the current time, because the model has no clock. **(b)** *Gated like its immediate dispatch.* The tools are built, and the plan verbs offered, only on a `direct` `dispatch-agents` grant (absent resolves to `direct`, ruling 98(b)): a scheduled run starts with nobody present, and under `recommend` a person starts every run the operator proposes. The action refuses the same way (`denied`), for the plan's sake, and the all-denied plan fallback never advertises the two verbs. An agent the operator could not dispatch NOW is a `noop` naming why: not deployed, held by a dependency (ruling 186's sentence, "so scheduling an agent run on it is refused"), or not eligible at the task's stage (ruling 133's `runEligibilityFor`). A closed task is refused by the writer's closure sentence (ruling 177). **(c)** *Its own task and its own entries.* An entry on another task is simply not there (`noop`, naming what is pending here), and an entry a person made through the task page or the controller is `denied`: theirs to cancel. **(d)** *The fire path.* The operator's own `run-agent` entry starts the agent the way its `run_agent` would: no `directiveFrom` (the prompt no longer says "A human (operator) asked you") and no triggerer to tag; the completion re-invokes the operator as any of its dispatches does. Its own `run-operator` entry passes `scheduledByOperator`, and the turn says "a SCHEDULED re-check you set earlier yourself" instead of "a human set earlier". A held dispatch (ruling 152(c)) made under the operator's authority writes its retry as the operator's too. **(e)** *What it can see.* `get_task` and the Codex snapshot carry `schedules`: the pending entries with action, due time, profile, prompt, `by` and `yours`. The spec supposed they already did; they did not, only the controller's `get_task` listed them. Every turn instruction names them when there are any, with whose each is, beside the other standing facts (rulings 397–437). **(f)** *Doctrine.* The shipped `operator.definition.md` (its outgoing hash in `PRIOR_SHIPPED_HASHES`) says a wait a clock explains is scheduled, never asked or routed through anyone, that a hold a pending schedule explains needs NO decision packet, only one timeline note naming the schedule before the turn ends, and that a packet is for a decision a person must make. Three sentences pushed every hold to a packet and are changed: the doctrine's and the non-negotiable rules' "never leave a pre-work or `auto` stage with nothing done and no packet" (now "no packet and no pending schedule", with the schedule as a way out, a rule that is appended whatever the persona says), the stage rule's tail, and the idle-stage nudge, which told the operator to record ANY hold with `open_decision_packet`. The nudge now schedules a wait on a time and keeps the packet for a hold a person directed (ruling 131(f)). The fallback persona says the same. **(g)** *Quiet.* The stranded sweep keeps treating a pending schedule as a reason for quiet (ruling 330), and so does the settle-time backstop now (`operatorLeftTaskStranded`): it read a task holding on a pending schedule at an `auto` stage as stranded, and its nudge is what asked for the WEB-9 packet. Tests (each red by canary, the source restored byte for byte and checked with `cmp`): `schedule.server.test.ts` "ruling 487": the tool writes the entry, the note and the row as the operator and `get_task` lists it as `yours` (canaries: the tool not built; `createdBy` back to the person's id; the note back to a human actor); a time outside 1 minute to 28 days is refused with the time now (canaries: either upper bound dropped); a `recommend` grant, a stage the agent does not work and a held task are refused (canaries: the tools built on `!== "deny"`; the action's grant refusal dropped; the stage check dropped; the hold check dropped); the entry fires on the profile deployed when it fires (Codex, after it moved from Claude) and the agent is not told a human asked (canary: `byOperator` dropped); its own re-run is not told a human set it (canary: `scheduledByOperator` dropped); cancel reaches only its own entries on its own task (canary: the `createdBy` check dropped). `stranded-sweep.server.test.ts` "ruling 487": a task holding only on an operator-made schedule is not nudged, and is once the operator cancels it (canary: the sweep's pending-schedule check dropped). `operator-run.server.test.ts` "ruling 487": the predicate and the settle-time backstop (canaries: the early return dropped; the caller not passing `schedules`); the plan verbs on a `direct` grant only and their schema fields (canaries: the verbs dropped; gated on `!== "deny"`); a Codex plan schedules and cancels as the operator (canaries: either executor case dropped); the idle-stage nudge, the stage rule's tail and the pending-schedules line (canaries: each old sentence restored; the line emptied). `operator-kb-injection.server.test.ts` "ruling 487": the non-negotiable rule (canaries: the rule dropped; the old sentence restored). `operator-toolkit.server.test.ts` "ruling 487": the tools' gate and the description's doctrine (canaries: built on `!== "deny"`; the no-packet sentence dropped). `default-assets.server.test.ts` "ruling 487": the doctrine's sentences and the outgoing hash (canaries: the doctrine reverted; the hash removed). (`app/server/tasks/schedule.server.ts`, `operator-actions.server.ts`, `operator-toolkit.server.ts`, `app/server/runtimes/operator-run.server.ts`, `app/server/seed/assets/operator.definition.md`.)

488. **Work on one task reaches another task in the same project, on the record** (owner, 2026-09-25, pass 40, F40-67; spec `planning/discovery-2026-09-24-pass40-akinozer-site/SPEC-488-cross-task-relay.md`). Measured live on WEB-9 at 12:56 UTC: the goal the controller wrote told the task to post its deployed CPU numbers on WEB-8, whose cron design depended on them. The Platform Engineer wrote two attachments instead, `WEB-9-post-for-WEB-8.md` and `WEB-9-post-for-WEB-8-1217Z.md`; the operator's acceptance packet said they were "handed to a person to post by hand, because neither the agent nor the operator can post on another task" and asked the owner to confirm they were on WEB-8; the owner's driver pasted 5,117 characters over by hand. It was true: the specialist's `post_comment` and the operator's comment tools write only to the task the run is on, and only the controller comments anywhere. Decided: **(a)** *One door.* `relayToTask` (`app/server/tasks/task-relay.server.ts`) is the only way text moves between tasks, whoever sends it. On the TARGET it writes a `comment` by the relaying actor, headed `**From <source> (<author>):**` above the text (the author is `operator`, or the deployed agent's name), marked `toAgent` so compaction keeps the hand-off (ruling 206); the text's @mentions notify as any comment's do, with the ambiguity disclosure (S5-G3); the audit row is `task.relayed {from, to}` on the target, attributed to the relayer. On the SOURCE it writes one `note` by the same actor, `Relayed to <target>: <first line>…` (the first non-blank line without heading marks, cut at 120 characters, the ellipsis when more follows); that line is how the source's operator sees in its snapshot that the relay went out. It then wakes the target's operator, fire-and-forget through `autoInvokeOperator`, with a new `relayed` trigger carrying `relay {fromTaskKey, by, text, occurredAt}`, the way an `@operator` comment wakes it. **(b)** *What is refused, with nothing written.* An empty text; the source task itself (`noop`); a key that is not a task in this project (`noop`, naming `read_board`); a task in another project (`denied`, naming that project: a relay reaches only its own project); an archived project; and a CLOSED target, Done or archived (`noop`, ruling 177's closure sentence plus "a closed task's operator starts no run, so the text would reach nobody"). The spec left the closed target to this ruling: it is refused, not allowed with a reason, because the target's operator refuses every trigger on a closed task, so a relay there wakes nobody and reads as delivered to finished work; reopening the task is a person's stage move, and the transition that reopens it coordinates again. The spec asked for the text to be capped "at the same limit as other comments": no comment carries a length cap (the owner ruled on 2026-08-31 that the record keeps a comment whole and the timeline clamps it), so a relay has none either, and none of the operator's comment guardrails applies, because the meaningful-comment drop and the evidence-separation trim would cut exactly the numbers a relay exists to carry. **(c)** *The operator.* `relay_to_task {taskKey, text}` on the Claude toolkit and as the Codex plan's sixteenth verb (the target in a new required nullable `taskKey` field, the text in `text`), both through `operatorRelayToTask`, gated on `append-typed-events`, the comment's own grant (withheld with it, and in the all-denied fallback like `post_comment`, since it has no effect outside Viberr). The tool's reply says whether an operator is deployed on the target to pick it up. A plan step that opened a packet does not pause a later relay, as it does not pause a comment (ruling 430). **(d)** *The woken operator.* The `relayed` turn quotes the text (cut at `AGENT_REPORT_CAP_TOOLLESS`, with the stamp `read_timeline_entry` takes for the rest), says it is data from another task and not an authority grant, says to act on it when it delivers what the task was waiting for and to leave it otherwise, and forbids asking a person to copy it here or to confirm it arrived; a reply the source needs is `relay_to_task` back. It is placed ahead of the held doctrine (ruling 131(d)), as a person's comment is, and neither an open packet nor a dependency hold refuses it. The lease queue keeps a queued relay in arrival order with the reason-carrying triggers (a newest-wins machine trigger would overwrite the text before any turn read it), and an overflow drop is noted with the source's key. **(e)** *Specialists, through the reporting path they have.* No free-roaming post tool: `report_outcome` gains `relay: [{taskKey, text}]` on every variant of the tool, at most `RELAY_MAX_ENTRIES` (2), a third refused by the schema by name so the agent re-reports in the same run; the Codex envelope gains the same field (required, nullable), every entry parsed and kept, because an envelope is the agent's last word and nobody is left to refuse it to; the staged row keeps it across a restart. At completion, after the reply and before the operator reacts, `postOutcomeRelays` posts the first two through `relayToTask` with the agent as the author (its actor ref on both tasks, the deployed profile's name in the header, the audit label the agent's). An entry past the cap, an entry the door refuses, and every entry of a profile no longer deployed (withheld, like its grants, R15-7) are named in ONE `note` titled "Not relayed" on the source task by `system:policy-engine`, saying the operator can post it with `relay_to_task` and nobody copies it by hand. The run prompt's Collaboration section names the channel wherever the outcome channel exists (`RELAY_NOTE_CLAUDE`, `RELAY_NOTE_CODEX`). **(f)** *Doctrine.* The shipped `operator.definition.md`, `viberr-app-expertise.skill.md` (its Tools list) and `developer-expertise.skill.md` (the specialist handbook's reporting rules) say it, each with its outgoing hash in `PRIOR_SHIPPED_HASHES`: text a goal, a person or a report says belongs on another task is relayed; nobody hands text to a person to copy, paste or post between tasks, asks for an attachment to be carried over, or asks a person to confirm a relay landed. The same rule is appended to the non-negotiable rules whatever the persona says, to the fallback persona and to the `agent-reply` turn ("a \"Relayed to …\" line means the agent's relay already went out"). No shipped text said cross-task posting was impossible; the operator inferred it from its tools. The controller's `create_task` and `create_goal` descriptions and the seeded personas were read for such a sentence and none assumes it, so they are unchanged. Tests (each red by canary, the source restored byte for byte and checked with `cmp`): `task-relay.server.test.ts` "ruling 488": the operator's relay posts on the target as the operator with the source named, audits `task.relayed`, and writes the source's line (canaries: the audit row dropped; the source line dropped; the header dropped); it wakes the target's operator with the `relayed` trigger and the payload (canary: the wake dropped); the woken operator's turn quotes the text and forbids the hand-copy (canaries: the relay instruction emptied; the payload dropped at the Claude prompt's call site); another project, the source itself, a missing task, Done and archived are refused with nothing written (canaries: the other-project lookup dropped; the self check dropped; the closure check dropped); the tool is withheld with the comment grant (canary: built outside that block); a specialist's entries are posted after completion as the agent and the operator's snapshot shows the line (canary: the completion's call dropped); at most two are posted and the rest named (canary: the cap dropped); another project is refused (canary: the other-project lookup dropped). `operator-run.server.test.ts` "ruling 488": the plan verb on the comment grant with its `taskKey` field (canary: the verb dropped from the list); a queued relay survives a later machine trigger and its turn quotes it (canary: the relay routed back to the newest-wins slot); a Codex plan's relay posts on the other task (canary: the executor case dropped); the all-denied fallback is eleven verbs (canary: the verb dropped). `operator-toolkit.server.test.ts`, `operator-kb-injection.server.test.ts` and `default-assets.server.test.ts` "ruling 488": the tool's gate and doctrine, the non-negotiable rule, and the three assets' sentences and outgoing hashes (canaries: the tool built outside its block; the sentence dropped; the rule dropped; each asset's sentence reverted; each hash removed). `agent-toolkit.server.test.ts`, `agent-outcome.server.test.ts` and `specialist-run.server.test.ts` "ruling 488": `report_outcome` stages two entries and refuses a third (canaries: the cap dropped; the field's copy onto the outcome dropped); the envelope declares and parses `relay` and a staged relay survives a restart (canaries: `relay` dropped from the schema's `required`; the parser's copy dropped; the staged row's field dropped); each backend's prompt names its relay note (canary: either note dropped). `mention-notify.server.test.ts`: the relay is one more comment writer, driven through its seam, that fans its @mentions out and stamps the event (canary: the fan-out dropped), and the source sweep of comment writers counts its site. The audit-coverage table has a `task.relayed` row.
