Tests: `line-diff.test.ts` (the shortest script and both sides replayed; the cost cap's fallback; a phrase marked across its spaces; an indentation change; no marks on a rewrite; words in any script), `edit-diff.test.ts` (context, removed then added and the counts; the marked pair and the unpaired line; folds past three lines and never of one; the trailing newline; every occurrence; a MultiEdit's markers; a Write numbered with no +/−; the preview's count, a fold's lines included), `console-todos.test.ts` (TodoWrite's steps, the step under way, an unknown status read as waiting, Codex's steps, nothing else), `runs-helpers.test.ts` (`filePathOf`; `hiddenArguments` naming nothing drawn), `wire-format.server.test.ts` (a completed `todo_list` carries its steps; an updated one is no row; a junk step drops out), `runs-panels.test.tsx` "ruling 499" (the Edit row: repo-relative path with the host path on hover, the stat, the rows and marks, no link; Show more on the row's disclosure; a fold opened in place; a Read shortened and a command not; the to-do card, its statuses and its fold; the shimmer only on the list a running agent wrote last; a Codex plan; "Thinking" on the live tail and "Thought for" once anything follows; `{ } raw` shows neither) and the updated thought-fold, output-block and orb tests, `app.css.test.ts` (F42: the orb is the 20px cell and pauses once the wait ends). Canaries: make the search give up at once and a two-line change costs twelve steps instead of four; drop the half-kept check and a rewritten line is marked word by word; set the context to 0 and every unchanged line folds away; count a Write's lines as added and it claims a +N the record cannot support; ignore the drawn keys and `+ old_string, new_string` returns beside the diff that shows them; mark every to-do list live and a stale list shimmers; drop `todos` from the Codex line and its plan is an empty row again; drop the orb's pause and a finished wait keeps animating; read an unknown status as done and a waiting step claims completion; never pass `live` to a thought fold and the tail never reads "Thinking"; print the host path and the row loses its repo-relative file. Each went red and was restored byte for byte.

500. **The task page takes AICSS's approval card, data table, code block and agent input: a decision packet leads with its tone and its keys, a comment's code and tables are cards, and the task composer is the controller's** (owner, 2026-09-26, "let's implement these components: https://www.aicss.dev/#components"; the task page's half of ruling 499). Measured: the packet carried its tone as a 3px left accent and a kind pill, and each option a radio circle on the left and its digit shortcut as a `kbd` chip at the far right, so the key that selects an option stood as far from it as the row allowed; a comment's fenced block was a bare scrolling `pre` with nothing to copy it by; a comment's table boxed every cell; and the task's composer was a 12px frame with a plain Comment button while the controller's composer, the other box a person addresses an agent through, is a 16px frame with a primary Send (the owner's ask of 2026-09-25). Decided: **(a)** *The packet is an approval card* (AICSS's Approval Card, its questions variant; `PacketHead`, `OptionKey`, `decision-packet.tsx`). The head is a 24px tile in the packet's tone (amber with a hand for a question, coral with an alert for a block), the kind beside it as the card's title (`.packet-kind`, no longer a pill) and "from <who>" at the right; the card sits on a hairline and `--shadow-card` at the box radius, and the left accent is gone. Each option leads with its key, the digit the radiogroup's shortcut selects, which the option now declares (`aria-keyshortcuts`), where the radio stood; the chip at the far right is gone, and the chosen key fills with the call to action. A decided card's options wear the same keys. The density and the one quiet column the owner asked for (the 2026-08-21 preferences #180 and #182) are kept. **(b)** *A comment's fenced block is a code card* (AICSS's Code Block; `MarkdownCodeBlock`, `app/ui/markdown.tsx`): a head with the `code` glyph, the language its fence names (or "code") and Copy, the copy mark trading for the check as every copy control's does; past one line, the attachment reader's gutter (`.code-view`, ruling 363), its numbers drawn by a CSS counter a selection skips. Each line keeps its newline, so the text reads, copies and is announced as written. It is not highlighted: a comment renders at once, and the reader keeps its grammars. A `pre` react-markdown hands over in any other shape renders as it came. **(c)** *A comment's table is one card* (AICSS's Data Table): the button radius, the header row a quiet band in `--muted`, hairlines between cells rather than a box around each; a wide table still scrolls in its own box with the cut-edge cue. **(d)** *The task's composer is the controller's* (AICSS's AI Agent Input): the controller composer's frame (`--radius-card`, the 4px focus ring on the frame's own edge) with Comment as its primary action. The buttons keep their words: ruling 368 has a busy button say what it is doing, so no send becomes an icon-only circle, and the composer grows no attach or model menu it has no feature behind. **(e)** Text Response is the app's inline code chip already, and is unchanged. Budgets (ruling 457): `bundle:root.css` +218 B gzip (the rules above, in the one stylesheet), so every route closure +249 to +265 B (with the `code` glyph in the shell's icon set); `routes/project.task` +758 B and `routes/controller` +692 B (the markdown code block, which the controller's replies render through too, and on the task page the packet's head and keys); ceilings raised to the measured figures with the reasons beside them. Tests: `markdown.test.tsx` "ruling 500" (the head's language and "code", the gutter past one line, the lines and their newlines, the one-line block without a gutter, Copy writing the text and trading its glyph), `task-detail-components.test.tsx` (the packet's kind and tile; each option's key and `aria-keyshortcuts`, and no radio; a checkout-failure note's two lines stay two), `app.css.test.ts` "ruling 500" (the task composer's radius and ring are the controller's; the tile carries the tone and no left accent is left; the chosen key fills with the call to action; no `.opt .radio` or `opt-kbd` rule is left; the table's hairlines; the code card). Canaries: render every `pre` plain and the head, Copy and gutter are gone; drop the lines' newlines and a checkout note's two lines read as one; blank the keys and the shortcut chips advertise nothing; drop `aria-keyshortcuts` and the digits go unannounced; put the kind back in a pill and the head is the old one; put the composer back on the box radius and the two inputs part; drop the chosen key's fill and selection is the tint alone. Each went red and was restored byte for byte. *(Amended 2026-09-27 by ruling 529: a question asked while an agent keeps working on the task sits on the hairline without `--shadow-card`, its tile neutral, and its first line says it is not blocking; a block, and a question the task waits on, keep (a)'s card and tone.)*

501. **The task's Details panel draws its properties the way Linear and GitHub draw theirs: each value is its own control, a value with nothing in it is a quiet line, and an edit posts only the property it changed** (owner, 2026-09-26, of the Details panel reading Priority "Normal", Labels "None", Due date "None", Blocked by "Nothing" over "Edit details" and "Edit what it waits on": "this looks so bad and dated design please make this better and coherent with the UI, check examples like linear github etc. to be inspired"). Measured: every value was set in the bold a side panel gives a fact (`.kv-row .v` is 700, and the `.sub` the empty ones carried has no rule of its own), so the four words with nothing in them were the loudest in the panel; editing was two outline buttons under the rows, 12px on the small radius and touching each other ("Edit what it waits on" under a lock), and the first swapped the whole panel for a three-field form that posted priority, labels and due date together as a full replace (the route read an absent labels field as an empty set). Linear's issue sidebar makes a property's value a ghost button that opens its menu, an empty one reading as the action ("Set priority", "Add label"); GitHub's edits a property where it is read, says "None yet" for an empty one, and since August 2025 lists "Blocked by" as issues with their state icons. Decided: **(a)** *Each value is its control* (`TaskDetailsPanel`, moved to `app/features/task-detail/task-details-panel.tsx`). For a person with `edit-task-meta` on a task that is not archived, the value is a ghost trigger (`.prop-btn`: no chrome at rest, the hover fill and a hairline under the pointer, a blue edge while its editor is open) named by its row and its value ("Priority urgent"), its padding running past the row's edge so the value lines up with the panels above. It opens its editor in a popover under the row (`.prop-pop`: the menus' ring and shadow at the box radius, `menu-in`, a fade under reduced motion): Priority a menu (Urgent, High, Normal, Low, most urgent first, each flag in its pill's tone, the current one checked and focused, arrows, Home and End); Labels the label picker with Cancel and Save (a Save with no change posts nothing); Due date the calendar (a pick saves; "Clear due date" when one is set); Blocked by the wait's own form, intent and refusal (ruling 131: prefilled with the canonical refs, a refused reference keeps it open beside the error, its example keys in the project's prefix) *(narrowed by ruling 548, 2026-09-28: the form's text field and its example keys are replaced by a picker, each entry a chip with a remove cross and a field that finds the project's tasks; the form, its intent and its refusal stay. For an editor the row's own chips carry the cross too, standing before the trigger, which is the plus after them)*. An outside press or focus leaving closes an editor where the person went; Escape, a pick, Cancel or a save hands focus back to the trigger. The "Edit details" and "Edit what it waits on" buttons and the three-field form are gone. A viewer's values are text, and so are an archived task's, over "Archived. Restore this task to edit its details." **(b)** *A value speaks the board's vocabulary, quietly when it is empty.* The rows keep the side column's shape (label left, value right, a hairline between) *(narrowed by ruling 520, 2026-09-27: the rows are a property grid, a label column of one width and every value starting on one left edge beside it, with no hairline between, and a trigger's padding runs past that left edge)* and draw the flag, the label chips and the due pill the board card draws. A value with nothing in it is a quiet line in the placeholder ink at 500 (`.prop-empty`), never bold: "Normal" under a flag for the default priority; "None", "None", "Nothing" for a viewer; for an editor, the invitation with its glyph, "Add labels", "Set due date", "Add dependency". **(c)** *A wait's entry is a chip with a status ring* (`.wait-chip`, the to-do family, ruling 499): a dotted ring open, a green check done, and a red ring on a red chip for an entry that can never complete (ruling 355); the words stay ("· done", "· archived"). **(d)** *An edit posts only its property.* `set-task-metadata` (`project.task.tsx`) writes an axis only when the form carries its field; a present empty field still clears its axis. Each property has its own fetcher, so a save touches exactly what changed and never overwrites a concurrent edit to another property, and the toast names it ("Priority updated", "Labels updated", "Due date updated"). No optimistic UI: the trigger that started a save reads "Saving…" with the spinning loader (ruling 368) until the server answers, stays focusable and ignores presses meanwhile, and its siblings claim nothing. `setTaskMetadata` was already partial and is unchanged, as is the controller's `update_task`. **(e)** *An unchanged task re-renders none of it* (ruling 457): the panel keeps its labels, suggestions and wait as the objects it last committed while their content is the same (`useStableValue`), and each row is memoised on those and on primitives, so a revalidation that brings the same task back renders the panel's shell and its head glyph and nothing under them. Budgets (ruling 457): `console:task-page.renders-per-noop-revalidation` 49 → 44 (the old panel re-rendered whole on every revalidation); `bundle:root.css` +379 B gzip (the rules above, net of the retired editor's), so every route closure +379 B; `routes/project.board` +742 B, the other 363 B being the calendar, which the panel now imports itself, leaving the date-picker chunk for a chunk of its own (the board loads the same code as two); `routes/project.task` +1,094 B (+1,142 B of panel, less the date picker it no longer loads); the render ceiling lowered and the byte ceilings raised to the measured figures, with the reasons beside them. Tests: `task-side-panels.test.tsx` "ruling 501" (a viewer gets text and no control, an editor one trigger per property and the empty ones as invitations; the priority menu's order, check, focus and arrows, a pick that posts `priority` alone and a pick of the current one that posts nothing; Escape hands focus back; the labels editor posts `labels` alone and an unchanged Save nothing; the calendar posts `dueDate` alone and Clear an empty one; an archived task's values are text under its note; the empty values are quiet lines; the wait's chips carry their state and ring), the ruling-131 block (the wait's own form is the Blocked by trigger's editor and closes once saved), `task-disposition.test.tsx` (a property's save reads "Saving…", busy, the loader spinning, on its own trigger alone), `task-detail-route.server.test.ts` "ruling 501" (a priority edit leaves VIB-142's labels and due date as they stand; an empty `dueDate` clears the date alone), `task-console.perf.test.tsx` (the no-op revalidation's renders, at the lowered ceiling), `app.css.test.ts` "ruling 501" (no bold value, the quiet line's ink and weight, the ghost trigger at rest, hovered and open, the editor's floating surface and its reduced-motion fade, the wait chip's rings; no retired `meta-edit` rule left) and the sheet's standing gates (the menu's check is a glyph at 3:1, as the stage menu's; the quiet value's and the chip's glyphs take the 2 stroke beside their 500 and 600 labels; the trigger presses at .96). Canaries: read an absent field as empty again and the route test clears VIB-142's labels; post the triple from the menu and `labels` rides along; drop the trigger's `aria-busy` and the save claims nothing; print the empty values bare, show the triggers to a viewer, save unchanged labels or drop the chips' state, and each test above goes red; drop the refocus on close and Escape leaves focus nowhere; take the weight off `.kv.props` or `.prop-pop` out of the reduced-motion list and the sheet test fails; drop a row's `memo`, or pass the wait unstabilised, and `task-console.perf.test.tsx`'s no-op revalidation goes over 44. Each went red and was restored byte for byte.

502. **Every operator run and every controller turn writes under the Humanizer skill, and nothing a person uses names it** (owner, 2026-09-26: "I want every operator and controller run on humanizer skill by default and hidden from the end user as well https://github.com/blader/humanizer/blob/main/SKILL.md"). The pass-21 humanizer sweep took em and en dashes out of the copy Viberr renders and out of its seed assets (P21 in `copy-ban.test.ts`), but the prose the two coordinating agents write reached the same people with no rule at all: the operator's timeline comments, notes, decision packets, recommendations, goals and directives, and the controller's replies and the documents it drafts. Neither prompt said more about writing than "Keep every comment concise". Decided: **(a)** *Vendored and pinned.* `SKILL.md` from `blader/humanizer` (version 3.0.0, by Siqi Chen, MIT) and its `LICENSE` are copied unchanged from commit `9862685f575c65a8247f90369951df1b3416e3d6` into `app/server/runtimes/humanizer/`, and `THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md` carries the licence. `humanizer.server.ts` records the source and the SKILL.md's sha256, and `humanizer.server.test.ts` fails on any edit to the copy until someone re-vendors it and moves the pin. Nothing fetches it at run time. The module reads it from disk when it loads, from its own folder or else `<cwd>/app/server/runtimes/humanizer`, which is where the image's `COPY app` puts it (read from disk for the reason `default-assets.server.ts` gives: a `?raw` import exists only under Vite). `entry.server.tsx` reaches the module through `boot.server.ts` and `controller-run.server.ts`, so an image without the file fails to start instead of running a coordinator without it. **(b)** *One section on every run.* `HUMANIZER_PROMPT_SECTION` is a "# How you write" section: three short paragraphs of framing, then the skill's body without its frontmatter. It is the last part of the static block of `buildOperatorSystemPrompt`, on Claude and on Codex, whatever the project's operator guidance and skill grants say, and of `buildControllerSystemPrompt`. The framing applies the guide to all the prose the agent writes, in the guide's embedded mode (the final text only, never a draft, a list of patterns or a note about the rewrite). It lets any other instruction win a conflict, and keeps @mentions, questions the agent needs answered, quotations, formats a tool asks for, identifiers, task keys, code, commands and paths as they are. It also tells the model that the people it writes for do not see the guide, so it never names it, quotes it or lists it among its skills and resources. The section is constant, so ruling 370's static block stays byte-identical across a project's tasks and a conversation's turns. It is 28,993 characters, about 7,000 tokens, on every operator and controller call: the operator's static block on a freshly seeded store grows from about 39,000 to 68,000 characters, and after the first call the prompt cache serves it. **(c)** *Hidden.* It is not a store skill and no profile grants it, so it never appears on the Agent resources tab, the Agents page, the controller's settings panel or a run's `run_inputs` skills row, and no edit, save or deployment lock can remove it. Ruling 344 discloses a run's grants and how they resolved; the guide is part of the built-in prompt, like the operator's non-negotiable rules, and `personaChars` counts it with the rest of the prompt the run was sent. There is no switch to turn it off. Residual, recorded: the raw provider transcript that `/resources/session-export` hands a project member (or a controller conversation's owner) to resume a session locally may hold the system prompt the provider recorded (the SDK records it on a session's first request wherever system-prompt recording is enabled for the account, and a Codex rollout can carry its developer instructions), and this section with it, as it holds the rest of the prompt. Tests: `humanizer.server.test.ts` (the pin, the licence in both places, a freshly seeded store whose skill list has no copy of it, the framing, and the operator's static block on both backends, under a project persona and skill grants, with a disclosure that lists only the grants), `controller-run.server.test.ts` (the controller's static block and its disclosure). `operator-kb-injection.server.test.ts` measures its two prompt-length bounds without the section: they were written about the skill budget and the knowledge-base index, and the guide spends neither. Canaries: drop either `parts.push(HUMANIZER_PROMPT_SECTION)` and its test fails; change one character of the vendored SKILL.md and the pin fails.

503. **Goal chains become epics: a named body of work in a project, which tasks join and leave one at a time, the way Jira draws an epic and Linear a project** (owner, 2026-09-26: "goal links should be epics instead and tasks can be independently added or removed to the epics just like jira, linear implement in every detail please"). Ruling 99(e)'s chained goal was automation: a file that owned an ordered list of links, an engine that minted each link's task when the work the link declared had landed, and a panel of chain controls (retry, skip, adopt, rename, cancel) that grew a ruling per defect. A task could not join or leave a chain; it was minted into one, and a person who wanted to regroup work had to cancel a chain and rebuild it. Decided, with the two defaults the ask left open taken as stated here (every existing chain becomes an epic and nothing it knew is lost; people, the operator and the controller can all put tasks in an epic and take them out): **(a)** *The epic.* `projects/<slug>/epics/epic-<n>.md` (`app/schemas/epic-file.schema.ts`, written only by `app/server/files/epic-writer.server.ts`, which mints the id from a directory scan under a per-project lock). Frontmatter: `id`, `title` (at most 120 characters), `status` (`planned`, `in_progress`, `paused`, `done` or `cancelled`: a person's call, as in Jira and Linear, never derived), `color` (one of ruling 364's twenty stage presets; a new epic takes the next in a fixed sequence of far-apart hues), `leadUserId` (Jira's assignee, Linear's lead: the person its notices reach), `startDate` and `targetDate` (planning facts; nothing waits on them), `createdBy`, `createdByLabel`, `conversationId` (the controller conversation that planned it, ruling 476(h)), `convertedFrom` (the goal it came from, (h) below) and the two times. Body: `## Description`, then the `## Timeline` history bullets, newest first. Projected to `epic_projections`, whose status CHECK `projectionCheckGaps` compares against `EPIC_STATUS_VALUES` at boot, and which an upgraded root gains at open. Nothing deletes an epic: a done or cancelled one stays readable, and a done one can be reopened. **(b)** *Membership lives on the task.* `task.md` gains `epic` (an epic id, or absent), projected to `task_projections.epic_id` (a partial index over the rows in an epic, so a read that names no epic keeps the plan and row order it had), the same project-to-task shape as `stage`. A task is in at most one epic, so joining another moves it. An epic's progress (done of total, started, not started, how many wait on other work, per stage; archived tasks counted apart and left out of the total, as Linear leaves a cancelled issue out of a project's progress) is counted from those rows when it is read, so it cannot go stale. `setTasksEpic` (`app/server/tasks/epic-actions.server.ts`) is the one writer, and every door lands there: the task page's Epic menu, the epic page's Add tasks and Remove, the controller's `update_task.epic` and `update_epic`'s `addTasks` and `removeTasks`, and the operator's `set_epic`. A removal from one epic names it (`fromEpicId`), so a stale page never takes a task out of the epic it has since moved to, and `update_epic` checks its task keys (`planTasksEpic`) before it writes the epic's fields, so a call lands whole or not at all. Each move writes an "Epic" note on the task's timeline, one line on the history of each epic it touched ("<who> added WEB-3 and WEB-4", "moved WEB-5 here from epic-2"), a `task.epic.changed` audit row, and an `epic` notification to the lead (not to the person who moved it). A task can also be born in an epic: `createTask` takes `epic`, which the board's New task dialog, the epic page's New task and the controller's `create_task` pass, and a task a person creates from an operator's `create_task` option joins the deciding task's epic; the epic's history and its lead hear of it as of a task added later ("<who> made WEB-7 in this epic"). **(c)** *Who may.* `manage-epics` ("Create & edit epics": admin, maintainer and contributor, the roles that can create the tasks an epic groups) gates creating an epic and changing what it is. Putting a task in an epic or taking it out is the task's own planning metadata, like a label, under `edit-task-meta` (the same three roles). The operator's `set_epic` moves its own task only, under the in-process authority its other task writes use. **(d)** *An epic starts, orders and holds nothing.* What a task waits on is its own `blockedBy` (ruling 131), and every entry is a task key: the `goal-1 link 3` spelling is retired, and the reserved task prefix moves from `GOAL` to `EPIC`, because an epic's id is `epic-N`. The release engine keeps the minute tick the goal runner gave it (`startDependencyRunner`). When the last open task of an open epic is done, archived or taken out, the epic's history says "Every task is done (N tasks)." once and the lead is told; a done task archived or taken out afterwards completes nothing new and says nothing. Setting it Done stays theirs, because "every task I filed is done" and "the work has landed" are different claims. **(e)** *Where a person meets it.* The project rail gains Epics after Board (`nav.ts`). `/projects/:slug/epics` lists the epics, open ones first by default (Open, Closed, All), each row its colour and name, its status, a progress bar in the project's own stage colours (the Home card's meter), its lead and its target date, with New epic for `manage-epics`. `/projects/:slug/epics/:epicId` is the epic: About (its markdown description), Tasks (the progress bar, then one row per task with its stage, the board card's status word as ruling 476(g) drew it on the chain, "waits on N" when it waits, its owner, and Remove; Add tasks offers every live task not in it and says which ones will move from another epic; New task makes one in it; archived tasks fold under the list), History, and Details (status, lead, dates, creator, and ruling 476(h)'s "Planned in" link for a viewer who may open that conversation). The head carries a status select and Edit, which opens the dialog that also creates an epic (name, description, status, lead, start and target dates, colour). The task page names the epic in its hero, as a chip linking to the epic, and in the Details panel's Epic row, a menu of the open epics with "No epic" first. The board gains an epic filter (`?epic=`, an epic's id or `none`; Clear resets it, and the empty copy names it) and the New task dialog an Epic select that starts on the filtered epic. The ⌘K palette finds an epic by its name or its id, between the projects and the tasks, open ones first and a done or cancelled one saying so, inside the same membership scope as its other hits. The card and the list row stay as ruling 172 left them: the epic is planning metadata, so it is not drawn there, as the goal link was not. Both epic routes read the project's domain and run facts (ruling 457), which a new project-routed `epic.updated` event (replacing `goal.updated`) and every task event move. The Activity audit column reads `epic.created`, `epic.updated` and `task.epic.changed` (on the task's chip) as a person's changes and the conversion's `epic.converted` as its own record; the `goal.*` rows a project already holds still read. Profile's `controller` notification category, whose only writer was chain progress, becomes `epics` ("Epic updates"), and a person who had silenced the old one keeps the new one silenced. **(f)** *The controller.* `list_epics`, `get_epic`, `create_epic` (its `tasks` puts existing tasks in as it is made) and `update_epic` (every field, `addTasks`, `removeTasks`, and no delete) replace `list_goals`, `get_goal`, `create_goal` and `update_goal`. `list_tasks` names each task's epic and filters by `epicId` (`none` for the tasks in no epic), `get_task` names it, `create_task` and `update_task` take `epic`, `get_project` summarises the epics, and the board context lists the open ones where it listed the chains (ruling 121). The project Controller page loses the Goals panel, its `goal-op` intent and the loader's chain reads, and keeps its conversations and the knowledge-base proposals. **(g)** *The operator.* Its snapshot carries `epic` (the epic this task is in, its description clipped, and its other tasks with their stage and `blockedBy`) where it carried `goalChain` (ruling 402), and `openEpics` for `set_epic`, which a Codex operator reaches through the plan schema's `set_epic` and its `epic` argument. **(h)** *Nothing is lost at the upgrade.* Boot converts every goal file once, after the rescan (`app/server/tasks/goal-epic-conversion.server.ts`). Each goal becomes the epic with its number (goal-3 becomes epic-3), keeping its title, description, creator, conversation and history, its status mapped (active: in progress, or planned while no link had started; paused and attention: paused; completed: done; cancelled: cancelled). Every task that carried a link, or named the goal in `goalRef`, joins it and loses the retired key. An unstarted link of a running chain becomes a task in the epic, waiting on what the link waited on, made on the goal creator's authority re-proven as the chain re-proved it and signed by the conversion; a link that cannot be made that way is listed in the epic's description with its text. Every stored `goal-N link M` wait, in a task's `blockedBy` and in an open decision's options, is respelled by the key of the task that carried the link, and notices that opened a goal on the Controller page open its epic. The goal file is then filed under `goals/converted/`, which makes the conversion run once, and every step is idempotent, so a conversion interrupted part-way finishes on the next boot. An upgraded root keeps `goal_projections` and the two retired `task_projections` columns, which nothing reads. **(i)** *Retired with the chains:* the goal file schema and writer, `goalRef`, `reconcileGoal` and its runner, the goal actions, `mirrorLinkWait`, `goal-anchor.ts`, the goal-planning backfill (ruling 476(j); a converted epic keeps the goal's `conversationId`), the dependency state `cancelled` (a link on a cancelled goal), and the Goals panel's styles. Ruling 477(b)'s signed creation stays as `createTask`'s `signedBy`, whose one caller is now the conversion: a task it makes for an unstarted link has its owner seat signed `system:epic-conversion` ("Epic conversion", which the Humans filter drops as it dropped the chain) and reading "Made for link 3 of goal-1 (<title>) when goal chains became epics, on <creator>'s authority". This supersedes rulings 155, 192, 194, 243, 260, 267, 335, 358, 359, 398, 402, 404, 411 and 425, and narrows rulings 99, 121, 131, 200, 300, 355, 419, 426, 476, 477, 483, 492 and 497; each says so in its own text. Ruling 492's rule keeps its substance, and its last sentence now reads "Planned work whose outcome needs such a proof is two tasks, in the same epic when it has one: the delivery task, and a read task whose `blockedBy` names it." The seeded controller doctrine, guide, profile and handbook and the operator's doctrine and skill describe epics, and each one's outgoing version is a recorded prior hash, so an unedited store copy upgrades at boot. Tests: `epic-writer.server.test.ts` (the file's round trip and key order, unknown keys kept, `diagnoseEpicFileContent`, id minting under the lock, the colour sequence); `epic-query.server.test.ts` (the list's order, progress counted from the task rows with archived tasks apart, rebuilds and pruning, a broken file's diagnostic); `epic-actions.server.test.ts` ((a) to (d): create and edit with their audit rows and notices, every membership move with its notes, history lines, rows and notices, `fromEpicId`, the permissions, a task made in an epic, and the all-done line said once); `goal-epic-conversion.server.test.ts` ((h) over three stores: a full upgrade of nine chains, an interrupted run finished, and an unreadable goal left alone with everything naming it); `controller-toolkit-epics.server.test.ts` ((f)); `operator-epic.server.test.ts` ((g)); `epics-page.test.tsx`, `epic-page.test.tsx` and `epic-routes.server.test.ts` ((e), the pages and their actions); the Epic row's cases in `task-side-panels.test.tsx`; the epic cases in `command-search.server.test.ts` and `command-palette.test.tsx`; "ruling 503" in `activity-feed.server.test.ts`, `dependencies.test.ts` and `file-formats-sync.test.ts`; and `e2e/09-epics.spec.ts` against the production image (an epic made from the list opens on its own page, tasks join and leave it from there and from their own page, the board filters by it, and the epic page and its dialogs pass the WCAG 2.2 AA sweep in both themes), with the empty Epics page added to `07-accessibility.spec.ts`. Writing them found five defects, fixed here: a new epic's page opened with the list still drawn under its address (the dialog navigated while the list's loaders were still reloading for the create, and React Router finished that navigation over the old page; it now waits for the fetcher to be idle); the all-done line repeated with a smaller count when a done task was archived or taken out; a task made in an epic went unrecorded on the epic's history; the Epic row's button read "Epic Epic <name>"; and the conversion lost a member's decision option naming a goal link (the join parsed the task before its waits were respelled, so the waits are respelled first), dropped an option whose only entry went, restamped tasks an interrupted run had already moved, respelled waits on an unreadable goal's links as dead, and doubled a refusal's full stop.

504. **A starter's bare `docker compose up` is the whole install** (owner, 2026-09-26: "we want to have a perfect UX experience for starters, and docker-compose up is the way to do it"; asked the two forks, the owner chose "Generate secrets on first boot", and for the store an opt-in guard, then none: "why would you be worried about the explicit volume deletion command where they can use down without it"). A fresh clone stopped three times before it served a page: Compose refused `env_file: .env` with no `.env` (`env file .env not found`); the app refused to boot without VIBERR_SESSION_SECRET and VIBERR_SECRET_ENCRYPTION_KEY; and ruling 473's `external` store volume failed the `up` with `external volume "viberr-data" not found` until someone ran `docker volume create viberr-data`, a step the README's quickstart never gained. A fourth waited on a small host: Docker refuses a CPU ceiling above the host's count ("range of CPUs is from 0.01 to 4.00"), and `compose.yml`'s was a fixed 7. Decided: **(a)** *The store.* This supersedes ruling 473: `viberr-data` is Compose's, so the first `up` creates it. `docker compose down` keeps it and `docker compose down -v` deletes it, as that flag asks (measured 2026-09-26 on the real project). An opt-in guard that made it `external` again (`VIBERR_STORE_EXTERNAL`, with `npm run deploy` creating the volume outside Compose) was built and dropped the same day: `-v` is already an explicit request to delete volumes. `npm run deploy` no longer creates the volume. **(b)** *No `.env`.* `env_file` is `required: false`. **(c)** *Generated secrets.* When the environment leaves either secret unset (missing or empty), `getEnv()` takes it from `<data root>/state/instance-secrets.json`, which the first process to need it creates holding both (`app/server/config/instance-secrets.server.ts`). The file is written whole under a `*.tmp` name and linked into place, so two first processes cannot both win and nothing reads half a file; it is 0600 inside the `state/` that boot holds at 0700, so no agent uid can open it (ruling 460). A value the environment sets wins, key by key. The file is never regenerated: one that cannot be read stops the process with a message that names it and never quotes it. The accepted cost: the key sits on the volume beside what it seals, so a copy of the volume opens every sealed secret. **(d)** *Backups carry it.* `npm run backup` copies the file into the artefact (0600) and says in `contains` that the artefact is now a secret; the "key is not in this artefact" exclusion is written only when there is no file. `npm run restore` puts it back and no longer counts it as data that needs `--force`, because its own env read generates one on a fresh volume. Over an occupied root, the root's own file moves aside with its displaced database, so that copy still opens. **(e)** *CPU ceiling.* `cpus: "${VIBERR_CPUS:-0}"`: none unless `VIBERR_CPUS` sets one. **(f)** *Docs.* The README's Docker section and `deployment.md`'s First run begin at `docker compose up`, and `.env.example` leaves both secrets unset and documents `VIBERR_CPUS`. Tests: `instance-secrets.server.test.ts` (generated once at 0600; the environment wins per key; a racing second creator adopts the first file; an unreadable file stops the process unquoted; `getEnv()` hands the file's values over), `backup.server.test.ts` "ruling 504" (carried, and restored onto a fresh root without `--force`; the replaced root's secrets move aside with its database) and `store-volume-wiring.test.ts` (the three compose lines, and both install docs start at `docker compose up` with no `.env` copy or volume create before it), each red by canary.

505. **Insights measures what the prompt-cache plan said to measure before building more: its baseline table, resumes by idle time and operator bursts** (2026-09-26, completing the prompt-cache plan of rulings 369–376, `planning/prompt-cache-2026-09-21/PLAN.md`: PR 1's acceptance, PR 5's count before the gate and PR 6's Codex retention probe). Measured: the plan shipped as rulings 369–376, but three of its pieces were measurement it asked for before deciding more, and none reached the page. PR 1's acceptance was "the insights page reproduces the baseline table above from the stored rows"; the card drew the warm-start rate, the write/read ratio, the large first writes and the TTL split, but not the table's average first-call write, cache reads per run or peak prompt (median · p90 · max), and it had no Codex row, so by run kind a Claude specialist's cold start (its prefix shared across tasks, ruling 371) and a Codex one (per thread, ruling 375(c)) read as one rate. PR 6 asked whether a Codex resume idle past ten minutes reads its prefix back before `CACHE_TTL_MS.codex` moves from ten minutes toward the 24 hours OpenAI documents (research S16); nothing sorted resumes by idle time, so the ten minutes stood "until measured" with nothing measuring it. PR 5 held back a per-project gate that would serialize simultaneous fresh operator starts until the bursts were counted; nothing counted them. Decided: **(a)** *The table carries the baseline's columns* (`CacheRow.avgFirstCallWrite`, `readPerRun`, `peakPrompt`; `cacheSummary`, `insights-query.server.ts`): the mean first-call write over the runs with a first call on a backend that reports writes (null otherwise: "not reported" when the group has no such run, as ruling 395 draws the write column, "n/a" when its runs never reached the provider), the cache reads per run over the runs that reached the provider, and the median, p90 (nearest rank) and max of each run's peak prompt over the runs that carried a per-call figure. A third group, by backend and run kind (`claude · primary`, `codex · primary`), gives Codex its own rows. **(b)** *Resumes by idle time* (`ResumeSummary`, `resumeSummary`). A resume is a run whose provider session an earlier run of the same backend used; its idle time runs from that run's finish (after any completion compaction, the last call that touched the cache) to its own start, and it lands in a bucket bounded by `RESUME_IDLE_EDGES_MS`: every TTL `CACHE_TTL_MS` assumes, then `EXTENDED_CACHE_RETENTION_MS` (24 hours), derived from the table so a TTL it gains moves the edges. A row is a backend and the credential kind the EARLIER run billed, the pair `cacheTtlMs` takes, so it names the TTL ruling 372's verdict assumes; each cell counts the warm resumes of all the resumes idle that long, and the cells past the assumed TTL are marked (`data-past-ttl`). A warm cell past it says the cache outlived the TTL (for Codex, the retention the probe looks for); a cold one inside it, that the cache lapsed sooner. Only resumes whose first call landed are counted; an earlier run that never finished gives no idle time. The set-aside column counts the fresh starts ruling 372 made instead of a replay, from their `runtime.run.started` audit (`continuityReset: "stale_large_session"`, typed against `ContinuityLossReason`), keyed by the fresh run's own kind. It is all read off rows the sink already writes, so an instance's history since ruling 369 answers at once; no column was added. **(c)** *Operator bursts* (`OperatorBurstSummary`, `operatorBurstSummary`). Over the Claude operator runs that reached the provider, a start within `OPERATOR_BURST_WINDOW_MS` (a minute) after the previous start of the same project, principal and model is in a burst, and the cold ones, with what their first calls wrote, are the most a gate could save. The minute is generous (an operator's first response begins seconds after its start), so the count is an upper bound. Codex is left out: its cache does not cross threads (ruling 375(c)), so no order of starts makes a second one warm. **(d)** *Not built.* The gate itself: `RESEARCH.md`'s re-measure (its note 4) found 1 cold start in the 141 operator starts within five minutes of the previous one, and a gate would delay every overlapping turn to save that; (c) now shows whether it changes. PR 2's "rework rate unchanged" check: the mid-run window it guarded was removed by ruling 376, and verdicts are not projected per revision. Codex 0.156.0's `model_post_turn_compact_threshold_percent`: ruling 376 already compacts a large session at the end of its run and keeps no mid-run window, so it is not set. Tests: `insights-query.server.test.ts` (ruling 505's three describes: the baseline columns beside a refused run and a row from before ruling 369; the backend-and-kind rows, where Codex's first write is null; resumes bucketed per backend and credential kind, five minutes exactly inside the five-minute bucket, keyed by the earlier run's kind, an unfinished earlier run and a first call that never landed left out, set-asides from the audit and scoped by project; bursts within the minute, a refused start neither opening nor joining one, and no pairing across project, principal, model or backend), `context-policy.server.test.ts` (the edges derived from the TTL table) and `insights-page.test.tsx` (the columns, the group rows spanning every column, the resume cells past each row's TTL, the burst sentence). Canaries: average first writes over every backend and Codex reads 0; key a resume by its own kind and an API-key session's resume lands under the sign-in; spell the edges by hand and a TTL the table gains leaves no edge; partition bursts by project alone and another principal's start reads as a burst; leave a group row at the old span and it stops short of the table's edge.

506. **A cached prefix no longer moves between sessions for three reasons nobody chose: a knowledge-base index prints a size class, its lists sort by code point, and the host's cache and compaction switches stay out of every child** (2026-09-26, the owner extending the prompt-cache plan of rulings 369–376: "let's extend this with prompt caching across sessions or researching what to do else to improve caching overall"; amends 283). Read against the pinned Claude Code 2.1.280 and Codex 0.156.0: two sessions of one kind share a prefix only while every byte before the dynamic boundary matches (the tools, then the system prompt; ruling 370), and three things moved it that no ruling had named. (1) *The knowledge-base index printed each document's exact byte count* (`` `conventions.md` · 20,632 chars ``). The index sits in the static block of the operator, of the controller and of every specialist profile it is attached to, and since ruling 498 an agent's correction is written straight into the document, so each correction re-priced the next fresh start of every one of them (about 65k for an operator turn by ruling 374(a), about 14k per specialist profile by ruling 371) and, where the CLI does not yet record the system prompt (`snapshot` is rolling out), every session resumed after it paid for its whole history again (inferred). (2) *Two lists in those blocks sorted with `localeCompare`*, a knowledge base's documents and the gateway section's OAuth grant lines, which follows the process locale, where every other list in a cached prefix sorts by code point (ruling 370's `sortedNames`). (3) *The CLI's prompt-cache and compaction switches passed through `filteredSpawnEnv`*. None of `DISABLE_PROMPT_CACHING` (and its per-model variants), `ENABLE_PROMPT_CACHING_1H` (and `_BEDROCK`), `FORCE_PROMPT_CACHING_5M`, `CLAUDE_CODE_PROMPT_CACHE_TTL` or `CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_PROMPT_CACHE_TTL` is credential-shaped or declared by the env schema, so one set on the host reached every Claude child, where it could turn caching off for the whole instance or force the lifetime 374(a) left to the CLI, and made `CACHE_TTL_MS` wrong without a sign. The compaction switches ruling 376(d) left to the CLI passed the same way (`CLAUDE_CODE_AUTO_COMPACT_WINDOW`, `CLAUDE_AUTOCOMPACT_PCT_OVERRIDE`, `DISABLE_AUTO_COMPACT`, `DISABLE_COMPACT`): a server started from inside a Claude Code session inherits the first two, and the container this ruling was written in did, which is why ruling 376's two hermeticity tests failed there. Decided: **(a)** *The index prints a size class* (`kbSizeClass`, `kb-injection.server.ts`): "under 1k chars", then "1k to 2k chars" and on up the 1-2-5 steps to "500k to 1M chars", then "1M chars or more". A correction to a document's body leaves the index byte-identical; a new heading, a new document or a crossed step still moves it, because then the index says something new. The class keeps what a run used the number for, whether a document is a note or a book: no tool description tells a run the read cap, and a read past it says so itself. **(b)** *Code-point order* (`sortedBy`, `prompt-prefix.server.ts`) for a knowledge base's documents (`collectKbDocs`) and the grant lines (`gatewayMcpSection`), so `README.md` now lists before `api.md`. **(c)** *The switches are stripped* (`PROMPT_CACHE_ENV_RE` and `COMPACTION_ENV`, `spawn-env.server.ts`) by the CLI's own names. A value Viberr chooses on purpose still arrives, because a run's own overlay (`spec.env`) is spread over the filtered base. The CLI's other caches (`CLAUDE_CODE_WEBFETCH_CACHE_TTL_MS`, `MCP_DISCOVERY_CACHE_TTL_S`) are not the prompt cache and pass like any undeclared name. `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` and `CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_EXPERIMENTAL_BETAS` also cost the operator's and the controller's prompts their global cache scope (read from the binary), but a deployment sets those on purpose, for a gateway or a proxy, so they stay. **(d)** *Codex has nothing to set.* 0.156.0 exposes no cache key and no retention: `prompt_cache_key` is a wire string the CLI fills per thread (ruling 375(c)), the SDK's options and `config.toml` carry no cache field, and the one occurrence of `prompt_cache_retention` is prose in a bundled OpenAI docs skill. The plan's "the CLI may already request 24-hour retention" (PR 6) is corrected: whatever the backend keeps is its own default, and ruling 505's resume table is the only evidence either way. **(e)** *Not built*, each for its reason. A resume onto a new model or effort replays the whole history cold (the CLI lists `model_changed` and `effort_changed` among its cache breaks), and `resumeVerdict` weighs only idle time and size. Counting a switch as cold would change almost nothing: since ruling 376 compacts a session above 100k when its run ends, a session reaches a resume above ruling 372's 150k only when its run was interrupted or its compaction refused, and below that line ruling 372 replays a cold session anyway. Effort is not stored on `agent_runs` either. Completion compaction's own cache hit is not recorded: the Claude call's usage is folded into the run's totals, and Codex's `thread/resume` for it carries the run's cwd, model and `compact_prompt` but not its `developer_instructions` or servers, a likely miss (inferred); measure it before changing it. On a subscription seat in overage the CLI drops the main conversation to five minutes while `CACHE_TTL_MS.claude.login` assumes an hour; the SessionStart hook's `prompt_cache_likely_expired` could check that without forcing anything. A specialist's static block is appended after the preset's boundary, which the CLI caches at organization scope rather than globally (read from the binary; the effect is inferred); where it goes belongs to the preset ruling 371(a) chose. Tests: `kb-injection.server.test.ts` (every step of the class, a body correction leaving the index byte-identical while a heading and a crossed step move it, code-point order), `prompt-prefix-determinism.server.test.ts` (the specialist's and the operator's static blocks unchanged by a correction, moved by a heading), `kb-prompt-block.server.test.ts` (the pinned index lines), `mcp-oauth.server.test.ts` (the grant lines in the names' order), `runtime-registry.server.test.ts` (every switch stripped, the other caches kept), and ruling 376's `harness-hermeticity.server.test.ts`, which now passes on a host that sets a window. Canaries: print the byte count again and the correction tests fail; sort with `localeCompare` and `README.md` lists after `api.md`; drop either list from the filter and its switches reach the child.

507. **A person keeps several agent accounts per backend and switches between them without signing in again** (owner, 2026-09-26: "Let's work on multiple accounts per user on codex and antropic and ability to switch between them without login"). Ruling 127 gave each person one credential per backend: `user_backend_credentials` carried `UNIQUE (user_id, backend)`, connecting a key logged the previous sign-in out and deleted its file, and a sign-in wrote into the one backend home the previous account's sign-in had lived in. A person with a work and a personal subscription, or one whose window was spent, could only swap accounts by signing out and running the vendor's browser flow again, and the account they left was gone. Decided: **(a)** *An account is a row.* `user_backend_credentials` holds one row per ACCOUNT and a person may keep up to ten per backend (`MAX_ACCOUNTS_PER_BACKEND`). Exactly one per (person, backend) is ACTIVE, the one every run on that backend bills: the most recently selected (`selected_at`, ties to the newer row, `ACTIVE_FIRST`). Connecting, by a hosted sign-in or a pasted key, ADDS an account and makes it the active one; nothing that was connected is logged out or replaced. A root created before this ruling has its table rebuilt once, in place, from the baseline's own DDL (`ensureBackendAccountsTable`, the recipe of ruling 481(a)): every row is carried, each becomes its person's active account, and each is marked `legacy_home = 1`. **(b)** *Each account has a home of its own.* An account connected since this ruling keeps its vendor sign-in in `<backend home>/accounts/<accountId>` (`backendAccountHome`), where the vendor's binary wrote it; a legacy account's sign-in stays in the backend home itself. Viberr never moves, copies or reads a Claude sign-in to switch accounts (ruling 127): a Claude run is pointed at the active account's home as `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR`, whose `projects/` is a link to the backend home's, so every transcript lands where resume, the exporter and the retention sweep look, whichever account wrote it; and two accounts never share one credential file, which matters because Claude rotates its refresh token on every refresh. A Codex run keeps ruling 181's private fork of the shared home, and the fork takes `auth.json` from the billed account's home and hands the refreshed one back there, under that home's lock, and only when the CLI actually refreshed it (a digest of the seed, `.auth.json.seed`, so a copy that went stale while another run refreshed the account never overwrites the newer token). The Codex completion compaction (ruling 376) runs in a fork of its own (`runs/<runId>-compaction`), seeded and settled the same way. The launcher still hands back the whole backend home after every process (ruling 460), and `agentLaunchFor` hands an account's home, and the shared directory it links to, to the person's uid when the server created them. **(c)** *Switching is a write, not a sign-in.* Profile → Agent accounts lists the person's other accounts on each backend with **Use this account** (`backend-account-switch`, `switchBackendAccount`): it stamps `selected_at` and nothing else, no vendor process runs and no file moves, it takes effect for the next run that starts, and a run already going keeps the account it started on (a Claude run's config dir and a Codex run's fork are fixed at spawn). It is refused, with a sentence, for the account already in use, for an account whose sign-in file this server no longer holds (the card offers that account's sign-in instead), and for an account that is not the person's. Audited as `profile.backend.switched`. **(d)** *Disconnecting is per account.* `backend-disconnect` names the account (`disconnectBackendAccount`): a sign-in is logged out by the vendor's own binary in THAT account's home, the home is removed as the person (ruling 485), and the row goes; a legacy account loses its credential file and nothing else of the backend home. Removing the active account hands runs to the account used before it, and the toast says which; removing any other changes nothing about which account runs bill. Account removal (`retireUserBackends`) retires every account, not only the active ones. **(e)** *Names.* A person may name an account (`label`, at most 60 characters, `backend-account-rename`, audited `profile.backend.renamed`); an unnamed account is named by what its vendor reported (the email Claude's `auth status` prints) or by its kind (`backendAccountName`). A name decides nothing. **(f)** *A sign-in is for one account.* Its account is decided before the vendor process starts (`loginTargetFor`), so the ceiling refuses before any process runs: a new account gets an empty home minted with its id, and signing an existing sign-in in again (the card's offer for a missing file, and Start again after a failure) runs in that account's home and updates its row. A sign-in into a new account that does not end connected (failed, cancelled, timed out or replaced) takes its half-made home with it once its process has exited, so an abandoned attempt leaves no credential that no row accounts for. **(g)** *Ruling 165 follows the active account.* The refusals and the reading Viberr observed are retired whenever the account that bills the next run changes (a connect, a switch, the active account's removal) and not otherwise; switching back to a spent account retires them too, and one refused run re-records the window. **(h)** *No fallback.* A run bills the active account or is refused (ruling 127); nothing moves a run to another account on its own. When the active account cannot run and another of the person's accounts can, the health sentence every refusal quotes says so ("Another of your Claude accounts is connected there: switching to it needs no sign-in."), and the quota and credential remedies say "switch to or connect a different account (or an API key)". **(i)** *The run records its account.* `agent_runs.credential_account_id` names the account a run billed; boot recovery hands an orphaned Codex run's refreshed sign-in, and its compaction's, back to that account, and to nobody when the account has been removed since. The model catalog's live list (ruling 127) is cached per account home, since two subscriptions of one person may offer different models. The continuity probe reads an EMPTY shared `projects/` as `unknown`, like an absent one, because Viberr now creates it before any CLI has written there. (`app/server/runtimes/backend-credentials.server.ts`, `user-homes.server.ts`, `backend-login.server.ts`, `codex-runtime.server.ts`, `run-recovery.server.ts`, `session-export.server.ts`; `ensureBackendAccountsTable` in `app/server/db/sqlite.server.ts`; the card in `app/features/profile/agent-accounts-panel.tsx`, the intents in `app/routes/profile.tsx`.) *Dated note (2026-09-27, ruling 515):* the card's other accounts are no longer the connections list's one-line rows: each account's name and facts sit over its buttons, because beside them an address, which cannot wrap, ran under Use this account.

508. **The code reader colours every scope family its theme emits, and a log's numbers whole and its levels by severity** (owner, 2026-09-26: "syntax highlighting fails, inspect carefully", with a screenshot of Node test-runner output open in the reader; amends 363). The screenshot's file was a `.log`, which ruling 363 maps to Shiki's `log` grammar (the Log File Highlighter grammar VS Code's Log mode is converted from). Its tokens reproduce exactly in Node, with the JavaScript engine the reader uses and with Oniguruma alike, so neither the engine nor the per-line clock was at fault, and every pattern of every mapped grammar compiles under the JavaScript engine. Three defects, all in what the reader does with correct tokens. (1) *Numbers were coloured in part.* The grammar's number rule is `\b([0-9]+|true|false|null)\b`: a digit run is a number wherever it stands as a word, and `.` ends a word. Node prints each test's duration as `(0.73575ms)`, so the `0` was a number and `.73575ms` stayed plain, because `73575ms` is not a word; `127.0.0.1` was four numbers and three plain dots, `85.123` two numbers, and the `004` of an id like `W-004` a number inside a name. The rule runs ahead of the grammar's own dotted-token rule, which would have taken `0.73575ms` whole. VS Code splits them the same way (inferred from the grammar, not run). (2) *Three scope families had no colour.* Shiki's css-variables theme resolves a scope to one of twelve families. Ruling 363's stylesheet coloured eight and left punctuation in the foreground by design, but `inserted`, `deleted` and `changed` had no rule, so every added and removed line of a `.diff` or `.patch`, its `---`/`+++` headers, and a log's INFO, WARN and DEBUG rendered in the plain foreground: a diff opened in the reader showed no colour at all. `app.css.test.ts` checked a hand-written list of the eight, so it passed. (3) *A log's levels were named for VS Code's default theme, not for their meaning.* The grammar scopes ERROR as `string.regexp` (with a stray comma, so a theme reads it as `string`), WARN as `markup.deleted` and DEBUG as `markup.changed`. Under GitHub's palette an ERROR read as a pale string, and with (2) fixed alone a WARN would have read red and a DEBUG orange. Decided: **(a)** *Every family the theme emits has a colour.* `--syn-inserted`, `--syn-deleted` and `--syn-changed` join both theme blocks with the text colours GitHub's own VS Code themes give those scopes (light `#116329`, `#82071e`, `#953800`; dark `#7ee787`, `#ffa198`, `#ffa657`), each at least 4.5:1 on `--bg` and `--surface`. They are text colours only, like every other family: GitHub's themes also tint the background, which the reader does for no family. `app.css.test.ts` now reads the families off the reader's own theme (`THEME_OPTIONS`, `code-highlight.ts`) through the reader's own token-to-class map (`toToken`), with a floor of the eleven so an unparsable theme cannot pass by listing none. A family a Shiki upgrade adds fails the test until it has a colour or joins punctuation in the foreground. **(b)** *A log's number is one token or none* (`log-grammar.ts`, which the `log` loader imports where it imported `@shikijs/langs/log`, so the repair rides the grammar's own chunk). Upstream's rule is replaced by one that takes an optional sign, digits, any `.digits` groups, an exponent, and a unit or `%` glued to it (`12ms`, `85.5%`, `1.5GB`), with no word, hyphen or dot on either side; a sentence's full stop may follow it. `true`, `false` and `null` keep a rule of their own. The grammar's 7-, 10- and 40-digit hash rule steps aside for a fraction, so `1727349634.123` is one number. So `(0.73575ms)` colours `0.73575ms`, `127.0.0.1` is one token, and `W-004`, `SHOP-65` and `x86_64` stay plain. **(c)** *A level wears its severity.* ERROR, and every rule upstream scopes `log.error` (FATAL, FAIL, `[E]` and the rest), is `markup.deleted` and bold, so red; WARN is `markup.changed`, orange; INFO stays `markup.inserted`, green; DEBUG is `constant.language`, blue. TRACE and VERBOSE stay comments, as do the dates and times. Everything else in the grammar is upstream's. Not changed: a string keeps GitHub's string colour, which on the dark ground (`#a5d6ff`) sits close to the foreground; that palette is ruling 363's. A test runner's pass and fail glyphs (`✔`, `✖`) stay uncoloured, since no grammar knows them, and a comment's fenced code stays unhighlighted (ruling 500). The stylesheet grew by 72 B gzip on every route and the task page's highlighter chunk by 16 B; the eight bundle ceilings are raised with that reason (ruling 457). Tests: `log-grammar.test.ts` (the owner's screenshot lines: durations whole, `2019` a number, `W-004` plain, strings still strings; a number as one token across addresses, units, signs, exponents, a sentence's full stop and a 10-digit time with a fraction; no part of a word coloured, while a hash, a UUID and `0x1f` stay whole; the level ramp; the grammar's own dates), `code-view.test.tsx` "a diff's added and removed lines take the inserted and deleted families", `app.css.test.ts` "code reader palette" (the families read off the theme, each with an AA token in both themes and a rule). Canaries: load `@shikijs/langs/log` again and all four `log-grammar.test.ts` tests go red; the stylesheet before this ruling fails the palette and rule tests on `--syn-inserted`. (`app/ui/log-grammar.ts`, `app/ui/code-highlight.ts`, `app/app.css`.)

509. **A review note may cover several lines, picked the way GitHub picks them** (owner, 2026-09-26: "multi line selection for comments are needed", with a screenshot of the Changes panel's note editor open under one line of a deploy runbook's status paragraph; amends 484). Ruling 484(b) made a line's number the button that opens a note under it, one note per line, so a remark about a paragraph, a list or a block of code went on one of its lines and named the rest in words, or was split over several notes. The comment could already quote a range (`path:start-end`, which 484(c)'s relay prints for GitHub's multi-line comments); nothing in the panel could make one. Decided: **(a)** *Picking the lines* (`changes-panel.tsx`). A primary mouse press on a number, dragged across the others, marks the lines while the button is held, and the release opens the note editor under the last of them; Escape during the drag drops it. With a note open, a shift-click on another number (Shift+Enter from the keyboard, which is how a keyboard reaches it) stretches or narrows the note from its first line, as a text selection extends from its anchor, and a drag that starts on one of its lines re-ranges it; both keep what was typed, and focus goes back to the box. A range stays inside one hunk, because the lines between two hunks are not in the patch, and stops before a line that has a note of its own (`noteRange`, `app/shared/diff-rows.ts`), so a line still carries one note and pressing any line of a note opens that note. Only a mouse starts a drag: a finger on the numbers scrolls the page, as it did, so on a touch screen a note covers one line. The rows being picked, and those of the open note, are washed in the focus blue over their own tint; a saved note's rows keep a bar at their left edge; a note on several lines, and its editor, are headed with them ("Lines 3 to 9", "Removed line 4 to line 7"), and the editor asks "What should change on these lines?". The footer's empty line says "Select a line number to add one, or drag across several." **(b)** *What the agent receives* (`review-notes.server.ts`). A note on several lines posts its first line and that line's side (`startLine`, `startSide`) beside its last; a range on one side never reads upward and a side without a line is refused like any malformed note. The comment quotes it as `path:start-end`, "(removed lines)" for the old file's, and by both ends when it runs from a removed line to an added one, which no single numbering covers: `` `path` (removed line 4 to line 7) ``. `ReviewNote` carries the start side for both doors, and the relay reads a GitHub comment's `start_side`, where it had printed such a range as `path:4-7` in two numberings. Still only the reference is quoted, never the lines' content, for 484(b)'s reasons: code carries `@` too, and the agent has the checkout. Not changed: one note per line, one comment per send, and nothing about a range reaches GitHub. Budgets (ruling 457): the stylesheet grows by 51 B gzip on every route, and the task page's closure by 52 B (the same CSS, and one byte where it names the reader's chunk, whose hash moved); the eight ceilings are raised with that reason. The reader chunk, loaded when the panel opens, grows from 3,291 to 4,485 B gzip. Tests: `diff-rows.test.ts` "ruling 509" (a range stops at its hunk's edge and before another note's line, passes the no-newline marker, reads first line first whichever way the pointer went, and starts nowhere a note cannot sit), `review-notes.server.test.ts` (the labels for a range on each side and across sides; the parse's start line and side, and its refusals), `pr-review-relay.server.test.ts` (a GitHub range from a removed line to an added one), `routes/task-changes.server.test.ts` (a range through the real intent) and `changes-panel.test.tsx` "ruling 509" (a shift-click, a range across sides, a drag and its Escape, no drag for a touch, a drag that re-ranges the open note and keeps its text, the stop before a noted line, a note's middle line opening it and a shift-click narrowing it), each red by canary. Checked in Chromium against a production build whose GitHub read was answered by a fixture: a drag, a shift-click and Shift+Enter, in both themes and at 390 px, with no text selected by the drag and no page scrolling sideways.

510. **A task's long attachment list folds the way a long comment does** (owner, 2026-09-26: "let's make this attachments foldable like comments copy the work from there", with a screenshot of WEB-3's Attachments panel listing fifteen files, twelve of them the logs of two gate runs). The panel listed every picture and file flat, so each gate run added six rows and pushed the timeline further down, while a long comment on that timeline clamps behind Show more. Decided: **(a)** *One fold.* `CollapsibleComment`'s measure, clamp and toggle move into `Collapsible` (`app/ui/collapsible.tsx`), which the comment and the panel both render: content taller than 340px (and the 24px of slack the comment had) clamps to 340px under the soft fade, with "Show more" / "Show less" and `aria-expanded` below it, and only the view changes. It measures after mount, as the comment did, so the server renders the whole list, and measures again whenever its content changes, which a clamped box's size never shows. **(b)** *What folds.* The panel's pictures, its files and the note that the list is partial are the fold; the heading, its file count and "Attach a file" stay above it. A short list renders as it did, with no toggle. **(c)** *Keyboard.* The rows under the fade stay in the tab order, and tabbing to one scrolled the clamped box so the row sat behind the fade, its ring too faint to follow, and left the box scrolled. Keyboard focus (`:focus-visible`) on anything whose bottom edge lies under the fade (past 78% of the box, where the mask turns; `app.css.test.ts` pins the two together) opens the fold. A row in plain sight keeps it folded, because closing an attachment's card with Escape hands keyboard focus back to the row that opened it, and a pointer's focus never opens it. A long comment's links take the same rule. **(d)** *The list's box.* A clamped box clips what paints outside it, and the file rows run the panel's full width, so the list (`.attach-list`) reaches 4px past them on every side (padding 4px, margin -4px) and the focus ring, 2px at a 2px offset, keeps its sides. The rows are spaced by the list's gap rather than a margin each, so the first row's space no longer collapses through the box, and no row moves when the fold clamps or opens. Not changed: the comment's fold, its height and its words; the attachment card; the 100-file cap and its note. Budgets (ruling 457): the stylesheet grows by 10 B gzip on every route, and the task page's closure by 162 B (the same CSS, the shared fold, its keyboard check and the panel's use of it); the eight ceilings are raised with that reason. Tests: `collapsible.test.tsx` (short content whole; the clamp at 340px and its toggle; a re-measure when the content changes; keyboard focus under the fade opens it, and neither a row in plain sight nor a pointer's focus does), `attachments-panel.test.tsx` "ruling 510" (the pictures and files fold, and the heading, the count and the attach control stay above it; a short list has no toggle) and `app.css.test.ts` "ruling 510" (any fold clips and fades at the keyboard check's 78%; the list's room for the ring, and its gap), each red by canary. Checked in Chromium against a production build with fifteen files on a task: the list folds to seven rows and a fading eighth, opens and folds again with every row where it stood, tabbing opens it at the first row under the fade, and a click on a row then Escape leaves it folded, in both themes and at 390 px; a long comment still folds as before.

511. **The PR card reads like GitHub's merge box** (owner, 2026-09-26, on a screenshot of the task page's PR card: "this is dated design, research online to find better stuff maybe shadcn like? I don't realy know but this has no taste"). Measured on VIB-142 (PR #318 in review, three commits, nine files, six passed gates) at 1440 px: the card stood 776 px tall in the 340 px side column. A black inverted bar carried the repository and the pills (the PR's number and state, and the gates, GitHub's checks and review and a conflict when they applied); a column of label and value rows set in the bold display face followed ("Checked no completed pass on record", "Last change recorded at delivery (nothing has changed since)", Branch, Diff), then the commits, the Gates row with its six-row table on every pass, and three full-width buttons (Run gates again, Force accept, Open on GitHub). Researched: GitHub's merge box (a section per check, review and conflict, each a status mark over a bold title and a muted line, the passing checks folded behind "Show all checks"), Primer's StateLabel, Vercel Geist's entity rows, shadcn's Card and Item (media, title, description, actions) and Linear's pull-request attachments. None needs a new library; a registry stays a reference (ruling 166). Decided: **(a)** *The bar, then what the pull request is.* The inverted bar stays the card's head: a first draft drew its mark, repository and state on the surface instead, and the owner answered "the old white/black headers were looking doog though". It holds the GitHub mark, the repository in the code face, the pull request's state pill (`prStatePill`, filled whatever its tier, as the bar always drew it, because the quiet outline's ink is made for the surface and fades on the bar) and the visually hidden "GitHub" heading (ruling 478(f)). The other pills it carried are the rows of (b), and the number moves to the title. Under the bar, on the surface, come the pull request's own title and number, which is the link to it ("Pull request #N" when the title is empty), then the branch as a chip that links to its tree, and the diff ("9 files +412 −87"). Those two links are the card's way to GitHub, and the "Open on GitHub" button is gone. A branch with no PR shows "no PR" on the bar and no title line. **(b)** *One status row per signal.* A branch collision (F31-1), Viberr's gates (ruling 482), GitHub's checks, review and conflict (P13-D-28, rulings 162 and 405(b)) and an unpushed revision (ruling 135) are each a row: a mark in its pill's tone (`github-pills.ts`), the pill's words as the title with a capital ("Gates passed", "1/4 checks failing", "Review required", "Conflicts"), and what the state rests on under it (the gates' server line, "GitHub's check runs on this pull request", "GitHub's review decision", "GitHub can't merge it into the base branch", the collision's and the unpushed revision's own sentences). The mark is the icon set's circle family (rulings 365 and 499), a check for a pass or an approval, a cross for a failure, the dotted ring for a wait and a plain ring otherwise, with the alert triangle for a risk and the upload arrow for the unpushed revision. A pass of the gates or the checks is filled green as its pill is (ruling 491); an approval keeps the ink alone, as its quiet pill does. The rows are drawn by a plain function rather than a component each, so they add no component renders of their own (ruling 457). **(c)** *A pass folds its gate table.* On a passing run the gates' row keeps the line ("Gates on a91f7c2: 6/6 exit 0 (run by Viberr)") and folds ruling 493's table behind "Show all" (`aria-expanded` and `aria-controls`; "Show all gates" to a screen reader); every other state keeps the table open, because then the table says what to do. Run gates stays in the row, under the table. **(d)** *The rest.* A commit leads with its subject in the text ink and closes with its SHA in the code face. The actions (deliver or push, complete merge, force accept, each container-sized for F19-42) stand together under a hairline. The two freshness facts (F19-22) close the card in small print on a well, their words and tooltips as they were. Full-width hairlines part the sections under the bar, and inset ones the status rows. This narrows ruling 162, whose card wore a "conflicts" pill; narrows ruling 482(e), whose card carried a gates pill in the bar and a Gates row; narrows ruling 491(b) on this card, where a pass is green in its row's mark rather than a pill; and narrows ruling 493(c), whose table stood open on the card after every run. Not changed: any fact, sentence, tooltip, refusal or control on the card, or when each shows. Budgets (ruling 457): the stylesheet grows by 447 B gzip on every route (the card's section, less the rules of the body, the commit list and the buttons it replaces), and the task page's closure by 977 B (that CSS and 530 B of the card's markup); the eight ceilings are raised with that reason. A no-op revalidation renders one component fewer (44 to 43, the button's glyph). Tests: `task-detail-components.test.tsx` "ruling 511" (the bar with the state alone, the title and branch links and no Open on GitHub; the rows in order with their words and tones; the fold, closed on a pass and opened by the click; a failing run's open table; a commit subject first; the actions together and the facts last), the card's earlier tests moved onto its new anatomy (F31-1, ruling 482, F19-22, UI-36 with a merged PR's pill filled on the bar, LV-09, C1 in `task-disposition.test.tsx`), and `app.css.test.ts` "ruling 511" (no hairline under the bar; the marks' inks and fills; the facts' weight and well; the 24 px targets; the chevron), each red by canary. Checked in Chromium on the dev server with the demo seed and one task added for the failing states: VIB-142 (a pass, folded and open), that task (a failing gate, failing checks, changes requested, a conflict and an unpushed revision), a merged PR (VIB-139), a branch with no PR (VIB-151) and a task with no branch (VIB-148), in both themes and at 390 px. axe (wcag2a, wcag2aa, wcag22aa) finds nothing on VIB-142 with the fold open or shut, on the failing task, on VIB-139 or on VIB-151, in either theme. VIB-142's card stands 504 px where it stood 776 px.

512. **Every test meets one value bar, and the suite was audited against it end to end** (owner, 2026-09-27: "let's work on our testing infra end to end using this skill's guidelines https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/main/.agents/skills/test-audit/SKILL.md. Go until you're done, you can break things if you must, no backwards compatibility needed."). The suite had grown to 520 test files and 266 K lines, `e2e/` included, against 226 K lines of production code. Each pass added a test per finding; the same contract was proven again in the server suite, the route suite and the component suite; and exports, reset hooks and injected parameters existed only so a test could reach inside a module. Decided: **(a)** *The bar.* A test earns its place by protecting a contract a person, an agent or a file on disk would notice. Before one is added or changed it answers four questions (what it protects, which edit breaks it, why nothing already catches it, and that it needs no seam only a test calls), is checked against the junk patterns, and stays only when the retention bar names the contract it alone guards. The text lives once, in `docs/development/testing.md` §0. `AGENTS.md` and `contributing.md` §7 point at it, and the `test-audit` skill (`.claude/skills/test-audit/SKILL.md`, adapted from OpenClaw's under its MIT licence, `THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md`) carries the audit workflow around it. It extends ruling 458(m). **(b)** *One owner per contract.* Each contract has one test, at the strongest boundary that reaches it: governed logic in its server suite through the real writers, what a route adds in the route suite, rendering in the component suite, what only a browser or the shipped image shows in `e2e/`, and a figure in one perf budget. Another layer gets a test only for a risk of its own. **(c)** *No test-only production code.* An export, a `*ForTests` hook, a parameter or a re-export that only tests use is removed, and its test moves to the public path; production code whose only callers are tests is deleted. What stays was kept on purpose, each with the reason recorded when it was judged: a hook that resets or stops process-global state (a lease map, a timer, a cache) where a test in the file needs a fresh instance; a way to reach or wait for work that a timer or a fire-and-forget call otherwise hides (`releaseDependents`, `releaseTask`, `whenProjectGatesIdle`); a pure function whose table of inputs the public path cannot reach cheaply (`classifyReviewerVerdict`, `deliveredWorkEvidence`, the Codex plan's `operatorPlanSchemaFor`); and two seams with no real boundary yet, `ownOperatorRunForTests` until a test can reach ruling 357's lease through a real delivery, and `openStuckLoopPacketForTest`, the only way into ruling 326's fallback, which no public input is known to reach. **(d)** *The audit.* Fifteen read-only lanes along production owner boundaries read every test file at `13b06a79` and recorded each candidate with its keeper and history. Editors applied the candidates lane by lane. The suite went from 520 test files and 9,264 tests to 510 and 8,800, and from 265.7 K lines to 255.2 K; `e2e/` went from 79 tests to 67. 158 exports left production modules, un-exported with their tests moved to the public path or deleted with the code only a test called, and production code is 504 lines shorter. The second pass compared all 600 deleted titles with the keepers they named: 26 contracts had lost their last proof and were restored, each as one assertion or row in its keeper and each red under a mutation of its production owner.
