A review of the finished branch found more tests that could not fail and seams the lanes had missed, and fixed them the same way. The full suite runs in 82–85 s where it took 96 s, and `npm run e2e`'s tests in 44 s where they took 51 s. **(e)** *What the audit fixed rather than deleted.* Tests that passed for the wrong reason now fail on the edit they name, each red-checked. They include a redaction proof whose fake secret a token pattern caught anyway; negative controls refused by a different guard than the one named (a non-member where a viewer was meant, an RBAC refusal before the last-admin guard, a project gate signed in as a member of no project); self-comparisons, tautologies and conditionals that could pass without asserting; and names that promised a case the input never reached. Eight source greps became behaviour tests: ruling 129's base refresh, ruling 179's work revision, the project rulings reaching the operator and a specialist, the migration CHECK scan (now boot's positive control), UX19-4's heading, the activity recogniser, and the diverged-branch remedy each door prints. Two tests no longer depend on the host: the wiped-volume credential tests failed on every macOS checkout, and a notifications test asserted only in the host's time zone. **(f)** *Harness.* `vitest.config.ts` sets `hookTimeout` beside `testTimeout`, one 20-second budget for tests and hooks. A hook that seeds the demo store kept vitest's 10-second default, which is how whole files timed out under load. A per-test timeout at or below the budget is removed; one above it stays only for a test that waits on a real process. `setupAppTest().cookieFor` and the demo seed hash each password once instead of on every sign-in. **(g)** *Kept, and left, on purpose.* The access-control refusal tests in the task page's route suite stay, although a stronger suite drives the same guard: the auto-mode permission check refused their removal, and a duplicate refusal test costs little. Two losses are accepted: which admin-only grant each settings panel follows (both grants are admin-only, so no test can tell them apart until a ruling widens one, and that ruling's change owns the test), and the audit scope tag's one declaration value. **(h)** *Citations.* A ruling's "Tests:" or "Budgets" line may name a test or a budget id this audit folded into a keeper or deleted beside a named keeper, and a ruling's body may name code the audit deleted: ruling 366's `foldWaits`, whose fold `createConsoleFolder` has done since ab65e7ab, and ruling 468's `primeRepoAccessForTests`, whose test now binds a PAT and answers through `fakeGithubFetch`. The ruling text is not rewritten (the convention above); the commit that moved the test says where it went. Three budget ids went, each because an exact pin already fails on any change the ceiling would catch: `render:css.main-thread-infinite-loops` (ruling 499's 1 → 3; `app.css.perf.test.ts` pins the three selectors themselves) and the two `console:sse.run-line-frames-per-line-*` ids (LIVE-5; `run-events.server.test.ts` pins one frame on the task's own stream and none on the board's). No ceiling was raised. Not changed: any product behaviour, except two repairs the tests exposed: ruling 507's selection stamp, because its test failed on a clean checkout (two account selections in one millisecond tied, and the random id decided the active account), and the macOS sign-in rule in `backendAccountHealth`, which now holds for Claude alone (a Codex account home without its `auth.json` read as signed in on a macOS host, and a run then started with no credential, because Codex signs in to that file and a run copies only it); `.github/workflows/ci.yml`, which has run no job since 2026-09-07 because GitHub refuses to start them over the account's billing (`testing.md` §1), so the local gates are the gates. Checked on the final tree: `npm run lint`, `npm run typecheck`, `npm test` (510 files, 8,800 tests, twice), `npm run build` with `measure-routes.mjs --check` (every ceiling held; none moved), and `npm run e2e` (68 passed, the setup included).

513. **The write cache knows its own write by the file it left there, never by the clock** (owner, 2026-09-27: "make the repair recognise its OWN write by file identity instead of a clock window"). `write-cache.server.ts` repairs VirtioFS stale reads (VIB-1, 2026-07-17: a verdict's locked read-modify-write, 2 ms after the reviewer's reply landed, read the pre-reply bytes and its write erased the reply). It remembered the content this process last wrote per path and the process clock at the write (`wroteAtMs`), and it took a read that disagreed for a stale copy of that write while the file's mtime stood at most 100 ms past `wroteAtMs`. Two defects followed. Any other writer that landed inside that window (a restore through `restoreStoreFile`, a person's editor, a test re-seeding with `writeFileAtomic`) read as stale, and the next locked read-modify-write silently put the app's write back over it. And the check set the file system's clock against the process's, so a skew past 100 ms between a Docker Desktop host and its container widened the window by the skew one way and switched the repair off the other way. Three suites carried `resetWriteCacheForTests()` after a re-seed to step around the first. With the resets taken out, on the old code, the specialist-run suite's "ruling 157: a dispatch on a held task lifts the hold on the record" failed in each of three runs, and the task page's route suite's "second resolve conflicts (409) instead of crashing" in one run of three; the goal conversion suite passed eleven runs, its re-seeds landing outside the window on that machine. Decided: **(a)** *Identity, not time.* `writeFileAtomic` renames a fresh temp file over the path, so every write puts a new inode there. The writers write through `writeAndRemember(absPath, content)`, which stats the path just before `writeFileAtomic` and right after its rename, and remembers both identities (inode number, size, mtime) with the content: the file the write put there and the file it replaced, because a cached mount can show either, fresh attributes over the old bytes or the old file itself. `freshestContent` repairs a disagreeing read only while the path still shows one of those two. Any other identity is another writer and wins, however soon after the write it landed, and no clock is read. Comparing contents could not have done this: a re-seed can put back exactly the bytes the write replaced, which are the bytes a stale mount serves. **(b)** *One door.* The nine writes that remembered themselves (the task writer's two, the project writer's three, the epic writer's two and the goal conversion's two) call `writeAndRemember`. `rememberWrite` and the project writer's wrapper of it are gone, and `writeFileAtomic` is unchanged for its other callers. **(c)** *What an identity cannot tell apart*, stated in the module rather than left to be found: an in-place rewrite of exactly the written file's size inside the timestamp tick of the write, and a new file that carries the replaced file's whole identity. That takes the replaced file's size, its mtime and its freed inode number, which ext4 hands to the very next file it creates (measured on the container this was built in: a file created right after an atomic replace got the replaced file's inode number). A copy put back with its mtime preserved (`cp -p`, `rsync -a`, `tar`) can carry it, and so can a re-seed of the same bytes inside the tick that file was stamped in, since Linux stamps files from a coarse clock. `restoreStoreFile` stamps a fresh mtime. **(d)** *The resets go.* The three test-side resets are removed, and `resetWriteCacheForTests` with them: no test needs a fresh instance any more (ruling 512(c)). The write cache's own suite writes each test's files into a fresh directory, and its bound tests hold whatever earlier tests left in the map, since that is older still and goes first. Not changed: the repair of both stale views (the writers' stale-read tests pass on the old code and the new), the warn line and its field names, the 500-path bound, and the parse memo. Tests: `write-cache.server.test.ts` "repairs a stale read of our own write" (fresh attributes over the bytes it replaced; the file it replaced, served again through `staleViewOf` in `test-support/stale-mount.ts`; the first again with this process's clock 10 s behind the file system's) and "another writer wins however soon after ours it lands" (a re-seed that puts back, as a new file, exactly the bytes ours replaced; a person's editor saving over ours in place). The clock row and both writer rows are red on the old code; leaving either identity out, or repairing whatever identity the path shows, turns the rows that need it red. The task and project writers' stale-read tests make their stale view with `staleViewOf`, since rewriting the file in place is another writer now; each goes red when its writer stops reading through the repair. Checked: `npm run lint`, `npm run typecheck` and `npm test` (510 files: 8,790 passed, 1 skipped, and the same 11 failures the unchanged tree shows in the same container, which runs as root), and each of the three suites run whole five times: the task page's route suite 66 of 66 and the goal conversion suite 28 of 28 every time, the specialist-run suite 162 of 163, its one failure ruling 485's checkout that cannot be replaced, which fails the same way on the unchanged tree whether run as root or as an unprivileged user.

514. **Saving a signed-in MCP server sends no credential its editor stopped showing, and a refusal about the credential is said at that field** (owner, 2026-09-27: "can't save and retest after the mcp oauth login, I think this is for API key login but confising in UX sense", with a screenshot of cloudflare-api's editor reading "Signed in (expires in 60 minutes, renews itself) · mcp.cloudflare.com" above its write tools, `execute` selected, and under them the refusal "cloudflare-api is signed in with OAuth. Sign it out first to use a pasted credential instead."; amends 469). Measured in Chromium against the dev server and ruling 469's in-test OAuth server (`test-support/mcp-oauth-server.ts`, started on its own on a loopback port): add the server bare (its probe records "needs sign-in"), open its editor, paste a key into Credential, then Sign in and approve. The editor turned to "Signed in" by itself (469(b)) and put its sentence where the field was (469(e)), but `McpModal` kept the field's value in state and posted it with every save: `mcp-save` carried `cred=a-pasted-api-token-123`, `saveMcpServer` refused a pasted credential over the live sign-in, and Save & re-test failed at the form's foot, under the write tools, about a credential the form no longer showed, whatever else the save changed. A value the browser fills into the field before the sign-in does the same (inferred, not reproduced). Decided: **(a)** *The draft goes with the field.* While the field gives way to the sentence (signed in, HTTP, the endpoint as saved), the editor holds no credential draft and no "Remove the stored credential" intent: it drops both while rendering, so a save of a signed-in server posts a blank credential (keep what is stored, which the sign-in emptied) and saves everything else, and a sign-out, or an edited endpoint, brings the field back empty rather than holding the old key, where a paste would land beside it. It is 469(e)'s "a sign-in that lands drops a pasted credential" applied to the one not saved yet. The server's refusal stays, for the controller's `save_mcp_server` and for an editor whose page has not read the sign-in yet. **(b)** *A refusal about one form field names it.* `AppError.fieldValidation(field, message)` carries the form field it is about, and `appErrorResponse` answers `{ ok: false, error, field }` (no `AppError` named a field before, so no other refusal changes). `saveMcpServer`'s two credential refusals, the 8-character floor (F20-7) and a key over a live sign-in, name `cred`. The org-settings modals' `useModalAction` keeps the field beside the error, and the MCP editor says a `cred` refusal under the credential input (`role="alert"`, the input `aria-invalid` and described by it, so the shared invalid border applies) instead of at the form's foot; typing in the field, or toggling "Remove the stored credential", clears it, as the other inputs clear theirs. A refusal that names another field, or none, stays at the foot. Not changed: the refusal's words, and the other fields' refusals (a name, an endpoint, a scope), which still read at the foot. Deliberate residual: an editor whose page missed the sign-in's live update still reads "Needs sign-in" beside that refusal until the page reads the row again, because a refused save does not revalidate the page (ruling 457). Tests: `mcp-sign-in.test.tsx` "a pasted credential and an OAuth sign-in in one editor (ruling 514)" (the owner's steps through a stub page whose row reads signed in once the start answers: Save & re-test posts a blank credential with the write tools and no `clearCred`; a sign-out brings the field back empty; a credential refusal under its field and a name clash at the foot, with the input's `aria-invalid` and description), `mcp-oauth.server.test.ts` (the refusal over a live sign-in names `cred`), `resources.server.test.ts` F20-7 (the floor names `cred`), `form-action.server.test.ts` (`appErrorResponse` answers the field). Canaries, each seen red and restored byte for byte: no drop (the save posts the pasted key and the sign-out shows it); a blank sent only at save (the sign-out test); the refusal's field ignored (the conflict at the foot); every refusal sent to the field (the name clash under it); each server refusal without its field, and the payload without it. Checked in Chromium, dark and light: before, the refusal of the owner's screenshot; after, the same steps save "cloudflare-api saved: 4 tools discovered · signed in with OAuth · 2 marked as write tools", and with the page's live updates blocked the refusal reads under the credential field. (`app/features/org-settings/resource-modals.tsx`, `resource-helpers.ts`, `use-org-action.ts`, `app/server/errors/app-error.server.ts`, `app/server/auth/form-action.server.ts`, `app/server/org/resources.server.ts`.)

515. **An account's name never runs under its buttons, and a long token stays inside the box that names it** (owner, 2026-09-27: "clipping issue", with a screenshot of Profile → Agent accounts' Other Claude accounts list, where "realvega1534@gmail.com" ran under its row's Use this account button). Measured in Chromium against the dev server with the screenshot's two Claude accounts: the card is 473px wide at every desktop width (Profile's two columns), and the row was the connections list's flex row (`.conn-row`), whose text column (`flex: 1` over a 150px floor) got what the row's three buttons left, 171px. An address has no place to wrap, and this one is 182px, so it painted 11px under the button. Decided: **(a)** *An account row stacks.* The name and its facts, then the row's buttons in the card's manage row (`.cred-manage`), then its rename form when open: the order the account in use has above it. Every row reads the same whatever its name's length, where a row that dropped its buttons only under a name too wide for the line would have mixed the two shapes in one list. The name keeps one line and ends in an ellipsis only where the row is narrower than it (a phone and a long address), with the whole name as its `title`. **(b)** *A long token breaks inside its own box.* Looking for the same flaw beside it: in Instance settings → Sign-in & SSO, a Google client ID (one 59-character token after its hyphen, `…apps.googleusercontent.com`) ran out of its row's text column into the pills at every width, and over the "off" pill and past the screen at 390px; at 320px a long address ran out of the account in use's green line, and past the card in "Disconnect <address>?", whose confirm button already broke it (interface review 2026-09-24, layo-1). The connection row's text column (`.conn-main`), the credential line's sentence (`.cred-ok`, `.cred-warn`) and the confirm card's title and sentence take `overflow-wrap: anywhere`, as the row's mono lines already did (acce-10). Not changed: the connections and SSO rows' layout, every button, its words and its order, and the account ceiling. Budgets (ruling 457): the stylesheet grows by 40 B gzip on every route, and Profile's closure by 51 B (the same CSS and the row's markup); the eight ceilings are raised with that reason. Tests: `app.css.test.ts` "ruling 515" (an account row is a block, and its name one line with an ellipsis) and "acce-10" (five selectors more break a long token), each red by canary. Checked in Chromium, dark and light, from 1440px to 320px: the screenshot's row reads the address, then its facts on one line, then Use this account, Rename and Disconnect; an address wider than the row ends in an ellipsis; a row whose sign-in file is gone carries its two sign-ins the same way; the Codex card's list matches; the rename form opens under the buttons; and the SSO row, the green line and the dialog keep their tokens inside. (`app/features/profile/agent-accounts-panel.tsx`, `app/app.css`.)

516. **The controller's suggestions are rows, the glyph of what each is about, the sentence and an arrow, at the foot of an empty dock** (owner, 2026-09-27: "make thiese suggestions better by shadcn stuff research", with a screenshot of the akin website board's dock: the scope's sentence at the top and ruling 314's three examples under it). Measured in Chromium against the dev server's demo board: each example was a `--surface` box outlined in `--border-control`, the outline the sheet keeps for inputs (3.44:1), with its sentence at 12px, so the empty dock read as three text fields over a fourth, the composer; two of the three board sentences wrapped in the 400px panel, and the block sat at the top of the transcript with the rest of its height empty under it. The references, read from their source: a suggestion that is a whole sentence a click sends is a full-width row or card in every kit, never a pill (AI Elements' `Suggestion` is an outline pill in a row that scrolls sideways and never wraps, which suits a short label, and Vercel's own chat template draws its sentences as two columns of cards); shadcn's `Item` is a leading glyph, the content and a trailing action, with a fill on hover; assistant-ui lists its suggestions under the composer, each a borderless row with a leading `>` mark; ReUI's chat blocks give each row a muted glyph for the task it starts. Decided: **(a)** *A row, not a box.* The three examples are one framed list (`--border`, `--radius-box`, its rows inset 4px so their corners are concentric) of borderless rows. A row is the glyph of what the example is about in `--muted`, the sentence at the body size (.88rem) in `--fg`, and an arrow in `--placeholder`, both marks on the sentence's first line however many it wraps to. Under a fine pointer the row fills `--tint-hover`, the glyph takes `--fg`, and the arrow turns `--blue-pressed` and steps 2px forward (not under reduced motion), as the review queue's "Review ›" does; the .99 press is kept. The glyphs are the app's own: the board's "waiting on you" hand and blocked mark, a clock, the pencil of a draft, the List view's three lines for where a task stands, the Insights pulse for cost, and the Agents glyph. They and the arrow are drawn, never read: a button's name is still exactly the sentence it sends. **(b)** *Where it sits.* In the dock the scope's sentence takes the middle of the transcript's space and the list its foot, over the composer; on the controller pages the list stays in the empty hero under its sentence, 30rem wide. **(c)** *The words.* Each keeps its intent and gets shorter: "What's waiting on me, and what's waiting on an agent?" (was "What is waiting on me right now, and what is waiting on an agent?"), "Draft a task this board is missing, but don't create it." (was "Draft a task for work this board is missing, but do not create it."), "Where does this task stand, and who is waiting on whom?" (was "Summarise where this task stands and who is waiting on whom."), "Draft a directive for this task's agent, but don't send it." (was "Draft a directive for the agent on this task, but do not send it."), "What's blocking <KEY>?", "What's blocked across every project I can see?" and "Show me the agent profiles on this instance and what each can do." (was "…what each one can do."). "Which tasks have been open longest, and why?" and "What did agent runs cost this week, by project?" are unchanged. Not taken from the references: the rows do not stagger in, because the dock's body mounts on every open and a panel the tab remembers open appears in place with no entrance (ruling 459, F24); and the list stays while the person types, where assistant-ui hides it, because ruling 259 already keeps a typed draft through a click on an example. Not changed: ruling 314's three per scope, the third a DO, a click that sends with the sentence as `submit`'s parameter, and the hold while a message is on its way or the composer can't send; ruling 419(g)'s one module, which now also draws the list for both composers (`ControllerExampleList`). Budgets (ruling 457): the stylesheet grows by 159 B gzip on every route, and the controller page's closure by 300 B (the same CSS and the list's markup); the eight ceilings are raised with that reason. Tests: the ruling 314 and 419(g) cases name the new sentences, and the dock's finds its example by the sentence alone (red by canary when the glyph carries a text alternative). Checked in Chromium, dark and light: the dock on a board and on a task at 1280px, the 375px and 320px sheets, and both controller pages; axe finds nothing on the list with its enabled look in either theme, and the accessibility and dock e2e specs pass against the production build. (`app/features/controller/controller-examples.tsx`, `controller-dock-panel.tsx`, `controller-page.tsx`, `app/app.css`.)

517. **A repository reading speaks only for the repository it was taken of, and a failing one is taken again** (owner, 2026-09-27: "still repo not found error in live", with a screenshot of a board's banner reading "akin-ozer/akin-website · repo not found. Agents clone the repository before they work, so runs in this project fail until GitHub can serve it."; extends U33-2). Read from the code and from GitHub, not from the live instance: the owner's account holds `akin-ozer/website` (private, pushed 2026-09-26 22:27 UTC) and no `akin-ozer/akin-website`. The banner and Home's repository pill read `project_github_health`, one row per project, which two probes wrote: project creation's and the GitHub page's (behind its 30-second memo). Nothing else wrote it, and only a project's deletion cleared it. So a repair in Project settings (`repairProjectRepo`), which probes the new repository with the bound credential and refuses one it cannot see, dropped the memo and left the row: the board kept naming the old repository as not found, and Home drew that verdict beside the new name. An edit of `project.md`'s `repo` did the same. And a repository created on GitHub after its project, or a token given access to it, changed nothing until someone opened the GitHub page. The reconcile poller (P11-14) asks GitHub every five minutes, but only about projects with a branched task, which a project whose clone fails never has. Decided: **(a)** *A reading is of a repository.* `readRepoHealthMany`, and `readRepoHealth` through it, joins `projects` and returns a reading only when its repository is the one the project points at now, compared without case as GitHub compares names. A reading of any other repository reads as no reading, as one never taken does. A renamed repository's `connected` reading carries GitHub's new name and so reads as none, which every surface draws as it draws `connected`. **(b)** *A repair records its probe.* A probed repair records `connected` for the new repository (its default branch and `private`, which the repair's probe now reads) once `project.md` is written. An unprobed repair (no credential bound) records nothing, and (a) keeps the old reading off every surface. **(c)** *The poller takes a failing reading again.* Each tick, and at boot, `recheckUnreachableRepos` runs `checkRepoAccess` for every non-archived project whose reading the board's banner and Home's pill show and records the answer, except `network_unavailable`: an outage is not an answer, and recording it would take the banner off a repository that is still missing, with nothing left to take the quiet reading again. A healthy project spends no call here, and a warning can clear or change here but never appear. The board still never calls GitHub to render. **(d)** *The surfaces' own test, written a third time.* "Shown" is `connectionPill`'s `risk` or `blocked` arm, the test the banner (`repoAccessNotice`) and Home's line (`RepoLine`) each make. Both carry a note that the two lines belong beside `connectionPill`, but moved there and shared, they cost Home 14 B, the board 36 B and the task page 27 B gzip, against ceilings that only move down (ruling 457). So `repo-health.server.ts` writes them out once more, and no client file changes. Not changed: the banner's words and link, the GitHub page's probe and memo, creation's probe, and U33-2's rule that the board reads a row rather than GitHub. Tests: `repo-health.server.test.ts` "ruling 517" (a reading of another repository is none; the same repository in another case is kept; the U33-2 cases now read a projected project and name its repository, which their fixture did not), `settings-actions.server.test.ts` "ruling 517" (the repair's probe is the reading read back), `reconcile-poller.server.test.ts` "ruling 517" (a failing reading GitHub now answers is recorded and a healthy one is not asked about on the next tick; an unreachable GitHub keeps the failure). Canaries, each seen red and restored: drop the repository comparison; drop the repair's record; drop the re-check from the poll; re-check every reading; record an outage. (`app/server/github/repo-health.server.ts`, `reconcile-poller.server.ts`, `app/features/project-settings/settings-actions.server.ts`.)

518. **The operator is one agent, called Operator, with no role** (owner, 2026-09-27: "no need to call it coordinator as well. It's a unqiue agent called Operator that's it. NO other roles needed.", with a screenshot of the task page's Execution profile, whose OPERATOR cell read "Coordinator" over "Decides which agent runs at each stage…"). The operator went by more than its name. The task page's OPERATOR cell put a hard-coded "Coordinator" in its value slot. The shipped template and the seed catalog gave it the role "Task coordinator", which its rows on Agents and Policy, its hero's pill and its glyph's tooltip showed; an operator whose role was empty fell back to "Orchestration", which also labelled a roster group of its own above "Agent profiles"; and its scope line read "System role · one per active task". Its editor asked for a Name and a Role like any agent profile's, and a save copied both onto the project's deployment with that scope line, so a project could rename the operator or give it another role. The fallback persona began "You are the Operator: the coordinator for one Viberr task", a specialist was told to close its report by tagging `@operator` "so the coordinator picks your results up", an `@operator` comment resolved to the role "coordinator", and Policy's autonomy note read "the operator (Operator) runs…". Decided: **(a)** *One name.* Every surface calls it Operator (`OPERATOR_NAME`, `deployment-view.server.ts`): `effectiveProfileView` gives the operator that name whatever its template or its deployment says. The task page's cell drops "Coordinator", so its kicker names the agent over the since line and what it does, and Policy's note reads "the operator runs at full autonomy…" (`OperatorAutonomyState.operatorName` is gone). **(b)** *No role.* The profile file requires `role` of every kind but the operator; an operator file that still carries one (a store copy from before this ruling) parses without it and warns of drift (`agent_profile.unknown_field`). The view gives the operator an empty role and `profileRoleLabel` gives it no label, so its rows, hero and glyph show the name alone; the "Orchestration" fallback and group label are gone, and "Agent profile" (`DEFAULT_SPECIALIST_ROLE_LABEL`) is the one fallback left. The shipped template and the catalog drop "Task coordinator", and an `@operator` target carries no role. **(c)** *No copy of either.* A deployment may not rename the operator, give it a role or reword its scope line (`OPERATOR_FIXED_FIELDS`). Resolving a deployment drops the three from its definition (`deploymentRuntimeIdentity`, so every reader agrees); the editor has no Name or Role field for the operator (Backend takes the first focus) and sends neither; `updateAgentProfile` writes none of the three for it, whatever an older tab posts; and boot (`ensureBaseAgentsDeployed`) removes the copies a save stored before this ruling, logging each project it cleaned. A save's snapshot no longer counts the three as fields still to fork, so the editor stops saying "Saving forks this profile" once one exists (`tracksTemplateLive`, ruling 479(g)). **(d)** *The scope line.* "System role · one per active task" said "role" too. The line under the operator's name reads "Built in · runs on every task" (`OPERATOR_SCOPE`), fixed in the view like the name, because `npm run seed` writes a template copy that boot never refreshes. The shipped template says the same (the parity test ties the two), and its outgoing hash is recorded so boot refreshes an unedited copy. **(e)** *The prompts.* The fallback persona opens "You are the Operator for one Viberr task.", and the reporting line reads "so the operator picks your results up". Nothing rendered, server-built or seeded calls the operator a coordinator, and the copy-ban test scans code and seed assets for the noun. Not changed: the operator's description ("Decides which agent runs at each stage, from the stage the task is at and the one it came from.") and its doctrine; everything else its editor edits (backend, model, effort, autonomy, stages, description, persona, capabilities and grants); "coordinate" and "coordination" for what it does; the controller's role ("Instance manager"); and an agent profile still needs a name and a role. Tests: the Agents page's roster, hero and editor (`agents-page.test.tsx`, "ruling 518"), the file parse (`agent-profile-file.server.test.ts`), the view and its fork signal on a store and a save from before the ruling (`agents-query.server.test.ts`), the boot pass (`base-agents.server.test.ts`), the save with an older tab's name and role and with neither (`agents-route.server.test.ts`), the refresh hash and the scope parity (`default-assets.server.test.ts`, `operator-parity.server.test.ts`) and the copy ban (`copy-ban.test.ts`), each red by its canary. Checked: lint, typecheck and the unit suite, whose remaining failures fail the same way on main in the same container. Not measured: the route budgets (ruling 457) and screenshots of the result, because the production build could not run in the session that made the change; the before screenshots were taken on main. (`app/server/agents/deployment-view.server.ts`, `app/features/agents/`, `app/features/policy/`, `app/features/task-detail/execution-profile.tsx`, `app/server/files/agent-profile-file.server.ts`, `app/server/seed/`, `app/server/runtimes/operator-run.server.ts`, `app/server/tasks/specialist-run.server.ts`, `agent-reply.server.ts`.)

519. **The operator moves a task into Review itself, and says why on the move** (owner, 2026-09-27: "review should be a automatic state not on confirmation", with a screenshot of a task's Operator recommendations card holding one pending STAGE card, "Move the task to Review", with Apply and Dismiss). The Standard template declared In Progress → Review an `approval` boundary, so under ruling 151 every move into Review the operator decided on became a card a person applied: the operator's own `transition_stage` filed one whatever its `stage-transitions` grant, and a supervised delivery that left none got Viberr's (ruling 58). Decided: **(a)** *The template.* `GOVERNED_TEMPLATE`'s In Progress → Review is `auto`, by "Operator, when the work is ready for review" (`TEMPLATE_REVIEW_ENTRY_BY`), so the operator crosses it under either autonomy, and on the Standard board a person's one gate is acceptance (review → done, `human` and locked). Ruling 151 is unchanged: a board that declares the move an `approval` still gets the card. The balanced preset is the template; the strict preset turns every `auto` short of the last stage into `approval`, this one included, so a strict board still asks at every advance. **(b)** *Boards already created.* Once at boot, after the rescan and before the watcher, `convertTemplateReviewEntry` gives a board the template's edge where its edge is still the template's old one: `approval`, with the words only project creation wrote ("Operator transition request, with evidence attached"; the Policy page writes `defaultTransitionBy`'s words when a person sets a boundary), on a board that is not strict (`humanGatesPreWorkAdvance`). Each conversion is a `project.policy.boundary_changed` audit row by the system (`ruling: 519` in its details), which the project's activity and the Policy page's last-change line show. An approval a person chose and every strict board stay as they are. A converted edge carries the new words, so a second boot changes nothing, and a project that fails is logged and tried again on the next boot. **(c)** *No card after a delivery where the move is `auto`.* `recordDeliveredNextStep` files nothing when the edge from the task's stage into the review stage is `auto`, which narrows ruling 58 to boards where a person approves the move. The drive that delivered goes on (the tool reply names the PR and the doctrine says to move the task), and a drive that stops at a stage with an `auto` way out is nudged once by the settle-time backstop, which ruling 58 recorded as not covering this moment. **(d)** *The reason is on the move.* The card carried the operator's reason, so the move now does: `transitionStage` quotes it under the operator's `transition` event the way ruling 381 quotes a person's, and the `task.transition` audit row's `reason` already held it. The `transition_stage` tool and the Codex plan's `reason` field say where it is shown. **(e)** *In Progress can be stranded now.* The settle-time backstop reads the stage's way out, so on the Standard board In Progress is a stage a drive can stop at with nothing following up: a drive that ends there with no agent run live (`settleWaitingAfterOperator`), no packet, no card, no wait and no pending schedule gets one nudge, and a nudge that holds again records the hold, as at Ready. Not changed: ruling 151; the edge into the terminal stage; the operator's prompt, which reads each boundary off `nextStages`; and a card already pending on a task, which stays until a person applies or dismisses it or the task moves (any move prunes pending transition cards). Tests: `operator-actions.server.test.ts` "ruling 519" (a supervised operator with `stage-transitions: recommend` moves the task into Review, files no card, quotes its reason on the event, and the audit row says `auto`, `operator` and the reason); `delivery-actionable.server.test.ts` "ruling 519" (a supervised delivery on the Standard board files no card, counts no decision and rings no bell); `review-entry-conversion.server.test.ts` (an old board converts once, on the record; a strict board and a person's approval are left alone); `project-create.server.test.ts` (strict gates the move into Review, balanced does not); `policy-route.server.test.ts` (the Policy page reads the move as `auto` and can set it back to `approval`). The suites whose contract needs a person to approve the move into Review, or an In Progress the backstop leaves quiet, name that board (`REVIEW_APPROVAL_WORKFLOW` and `approveReviewEntry` in `test-support/test-store.ts`). Canaries, each seen red and restored: the template's edge back to `approval`; the operator's quote dropped; the `auto` return in `recordDeliveredNextStep` dropped; the conversion's write skipped; its strict check dropped; its match on the boundary alone. (`app/shared/workflow/templates.ts`, `app/server/seed/review-entry-conversion.server.ts`, `app/server/boot.server.ts`, `app/server/tasks/task-actions.server.ts`, `operator-toolkit.server.ts`, `app/server/runtimes/operator-run.server.ts`, `app/features/home/project-create.server.ts`.)

520. **The task page's Current state card draws the property grid Details draws: one label column, every value on one left edge, each led by its mark** (owner, 2026-09-27: "these look unorginized somehow not aligned, not standard etc. please make it look better", with a screenshot of the card: Stage a bordered "Review" pill with a caret, Waiting on "Agent work" in large violet, Last activity "just now" in bold, Owner an avatar, "Arda (you)" and a cross, Repo "akin-ozer/website", over "Accept completion → Done" and "Not acceptable yet. Waiting on 1 required reviewer approval of the current revision."; narrows 501). Measured in Chromium against the dev server with the demo seed at 1440 px: the card's five values were right-aligned and set five ways. The stage was a bordered pill (the board card's trigger); who the task waits on 14px bold in blue or violet (`.by-human`, `.by-agent`); the last activity 14px bold; the owner's first name 12px bold between a 22px avatar and the release cross; and the repository 14px bold in the display face, because `.kv-row .v`'s font family overrode the `.mono` on the same element. No two values started at the same x, the cross rather than the name ended the owner's row, a hairline ran under every row, and "Waiting on" broke over two lines to make room for a hold. The Details panel under the card (ruling 501) and the PR card's facts over it (ruling 511(d)) right-aligned theirs too. Compared with Jira's issue details and Notion's page properties, which draw a label column of one width with every value starting on one left edge beside it, and Linear's issue sidebar, which leads each value with its glyph and makes it a ghost button. None needs a new component; a registry stays a reference (ruling 166). Decided: **(a)** *One grid.* `.kv.props` is a two-column grid: a 5.5rem label column, a .75rem gap and the values, with no hairline between rows. Current state draws its facts as `.kv.props` rows, the rows Details draws, so the side column's property panels share one value line; the epic page's Details (also `.kv.props`) follows, its creator's date a step quieter than the name, and the PR card's two freshness facts take the same label column, so their words start on that line too. A value's lines are 20px and start 6px down the 32px row, so a value that wraps (a long hold, a long label list, an epic's creator and date) keeps its first line on its label's; a ghost trigger's padding and border hang outside those lines and past the column's left edge, so its words sit where a text value's do. A value is one run of text, so it wraps between words, and a held entry's key stays whole: in the narrower column Chromium broke "VIB-151" after its hyphen, and no CSS property prevents that, so the card sets each entry's label in a `.hold-ref` span. **(b)** *Each value is led by its mark*, in a 16px column: the stage's dot; who owes the next move in the board card's marks (ruling 365), the hand for a human or a goal edit, the clock for a schedule, the ring for a queued run, the live pulse for agent work (ruling 457's dot, stilled under reduced motion) and the ban for other work (ruling 131); the activity pulse for the last activity; the owner's avatar; and the GitHub mark for the repository, which is printed in the code face. **(c)** *One size and weight.* Every value reads at the body size and 400 in the text ink. The tone moves from the words to the mark: the hand takes `--blue-pressed` and a queued run's ring `--agent-dark`, where the whole phrase used to (the pulse keeps the house's violet), and the other marks take `--faint`; a schedule's words keep ruling 225's muted ink, and "(you)" reads a step quieter than the name. An empty value is the quiet line ruling 501(b) gives Details ("Nothing", "Nothing on the timeline yet", "Unowned"), and "Assign me" is the invitation Details makes ("Add dependency"), a ghost trigger led by its plus. **(d)** *The stage is a ghost trigger.* In the row the stage menu's trigger has no chrome at rest, the hover fill and a hairline under the pointer and a blue edge while open, as a Details value does, and its caret points down, and up while open, as the PR card's fold does. The menu hangs from the trigger's left edge (`StageMenu`'s `align="start"`), so it opens over the values rather than the labels; the board card's menu still hangs from its trigger's right edge. Not changed: any fact, sentence, tooltip or control on the card, or when each shows (the stage menu's stages and keyboard contract, the release cross and its titles, the owner seat's rules of rulings 118 and 127, the wait's words of rulings 131, 138, 225 and 349, the quiet note, and the acceptance and archive dispositions under the rows). This narrows ruling 501, whose rows kept the side column's shape (label left, value right, a hairline between) with the trigger's padding past the right edge. Budgets (ruling 457): the stylesheet grows by 373 B gzip on every route (the grid, the marks and the ghost stage trigger, less the rules they replace), the board's closure by 406 B (that CSS and the menu's `align`) and the task page's by 673 B (that CSS and 300 B of the card's markup); the eight ceilings are raised with that reason. The card's new marks are elements hoisted out of the panel, so a revalidation that re-renders it hands React the same elements and renders no `Icon` again: drawn inline they took `console:task-page.renders-per-noop-revalidation` from 43 to 45, and with the hoist it stays at 43. Tests: `task-side-panels.test.tsx` "ruling 520" (each wait's mark, the board card's, leads its words; a held entry's keys stay whole; the empty values are quiet lines and Assign me a ghost trigger; the repository leads with the GitHub mark in the code face), `stage-menu.test.tsx` "ruling 520" (a property row's menu hangs from the trigger's left edge, a card's from its right), `app.css.test.ts` "ruling 520" (the grid, and the PR facts on its label column; the first line on the label's line and the triggers' hanging padding; the ghost stage trigger at rest, hovered and open, and its caret; the tone on the marks and none on `.by-human` or `.by-agent`; the house's pulse) and "ruling 501" (the trigger's padding past the left edge). Canaries, each seen red and restored byte for byte: the values right-aligned again; the values' padding dropped; the stage trigger's rest rule dropped, or its hanging padding; `.by-agent`'s colour put back; the card's pulse out of the pulse rule; the trigger's margin back on its right; a queued run drawn with the pulse; "Nothing" printed bare; the repository without its code-face span; Assign me a `.btn`; the hold printed as one string, or `.hold-ref`'s nowrap dropped; the menu's `align` arm dropped; the marks drawn inline, and `task-console.perf.test.tsx`'s no-op revalidation renders 45 against 43. Checked in Chromium on the dev server, light and dark: VIB-142 (agent work, owned by the viewer), a task waiting on a human with no owner, one held by three entries, the menu open, hovered and focused, a contributor's view, 390 px (no sideways scroll) and the epic page's Details. Every row's label and its value's first line stand within 1px of each other, except a Details wait list that wraps to a second row of chips, whose 15px chips sit 3px high (4px before). (`app/features/task-detail/task-side-panels.tsx`, `app/ui/stage-menu.tsx`, `app/features/epics/epic-page.tsx`, `app/app.css`.)

521. **The offer to accept a task carries Operator's completion packet: its summary, each reviewer's verdict on the work under review, the screenshots and the change** (owner, 2026-09-27: "up to date reviewer verdicts should be visible on a completion to done packet summarized by Operator, including the UI screenshots, code changes(if small full if not summary of code changes)", with a screenshot of AWS-1's "Decision required" card, whose REVIEWER VERDICT row read "approve on 060fc72: build, test (153 pass), …" above an option to accept AWS-1 now). The decision a person took at the acceptance boundary carried what the operator chose to type into it. On AWS-1 the approval was an observation the operator wrote, text bound to nothing, so nothing on the card could say whether it still described the head that would merge; the change was not on the card (ruling 484's Changes panel stood further down the page, closed); and the reviewer's screenshots were in the attachments panel in the side column. Measured in Chromium on the demo seed: VIB-142's "Accept completion, or send back for one fix?" showed the operator's body and four observations ("Changed 9 files · +412 / -87", validation, branch, a flag) over its options, and nothing else. Decided: **(a)** *The packet.* `completionPacket` in task.md (file-formats §2): the operator's `summary` of what was done against the goal and why it is complete (markdown, under 4,000 characters); `changes`, its summary of the code changes by area, required when the change runs past 200 changed lines (`COMPLETION_SMALL_CHANGE_LINES`, additions plus deletions from `github.changed`) and otherwise left null so the diff is shown whole; and up to six `screenshots`, image attachments of the task named exactly, each with a caption of at most 200 characters. It binds to the review subject (`reviewSubjectId`: the revision id, or `files:<deliveredAt>`) as a verdict does, keeping the head sha for display, so a new revision or a new delivery of files makes it stale. The verdicts and the change are never copied in: the page reads them live beside it. **(b)** *Operator writes it.* `write_completion_packet`, on the `completion-for-acceptance` grant, since the packet exists only to go with an offer; the Codex plan carries it as an action with the summary in `text`, the changes in `reason` and a new `screenshots` field. `writeCompletionPacket` refuses (`noop`) a task with nothing delivered, an empty or oversized summary, a change over 200 lines with no `changes`, more than six screenshots, and a name that is not an image or not among the attachments, listing the images the task has; it writes a `note` titled "Completion packet" ("The operator summarized revision `a91f7c2` for the person who accepts it, with 3 screenshots and a summary of the code changes.") and the audit row `task.completion_packet.written`. `get_task` carries `completionPacket`: its state (`current | stale | none | not_applicable`), the change's lines, whether `changes` is required, the newest 20 image attachments and a note saying what to do. **(c)** *Every operator offer waits for it.* `completionPacketRefusal` refuses (`noop`) the operator's own `accept_completion` inside a drive (either backend, and a `transition_stage` to the terminal stage, which reroutes there), the fold's acceptance card after a move onto the boundary (`requirePacket`), and a decision packet with an `accept_completion` option (after pass 32's boundary check), until the packet describes the current subject: "Write the completion packet for revision `a91f7c2` first (write_completion_packet), then offer VIB-142 for acceptance: the person who accepts it reads your summary, the screenshots you pick and the change beside each reviewer's verdict (ruling 521).", with "The packet on file describes earlier work, so write it again for what is delivered now." for a stale one. It is checked after every acceptance gate, so an offer the gate refuses hears the gate's own sentence. A fold refused this way after a person's move wakes the operator, as one the gate refuses does, and after the operator's own move its reply carries the sentence; either way the drive writes the packet and makes the offer itself. A person's acceptance, the accept dialog and Force accept never wait for it, and a task with nothing delivered is not refused over it. The tools, the Codex system prompt and the shipped operator definition say so (its outgoing hash is recorded so boot refreshes an unedited copy), and the decision tool's observation example no longer suggests a "Reviewer verdict" row. **(d)** *The card.* The task page draws the packet inside the decision that offers acceptance, between its observations and its options, and as its own card where the decision stands while an acceptance recommendation waits or while the task stands at the boundary with a packet written; never on a closed task. "Completion", "Summarized by Operator <time>" and the subject's sha head it. A packet written for earlier work opens with "Operator wrote this for earlier work (<sha>), before <sha> was delivered.", and a missing one reads "Operator has not summarized this work yet. The verdicts and the change below are current." *Reviewers*: the reviewers acceptance waits on, those engaged on the task in engagement order and then those the project's rules require (ruling 178), engaged or not; then anyone else who gave a verdict, marked "not required"; each with its verdict on the subject, "Approved" or "Requested changes" in ruling 491's tones, when, and its reason folded at 72px, or "No verdict on <sha> yet" with its latest verdict on earlier work under a "Stale" tag ("Approved on 3b7a0e1 3h ago, before the work under review was delivered."); and a GitHub approval that carries the gate (R19-B). *Screenshots*: the attachments panel's thumbs with Operator's captions, opening the lightbox; a viewer who may not see attachments sees none, and a count says how many are not shown. *Changes*: "N files changed +a −d", and at 200 lines or fewer ruling 484's reader inline, open from the first paint and reading the diff as the page mounts; past that, "Over 200 lines, so this is Operator's summary" over the summary, and "Show the diff". While the packet carries the reader, the Changes panel steps aside, so the page holds one reader and one set of unsent notes. **(e)** *The loader.* `completionView` is built from the task file, the names the loader already holds (a reviewer's profile name, else the deployed agent's, else its role) and the project's rules as the acceptance affordance read them (`acceptanceStanding`, the one read of project.md), and checks each screenshot by name (`taskAttachmentExists`, a stat rather than a read, so ruling 457's store-read count holds; the attachments list stops at 100). Not changed: the acceptance gate and its refusals; who may accept; the operator's body, observations and options; decisions that offer no acceptance; ruling 484's panel wherever no packet carries the reader. Budgets (ruling 457): the stylesheet grows by 512 B gzip on every route (the card), every route's shell by 69 B more (the task file's `completionPacket` key in the schema the shell parses with) and the task page's closure by 2,014 B in all (those, the card's component, the reader's inline form, the reason's shorter fold and the page placing the card); the task loader's result grows by 234 B on VIB-142 (`completion`: its one required reviewer, no verdict yet, and the change's size), 222 B over both console payload ceilings, which it had come 12 B under since ruling 475; the ten ceilings are raised with that reason. The loader's store reads and SQL statements hold at 31 and 50. Tests: `completion-packet.server.test.ts` (the writer stores the packet for the subject with its note; six refusals write nothing; a large change with its summary; the view's rows, required reviewers first, a stale approval; a project rule's reviewer required though nobody engaged it; screenshots by what the viewer may see, and a packet made stale by a redelivery), `operator-actions.server.test.ts` "ruling 521" (the offer refused until written, and the snapshot's state; a packet for a replaced revision refused with both sentences), `task-actions.server.test.ts` "ruling 521" (the fold files no card without the packet and wakes the operator; with it, the card and no wake), `operator-toolkit.server.test.ts` "ruling 521" (a decision offering acceptance refused until `write_completion_packet` writes it), `operator-run.server.test.ts` "ruling 521" (a Codex plan writes the packet, then offers on it), `project.task.server.test.ts` "ruling 521" (the loader ships the packet with the reviewer's name and the screenshot, and counts a reviewer project.md requires), `completion-packet.test.tsx` (the verdict words and the stale tag; a small change open and read at mount, a large one summarized and read only on a press; captions, the hidden count, the stale and missing notes), `task-disposition.test.tsx` "ruling 521" (inside the decision, the Changes panel stepping aside; its own card beside a recommendation or at the boundary once written, and nowhere else) and the audit table's row. Checked in Chromium on the production build with the demo seed, light and dark: VIB-142 (a 499-line change: the summary, three screenshots, the reviewer's approval, the changes summary and "Show the diff") and DEP-31 (a 58-line change: the diff open, and a reviewer whose approval was of the earlier revision, marked stale). The session had no GitHub credential, so the open diff shows the reader's own failure row ("Could not read PR #74 from GitHub: no GitHub credential is configured for this project."), not the patches. (`app/server/tasks/completion-packet.server.ts`, `app/shared/completion-packet.ts`, `app/schemas/task-file.schema.ts`, `app/server/tasks/operator-actions.server.ts`, `operator-toolkit.server.ts`, `app/server/runtimes/operator-run.server.ts`, `app/server/seed/assets/operator.definition.md`, `app/server/tasks/task-actions.server.ts`, `app/routes/project.task.tsx`, `app/features/task-detail/completion-packet.tsx`, `changes-slot.tsx`, `decision-packet.tsx`, `task-detail-page.tsx`, `app/ui/collapsible.tsx`, `app/app.css`.)

522. **A timeline entry's pictures show their first row, and the rest fold with its text** (owner, 2026-09-27: "comments including attachments still collapses with text but the images can take lots of space, let's make them visible on first row then the rest is collapsed as well, it should be uncollapsed with the text though so this requires good UI/UX from you to implement correctly", with a screenshot of an agent's comment folded behind Show more over two full rows of four pictures; extends 510). Ruling 510's fold clamps a comment's text alone; the files the event's run saved (`ev.attachments`) sat under the card, every one drawn, pictures first. Measured in Chromium against the dev server on a task carrying four such entries: the strip is 1008 px wide at a 1728 px window, four 240 px tiles to a row, and 258 px at 390 px, one to a row. A long comment with ten pictures stood 991 px tall at 1728 px and 2,279 px at 390 px with its text folded; a short one with seven, 462 px and 1,404 px; a completion report with five pictures and a gate log, 453 px and 1,231 px. Decided: **(a)** *The first row stays, the rest fold.* An entry shows as many of its files as stand on its strip's first line, in the strip's order (pictures, then the rest); the rest are not drawn while folded, so they leave the tab order and their pictures do not load. `useFirstRow` (`app/ui/collapsible.tsx`) counts that line from widths: every tile takes one width (a file tile, `.tl-attach-file`, shares a picture's 240 px, capped at the strip, which `app.css.test.ts` now holds them to), so the line holds floor((room + gap) / (tile + gap)) of them, a count that holds whether the rest are drawn or not and follows the strip when the window resizes. Until it has measured (the server's render, a strip laid out at no width) every tile is drawn, as before. **(b)** *One toggle.* A comment's pictures fold with its text: the entry holds one state that the comment's `Collapsible` and the strip both read, so Show more opens the text and every picture at once and Show less folds both. The toggle stays at the foot of the card, above the pictures, so opening it never moves it. It says what it hides beyond the text: "Show more · +6 images" when the text is cut too, the count in the muted, lighter voice (`.md-collapse-more`); "Show 3 more images" when only pictures fold, which a comment with short text now gets for its pictures alone; "files" once anything but a picture is among them; and "Show less" while open. A typed event (a completion report, a gate note) has no card, so its toggle follows its strip and folds the strip alone. An entry whose text is short and whose files fit the first row has no toggle, as before. Folded, the four entries stand 623, 305, 623 and 296 px at 1728 px, and 623, 326, 624 and 337 px at 390 px. **(c)** *Show less keeps its place.* Closing a fold pulled its toggle up by the height folded above it (a long reply's text, or the rows of pictures above a typed event's toggle), so a person who opened a long comment, read to its end and pressed Show less watched the toggle leave the screen, and the next entry landed under the pointer. With the ten-picture comment open and its toggle 120 px above the foot of the window, Show less moved it from 997 to 812 px down at 1728 px, from 780 to 595 at 1440 px, and from 724 to 54 at 390 px, under the sticky header. The toggle (`FoldToggle`) now notes where it stood and the nearest box that scrolls it (`scrollingBox`, taken out of ruling 497's `revealTarget` in `app/ui/use-hash-target.ts`) when pressed to close, and scrolls that box back by what it moved before the browser paints; it stays within a pixel at all three widths. Every fold takes it, the attachments panel's (ruling 510) included; opening moves nothing, and nothing scrolls when no box around the toggle does. **(d)** *No flash.* The fold measures in a layout effect instead of an effect, so a client render (a navigation to the task) paints the folded text and the first row at once, where it drew everything for a frame; a document load still draws everything from the server and folds on hydration, as ruling 510 left it. Not changed: ruling 510's 340 px clamp, its fade and its keyboard rule; the attachment card; the strip's order; a comment's embedded pictures, which are its text. Budgets (ruling 457): the stylesheet grows by 11 B gzip on every route, the task page's closure by 631 B (the toggle that counts and keeps its place, the first-row measure, the timeline's use of both, the shared scrolling-box helper and the same CSS), and the controller's by 25 B (the CSS and the helper its knowledge panel shares), measured on ruling 520's main; the eight ceilings are raised with that reason. Tests: `collapsible.test.tsx` "ruling 522" (the toggle counts what it hides, and shows for pictures alone under short text; closing keeps the toggle where it stood in the box that scrolls it), `task-detail-components.test.tsx` "ruling 522" (a long comment with ten pictures shows four and one toggle in its card, "Show more · +6 images", which opens the text and all ten and folds both; a completion with five pictures and a log shows four, and its toggle under the strip reads "Show 2 more files" and opens every file) and `app.css.test.ts` "ruling 522" (a file tile takes a picture's width, and the strip wraps), each red by canary. Checked in Chromium against the dev server, light and dark, at 1728 and 390 px: each entry folds to its first row with the counts above and opens with its text, and the toggle's accessible name reads "Show more · +6 images". (`app/ui/collapsible.tsx`, `app/ui/use-hash-target.ts`, `app/features/task-detail/timeline.tsx`, `app/app.css`.)

523. **A notification's mark lasts until the person's next press, which takes its anchor out of the URL** (owner, 2026-09-27: "clicking inside the page on anything should clear the highlight borders after notification moving", with a screenshot of a task timeline's Operator comment still in ruling 497's wash and outline after a notification had taken them to it; narrows ruling 497(c)). Ruling 497 marks the place a notification opens (a timeline event's wash and outline, the ring on the packet or the recommendation cards, the border on a Controller page entry) for as long as the URL's hash names it, and nothing on the page took the hash away: the mark outlived every click, key and revalidation, and a reload drew it again. Decided: **(a)** *The next press ends it.* `useHashTarget` (`app/ui/use-hash-target.ts`), the one hook every marked place goes through, listens on the document while the hash names a place it claims, in the capture phase so a control that stops its own event still counts. A pointer pressed anywhere (the marked place included; any button, and touch and pen too) or a key other than a modifier on its own (one the browser reports as the modifier it now holds: Shift, Control, Alt, Meta and their kind) and other than a key held down from before navigates to the same path and search without the hash: the history entry is replaced, the scroll is not reset and the location's state is kept. Every reader of the location lets go at once (the timeline's steps toward an event it has not reached stop too), a reload and Back come back without the mark, and the press goes on to do what it does. A second click on a row about the page on screen is a new location carrying the hash, and it marks the place again as ruling 497(c) says. **(b)** *Taking the hash away reloads nothing.* React Router hands the loaders a navigation that removes a hash (a browser would request the page again), and the revalidation policy's reload for a navigation to the URL on screen compared the path and the search alone, so every such press would have re-run root, the workspace layout and the task page. `samePlace` (`revalidation-policy.ts`) compares the hash too, so a navigation that only takes the hash away re-runs what a live event left owed and nothing else. A link to the URL on screen with no hash on either side reloads as before; one carrying the hash already on screen never reaches the loaders, which React Router skips for a hash it keeps or adds. **(c)** *The focus stays where the link put it.* The timeline gave the marked event its `tabindex="-1"` only while it was marked, and Chromium drops the focus to the body when a focused element loses it, so the keys that scroll `.detail` from it (G7) stopped after the first. The event the latest link named keeps it (`TimelineItem`'s `focusable`); the packet, the recommendation cards and the Controller page's entries always had one. A place focused this way is a region, not a control, so once its mark is gone it paints no focus ring, as `.detail` paints none (`.tl-item`, `.detail-packet`, `.op-recs` and `.ctl-proposal` at `:focus-visible` without `data-targeted`). **(d)** *A Controller page entry is marked by `data-targeted` alone.* `.ctl-proposal:target` is gone: the press takes the hash away with the router's `replaceState`, which never updates `:target`, so an entry a reply's plain `#proposal-` or `#correction-` link opened would have kept its border. That link's fragment navigation reaches the router, and `useHashTarget` marks the entry as it marks a notification's. Not changed: what is marked, how it looks, and the reveal once per navigation (ruling 497). Tests (each red by its canary, the source restored): `timeline-target.test.tsx` "the next press ends the mark (ruling 523)" (a press on the page drops the hash and the mark, keeps `?events=` and the event's tabindex, and the bell's row marks again; a key ends it, a lone modifier and a held key do not; listening for pointers alone, dropping `focusable` or taking every key each turn one red) and `revalidation-policy.test.tsx` "taking the hash away from the URL on screen reloads nothing" (with path and search compared alone, root, the layout and the task page reload). Verified in Chromium on a production build of a demo root, light and dark: the bell's VIB-151 row ringed the packet, a press beside it and one on it each cleared the ring and the hash with no `.data` request, and a reload drew nothing; an event reached through the router was marked and focused, Shift kept the mark, PageUp cleared it and scrolled the page column, and the next PageUp scrolled again with the focus on the event and no ring; a plain `#decision` link marked the packet and a press cleared it. The bundle ceilings rose by what this costs, each with its note: 23 B in the stylesheet every route loads, 207 B on the task page and 171 B on the Controller page, which run the listener, and 14 to 26 B on the other first routes. (`app/ui/use-hash-target.ts`, `app/features/task-detail/timeline.tsx`, `app/features/live-updates/revalidation-policy.ts`, `app/app.css`, `test-support/perf-budgets/bundle.json`.)

524. **The Controller page is one band as tall as the screen, with the run in a column of its own** (owner, 2026-09-27: "this looks bad compared to task view, but it doesn't have the same page limitations so make this page more better for experience it show lots of empty space everywhere. It's not polished", with a screenshot of /controller's Live run card; extends ruling 380, narrows ruling 419(b)). Measured in Chromium on a dev root with a streaming controller turn, before: the standalone page was a 1200px column centred on the screen (120px of empty margin each side at 1440, 360px at 1920); the run card sat above the transcript, its four facts separate boxes floated right of the phase and Hide console and Interrupt on a row of their own under them, the step cut at 44ch with the row half empty; the console under the composer was a 320px box however tall the screen; the transcript was capped at the viewport less 320px and the 340px rail pinned at its own content's height, so each column ended at a height of its own over empty page; and every column kept 80px at its foot for the dock's button, which the controller routes do not render. The screenshot also showed the Elapsed cell reading "03:1" over a clipped glyph and the card's head reading "Controller · Controller". Decided: **(a)** *One band, the run in a column of its own.* Above the 1100px collapse the page is one grid row that fills the height the shell leaves (the standalone page is the screen's height, and up to 1920px wide): the conversation's column (transcript and composer), the run pane (`.ctl-run`) and the rail, now 17rem, each filling it and scrolling itself, so the composer, the console and the rail all end at its foot; a screen shorter than the band's 30rem floor scrolls the page instead. The pane holds the Live run card while a turn streams and ruling 380's archive of settled runs after it, and its console fills what the strip leaves (12rem at the least). A thread that has not run has no pane, and the rail sits beside the conversation. With the console hidden the pane is the strip alone: it goes under the composer and the rail comes back beside the conversation. Where three columns do not fit (75rem of page, which a project's page beside the shell's rail lacks at 1440), the conversation and the run split the band, the rail follows under it with its panels side by side, and the head shows ruling 419(a)'s thread switcher, since the list is out of view. `data-console` on the pane (`open`, `closed`, `archive`) is what the sheet reads. The band's query is `(width > 1100px)`, the collapse's exact complement, so no zoomed width falls between the two blocks; the breakpoint map (P16-F8) names it, and a complement whose breakpoint moved without it fails there. At 1100px and under the page flows as before except that the pane comes after the composer, so a phone shows the conversation and the composer first and the run card under them (it used to push both a console's height down); the transcript keeps ruling 419(b)'s cap and the console its 320px. The blank transcript's examples keep no scrollbar gutter, so their frame lines up with the composer's edge (it stood 15px short). **(b)** *The clock's digits land.* `@number-flow/react` rolls a digit with a 900ms spring and the Elapsed clock ticks each second, so its seconds were mid-roll nine tenths of the time, two glyphs half in view in the cell. Every field of the Elapsed clock and of a wait's clock (`RunClock`, `WaitClock`) rolls in 300ms eased out (`CLOCK_ROLL`, the sheet's `--ease-out`), so the digit stands for most of each second; the digits still roll (rulings 366(e), 451(e)). **(c)** *A run is named once.* `runLabel` put the run's role after its name, and a controller turn is named "Controller" in the role "Controller"; the stream picker's trigger read "Operator · operator" the same way. `roleAfterName` (`runs-helpers.ts`) leaves out a role that only repeats the name, letter case aside, on the card's head, the picker, its options and the console's label; a renamed agent keeps its role ("Atlas · Controller"). **(d)** *The run card reads as a strip.* One `LiveRunPanel` draws this page's card and the task page's, and both change. Its body is a grid: the phase and step, with Hide console and Interrupt beside them; the four facts under them as one strip of equal cells divided by hairlines, their figures a step larger; and the console under that. The step's 44ch cap is gone, so it cuts at the strip's edge (ruling 478(c)). A narrow card (under 27rem) stacks the phase, the actions and the strip, and under 24rem the strip is two by two. In the console's toolbar the SDK line takes the row's free space and wraps inside its own box, and "{ } raw", "follow" and a retry wrap as one group, right-aligned, where in the pane the whole line dropped under the state pill and pushed the toggles to a third row. **(e)** *An aborted console load is not a failure.* Found on main while ruling 526 was checked on the dev server: a new conversation's console read "Could not load this console: the request failed." for about its first second, and one opened from the rail while its turn streamed read it until the console mounted anew (over 3 s, measured). Under StrictMode (`entry.client.tsx`) React's development build rehearses every mount: the console showed its thread and asked for its window (`/resources/run-log?window=1`), the page's cleanup disposed the store, which aborts every request in flight, and the console showed the thread again while that load still counted as in flight, so nothing asked again and the abort landed as the failure. A production build mounts once: built from this branch, the same navigation asked once and drew the lines at 260ms. `dispose` now hands each window load it cuts short back to its thread (`unloaded`), and `loadWindow` takes an aborted request for neither a failure nor an answer, so the next show asks again. Not changed: what the page shows and every control on it, the Conversations list's rows, the dock, and ruling 516's examples. Tests (each red by its canary, the source restored): `app.css.test.ts` "app.css controller band (ruling 524)" (the three columns, the split with its switcher, the hidden console's strip and rail, the standalone frame; the console's fill and every box between it and the pane; the card's grid, strip and two-by-two; the toolbar's wrap), the breakpoint map's "a complement starts exactly where the breakpoint it names ends" (the collapse moved alone) and ruling 419's rail test, rewritten for the band; `controller-page.test.tsx` (the pane between the conversation and the rail, `data-console` open, closed and open again; a finished turn's archive in the pane; no pane for a thread that has not run); `runs-panels.test.tsx` "ruling 524(b)" (every Elapsed field rolls within half a tick; number-flow's default fails it) and "ruling 524(c)" (the controller's card and the operator's picker, and a renamed one keeping its role); `use-run-log-stream.test.tsx` "ruling 524(e)" (under StrictMode at the root the console asks twice, the first request aborted, and loads without the failure sentence; red with the catch failing the thread whatever aborted it, and with only the hand-back dropped). Verified in Chromium on a dev root with a staged streaming controller turn, light and dark: /controller at 1024, 1280, 1440 and 1920; a project's controller at 1440 (two columns, the rail under them) and 1920 (three); the console hidden, the settled archive, a new conversation, a phone at 390, and the task page's card at 1440 and 390; and (e) on the dev server, the staged turn opened from the rail (the rehearsal's request aborted, the second answered, the lines at 310ms and no failure sentence). The bundle ceilings rose by what this costs, each with its note: 447 B in the stylesheet every route loads, 606 B on the task page and 635 B on the Controller page (42 B and 41 B of them (e)'s). (`app/features/controller/controller-page.tsx`, `app/features/runtime/runs-panels.tsx`, `app/features/runtime/runs-helpers.ts`, `app/features/runtime/run-log-store.ts`, `app/app.css`, `test-support/perf-budgets/bundle.json`.)

525. **A controller conversation can be deleted: by its starter, by an org admin, and, when it is about a project, by whoever holds that project's `delete-controller-conversations`** (owner, 2026-09-27: "I want controller conversations deletable by it's invoker or from admin(or RBAC enabled people)", with a screenshot of `/controller` as an org admin: two threads both titled "I want to build a deep agentic workflow…" at 18:58, the open one's turn "stopped before I could answer", and nothing on the rail to take either away; narrows rulings 274 and 99(d)). Nothing deleted a conversation before this. The pages had no control for it, the controller's toolkit has no tool that deletes one (ruling 99(c), as ruling 464 narrowed it), and a deleted project releases its conversations rather than deleting them (ruling 274), so a thread started by mistake, or twice, stayed in its starter's rail, and in every org admin's "Show everyone's", for good. Decided: **(a)** *Who.* Its starter, always, whatever it is about. An org admin, any: they already read every one (ruling 100(b)). For a conversation about a project (bound to its board, or anchored to one of its tasks), whoever holds the new row `delete-controller-conversations` on that project ("Delete anyone's controller conversations", covering "the ones about this project's board and tasks; everyone may delete their own"), which the admin role holds. The role matrix is fixed per role, so a person gets the row the way they get any other, by being given that role on the project; an org admin passes it as the audited D2 override, as on every project action. A conversation about no project has no project role to hold, so it stays its starter's and the org admins', and anyone else gets the 404 every non-reader gets (ruling 99(d)). A project member without the row gets the guard's 403, "Only project admins can delete another person's controller conversation.", audited `project.authority.denied` like every refusal of the matrix. Each page deletes only the scope it lists (ruling 121): `/controller` its instance threads, `/projects/:slug/controller` its board's and its tasks'; an id of another scope is not found. The page draws the button from `mayDeleteConversation`, and the delete re-decides through the guards (`deleteControllerConversation`, `controller-deletion.server.ts`). **(b)** *What goes.* The conversation and its messages, in one transaction, and what its turns said and did: their console lines (`run_log_lines`), their raw NDJSON, and the provider's session transcript in the starter's runtime home with the folder Claude keeps beside it, removed as the starter (ruling 485) (`controller-purge.server.ts`). The turns' run rows stay, with their last tool step cleared, as the instance's record of what was spent: Insights still counts them under `controller (instance)`, and nothing opens them, since a controller run is readable only through its conversation (`canReadControllerRunLog`). It is permanent: nothing restores a deleted conversation. **(c)** *A turn still working stops first.* The deletion drops the conversation's lease with the queue of messages waiting behind its turn (they go with the conversation, with no note), then stops every queued or running turn of it as the deleter (`interruptRunOnConversationDeletion`: `runtime.run.interrupted` under the system actor with `reason: "conversation-deleted"` and `deletedBy`, the shape a closing task's stop has, ruling 177), so nothing answers into it and nothing it was about to apply is applied. The turn settles into a conversation that is gone: it posts nothing, and its settle purges the lines it wrote on its way out. A turn still in its pre-flight when the deletion lands starts no run, so it spends nothing, and boot finishes the purge for a turn a restart cut off before it settled (`purgeOrphanedConversationLogs`); nothing else deletes a conversation, so a controller run with no conversation is always one of these. **(d)** *The record.* `controller.conversation.deleted` names the starter (`ownerUserId`, `ownerLabel`), how the actor held the delete (`starter`, `org-admin` or `project-role`) and how much went (`messages`, `turns`, `stoppedTurns`), with the project and the task it was about; never its title or a word of it. It is on the org Audit log and its export, not on the project's Activity feed, since whether a person had a conversation is theirs to know. **(e)** *The rail.* Every row the viewer may delete carries the shared row ✕ (`.stg-x`, destructive, drawn always like every row action since P16-UI-25) at its right edge. It asks first, in the shared confirm (ruling 459): "Delete this conversation?", or "Delete <name>'s conversation?" for someone else's, over "“<title>” goes for good: its messages and the logs of its turns. This cannot be undone.", which adds ", for <name> too" for someone else's and "The turn it is working on stops first." while one is; "Delete conversation" commits it in the shared `danger`. Deleting a thread the page is not showing answers the toast "Conversation deleted.". Deleting the one on screen answers a redirect to where a bare visit lands (U33-8), `?all=1` kept, replacing the history entry that named the thread, and the page says "Conversation deleted." once it lands (a fetcher keeps its data across a redirect, so the rail compares what it holds with what it held before the post). A project admin who is not an org admin now gets "Show everyone's (project admin)" on their project's page, as an org admin gets "Show everyone's (org admin)". It lists the other people's threads about the project SEALED: each titled "<name>'s conversation" with when it was last active, not a link, and left out of the phone's thread picker, and its confirm names the task it is about (or "about this board"). Their words stay their starter's (ruling 99(d)). Not changed: who reads a conversation (rulings 99(d) and 100(b)); the controller's toolkit, which deletes no conversation (ruling 99(c), as ruling 464 narrowed it); a deleted project releasing its conversations (ruling 274), because deleting a project is nobody's decision about anyone's conversation; the dock, which falls back to its scope's newest thread when the one it held is gone, as for any stale selection.
