A person with a conversation open when someone else deletes it reads the page's "Conversation not found." on its next load. Budgets (ruling 457): the stylesheet every route loads grows by 79 B gzip (the row's ✕ and the sealed row); the board's, the task page's and Profile's closures by 71 to 75 B more (the permission table's new row, which the project layout and Your access ship); and the Controller page's by 530 B more (each row's delete and its confirm, the sealed row, and the toast for deleting the thread on screen). The eight ceilings are raised with that reason. Tests: `controller-deletion.server.test.ts` (who: the starter in every scope; a project admin, another person's about the project, and neither a maintainer nor a stranger; an instance thread its starter's and the org admins'; a thread of another scope, and a missing one, not found; the page's `mayDeleteConversation` agreeing with the server over two starters, four scopes and five viewers. What: the messages, the lines, the raw log, the transcript and its folder gone, the run row keeping its cost and tokens, no log readable, the other thread untouched, the audit row's counts and no title, and the purge refusing a conversation that still exists. A working turn: stopped as the deleter, no reply, no queued message started, no longer counted as working at once, and the lines it writes on its way out purged when it settles. Boot: the sweep clears a deleted conversation's lines and keeps a live one's), `routes/controller.test.ts` "POST intent=delete-conversation" on both surfaces (a thread the page is not showing answers the toast; the open one the replacing redirect, `?all=1` kept; a member who may not gets 403 on the project page and 404 on the instance page, and the thread stays), `controller-query.server.test.ts` "other people's threads for a project admin" (sealed, with Delete, only on their project's page and only when asked; none of their words reach the page), `controller-page.test.tsx` "ruling 525" (Delete on the deletable rows, asking before it posts; the redirect's toast after an earlier result; a sealed row that opens nothing and is out of the picker; the link naming the role), `app.css.test.ts` "ruling 525" (a sealed row, a `<div>` and so never a `.ctl-conv`, which presses (ruling 459's F31), draws that row's box with none of its hover or press), and the permission's rows in the policy matrix (`policy-rbac.server.test.ts`), the role floor (`rbac.test.ts`) and the audit table (`audit-coverage.server.test.ts`). Canaries, each seen red and restored: the row given to maintainers; `mayDeleteConversation` answering true for a maintainer; the purge's `run_log_lines` delete dropped; the interrupt loop dropped; the purge dropped from the settle's deleted branch; `dropConversationLease` dropped; the boot sweep returning early; the scope check dropped; a sealed row titled by its starter's words; the open thread's redirect dropped; the rail posting without the confirm; the redirect's toast said only while the fetcher holds no data; every row a link; the picker listing sealed rows; the sealed row's padding off the row's; a hover on the sealed row. Checked in Chromium on a production build of the demo seed with seven conversations written into it, light and dark: as Arda (an org admin) on `/controller`, the ✕ on each of Arda's three threads, the confirm for one not on screen, and, on deleting the one on screen, the page on the bare URL with the next thread open, two threads left and "Conversation deleted.", the audit row saying `deletedAs: "starter"` and two messages and carrying no title; as Elif (viberr-core's admin) on its page, "Show everyone's (project admin)" listing Elif's own thread with Murat's and Selin's sealed, neither a link, and Murat's confirm reading "This conversation about VIB-142, last active 17:02, goes for good, for Murat Yıldız too: its messages and the logs of its turns. This cannot be undone."; as Murat (a maintainer), Murat's own thread and no such link. A working turn was not staged in the browser, since the container has no Claude account; the tests above stop one. (`app/shared/rbac.ts`, `app/server/controller/controller-deletion.server.ts`, `controller-purge.server.ts`, `controller-run.server.ts`, `app/server/runtimes/run-service.server.ts`, `session-export.server.ts`, `app/server/boot.server.ts`, `app/features/controller/controller-query.server.ts`, `controller-page.tsx`, `app/routes/controller.tsx`, `project.controller.tsx`, `app/app.css`, `test-support/perf-budgets/bundle.json`.)

526. **A reviewer's verdict is a card around its checklist, and every outcome's evidence row says what was checked, how it came out and whether it passed** (owner, 2026-09-27: "review comments still fails the UI taste part, lets do it in shadcn like something or redesign the output as well just go for it", with a screenshot of a reviewer's verdict on a task's timeline: "Changes requested", then "Validation: failing. Estimate Reviewer requested changes on `07e57314c533`.", then a monospace block whose rows ended in "— —", "102 passed 0 failed" and "75 right 2 wrong", then the log a row cited drawn again as a tile; extends P13-D-26 and ruling 493). Measured in Chromium at 1440 px on a dev root with a verdict of that shape staged (eight rows, two of them counted, and the log): the entry stood 456 px tall. An evidence row was a label and two diff-count cells, `add` and `del`, so the reviewer had put its results in them, and the timeline painted the first cell green and the second red whatever they said: "0 failed" read as the failure on the entry. Every row without counts printed "— —" once one row had them, a row that failed looked like every other, and the whole block was the code face at .75rem on a grey well. The title said "Changes requested" and the line under it said the verdict again, and the log the last row linked stood again under the block as a tile. Decided: **(a)** *A row says how it came out and whether that passed.* An evidence row is its `label` (what was checked or cited), its `result` (how it came out in a few words, at most 40 characters, or nothing) and its `status`: `pass`, `fail` (a failed check, or a finding that blocks) or `info` (a reference that is neither: a source read, a file attached, the change's size). task.md writes it `- [<status>] <label> · <result>`, `—` standing for no result; a label may hold ` · `, since the result is the last segment. A row in the old `- <label> · <add> · <del>` form still reads, as an `info` row whose result is its two cells (a diff's signed counts spaced, "+412 −87"; any other pair joined by a comma, "102 passed, 0 failed"; `—` dropped), and the file's next write puts it in the new form; the projection's derivation version is 6, so a store rebuilds its rows from the files on its next start. `report_outcome`'s evidence rows require `status`, and a row without one is refused by the schema, which names the field; `result` is optional. The Codex envelope's items require all three, `result` nullable. A status no writer knows reads as `info`, never as a pass. The specialist prompt and the seeded reviewer skill ask for one row per thing checked with its result and its mark, and for a row that blocks to be marked `fail` (the skill's outgoing hash is recorded, so an unedited copy upgrades). The delivered work's rows are references ("9 files changed on `vib-142-attach-workspace`" with "+412 −87", "2 commits delivered, revision …"), and a gate run's rows are marked by each gate's exit. **(b)** *The verdict is a card.* The timeline reads a reviewer's verdict note (a `quality` event titled Changes requested, Review passed or Approval noted …) back into its result, the revision it judged and whatever its sentence adds beyond them (`verdictNoteView`), as ruling 493 reads a gate run's note, and draws one card. Its head is the title in the verdict's colour (the blocked red for changes requested, the success green for an approval) with the tally of its checks under it ("2 of 4 checks failed", "4 checks passed", nothing when no row is a check) and the judged revision as a small code chip at its end, spoken "on revision …"; what the note adds follows (who else must review, why nothing is bound yet); then the checklist on the card's own edge. The note's "**Validation:** failing." lead and its opening "… requested changes on `…`." are not drawn, since the title, the actor line and the chip say them. The rail's mark is the reviewer's own verdict, the check on green for an approval and the cross on red for changes requested, and the pill stays "Review verdict". The note's words are unchanged in task.md, where agents read them, and on the bell. **(c)** *Evidence is a checklist.* Every outcome's rows (a completion, a verdict, an agent's report) draw as one list in the body face at the timeline's size: each row is its mark (the icon set's circle family the PR card's rows use, ruling 511: a check, a cross, a plain ring for a reference), its label and its result at the row's end, which drops under the label when the two do not fit. Failures come first and are tinted as a failing gate's row is (ruling 493), then passes, then references; the file keeps the agent's order. A screen reader hears "Failed:" or "Passed:" before a check's label. A label's backtick span is a code chip, as in the event's text, a label that names one of the task's files links it (R19-19), and a result's `+N` and `−N` keep the diff's colours. A file a row already opens is not drawn again as a tile under the event, a picture excepted. The list and the card stop at the gate table's 36rem measure. **(d)** *The review PR's evidence lines* lead with "**Passed:**" or "**Failed:**" for a check and with nothing for a reference, and a row's result follows its label after " · ". The design reads shadcn's card (a bordered surface, a head of title and description over its content) and a pull request's list of checks as references; nothing is installed (ruling 166). Not changed: which events carry evidence and who may write it (P13-D-26's grant), the eight rows and 200-character labels, the gate table (ruling 493), a verdict note's title and words, the bell, and the evidence-separation guardrail. Budgets (ruling 457): `bundle:root.css` +274 B gzip (the rules above, in the one stylesheet), so root and every route's closure +274 B; `routes/project.task` +955 B (the checklist and the card, `evidence-list.tsx`); the console's two task payload budgets +26 B (VIB-142's two rows as a result and a mark in place of two cells); ceilings raised to the measured figures with the reasons beside them. The shared schema checks a row's status with a lookup, not a schema of its own, so the shell chunk every route loads did not grow. Tests (each red by its canary, the source restored): `task-file.server.test.ts` "ruling 526: reads a row in its status form and in the two-column form it replaced" (the two-column branch dropped); `evidence-rows.server.test.ts` "reads a missing or unknown status as a reference, and an absent result as none" (the default made `pass`); `agent-toolkit.server.test.ts` "ruling 526: report_outcome refuses an evidence row with no mark, and stages a marked one" (`status` made optional); `agent-outcome.server.test.ts` "ruling 526: asks every row for how it came out and a pass, fail or info mark" (`status` out of `required`); `project-gates.server.test.ts` (each gate's row marked by its exit; every row `info`); `task-actions.server.test.ts`, ruling 478(g)'s test reading the verdict back (the note's opening reworded); `task-detail-components.test.tsx` "TimelineItem — a reviewer's verdict (ruling 526)" (the title, the tally, the revision, failures first, the log linked once, no "Validation:"; the verdict branch dropped, the sort dropped, the cited-file filter dropped) and the completion's checklist (the sort dropped); `attachments-panel.test.tsx` (a cited file inside a code span; the code split dropped); `default-assets.server.test.ts` "ruling 526: the reviewer skill asks for each row's result and mark, and its outgoing hash is recorded". Checked in Chromium against two local servers, light and dark: the staged verdict before, after as written in the new form, and after as a verdict written before this change (rings, its results joined), at 1440 px (456 px before; 364 px after, the verdict written anew as seven rows; 407 px for the older eight), 375 and 320 (no horizontal overflow, the results under their labels), axe clean. (`app/features/task-detail/evidence-list.tsx`, `app/features/task-detail/timeline.tsx`, `app/shared/verdict-note.ts`, `app/shared/mapping/task-event.server.ts`, `app/schemas/task-file.schema.ts`, `app/server/files/task-file.server.ts`, `app/server/tasks/agent-toolkit.server.ts`, `app/server/tasks/agent-outcome.server.ts`, `app/server/tasks/task-actions.server.ts`, `app/server/tasks/project-gates.server.ts`, `app/server/github/pr-open.server.ts`, `app/server/seed/assets/reviewer-expertise.skill.md`, `app/app.css`, `test-support/perf-budgets/bundle.json`, `docs/architecture/file-formats.md`, `docs/domain/agents-and-runtime.md`, `docs/ui/surfaces.md`.)

527. **A message sent while a Controller turn works steers that turn, unless its sender queues it, and a message still waiting can be sent now or taken back** (owner, 2026-09-27: "we need steering from prompts", with a screenshot of a correction, "I deleted old calculator agent and kb btw", waiting "queued · 1 ahead" behind the turn it was meant to correct; then "I also want queued vs steered just like claude code but I want bot send now and retracting if queued as well"; narrows ruling 99's FIFO and narrows ruling 465(c) and (d)). Ruling 99 gave each conversation one turn at a time and a FIFO of queued messages, so every message sent while a turn worked waited for that turn to end, and a correction reached the model only after it had acted on what the correction took back. Decided: **(a)** *Steer is the default.* A message sent while a turn holds the conversation's lease goes INTO that turn at its next step. The lease keeps it (`LeaseEntry.steering`) until the run asks, through the run's steering channel (`RunSpec.steering`, `take` and `close`, built per turn by `steeringChannel` in `controller-run.server.ts`). The Claude adapter asks from the SDK's `PostToolBatch` hook, which fires once every tool call of a batch has answered and before the next model request, and hands the messages to the model as that hook's `additionalContext`, beside the tool results: `steeringText` says who sent them while the turn worked, that they are part of this turn, and that the turn's reply answers them. What `take` hands over is marked steered (`controller_messages.steered_into`, the message the turn answers; baseline and `BASELINE_COLUMNS`, no backfill), and the console writes a `run·steered` line ("1 new message from the person went into this turn here"), because the SDK echoes nothing for a hook's context. The SDK's own mid-turn input is not used: measured on SDK 0.3.280, a `next`-priority user message that lands while the model writes its final answer starts a second model turn inside the same run, after its result, and neither closing the input nor `cancelAsyncMessage` at the result stopped it; the hook only ever speaks at a boundary the run is already at. **(b)** *What misses the turn goes next.* The SDK's `Stop` hook (the model has written its final answer) closes the channel: a message still waiting, or sent after, joins the queue at its front, behind any other message that missed a turn and ahead of the messages queued on purpose, and starts the next turn, which takes steering again from its start. The settle does the same for a message the turn never read because it stopped or failed first, and a message sent to steer a turn that could not start gets ruling 465's "I dropped this message" note, as a queued one does. A conversation deleted while its turn works (ruling 525) drops its steering messages with its queue (`dropConversationLease`), so the stopping turn reads none of them. **(c)** *Queue is a choice.* While a turn works, the composer on the page and in the dock offers **Steer** (primary, ⌘↵) and **Queue** (⌘⇧↵; the hint names the viewer's modifier); with no turn working it is **Send** as before. The form carries `mode`, and only `queue` queues (`sendModeOf`), so a form without it steers. A queued message waits for a turn of its own, exactly as every message did before this ruling. Steering and queued messages share ruling 99's bound of 8. **(d)** *Send now and Retract.* A message still waiting offers its sender two moves, beside its state: **Send now** on a queued one moves it into the running turn's steering (`sendQueuedMessageNow`; once that turn has written its answer it goes to the queue's front instead, and the toast says which), and **Retract** on a queued or steering one that nothing has read deletes the row (`retractWaitingMessage`, `retractMessage`; `last_message_at` recomputed, `controller.updated` published) and hands its text back to the composer, under whatever is typed there (`withRetracted`), so nothing typed is lost. Both are the conversation owner's alone, checked in the engine (the buttons render for the owner only), and a message that is not waiting any more answers 409 with a sentence. The two pages and the dock's resource route share one handler (`waitingMessageAction`, `app/features/controller/waiting-actions.server.ts`); the dock's posts do not re-run the page's loaders (ruling 457, CTL-4). **(e)** *How it reads.* A steering message sits in the turn it steers, under the message the turn answers and above the working row and the turn's reply, and does not move when the turn reads it: `inReplyOrder` places a user message under the message its `steered_into` names, and one still waiting under the live turn's (`turn.steering`, on both views). It says "steering · next step" while it waits and "steered" for good once read (`MessageState`), and has no reply of its own. The turn's digest (`messagesUpTo`) includes a message that steered a turn it includes, whatever its own `seq`, and boot recovery writes no restart note under it: it was part of its turn, whose own message carries the note; one still waiting when the server stopped was never read and is noted like a queued one. Task agent runs are not conversations and have no such queue; the operator's triggers keep their own lease, unchanged. Tests: `controller-conversations.server.test.ts` "ruling 527" (a steered message is taken once, marked, answered by the turn's reply with no turn of its own, and in the digest of a turn queued before it; a closed turn sends what waits, and what is sent after, to the queue's front ahead of a message queued on purpose; the next turn steers again; a stopped turn's unread steering goes next behind an earlier one that missed; Send now, Retract, the owner check, the 409s and Send now on a closed turn), its boot recovery case (a steered message gets no note) and its first-turn start failure (the steering message gets its dropped note); `claude-runtime.server.test.ts` "ruling 527" (the hook's context and console line, nothing with nothing waiting, `Stop` closes, no hooks without a channel); `controller-page.test.tsx` "ruling 527" (order and labels live and once read, the owner-only buttons, Retract under what is typed, Send now, Queue and ⌘⇧↵ post `mode=queue`, Steer posts `steer`); `controller-dock.test.tsx` "ruling 527"; `controller.test.ts` "ruling 527" (both pages) and `resources.controller.test.ts` "ruling 527" (the doors: `mode`, Send now, Retract, a stranger's 404, the 409); `controller-deletion.server.test.ts` (ruling 525's working turn also has a message sent to steer it, which the stopping turn never reads). Canaries, each seen red and restored: no `markSteered` in `take`; `take` leaving what it took; no steering arm in `messagesUpTo`; no move in `close`; `steer` ignoring `steerable`; no `steerable` reset per turn; no move of unread steering in the settle; no owner check on Retract; no steering filter in recovery; no steering in `drainWaiting`; `queueNext` appending; Send now queueing; the hook's context emptied; no `Stop` hook; no console line; the page's and the dock's `inReplyOrder` without the live turn; no `steered` label; Retract replacing the box, in the page and the dock; no ⇧ check; the buttons for a non-owner; no `mode` on the dock's send; at each of the three doors, no `mode` and no `waitingMessageAction` branch; and `dropConversationLease` emptying only the queue.

528. **The dock opens on the newest conversation where the person stands, and its button's one dot is a reply they have not read** (owner, 2026-09-27: "this view shows old run(I made a new one), also shows like there is a pending message that I didn't read yet which is awesome but I don't have any new messages. I want this for real but for only new messages else I don't want it.", with a screenshot of the instance dock open on an older conversation under a dotted button; narrows ruling 121(e), changes ruling 448). The dock showed a thread the owner had left for a newer one, and its button wore a dot while nothing new waited for them. Decided: **(a)** *Every open asks for the scope's newest thread.* Ruling 121's owner answer was that the panel reopens the newest thread of the current scope, and 121(e) also kept the thread selected per scope for the life of the tab (`viberr.dock.selected` in `sessionStorage`). A thread picked in the dock, started with New or sent in stayed pinned there, so a conversation started on the full Controller page, in another tab or on another device never came up in that tab's dock, which reopened the old one after every reload and every return from a page it stays off. (That the owner's pin came from an earlier send or pick in the dock is inferred: nothing else writes it.) Nothing stores the selection now. Every open (a click on the button, a reload with the panel open, a return from a page the dock stays off) asks `/resources/controller` with no `c`, which answers the scope's thread with the latest message, the one the full page opens with no `?c=` (`listConversations`' order). A thread the person picks, starts or sends in holds while the panel stays open, across navigation, and the button's next open lets it go. The open/closed state still survives a reload, and `staleSelection` still makes the dock forget a picked id the server cannot honour (121's correction (ii)). **(b)** *The button's one dot is a reply not read.* The dot on the owner's button was not ruling 448's. It was 121(e)'s pulsing `.live-dot`, lit while a turn of theirs worked in the dock's scope, and the same condition hid 448's still blue dot (`!working`). A turn runs one to five minutes, so every turn the owner started dotted the button, and a reply that landed elsewhere meanwhile was drawn only as that working dot. The trigger now wears one dot, 448's `.unseen-dot` with "a new reply" in its name, whenever a conversation of the viewer's holds a reply they have not seen, a turn working or not. A turn at work shows in the open panel (its working row and step line) and in the button's announcer ("<name> is working", ruling 476(d)), never as a dot on the button, and `.dock-fab .live-dot` is gone from the stylesheet. The 5 s status poll still runs while a turn works, open or closed, so a settle the stream missed still lights the dot. Not changed: what counts as unread (ruling 448: a reply past `seen_seq`, read only by the open dock and the controller pages) and when the dock loads its status (ruling 457). Tests (each red by its canary, the source restored): `controller-dock.test.tsx` "ruling 528: the dock opens on the newest thread, and its one dot is a reply not yet read", (a) every open asks for the newest thread and a pick holds only while the panel stays open (a pick kept across the button's open, or kept in `sessionStorage`, turns it red), and (b) the button shows no dot for a working turn and the unread dot while one works (the `.live-dot` back on the trigger, or the unread dot gated on `!working` again, turns it red); "forgets a picked thread the server could not honour (review finding 2)" replaces the stored-selection test, and the routed stub's task page links to the full controller page and back. Verified in Chromium against a local server, light and dark, on the owner's path: an older instance thread picked in the dock, the full Controller page opened and a newer conversation started there, then back to Home. Before, the restored panel and a reopened one showed the older thread, and once a reply landed in the newer one, opening the dock showed the older thread again and the button's dot stayed lit after it closed. After, the panel showed the newer conversation each time, opening it on the reply read it, and the dot went out. The missing working dot is proven by the component test alone: a live turn needs a connected Claude account. The closed dock still loads 21 static modules (`controller:closed-dock.static-modules`), and the bundle ceilings fall by what this saves: 8 B in the stylesheet every route loads and 103 to 119 B on each first route. (`app/features/controller/controller-dock.tsx`, `controller-dock-query.server.ts` (comments), `app/app.css`, `test-support/controller-dock-stub.tsx`, `test-support/perf-budgets/bundle.json`, `docs/domain/controller-and-epics.md` §2.1, `docs/ui/surfaces.md`.)

529. **A decision that does not hold the work says so: the board card names the viewer beside a working agent, and the task page draws the question as not blocking** (owner, 2026-09-27: "this doesn't say waiting for you, it says agent working where it actually waits for a decision from me", with a screenshot of CALC-1's card in Review reading "agent working" and "validation failing"; then "actually it still runs when I rechecked but it still offers the packet, it shouldnt do that"; then, once the packet turned out to be Operator's question, "it was a decision it said this after selecting" and "Then it makes sense but it should be different kind of packet because it confused me, UX should be more clear that it's not a blocking packet and maybe different theme like completion packet?"; amends ruling 365(c) and ruling 500(a)). CALC-1 had an agent's wait (`waiting: agent`, a run in flight) and an open question from Operator (`type: input`, "Decision required") at once, and both were true. The card's one seat said the wait, which ruling 365(b) reads before a human's, and nothing on the card said a decision was the owner's, though the board's own "Waiting on me" filter selected the card and counted it in its tally (`matchesBoardFilter` reads `waitingOnMe` alone, R8-3). On the task page the question drew as one the task waits on (500(a)'s card: the amber hand tile, the hairline and `--shadow-card`) while Current state said "Waiting on: Agent work", so the owner read it as holding the work. What the agent did meanwhile was not seen, since the owner's server is not reachable from here; that it was the specialist reworking the review's findings is inferred from the "validation failing" chip and the owner's second screenshot (Operator writing the pick into the project's rulings, then re-engaging the specialist). Decided: **(a)** *The board card names a decision the viewer owes beside a working agent.* When `waitingOnMe` holds and the seat is an agent's wait, working or queued, `cardProblems` leads its chips with "waiting on you", the seat's own words and hand, outlined like every chip and in the viewer's blue ink (`.chip.pb.blue`, `--blue-pressed`), since the seat's one tint stays the agent's. Both facts show, the viewer's own first, as a hold displaced by a working agent joins the chips (168(a)). It counts toward the cap of two like any chip, so CALC-1's card draws "waiting on you" and "validation failing" beside "agent working". A human wait already says it from the seat, and R8-3 names only the viewer who can act, so no other card changes. **(b)** *A question the work does not wait on reads as not blocking.* An open question (`type: input`) while the task's wait is an agent's (`waiting: agent`, the wait the card's seat and the "Waiting on" row read) sits flat on its hairline, without the `--shadow-card` a question the task waits on keeps, and its tile turns neutral (`--tint-press`, muted ink) in place of the amber, toneless like the completion packet (ruling 521); its first line says "Not blocking: an agent keeps working while you decide." beside the agent pulse, stilled under reduced motion (`DecisionPacket`'s `aside`, `data-aside`, `.packet-aside`). Its options, keys, note, Ask operator and Confirm are unchanged: the decision is still the viewer's to make. A block (`type: blocked`) never takes it, and a question the task waits on keeps 500(a)'s card and amber tone. Not changed: when Operator asks, and where a pick goes (into the rulings and back to the specialist, as CALC-1's did); the task's wait and readiness; the "Blocked or waiting" filter, which selects work that cannot proceed and so still leaves out a question beside a working agent (rulings 36 and 91); the review queue. Budgets (ruling 457): `bundle:root.css` +56 B gzip (the rules above, in the one stylesheet), so root and every route closure +56 B; `routes/project.board` +69 B (the chip) and `routes/project.task` +129 B (the packet's line and the page's condition); ceilings raised to the measured figures with the reasons beside them. Tests: `card-status.test.ts` "a decision the viewer owes beside a working agent is the first chip, in the seat's words (ruling 529)" (the seat stays the agent's; the chip leads, blue, before "validation failing"; queued too; no chip for a viewer who cannot act, nor beside a human wait) and `task-disposition.test.tsx` "ruling 529: a question asked while an agent works reads as not blocking" (a question beside an agent's wait wears `data-aside` and the line; beside a human wait it does not, nor does a block beside an agent's wait). Canaries, each seen red and restored: the `waitingOnMe` arm dropped from `cardProblems`; the page's condition without the wait; the page's condition without the packet's type. Checked in Chromium against a local server, light and dark, with the demo's VIB-142 staged as CALC-1 stood (an agent's wait, validation failing, an open Operator question with two options): before, the card read "agent working" and "validation failing" and the question drew as a blocking card; after, "waiting on you" stands between them and the question reads "Not blocking" on the quieter card. (`app/features/board/card-status.ts`, `app/features/task-detail/decision-packet.tsx`, `app/features/task-detail/task-detail-page.tsx`, `app/app.css`, `test-support/perf-budgets/bundle.json`, `docs/ui/surfaces.md`.)

530. **A board can deliver results, not only software: the controller settles which before it designs a project, and builds a results board out of the board itself** (owner, 2026-09-27, on the controller conversation that brought up `aws-cost-calculator`: "this controller run generated an app instead of doing the work on the board itself. Viberr should consider that people might be using the board itself to deliver results not generate an app to do it"; the person in that conversation had answered the plan with "I wanted this board to create the cost estimation not an extra app"). They had asked for "a deep agentic workflow to create AWS Cost Calculator as a viberr project": a person gives the project "a task with inventory as a file, screenshot or a text", and "this project's agents, mcps etc. will ask correct questions in every step and give a calculator.aws compatible outcome". The controller deployed the estimating agents and wrote their skills and knowledge bases, then planned the work as software: CALC-2 "Repository foundation: TypeScript toolchain, inventory and mapping schemas, measured gate commands" and CALC-4 "Estimate pipeline v1: calculator.aws outcome generator, validator, fresh price reader and a worked example", with the base Developer and Reviewer deployed "for the tooling" and real estimates to be filed "once CALC-4 lands". That plan is the controller guide's. Its "Bringing up a new project" told every bring-up to verify the toolchain, "wire the first task to prove it empirically" and declare the gates a task measured, and CALC-2's done signal posts the measured commands "so they can be declared as the project's gates"; the handbook opened with "Viberr manages AI software delivery". Nothing in the doctrine said a board's tasks may deliver the person's own work, though the runtime has delivered such work since rulings 385, 388 and 391 (the files a delivering agent saves on the task are the delivery, a verdict binds to `files:<deliveredAt>`, and acceptance merges no pull request) and ruling 482 owes it no gates. Told, the controller re-planned the same board in one turn with tools it already held: CALC-2 went back to Triage, out of the epic; the rulings gained the first rule "The board is the estimator, not an app"; four skills and two agents' instructions were rewritten; CALC-4 became a pilot estimate the agents make in calculator.aws; and CALC-5 and CALC-6 now score the board's own estimates and put the fixes into its knowledge bases, rules, skills and instructions. Decided: **(a)** *The controller settles what a board delivers before it designs one.* A software board's tasks change the repository and ship as pull requests. On a results board the board itself is the workflow: a person files a task with an input (an inventory, a brief, a dataset, a question), the agents do the steps and ask what they need, and the result comes back on that task. The controller reads which one the person wants from their words: a task they would file and what comes back on it ("give it a task with X, and the agents ask the right questions and hand back Y") is a results board, whatever it is called; an app, a site or a tool to build is software; and words that only name the work ("our invoice processing") fit both, so it asks that one question before it creates anything. **(b)** *A results board is built out of the board.* One task is one piece of the person's work. Its deliverable is the result, saved on the task by its delivering agent, and its done signal is the required reviewer's approval of those files. Each step is an agent with its skill and knowledge bases, deployed at the stages where the step happens, and the agent that makes the final result delivers the task: the operator's playbook skill names it and hands it delivery (`run_agent` with `delivers: true`), since only the delivering agent's saved files are the delivery. What a task on the board is (what a person files, what comes back, what the reviewer checks) goes into the rulings knowledge base; research lands as knowledge, not in the repository; and the workflow improves on the board: sample inputs run as ordinary tasks, their expected answers given only to the judging agent, then the skills, knowledge bases, instructions, stages or reviewers change where the scores point, and the samples run again. **(c)** *No software to do the agents' work.* A repository foundation, toolchain, pipeline, generator, validator or CLI for what the agents do on each task, and the gates and the Developer and Reviewer that would build it, are planned only when the person asked for that software; an agent may still write a throwaway script inside its own run. The guide's toolchain and gate bullets now begin "On a software board", and a results board declares no gates. **(d)** *The agents' own prompt no longer sends a result to the pull request.* The "Files on the task thread" section every agent granted `attach-evidence-references` reads said the folder held what earlier runs attached and that "code and large artifacts belong in the repository and the pull request, not here", which is where an estimate's exports would have gone. It now says the folder also holds what people attached to the task (ruling 379 writes a person's upload there), such as the input the goal names, and that on a task whose deliverable is a result rather than a change to the repository, the result's files go there and never into a commit; the large-artifact rule stays, for a task that changes the repository. Where it lives: the controller's doctrine (`controller.definition.md`), its guide ("Bringing up a new project", the new "A board that delivers results", "Creating a task"), the handbook's first paragraph, and `attachmentsDropSection`. The three outgoing hashes are recorded, so a store whose copies nobody edited, the owner's live one among them, takes the new text at its next boot. Not changed: every project still needs a repository, since every run works in a checkout of one; the operator and the delivery, review and acceptance machinery, which already carry a result that is not a commit; a board already brought up, which the controller changes when asked, as it did here. Tests: `default-assets.server.test.ts` "ruling 530: the controller's doctrine, guide and handbook settle what a board delivers and build a results board out of the board itself", the three outgoing hashes as `beforeResultsBoards` in "every rewritten asset's outgoing version is a recorded prior hash, and the shipped version is not", and `specialist-browser-mcp.server.test.ts` "ruling 530: names a person's attachment as input to read, and keeps a result that is the deliverable out of every commit" (ruling 306's case reads the reworded READING half). Canaries, each seen red and restored: the doctrine without its paragraph; the gate bullet on every board again; the guide's outgoing hash dropped; the drop section's old text. Checked, one sample each, by handing fresh agents the controller's doctrine and guide, old and new, with the same messages and no tools. The owner's AWS request under the old text planned no app this time but committed every estimate, the research and the test inventories to the repository, a pull request per result. Under the new text it built the board: step agents at the stages, the Estimate Builder delivering on each task, research into knowledge bases, calibration as ordinary tasks with the answer keys in a knowledge base only the judge reads, no gates, nothing committed. "Build me a small web dashboard app ... Next.js" still got a software board. "Set up a viberr project for our supplier invoice processing" got a question under the old text and, under the first draft of the new one, a results board built without asking, which is why (a) says that words naming only the work fit both; with that sentence it asks, naming both shapes. (`app/server/seed/assets/controller.definition.md`, `app/server/seed/assets/controller-guide.skill.md`, `app/server/seed/default-assets.server.ts`, `app/server/tasks/specialist-browser-mcp.server.ts`, `docs/domain/controller-and-epics.md` §1.1, `docs/domain/agents-and-runtime.md`, `docs/product/overview.md`.) *(Completed 2026-09-28 by ruling 531: the operator's own triage and delivery rules now know a task whose deliverable is a result, and the engaged reviewers' acceptance gate, which "Not changed" above said already carried a result that is not a commit, refused one until then.)*

531. **The operator scopes and delivers a result on its task, and an approval of the files a result came back in releases acceptance** (owner, 2026-09-28: asked "is operator aware as well from this change?", told it was not and that the live CALC-4 pilot estimate had gone out as a pull request, "yes add it"; completes rulings 388 and 530). Ruling 530 taught the controller to build a board that delivers results and changed the file-posting section every agent reads; the operator's own doctrine and turn were untouched. Its triage gate asked for "a deliverable (what changes, and where)" and read the repository first, and its delivery rule, in the doctrine, the stage rule and the `agent-reply` instruction, delivered whatever the deliverer committed. Live on aws-cost-calculator, the CALC-4 pilot estimate (its goal, written before ruling 530, said "Deliverable, on the task branch: estimates/CALC-4/") was committed by the Pricing Estimator, delivered by the operator as PR #4 and approved on that commit, so accepting the estimate merges it into the repository. Following a results task's path to Done found a second gap: `acceptanceBlockedReason`, the engaged reviewers' gate, answered "No reviewed revision yet, so there is nothing for the required reviewers to approve" whenever no commit revision stood, although ruling 388 had bound the verdict, the derived validation and the project's rule to the files a delivering run saved. Ruling 388's own release test passed only because its fixture never engaged the reviewer, which every real review does, and the AX-12 report that ruling came from was force-accepted (ruling 393). Decided: **(a)** *The operator's triage knows a results task.* Such a task (an estimate, a report, a dataset made from what a person gave; its goal and the project's rulings say which) is concrete when it names the result, the files it comes back in on the task and the reviewer whose approval proves it, and it is scoped from its goal, the rulings and its attachments, not from the repository. **(b)** *A result is delivered on its task, never in a pull request.* The files its delivering agent saves there are the delivery, what its reviewers judge and what the person accepts. The operator hands delivery to the agent that makes the result (`run_agent` with `delivers: true`), directs it to post the result on the task and commit nothing, and never calls `deliver_for_review` for it, even when it committed something: a stray commit stays undelivered, and with no pull request an acceptance merges nothing. Both rules live once, in `result-delivery.server.ts` (`RESULT_GOAL_RULE`, `RESULT_DELIVERY_RULE`): the triage gate, the stage rule and the `agent-reply` instruction carry them on every drive, on both backends; the shipped doctrine quotes them word for word; and `deliver_for_review`'s description says it never serves such a task. **(c)** *The engaged reviewers' gate reads the review subject.* `acceptanceBlockedReason` keys on `reviewSubjectId`, so an approval bound to `files:<deliveredAt>` releases it, a later save holds it again, and its refusals say "the work delivered on this task" where no revision stands; a task that delivered nothing keeps the F19-21 sentence. The doctrine's outgoing hash is recorded, and the owner's live copy was unedited, so it takes the new text at its next boot. Not changed: the delivery of a task that changes the repository; the agents' own rule (ruling 530(d)); CALC-4, which stands delivered as PR #4, where accepting still merges the estimate. Tests: `operator-run.server.test.ts` "ruling 531: triage says when a results task is concrete, and every turn says a result is delivered on the task" (the triage turn, and a manual and an agent-reply turn at work); `default-assets.server.test.ts` "ruling 531: the operator doctrine quotes the result rules word for word, and its outgoing hash is recorded"; `task-file.schema.test.ts` "ruling 531: an engaged reviewer's approval of the delivered files releases acceptance, and a later save holds it again"; and ruling 388's case in `required-reviewers.server.test.ts`, which now engages the reviewer as a real review does and is red on the old gate. A throwaway test through `resolvePacket` confirmed that a person's acceptance moves a reviewed files-only task to Done with the fix and leaves it in Review without it. Canaries, each seen red and restored: the goal rule out of the triage gate; the delivery rule out of the stage rule; out of the `agent-reply` turn; the doctrine's delivery sentence reworded; its outgoing hash dropped; the gate keyed on `activeWorkRevision` again. (`app/server/tasks/result-delivery.server.ts`, `app/server/runtimes/operator-run.server.ts`, `app/server/tasks/operator-toolkit.server.ts`, `app/server/seed/assets/operator.definition.md`, `app/server/seed/default-assets.server.ts`, `app/schemas/task-file.schema.ts`, `docs/domain/operator.md` §4 and §5, `docs/domain/task-lifecycle.md`.)

532. **Home lists what the instance and the person still need before Viberr can work, until nothing is left** (owner, 2026-09-28, on a screenshot of a fresh install's Home: "We need onboarding experience. When logged in with default admin account we need to list gaps: github connection for instance level, create a real user, at least 1 of the codex/claude logins"; asked three forks, the owner chose every org admin for who sees it, answered the backend fork "not just admin every user gets it, since it's a personal connection for each", and took the first project as the last step). A fresh `docker compose up` (ruling 504) signed its bootstrap admin into a Home that said "No projects yet. Create your first project below." over a dashed box whose three steps ("Connect a repository", "Define workflow stages", "Put agents under policy") were decoration. Its New project opened a dialog that cannot create anything without a GitHub connection; nothing said the bootstrap admin is the instance's default account rather than a person's own; and nothing said that an agent runs only on its task owner's own Claude or Codex account (ruling 127), so the first run anyone started was refused. Decided: **(a)** *The checklist.* While any of the viewer's steps is open, Home's first section is "Finish setting up": a numbered row per step, the count done ("2 of 4") and a meter; once every step is done the loader sends null and the card leaves Home. An org admin gets four steps: **GitHub**, done while one connection's token was not refused at its last check (when every token was, the row names that connection and links its Update token); **Your own account**, done once an enabled account other than the bootstrap admin exists, the bootstrap admin being the first account the instance holds, made by nobody with a password of its own (`bootstrapAdminOf`: the environment's email is no test, it may have changed since); **Claude or Codex**; and **First project**. A member gets the last two. **(b)** *Claude or Codex is the viewer's own.* It is done when the viewer holds a Claude or Codex account that can bill a run. Another person's account never closes it, and an account whose sign-in is gone from the server asks for a sign-in again. **(c)** *The first project* is done once the viewer can see a project and waits ("After GitHub") while the instance has no connection; otherwise it opens Home's New project dialog. The checklist takes the place of Home's empty-state box, which is deleted with its decorative steps, and the hero adds no sentence while there is no project. **(d)** *One path, in order but not gated.* The first step the viewer can take leads: its number is blue, its sentence shows and its action is the primary one, full width at phone width. Every other open step keeps its own action beside its title. A done step is a green check (a pass is the success green), and GitHub and Claude or Codex name what closed them: the connection's owner, the backend. **(e)** *Each action opens its place.* `/org/settings?tab=connections&add` opens the New GitHub connection dialog; `/org/settings?tab=users&add=admin` opens Allow access with Admin chosen; `/profile#agent-accounts` brings Profile's Agent accounts panel to rest below the overlay's pinned head, ringed and focused the way ruling 497's places are. Tests: `home-query.server.test.ts` "ruling 532" (a fresh instance's bootstrap admin through the four steps; the backend step each person's own, a sign-in gone stale, a member's two steps; a refused token), `home-page.test.tsx` "ruling 532" (the lead and each action's place; the project step's dialog), `org-settings-page.test.tsx` and `users-panel.test.tsx` (the two `add` links) and `profile.test.tsx` (the anchor), each red by canary. The Home payload ceiling rises by the 136 bytes the demo seed's open checklist costs, and the bundle ceilings by the measured 329 B (the stylesheet, on every closure) to 1,393 B (Profile, which lands the link through `useHashTarget`, ruling 497's one mechanism; sharing it moves `use-hash-target` and `page-anchors` out of the chunk the task page and the controller share, about 250 B on each). Home spells `/profile#agent-accounts` itself rather than import `page-anchors` for one string, as ruling 457 lets a closure with no room spell a label; the Home and Profile tests hold the two ends to one spelling.

533. **A task is filed with its input, and a coordinator reads the input it was given** (goal, 2026-09-28: the owner's AWS calculator board is to take "a task with inventory as a file, screenshot or a text as their current state"; narrows ruling 293's text-only reader; completes rulings 379 and 530). The New task dialog took a title, a goal and metadata and no file, and `createTask` fired the operator's `create` trigger the moment the task was written, so an inventory could reach its task only after triage had already scoped a goal that could not show it, and attaching it then woke nobody. The two readers a person relies on could not read it anyway: `read_task_attachment` returned text files only, while an inventory is a spreadsheet (an RVTools export, an Azure Migrate assessment) or a screenshot of a portal far more often than text, and a spreadsheet could not even be uploaded (ruling 379 stores only what Viberr can show or read back). And a file a person attached while an agent ran fell in that run's mtime window, so the completion credited the run with it and, for a deliverer, stamped `deliveredAt` from the person's own input. Decided: **(a)** *The dialog files the task with its files.* A Files field takes a picker, a drop and a pasted screenshot (a paste into a text field that carries text stays text, so copied spreadsheet cells are not turned into a picture of them; a browser's `image.png` is filed as `screenshot.png`, numbered when there are two). The route hands every file to `createTask`, which checks them all before it allocates a key (the upload's own rules, at most 10 files and 25 MB, no two names one case apart, the `attach-file` tier) and writes them before the task file and the `create` trigger, so triage reads a task whose input is already on it. One "Attachment added" note in the creation's own instant names them, and each gets the `task.attachment.added` audit row a later upload writes. **(b)** *A person's file is the person's.* The note, and a later upload's note, claim the file names (`attachments:`), so the panel says who added each file, and a completion leaves out of its run's files every name a person's note claimed during the run. **(c)** *The readers read the input.* `read_task_attachment`, on the operator's and the controller's toolkits, returns an image (`.png`, `.jpg`, `.jpeg`, `.webp`, `.gif`) as the picture itself after checking its own header (a file named as an image that is not one, or one wider or taller than the model API's 8000 pixels, or over 3.75 MB, is named and refused rather than sent, since the API would refuse the whole turn), and a spreadsheet (`.xlsx`) as its sheets in CSV (`xlsx-text.server.ts`: the zip's central directory, the workbook's sheet list, shared strings including rich text, inline strings, booleans and a formula's cached value; every part inflated under a ceiling). `.xlsx` joins the uploadable set on that strength. Tests: `task-actions.server.test.ts` "ruling 533: a task filed with its input" (the create trigger finds the files on disk and claimed for the person; one refused file refuses the filing and burns no key), `project.board.server.test.ts` "create-task carries the files the task is filed with", `filed-files.test.ts` (the picks the server would refuse; a paste of cells stays text and a screenshot is filed), `agent-completion.server.test.ts` "ruling 533: a file a person attaches while a deliverer runs stays theirs, and delivers nothing", `controller-run.server.test.ts` (an image read as the picture, a fake image refused), and `xlsx-text.server.test.ts` against two real workbooks (openpyxl's inline strings, and XlsxWriter's Excel layout). Canaries, each seen red and restored: the files left out of `createTask`'s own writes; the `personFiled` filter dropped; the dialog's extension check and its text-paste check dropped; the shared-string table bypassed. (`app/features/board/filed-files.tsx`, `app/features/board/board-page.tsx`, `app/routes/project.board.tsx`, `app/server/tasks/task-actions.server.ts`, `app/server/files/task-attachments.server.ts`, `app/server/files/xlsx-text.server.ts`, `app/shared/attachment-kinds.ts`, `app/server/tasks/operator-toolkit.server.ts`, `app/server/controller/controller-toolkit.server.ts`, `app/server/controller/controller-tool-guards.server.ts`, `app/server/runtimes/strict-tool.server.ts`.)

534. **A Codex run behind the agent launcher reads its own output schema** (live, 2026-09-28: the first operator run of every task on the AWS calculator board failed before its first turn). The Codex SDK writes a turn's `outputSchema` into a directory of its own (`mkdtemp`, 0700, the server's user) and passes the CLI `--output-schema <path>`, but since ruling 460 the CLI runs as the person's own agent uid behind `viberr-launch` and could not enter that directory: "Failed to read output schema file /tmp/codex-output-schema-…/schema.json: Permission denied (os error 13)". Every Codex run given a schema failed that way: the operator's decision plan, and every specialist whose outcome envelope rides the schema (a verdict, a question or evidence grant), which is nearly all of them. The controller diagnosed it from the two failed runs itself. Decided: the adapter's real factory, when a launcher stands in for the CLI, wraps the one SDK method that hands the file over (its private exec's `run`, parsed rather than asserted, and refused loudly if a future SDK no longer has it) and shares the file for the agent group to read before the spawn (`shareFileForAgentsToRead`: the directory 0710 and the file 0640, both in the agent group, through the no-follow descriptor every share uses, and a throw when the share did not take). The launcher is unchanged: the file is the server's own and so is the share, and nothing a caller controls widens what the setuid binary does. Test: `codex-runtime.server.test.ts` "ruling 534: a turn's output schema is readable by the agent the launcher runs", which drives the REAL SDK class against a fake CLI that records the mode and group of the file it was handed; canary, the share call dropped (0700 seen). (`app/server/runtimes/codex-runtime.server.ts`, `app/server/runtimes/agent-isolation.server.ts`.)

535. **An agent that makes a result can deliver it without a repo-write grant** (live, 2026-09-28, AWSC-1; narrows ruling 98(a); completes rulings 388 and 531). Ruling 531 tells the operator to hand a result's delivery to the agent that makes it (`run_agent` with `delivers: true`), and ruling 388 makes that engagement's saved files the delivery, the subject its reviewers' verdicts bind to. But `delivers: true` was refused to any profile without a repo-write grant ("holds no repo-write grant, so it cannot own delivery"), a rule from before files could be a delivery, when a deliverer that could not commit shipped nothing. On a board that delivers results the agent that makes the result must never write the repository, so the controller rightly granted none, and the operator's hand-off to the Workflow Researcher was refused: it ran as a supporting agent, its files could never stamp `deliveredAt`, its required reviewer's approval could bind to nothing, and the task could never be accepted without a force. The operator's note told the owner this "doesn't change the result". Decided: `canOwnDelivery`: a repo-write grant still makes an agent a deliverer, and an EXPLICIT hand-off also makes one of an agent that can post files on the task (`attach-evidence-references`, surfaced to the operator as `postsFiles`). The implicit posture, when no hint is given, still keys on repo-write alone, so a reviewer run first on a fresh task never becomes its deliverer by accident. An agent that can do neither is refused with a sentence naming both grants. A deliverer that cannot commit and can post files is told its delivery is the files it saves on the task, and to report their names, where it used to be told a human would publish its workspace to a pull request. Tests: `operator-actions.server.test.ts` "ruling 535: an explicit hand-off to an agent that posts files but cannot write the repo makes it the deliverer" (and without the hint it stays supporting), the refusal of an agent that can neither, and `specialist-run.server.test.ts` "ruling 535: a deliverer that posts files but cannot commit is told the files ARE its delivery"; canary, `canOwnDelivery` requiring repo-write again. (`app/server/tasks/specialist-run.server.ts`, `app/server/tasks/operator-actions.server.ts`, `app/server/runtimes/operator-run.server.ts`.) *(Amended 2026-09-28 on review: the prompt tells a deliverer its delivery is files only when it holds no repo-write grant at all (`DeliveryPermissions.repoWrite`), the fact `canOwnDelivery` reads; one that may write the repo with commit withheld is still told a person publishes its workspace.)*

536. **The completion compaction adds only its own cost to a run** (live, 2026-09-28: the controller's first turn on the AWS calculator board). Ruling 376 compacts a finished Claude run's session with `/compact` on the resumed session and adds that call's cost and tokens to the run. The CLI restores a session's saved cost state when it resumes it, so that result reports the SESSION's totals, the run's own figures plus the compaction call, and adding them recorded the run twice: the $1.87 turn was recorded as $3.85, its input as 4.77M tokens where 2.44M were sent, and the console line said "compaction request · $1.98 · 4768k in", adding the cached share into a figure that already held it. Decided: the adapter remembers what the run's result reported until its compaction reads it: when every figure the compaction reports is at least the run's, the report is cumulative and the compaction's share is the difference ($0.11 on that turn); when one is below it the CLI restored nothing and the report is the call's own. (Ruling 542 found every resumed run doing the same and made this one mechanism: `sessionShareOf` over the totals each session last reported.) The console line states that share, with the cached part named inside the input rather than added to it. Test: `claude-runtime.server.test.ts` "ruling 536: records the compaction's own share when the resumed session reports its totals", with the live turn's figures; canary, the baseline dropped. (`app/server/runtimes/claude-runtime.server.ts`.)

537. **An MCP server is probed by its name as well as its id** (live, 2026-09-28). `save_mcp_server` answers with the server's name, the key every grant uses, and `test_mcp_server` took only the id, so the controller's probe right after saving `aws-pricing` was told "No such MCP server." about a server that was installing, and it had to list the servers to recover. Decided: `resolveMcpServerId` takes an id or a registry name, and a reference that is neither is refused naming the servers that are registered. Test: the ruling 486 case in `controller-toolkit.server.test.ts` probes by name and by an unknown reference; canary, the reference passed unresolved. (`app/server/org/resources.server.ts`, `app/server/controller/controller-toolkit.server.ts`.)

538. **A relay carries files** (goal, 2026-09-28: the AWS calculator board's benchmark tasks AWSC-4 to AWSC-7, as the controller planned them, take as input "the file `sample-0N-input.*` delivered on AWSC-3", a spreadsheet and a screenshot among them; completes ruling 488). Ruling 488 let work on one task post TEXT on another task of the project; nothing could put a FILE there. Each agent reads only its own task's attachments, the operator had no file tool, and so a benchmark input made on one task could reach the task that works from it only through a person downloading it and attaching it again, which is the hand copy ruling 488 exists to end. Decided: **(a)** *A relay names files.* The operator's `relay_to_task` (on both backends: the Claude tool's `files`, the Codex plan's `files`) and a specialist's `relay` entries (`report_outcome`'s and the Codex envelope's, where `files` is required and nullable as the strict schema demands, and a garbled list costs the files, never the relay) name attachments of the source task. **(b)** *All or none, never over another file.* `relayToTask` checks every file before it writes anything: a name the source does not hold is refused with what it does hold, a kind the target could neither show nor read back is refused by the upload's own rules (ruling 379), and more than ten are refused. A file the target already holds with the same bytes stays as it is; one it holds with other bytes gets the relayed file under the next free name, which the comment states. **(c)** *The relay comment claims what it carried.* The files land on the target's attachments, where its agents read them, render on the relay comment, which names them, and `task.relayed` records them; the source task's line says how many went. A completion leaves out of its run's files every name a relay comment claimed while the run was in flight, as it does a person's (ruling 533), so a relayed input never reads as a run's work or stamps `deliveredAt`. Claims by other RUNS are not excluded: a supporting run that finished first claims what fell in its own window, the deliverer's files among them. Tests: `task-relay.server.test.ts` "ruling 538: a relay carries files" (the files land, claimed and named; the same bytes stay and other bytes get the next free name; a missing file or an unreadable kind refuses the whole relay and writes nothing), `agent-completion.server.test.ts` "ruling 538: a file a relay carries here while a deliverer runs is the relay's, and delivers nothing", `agent-outcome.server.test.ts` "ruling 538: an entry's files ride with it, and a garbled list costs the files, never the relay", and the operator's system-prompt rule in `operator-kb-injection.server.test.ts`. Canaries, each seen red and restored: the copy dropped from `relayToTask`; relay comments left out of the completion's exclusion. (`app/server/tasks/task-relay.server.ts`, `app/server/tasks/operator-actions.server.ts`, `app/server/tasks/operator-toolkit.server.ts`, `app/server/runtimes/operator-run.server.ts`, `app/server/tasks/agent-outcome.server.ts`, `app/server/tasks/agent-toolkit.server.ts`, `app/server/tasks/task-actions.server.ts`, `app/server/files/task-attachments.server.ts`.) *(Amended 2026-09-28 on review: a relay comment is told by its whole first line, so an author named "Reviewer (Opus)" still reads as one; a relay comment's files are never "files another agent saved" on the target (ruling 543); and a relayed file is read through no link and no bigger than an upload, before a byte is read (ruling 552). Residual, recorded: the files are written a moment before the comment that claims them, so a deliverer's completion on the target in that moment could claim them.)*

539. **Changing a project's repository is called Change** (owner, 2026-09-27, on the new `akin-website` project: "I repaired (which is a wrong term, let's update that) the github repo but the board still shows the old repo and connection error"). The board half of that report is ruling 517's, decided the same day in another session: a reading speaks only for the repository it was taken of, and the change records its own probe as the new repository's reading. This ruling is the word. Decided: the owner decision of 2026-07-26 stands (one repository per project, the new `owner/name` typed by a person and checked with the bound credential before anything is written, the acknowledgment when tasks carry PRs or pushed commits, `edit-policy`, audited as `project.repo.updated`); only its name changes, because "repair" framed pointing a project at the repository it should have had as mending something broken. The button beside the repository reads **Change…**, the dialog and its primary **Change repository**, the toast "Repository changed: <from> → <to>", and a refusal ends "then try again. Nothing was changed." The dialog no longer says it "is for the project that was misconfigured at creation, not for moving healthy work": the footprint acknowledgment is what guards a project with work on the old repository. The intent is `change-repo` and the server function `changeProjectRepo`; ruling 517's `repairProjectRepo` and "a repair" are this door under its old name. The home card's hint stops sending people to the GitHub page for "the repair", which never lived there. Not changed: what the change does, its checks and its record, ruling 517's included. Budgets (ruling 457): no ceiling moves; every measured route stays within its ceiling. Tests: the renamed cases in the settings action, route and page suites.

540. **A change to a project's credential, or to the token behind it, takes a new repository reading for the board** (owner, 2026-09-27: started the follow-up to ruling 539, the credential and connection changes that left the board's reading as it was). The board's Repository strip and the home card read the repository reading remembered per project (`project_github_health`, U33-2). Ruling 517 made that reading speak only for the project's current repository and has the reconcile poller take a failing one again every five minutes, but the changes that decide what GitHub will answer still took no reading of their own. Attaching, re-attaching or removing a project's credential and Re-check scopes (`runSetCredential`, `runClearCredential`, `runGrantScope`) dropped only the 30-second memo in front of the reading, and a connection's Update token, Re-check and removal (`replaceConnectionToken`, `recheckConnection`, `removeConnection`) touched no project at all. So "token revoked" stayed on the board for up to five minutes after a working connection was attached, and a healthy reading stayed quiet after Re-check scopes found the token revoked, because the poller takes only failing readings again and never makes a warning appear. Decided: **(a)** *A change takes a reading.* `refreshRepoAccess` (`github-query.server.ts`) drops the memo, checks the repository with the project's credential as it now stands, and records the answer. Deleting the row would not do: it clears a failure the change did not fix. As in ruling 517's re-check, an unreachable GitHub is not an answer and records nothing. **(b)** *Which changes.* A project's own: attaching or re-attaching its credential, removing it, and Re-check scopes. A connection's, for every project bound to its token (`project_github_credentials`; a project talks to GitHub only through its own binding): Update token, Re-check (unless GitHub was unreachable, which evaluates nothing) and removal, which reads the bindings before the token's delete cascades them away. Removing a person whose token was bound (`deleteOrgUser`) does the same for the projects that cascade unbinds. A project left without a credential answers `no_pat_configured` with no GitHub call; any other costs one `GET /repos/{repo}` (two for an empty repository), one project after another. The repository change keeps ruling 517's record of its own probe. Not changed: the strip, the home card, the poller and their words. The 24-hour re-proof of a connection (`ensureConnectionFresh`) runs when a token is about to be used, not on a person's change, and takes no reading for the projects bound to it. Budgets (ruling 457): server code only; no ceiling moves. Tests: `github-actions.server.test.ts` "attach, Re-check scopes and remove each leave the check describing the credential as it now stands" and `connections.server.test.ts` "Update token, Re-check and removal re-check the bound project and leave every other project's check alone" (both red on the old code at their first reading), and the person-removal case in `org-users.server.test.ts`; the attach test counts two repository reads now, the scope proof and the new reading.

541. **A Codex run's Turns and Tokens climb while it works, from the provider's own figures for each model call** (owner, 2026-09-28, on a screenshot of a GPT-6 Luna Workflow Researcher run's Live run card reading Turns 0 and Tokens "pending" twenty minutes in: "tokens pending for chatgpt based ones and no turns"). A Viberr run is one Codex turn: the adapter calls `thread.runStreamed` once, and the SDK streams usage only on `turn.completed`, which is also where the adapter counted turns, so every Codex run read Turns 0 and Tokens "pending" until it ended, and Turns 1 after. Driving the real 0.156.0 CLI through the adapter and the run sink against a scripted model showed both, and showed where the figures are: the CLI writes a top-level `token_usage_record` line into the rollout the moment each model call completes, before the tool the call asked for runs (the `token_count` event waits for the tool's output), carrying the call's usage, the turn's running total and the thread's. It also showed a second fault: on a resumed thread `turn.completed.usage` is the thread's running total, every earlier run's calls included, so a resumed run stored the conversation's earlier tokens again (a four-call first run of 51,000 tokens, resumed for two calls of 23,300, stored 74,300 for the second run) in its row, its console result line, its cache-read chip and the Insights sums. Decided: **(a)** *The adapter reads the rollout while the run works.* `codexUsageTail` (`session-export.server.ts`) follows the run's rollout in the principal's shared home: a new thread's once `thread.started` has named it, a resumed thread's found before the CLI starts and read from where it ends, so the thread's earlier runs stay out. Each read takes only the whole lines written since the last one, so a record the CLI is still writing is read whole the next time. The first SDK event after a new record carries the turn's running total as the run's usage, marked as the provider's figures (`outputEstimated: false`), so the strip prints them plain from the first call on and says "pending" only until that call completes. **(b)** *A Codex run's Turns are its model calls*, one record each, the way a Claude run's `num_turns` counts its model round trips; the step's fallback "turn N" follows the same count. **(c)** *A run stores its own turn's usage.* On `turn.completed` a new thread's figure stands, being its one turn's total; a resumed thread's is replaced by the rollout's turn total on the stored facts and the console's result line, and the raw line keeps the CLI's figure. This narrows 369(g), which measured the turn's total on runs stored before the CLI moved to 0.156.0 (2026-09-23). A Codex run stopped or failed after a model call now keeps the provider's figures for the calls it made, with `usage_final = 1`, where before it had none. Not changed: the sink's fold; the finalize read of per-call prompt sizes and compactions (`codexRolloutRunStats`, windowed by the run's start); the Claude adapter; and resumed runs stored before this change, which keep the thread totals they stored. Tests: `codex-runtime.server.test.ts` "ruling 541: a Codex run's Turns and Tokens while it works" (each call's record reaches the line after it, a record torn mid-write included; a resumed thread counts only this run's calls and stores its turn's total while the raw line keeps the thread's). Canaries, each seen red and restored: no tail; the unterminated last line parsed; a resumed rollout read from its start; the SDK's figure kept on a resumed `turn.completed`. Checked end to end on the real CLI, the adapter, the sink and a migrated database, reading `runLiveFacts` every second: main read Turns 0 and "pending" for the whole eleven-second run, then Turns 1 and 51,000; with the change Turns went 1, 2, 3, 4 and Tokens 11,100, 23,300, 36,600, 51,000, and the resumed run stored 23,300 where main stored 74,300. (`app/server/runtimes/codex-runtime.server.ts`, `app/server/runtimes/session-export.server.ts`, `app/server/runtimes/wire-format.server.ts`, `app/server/runtimes/run-sink.server.ts`, `docs/domain/agents-and-runtime.md` §2.5, §3.1 and §3.7.)

542. **A resumed Claude run records only its own spend** (live, 2026-09-28: the second turn of the AWS calculator controller conversation; generalizes ruling 536, completes ruling 175). The CLI restores a session's saved cost state whenever it resumes that session, so every Claude result after a session's first reports `total_cost_usd` and `modelUsage` for EVERY query the session has made; only `usage` and `num_turns` are the query's own. Ruling 175 records `modelUsage`, so each resumed run recorded all its session's earlier spend as its own: the controller's second turn, 8 turns in 29 seconds whose four calls read 188k tokens in, recorded "$2.51 · in 2627.6k (cached 2460.4k) · out 35.2k", the first turn's $1.98 included, and every later turn, operator re-run and agent follow-up on a thread counts the whole thread again. Ruling 175's spending cap is the same fact in a second place: the CLI measures `maxBudgetUsd` against the restored total, so a resumed session that had already spent past the cap would be stopped at once. Decided: the Claude adapter keeps, per session id, the totals that session last REPORTED (`reportedBySession`: every run's result and every completion compaction's result updates it, bounded, oldest out). A result is projected against them (`sessionShareOf` in `wire-format.server.ts`): when every figure, model by model, grew from the session's last report, the report is cumulative and the run's share is the difference; when one did not, the CLI restored nothing (another session ran in the same directory in between) and the report is the query's own. The result line, its per-model breakdown and the run row all carry that share, and ruling 536's compaction share is now this same projection. A resumed run's cap is raised by what its session had already spent, so the cap binds the run's own spend. After a restart the map is empty and a resumed session's first result is recorded as reported, as before this ruling. Test: `claude-runtime.server.test.ts` "ruling 542: a resumed run records its own share, and its spending cap starts from what the session had spent", with the live turn's figures; canary, the result projected without the session's totals. (`app/server/runtimes/wire-format.server.ts`, `app/server/runtimes/claude-runtime.server.ts`.) *(Amended 2026-09-28 by ruling 559: after a restart the baseline is read from the run log, so the first resumed run records its own share too. Narrowed 2026-09-28 by ruling 553: the cap is raised only when the CLI will restore the session's spend.)*

543. **An approval binds to delivered files in words as in fact, and files another agent saved are never "nothing to deliver"** (live, 2026-09-28, AWSC-2; completes rulings 388 and 535; narrows R19-8). Two sentences keyed on the commit revision after ruling 388 bound verdicts to the review SUBJECT. First, the verdict note: an approval of the files a result was delivered in was recorded against `files:<deliveredAt>` and derived a healthy validation, while its note read "Approval noted … there is no delivered revision to bind the verdict to yet". Second, R19-8's no-change verification: a verdict-capable reviewer approving a task with no deliverer, no branch and no revision mints a verified revision at the default branch's head and marks the task "no changes", and a results task whose result a SUPPORTING agent had saved (the Workflow Researcher on AWSC-2, before ruling 535 let it deliver) met every precondition, so the Estimate Judge's approval of the research would have been recorded as a verification of `main`. Decided: **(a)** the note keys on the review subject: an approval of delivered files reads "approved the work on the files delivered on this task", a request for changes likewise. **(b)** R19-8 mints nothing on a task where an agent other than the approving reviewer saved files (the timeline's claims, gate logs aside), and the approval's note says who saved which files without being handed delivery and to hand delivery to the agent that made the result (`run_agent` with `delivers: true`), have it save the final versions and run the review again. Tests: `no-change-acceptance.server.test.ts` "ruling 543: files another agent saved are not \"nothing to deliver\": no mint, and the note says to hand delivery" and "ruling 543: an approval of the files a result was delivered in says it bound to them"; canaries, the new precondition dropped and the note keyed on the commit revision again. (`app/server/tasks/task-actions.server.ts`.)

544. **A verdict binds only to what its run was dispatched to judge** (live, 2026-09-28, AWSC-2; completes rulings 388 and F10-15; narrows ruling 362). A verdict bound to the task's review subject at the moment the reviewer's run COMPLETED, while the reviewer read the subject as it stood when the run was DISPATCHED: a support checkout is pinned there (ruling 179), and files are read as they stand. On AWSC-2 the Estimate Judge was dispatched at 08:26 on research nothing had delivered yet; the Workflow Researcher, handed delivery (ruling 535), saved the final files and was stamped delivered at 08:37:02; the Judge's `request_changes` five seconds later bound to `files:2026-09-28T08:37:02.629Z`, content it never read, and the operator had to say so in words ("It reviewed the files as they stood before your 08:37 save"). An approval in those five seconds would have derived a healthy validation and released acceptance on a result no reviewer read, and a commit revision minted mid-review (a rework push, an external head) had the same hole. Decided: **(a)** every task agent's run records the task's review subject when it is dispatched, from the task-file read that pins its checkout: `agent_runs.review_subject` holds `reviewSubjectId`, or `none` when nothing had been delivered (`dispatchAgentRun`; the @mention resume records what is delivered when the resume is dispatched, and a continuity reset carries it to the fresh run). **(b)** At completion the verdict binds only if the task's subject is still the one recorded. When it moved, nothing binds: no `verdicts` entry, no round toward a deadlock (ruling 237), no no-change mint (R19-8). The verdict's note keeps the reviewer's result in its title and says what moved, for example "Review & validation approved, but it started before the files on this task were delivered, so the verdict does not bind to what is delivered now. Run the review again."; a completeness question the run was asked counts as answered (ruling 421). **(c)** An approval that bound to nothing opened no gate, so it no longer resets the operator's react depth or hop count (rulings 362, 489(d)); that hop counts like any other. A row with no recorded subject (a run dispatched before this ruling, or one no task agent made) binds as before, to the subject at completion.
