Tests: `agent-completion.server.test.ts` "ruling 544: a reviewer's run records the subject it was dispatched on", "ruling 544: a verdict does not bind when … during its run" (files delivered while it reviewed, files delivered again, a new revision) and "ruling 544: a verdict binds when the subject it was dispatched on is still delivered"; `agent-reply.server.test.ts` "ruling 544: a resumed agent's run records what is delivered when the resume is dispatched"; canaries, the dispatch's record dropped, the resume's record dropped, and `!moved` dropped from the binding. (`app/server/tasks/task-actions.server.ts`, `app/server/tasks/specialist-run.server.ts`, `app/server/runtimes/run-store.server.ts`, `app/server/runtimes/run-service.server.ts`, `app/server/db/sqlite.server.ts`, `db/migrations/0001_baseline.sql`.) *(Amended 2026-09-28 on review: an @mention resume re-pins nothing, so on a commit subject it records the subject of the run it resumes, where its checkout still stands, and on files today's subject, which it reads as they stand; and a verification revision (R19-8) a sibling reviewer's approval minted since the dispatch is not a move for a run sent to judge a task with nothing delivered.)*

545. **A controller-built project's operator can run on either backend from the start** (live, 2026-09-28: the controller building the AWS calculator board; amends ruling 464(a)). Ruling 464 gave `create_project` an `operator: { model?, effort? }` judged against the operator's own backend, which is Claude, and the owner's prompt asked for every agent on GPT-6 Luna at max. The first call was refused "GPT-6 Luna is a Codex model. Claude cannot run it. Pick a model from the Claude list.", a sentence that named only the way back; the controller created the project without the operator's overrides and then switched the operator with `update_agent_deployment { backend: "codex", model: "gpt-6-luna", effort: "max" }`, a door the refusal never named. Decided: `operator` takes `backend` (`claude` or `codex`); its model and effort are judged against the backend named, else the operator's own, and a switch writes what `update_agent_deployment` writes for one: the new backend, that backend's default model unless one is given, and no effort carried across. A model of the other backend with no `backend` is refused with a sentence that names the option ("GPT-6 Luna is a Codex model and the operator runs on Claude. Pass `backend: "codex"` in `operator` to run it on Codex, or pick a Claude model. Nothing was created."). Roster entries keep their template's backend, which the controller sets when it saves the template. Tests: `project-create.server.test.ts` "ruling 545: the operator runs on the backend `operator` names, with that backend's model and effort", and two rows of the ruling 464 refusal table (a Codex model with no backend, a Claude model for a Codex operator); canary, the backend switch dropped. (`app/features/home/project-create.server.ts`, `app/server/controller/controller-toolkit.server.ts`.)

546. **Entering Review does not announce a missing pull request on a task delivered as files** (live, 2026-09-28, AWSC-2; narrows R15-2's safety net (a); completes ruling 531). R15-2 writes a "Review reached with no PR yet" `github` event whenever a task enters the review-role stage without a live PR: "AWSC-2 entered Review with no live review pull request. The operator decides delivery (push + review PR); a maintainer or the task owner can also deliver from the task page's GitHub panel." AWSC-2 is a research task whose delivery is two files its deliverer saved on it (rulings 388, 531), and ruling 531 forbids `deliver_for_review` for such a task, so the note told the person a push and a PR were pending that must never happen. Decided: the event is not written when the task was delivered as files: no active work revision and a review subject, which is then `files:<deliveredAt>` (`reviewSubjectId`). A task that has delivered nothing at all still gets the event, since its gap is real. Test: `delivery-decision.server.test.ts` "ruling 546: no safety-net event for a task delivered as the files saved on it"; canary, the files condition dropped. (`app/server/tasks/task-actions.server.ts`.)

547. **A notification lands on its place once the page has settled, and a decision's row follows its packet to the entry that closed it** (owner, 2026-09-28, on AWSC-2 during the AWS calculator run: "click notifications here top 2 anchor misses the highlight section after switching clicks"; asked to replicate it, then "yes fix it, and the #decision one too"; extends ruling 497(a) and (c), keeps ruling 523). Measured live in the Browser pane at 800×847: between the bell's two "is now running on" mention rows, a click from AWSC-2 to AWSC-1's event landed it 8 px under the top of the page column, and the click back marked and focused AWSC-2's event 606 px ABOVE the column's top, with the column scrolled to its end (6,848 of 7,676 px), three times out of three. The task route remounts `TaskDetailPage` per task (`key={task.key}`), so every fold on the page a link opens (`Collapsible`, `useFirstRow`) draws whole and folds in the render its layout effect starts; React flushes the pending passive effects before that render, and `useHashTarget`'s reveal is one of them. It scrolled a page 11,842 px tall to the event, then four comments above it folded from 1,353, 537, 1,269 and 1,994 px to 436 and 623, taking 3,222 px out from above it. The other direction lost 6,952 px the same way and landed only because Chrome's scroll anchoring put the event back: no script set the column's scroll. The second finding, from the same bell: "Workflow Researcher asks: Approve the Mapping-stage hours and pricing baseline?", answered minutes before, linked `#decision`; the page shows a packet only while it is open, so the click moved nothing and the bell took the focus back. Decided: **(a)** *The place holds while the page settles.* `useHashTarget` (`app/ui/use-hash-target.ts`) keeps the element its reveal returned (a `reveal` now returns the element, or null while the page cannot show it) where the reveal put it in the box that scrolls it (`holdInView`): whatever changes size in that box (a fold, a picture loading, an event arriving above, a region drawn into it) scrolls the box by what the place moved, until the person's first wheel, touch, press or key, or the next navigation. The hold belongs to the navigation that named the place, so React's StrictMode, which mounts the effect twice, holds it again. **(b)** *A decision's link names its packet.* `taskDecisionLink` writes `#decision-<packet id>` (`decisionAnchor`, `app/shared/page-anchors.ts`), and every notice about a packet passes its id (`NoticeSubject` `{ decision }`). The task page opens the card for the open packet a link names, and for a bare `#decision` (a row written before this ruling) whichever packet is open. **(c)** *A closed packet's rows open the entry that closed it.* Every door that clears a packet moves the rows naming it to the timeline entry it wrote (`followClosedDecision`, `notifications.server.ts`): a person's answer (`resolvePacket`; an `edit_goal` answer keeps its packet on the page, decided, until the goal lands), the goal edit or the operator's drafted goal that fulfils it, the operator's withdrawal, a stall or a conflict made moot, an acceptance-offer packet withdrawn on a PR conflict, a direct acceptance that answers or withdraws it, and an archive. The rows keep their read state. **(d)** *A link to a place the page no longer shows lands on the timeline.* A decision link whose packet is not the open one (or with none open), and `#recommendations` with none pending, reveal the Timeline panel (`#timeline`, `TASK_TIMELINE_ANCHOR`), ringed as any `.panel` a link opens and focused, instead of moving nothing. Not changed: what is marked and how, the reveal once per navigation (ruling 497), and the mark's end at the next press (ruling 523). Tests (each red by its canary, the source restored): `operator-actions.server.test.ts` "ruling 547" (a packet the operator opened is linked by its id; a person's answer, the operator's withdrawal, an archive, an acceptance, a landed goal edit and the operator's drafted goal each move the row to the entry that records it, and an `edit_goal` answer leaves it on the decided card; dropping one door's call, the id, or `clearPacket` from the answer's condition each turn rows red), `task-disposition.test.tsx` "ruling 547" (the card for its packet; the timeline for a packet closed since, for none open, for a bare `#decision` and for no pending recommendation) and `e2e/10-notification-anchors.spec.ts` (Murat mentions Arda on VIB-148 under three 30-line replies; from VIB-142, with scroll anchoring off, Arda's bell row lands the event under the top of the page column; without the hold it sat above it). Verified in Chromium on the production image (the e2e stack): with the hold taken out of `useHashTarget`, the spec's event, revealed on a page 6,866 px tall, sat 841 px above the top of the page column once the five replies folded (5,450 px); with it, the event stays at the top of the column. The first version of that spec passed both ways: its replies were one soft-wrapped paragraph each (344 px, nothing folded), so it now counts the folds before it measures. The rows' moves and the timeline landing are verified by the tests above; not yet deployed, so a row written before the deploy keeps `#decision` and, once its packet is gone, opens the timeline (d). The bundle ceilings rose by what this costs, each with its note: 474 B on the task page, 329 B on the Controller page and 336 B on Profile, the three pages that reveal through `useHashTarget`. (`app/ui/use-hash-target.ts`, `app/shared/page-anchors.ts`, `app/server/projections/notifications.server.ts`, `app/server/tasks/task-actions.server.ts`, `app/server/tasks/operator-actions.server.ts`, `app/server/tasks/task-mutation.server.ts`, `app/server/tasks/agent-toolkit.server.ts`, `app/server/github/github-reconciler.server.ts`, `app/server/github/update-branch-operator.server.ts`, `app/features/task-detail/task-detail-page.tsx`, `app/features/task-detail/timeline.tsx`, `test-support/perf-budgets/bundle.json`.)

548. **What a task waits on is edited the way the Owner row releases its owner: each entry, on the row and in its editor, is a chip with a remove cross, and the editor's field finds the project's tasks and says which ones the writer would refuse** (owner, 2026-09-28, on a screenshot of the Blocked by editor open under the Details panel, "WAITS ON" over an empty field showing "AWSC-12, AWSC-14", "Task keys in this project, comma-separated. Empty clears the wait and releases the task.", Cancel and Save: "make dependencies section autocomplete and multiple dependencies and removing by clicking x section, just like owner section"; then, on the first version, whose row still drew its chips inside the trigger: "add the × on the row chips too"; narrows 501). The editor was one text field of comma-separated keys, prefilled with the canonical refs. Nothing in it listed the project's tasks, so a person had to know each key or look it up on the board; a key the writer refuses (not a task here, archived, already done, or one that would close a cycle) came back only as the toast after Save; and taking one entry out meant editing the text around it. Decided: **(a)** *Each entry is the row's chip with the Owner row's release cross.* The editor draws every entry as the Blocked by row does (the status ring and, once it has settled, "· done" or "· archived", ruling 501(c)) with `.own-x` after it, sized to the chip (`WaitChip`'s `onRemove`, `wait-chip.tsx`); a press takes that entry out of the draft, and Backspace in the empty field takes the last one. For an editor the Blocked by row's own chips carry the cross too: they stand before the trigger rather than in it, since a button cannot hold one, and the trigger is the plus after them (`PropRow`'s `lead`), still named "Blocked by Add dependency". A press on a row's cross saves the wait without that entry at once, through the same intent; the cross spins until the server answers (ruling 368), and the other crosses and the plus ignore presses meanwhile, since a second list posted before the first answered would put the first entry back. A cross that leaves nothing still open is the release (ruling 131(e): an emptied list at once, or only done entries, which the engine's next sweep clears), so it asks first, as the Owner row's cross does: "Release VIB-148?", then "VIB-153 is the last task VIB-148 waits on." or "Everything else VIB-148 waits on is done.", then "Taking VIB-153 off releases VIB-148: it can move again, and Viberr hands it to the operator.", with "Keep the wait" and "Release VIB-148", each key kept on one line. The cross that had the focus leaves with its chip once the wait comes back without it, and the trigger takes the focus. A viewer's and an archived task's chips carry none. The crosses keep WCAG 2.2's 24px of clear space (2.5.8): drawn 3px outside their chips, two of them had 23px against the field wrapped under them (axe, VIB-148 waiting on two tasks), so each sits inside its chip and the field's rows stand .375rem apart. **(b)** *The field finds the project's tasks.* The route component hands the page the read's URL, as it does the Changes panel's (`dependencyCandidatesUrl`); `GET /projects/:slug/tasks/:key/dependency-candidates` (`task-dependency-candidates.ts`: member-only, a 401 for a signed-out fetch rather than a login redirect, the task page's 404 for a non-member or a key the project has no task for, `shouldRevalidate` false, and a `clientLoader` that turns a failure into the picker's own line) answers `listDependencyCandidates` (`projections/dependencies.server.ts`): every task in the project but this one, newest key first, each with its title, its stage's name and the refusal the writer would give it as a new entry, in the order the writer checks: `archived`, `cycle` (it already waits on this task, directly or down the chain: the writer's walk run backwards over the stored lists, archived tasks' lists included, keeping the way back as the cycle's `chain`) or `done`. The picker says each refusal in the writer's own words: `validateDependencyRefs` and `setTaskDependencies` throw the sentences `app/shared/dependency-candidates.ts` builds, and the picker builds the same ones from the read (ruling 186's rule: the words a person meets before the click are the words the server answers with). With nothing typed the list offers the free tasks; typing matches a key or a title and puts the task whose key it is first, free or barred, so Enter never adds another in its place, then the free matches before the barred (a key it starts before a key or title it is in); a barred one is dimmed and `aria-disabled`, the reason where the stage was ("done", "archived", "waits on AWSC-7"), and picking it adds nothing while the live region says the writer's sentence. A done task the wait already holds, taken out, goes back in as it was, because the writer refuses done work only among the entries a save adds. Typing highlights the best match and Enter adds it; a key already on the list highlights nothing ("AWSC-7 is already on the list."); with nothing highlighted Enter saves. A row is highlighted by a pointer that moves over it, not one it scrolled under as the editor opened, and loses the highlight when the pointer leaves the list, so an Enter meant to save never adds the last row crossed on the way to Save. A key typed in full before a comma, or a pasted list, goes in key by key, and a key the picker refuses stays typed. At most 50 rows are drawn ("Showing 50 of N. Type to narrow them."). When the read fails the list says "The project's tasks could not be loaded. A key typed in full still goes in, and Save checks it." **(c)** *The list stays under the field while the editor is open.* Measured on the Labels editor, whose list folds when its field loses the focus (VIB-151, 1440 px): in Chromium a press on Save takes the focus on mousedown, the folding list moved Save from y 893.6 to 803.6 under that press, and the click saved nothing (a second one did). The picker's list folds for nothing, so its Save lands on the first press. **(d)** *It is still the wait's own form* (ruling 131): the draft posts as the full list of canonical refs through `set-task-dependencies`, a refusal keeps the editor open beside the toast, an unchanged Save closes without a request (as the Labels editor's does), and an empty list is the release. The writer refuses the whole list while it holds an entry that can never complete (ruling 355), so the editor says "AWSC-3 can never complete: take it out to save." under the field until it is out. The field says "Search by key or title" in place of the example keys, and the line under it reads "Tasks in this project. Empty clears the wait and releases the task." **(e)** *The picker is its own chunk* (ruling 457): `dependency-picker.tsx` is fetched when the pointer or the focus reaches the Blocked by trigger (`PropRow`'s `onIntent`), or as the editor opens, while the editor reads the tasks it offers, so a task page on which nobody edits the wait loads neither. It can arrive after the editor opened, so it takes the focus into its field as it mounts. A chunk that fails to arrive says "The task picker could not be loaded. Reload the page to try again.", since a browser may keep a failed module load for the page's life. Not changed: the intent and the route action, what `setTaskDependencies` refuses and its words, the hero's wait chips, and the operator's and the controller's doors. Budgets (ruling 457): the stylesheet's ceiling rises 152 B gzip (the chip's cross and its clear space, the row's plus, the task rows and the wider editor), and every closure's with it; the task page's rises 1,412 B (that CSS; the row's crosses, their saves and the release's confirm; the chunk's loader; and the editor's read and its note). The picker itself, 2.19 kB gzip, is a chunk no route loads first; drawn into the task page's own chunk (before the review below added to it) it cost that page 1,608 B. Tests: `dependencies.server.test.ts` "listDependencyCandidates (ruling 548)" (every other task newest first, each barred exactly where `setTaskDependencies` refuses it as a new entry and in the sentence it throws: archived, a cycle one and two hops back and one through an archived task's list, done; the one free task is written), `task-dependency-candidates.server.test.ts` (a signed-out fetch 401, a non-member and an unknown task the page's 404, a member the list without the task itself), `task-side-panels.test.tsx` "ruling 548" (the field has the focus once the picker is in; the note for an entry that can never complete, gone once it is out; a cross takes an entry out, a held done entry goes back in as it was, a picked task joins, and Save posts the full list alone; the free tasks with nothing typed, a barred match dimmed with its reason and refused in the writer's words, a key typed in full chosen over the matches after it, a listed key highlighting nothing, Enter adding the best match, a pasted list going in key by key with the refused key left typed; the pointer's highlight gone when it leaves the list, Backspace, an unchanged Save that posts nothing and a cleared one that posts an empty list; a typed key taken when the read fails) and "the Blocked by row's chips carry the remove cross" (a press posts the list without that entry and the other crosses wait for its answer; a cross that empties the list, or leaves only done work, asks first, and Keep the wait posts nothing; the focus goes to the trigger once the chip goes; a viewer's and an archived task's chips carry none). The sheet's refusal-box check (`app.css.test.ts`, ruling 451(g)) flagged the Epic row's `PropRow` as "an alert keyed per refusal that never shakes": its tag scanner skipped a line comment only outside an attribute's braces, so the apostrophe in "the project's epics" opened a string that ran the Epic row's tag on for 333 lines, into this editor's alert and the rows' keyed chips. It now skips a line comment anywhere, still finds its 21 boxes, and still names a keyed alert at its own line (the editor's alert, keyed for the check, went red at line 796). A review of the finished change found five of the behaviours above missing (the key typed first, the listed key, the pointer's highlight, the note, the reload wording), the sentences copied rather than shared, the read's URL built in the panel, and the reverse walk copying each list per edge; all were fixed here. Canaries, each seen red and restored byte for byte: the backwards walk stopped at the direct waiters; archived tasks' lists skipped; the keys sorted as text; a cycle's chain cut to its first hop; the membership gate dropped; the picker's focus as it mounts dropped; the note dropped; a held done entry barred; the hidden list dropped; the unchanged check dropped; the barred tasks offered with nothing typed; the bar check dropped from a pick; the free matches sorted before the key typed; a listed key highlighted; the pointer's highlight kept on leaving; every key refused while the list is missing; the row's one-save-at-a-time guard dropped; the confirm asked only for an emptied list; the focus hand-off dropped; the row's crosses given to a viewer. Checked in Chromium on the dev server with the demo seed, light and dark: VIB-148 with no wait, then two tasks picked and saved, then one of them archived (a red chip with its cross, the note, and a Save refused beside "VIB-166 is archived; a task cannot wait on abandoned work."), a live cycle (VIB-153's editor reading "waits on VIB-153" on VIB-148's row once VIB-148 waited on VIB-153), five chips wrapping, the keyboard alone, the highlight on opening, hovering and leaving, the row's crosses (a press refused while archived VIB-166 was still listed, which kept its chip and the focus; the archived one taken out; the confirm, its Keep and its Release; the focus on the trigger after each), three chips wrapping with their crosses, 390 px (no sideways scroll), and axe's WCAG 2.2 AA rules on the open editor in both themes, with no chip, two and five (none failed once the crosses kept their space). (`app/shared/dependency-candidates.ts`, `app/server/projections/dependencies.server.ts`, `app/server/tasks/dependencies.server.ts`, `app/routes/task-dependency-candidates.ts`, `app/routes.ts`, `app/routes/project.task.tsx`, `app/features/task-detail/task-detail-page.tsx`, `app/features/task-detail/task-details-panel.tsx`, `app/features/task-detail/dependency-picker.tsx`, `app/features/task-detail/wait-chip.tsx`, `app/app.css`, `app/app.css.test.ts`, `test-support/perf-budgets/bundle.json`, `docs/ui/surfaces.md`, `docs/domain/task-lifecycle.md`.)

549. **A browser snapshot a run's saved files cite is kept** (live, 2026-09-28, AWSC-1; amends ruling 105). Ruling 105 deletes the browser's working artifacts a finished run leaves (`page-*.yml` snapshots, `console-*.log` dumps) unless the run cites the exact file name, and it looked for citations in the reply, the envelope, the evidence rows, the question and the timeline since the run started. A run whose delivery is files (ruling 531) cites its evidence in those files: the Workflow Researcher's `calculator-findings.md` named eleven snapshots and its report named none, so the completion deleted all eleven, and the Estimate Judge rejected the findings for citing files that were not on the task, a defect Viberr had made. Decided: the citation corpus also holds the text of the files the run saved (`savedFilesText`: text files only, never the working artifacts themselves, each up to 4 MB). Test: `agent-completion.server.test.ts` "ruling 549: a snapshot cited only in a file the run saved is kept"; canary, the saved files left out of the corpus. (`app/server/files/task-attachments.server.ts`, `app/server/tasks/task-actions.server.ts`.)

550. **Accepting a task delivered as files records it delivered, never "completed with no changes"** (live, 2026-09-28, AWSC-2; narrows R20-2's auto-detect; completes rulings 531 and 546). Acceptance treats a task with no pull request as a candidate for "no changes" and probes GitHub (R20-2): no task branch, or an empty one, proves there was nothing to deliver, and the task closes with the no-change completion event and `noChanges: true`. A task delivered as the files saved on it (rulings 388, 531) never has a branch, so accepting AWSC-2, a research task whose two files the Estimate Judge had approved, would have recorded it as "Completed with no changes". Its confirm said so in advance: "Nothing to merge yet ... Accepting re-checks awsc-2 on GitHub: if it carries no commits the task closes as completed with no changes", and its Revision row read "No delivered revision recorded." Decided: **(a)** `acceptanceNoChangeCheck` skips the probe for a task delivered as files (`deliveredAsFiles`: a review subject with no work revision behind it, the predicate ruling 546 uses too); such a task is accepted as the ordinary PR-less completion ("Completion accepted ... (no linked pull request)"), since the verdict gate already passes it on its files' verdict. **(b)** The task page's confirm is handed the delivery's time (`filesDeliveredAt`) and says what is true: Merges "Nothing: the delivery is the files saved on this task, so no pull request merges.", Revision "The files delivered on this task at <time> UTC.", and no GitHub re-check. The board's confirm carries no delivery facts and already says nothing false ("No linked pull request. The task closes without a merge."). The operator's acceptance card already said there is no pull request, so nothing merges. Tests: `no-change-acceptance.server.test.ts` "ruling 550: a task delivered as files is accepted as delivered, never as \"completed with no changes\"" (no GitHub ref read, no `noChanges`, the ordinary completion event), `accept-confirm.test.tsx` "names the files as the delivery and promises no merge and no re-check" and `task-detail-route.server.test.ts` "hands the accept confirm the delivery's time, and nothing for a task with a commit revision"; canaries, the probe exclusion dropped, the dialog's files arms dropped, and the loader's field dropped. Bundle ceilings raised with the reason recorded: the task page by 99 B and the board by 69 B. (`app/server/tasks/no-change-completion.server.ts`, `app/schemas/task-file.schema.ts`, `app/routes/project.task.tsx`, `app/features/task-detail/task-detail-page.tsx`, `app/features/task-detail/accept-confirm.tsx`.) *(Amended 2026-09-28 on review: the re-check inside the lock uses the same predicate as the check before the probe (`probeCandidate`), so a files delivery that lands while GitHub is being read stops the no-change close instead of slipping past it.)*

551. **A task attachment reads in pages** (live, 2026-09-28: the controller on AWSC-2; amends rulings 293 and 533). `read_task_attachment` returned the first 40,000 characters of a file and said `truncated`, with no way to read on. Asked to promote the "KB-ready corrected table" at the end of AWSC-2's 55,818-byte `mapping-review.md` into the mapping knowledge base, the controller could read 11 of the table's 25 Azure rows and none of its on-premises rows, refused to copy a partial table, and asked the owner to hold the acceptance. The operator's reader had the same wall, and a large inventory (an RVTools export) would meet it on intake. Decided: both coordinators' `read_task_attachment` take `offset` (characters, default 0). A read returns up to 40,000 characters from it; a truncated read carries `nextOffset`, and a page past the first carries its `offset`, so pages read in turn join into the exact file. A spreadsheet pages through its sheets-as-CSV text the same way: the workbook's whole text is rendered (up to 16 million characters, `truncated` on its last page beyond that) and sliced exactly like a text file, because the renderer stops at whole lines and a page cut at its own budget would skip the rest of the line it stopped before. An offset past the end is refused with the file's length in characters. Test: `controller-run.server.test.ts` "ruling 551: a long attachment reads in pages that join back into the whole file" (100,000 characters in three pages, joined and compared, and the past-the-end sentence); canary, `offset` ignored in `textPage`. (`app/server/files/task-attachments.server.ts`, `app/server/controller/controller-toolkit.server.ts`, `app/server/tasks/operator-toolkit.server.ts`.)

552. **An attachment is read and written as the file it is, and read within bounds** (review of this branch, 2026-09-28; amends rulings 293, 533, 538 and 549; completes ruling 460). Ruling 460 made a task's attachments folder writable by every agent in the group, so a name in it can be a symlink an agent planted to a file only the server may read (another person's credentials, the store's state), and every reader followed it: the coordinators' `read_task_attachment`, the citation corpus (ruling 549), the relay (ruling 538), which copied the file onto another task as an ordinary file every agent can read, and the serving route, which handed it to anyone in the project. Every writer (`writeTaskAttachment`: a person's upload, a filed task's input, a relayed file) wrote through such a link into the file it pointed at. The new `.xlsx` reader (ruling 533) was unbounded in three ways: a cell reference past Excel's last column padded a row to that column, so a 1 KB workbook ended the process out of heap; unclosed `<row>`, `<c>` or `<si>` tags made each lazy pattern re-read the rest of the part, minutes of a blocked event loop for 2 KB compressed; and many sheets naming one part inflated it once each. Decided: **(a)** every reader of an attachment reads through `readAttachmentBytes`: a descriptor opened with `O_NOFOLLOW`, a regular file only, its size checked against the reader's cap before a byte is read (images 3.75 MB, workbooks 25 MB, text 16 MB, a relayed file 10 MB, the serving route 50 MB, a citation 4 MB). A link reads as no file: the reader says there is none, the relay refuses it by name, the route answers 404. **(b)** `writeTaskAttachment` writes the whole file under a fresh hidden name (`O_EXCL | O_NOFOLLOW`) and renames it over the entry, which replaces a link there instead of writing through it. **(c)** The workbook reader finds elements by a forward scan whose cost is linear in the part, skips a cell past column XFD, shares one 128 MB inflate budget across the workbook's parts, reads a part two sheets name once, reads at most 256 sheets, and keeps a character reference outside Unicode as written instead of throwing. **(d)** An upload's name is refused, by a sentence and before a task key is taken, for every character the store's resolver refuses (`/`, `\`, NUL): a filing with `a\b.png` used to take the key and fail on the write. Tests: `task-attachments.server.test.ts` "ruling 552: a link in the attachments folder is never followed" (the reader and the citation corpus read nothing through a link; a write replaces a link and leaves the file it pointed at alone), `xlsx-text.server.test.ts` "xlsxToText against a hostile workbook" (a cell past XFD, 200,000 unclosed rows under two seconds, a code point past U+10FFFF), and `task-actions.server.test.ts` "one refused file refuses the filing, and burns no key" (the crafted name); canaries, `readFileSync` through the link, `writeFileSync` through it, the code-point guard dropped and the separator test dropped. (`app/server/files/task-attachments.server.ts`, `app/server/files/xlsx-text.server.ts`, `app/server/tasks/task-relay.server.ts`, `app/routes/task-attachment.ts`.)

553. **A resumed Claude run's spending cap makes room for restored spend only when the CLI will restore it** (review of this branch, 2026-09-28; narrows ruling 542). Ruling 542 raises a resumed run's cap by what its session had spent, because the CLI measures the cap against the cost state it restores. The CLI restores that state only when the resumed session was the last one it ran in the working directory, per account home, and every controller conversation shares one scratch folder: a turn of another conversation in between means nothing is restored, and the raise was spend the run could overrun its cap by. Decided: `startRun` sets `costStateRestored` when the newest other Claude run under the same account, working where this one will (a controller turn: any controller turn; a task run: the same task, agent and kind), belongs to the resumed session (`lastClaudeSessionWorkingThere`), and the adapter raises the cap only then. The completion compaction still raises it: it resumes the session right after the run, where the run worked. Tests: `claude-runtime.server.test.ts` "ruling 553: a resume the CLI will not restore keeps the cap at the run's own" and the `costStateRestored` assertions in `run-service.server.test.ts` "ruling 559 …" (true when the session worked there last, false once another session has); canaries, the cap raised whenever the session has totals, and the flag forced false. (`app/server/runtimes/run-store.server.ts`, `app/server/runtimes/run-service.server.ts`, `app/server/runtimes/claude-runtime.server.ts`.)

554. **A page that stops answering does not take the agent's browser with it** (AWSC-9, 2026-09-28; extends ruling 75). Playwright MCP builds every answer from the page: an action's answer carries a snapshot of the current tab, and the tab list reads each tab's title. So a page whose script never yields holds every later call, and none of the agent's ways out works: a navigation to another route of the same single-page app stays in the same document, a new tab on the same site shares the page's renderer, and `browser_close` reads the page before it closes anything. Live on AWSC-9 calculator.aws's S3 form spun its renderer at 90% CPU and 2.4 GB after the Calculator Builder set a checkbox. The builder spent its last twelve minutes on snapshot, navigation, new-tab and screenshot calls that timed out or never came back, then reported the estimate it had built as lost. Reproduced against a private server in the image with a page whose button loops forever: every one of those calls hung, `browser_close` included. Decided: **(a)** `viberr_browser` runs under `browser-supervisor.server.ts`, a pass-through on the server's stdio that node runs as TypeScript, from beside the module or from the image's `app/`. It gives every tool call a deadline, `BROWSER_CALL_DEADLINE_MS` = 90 s, passed as `--deadline-ms`. The deadline is longer than any answer the server gives while its page still answers: a navigation times out at 60 s, then waits up to 10 s for the load and reads the page, and a wait is capped at 30 s. **(b)** A call still unanswered at the deadline makes the supervisor answer every request waiting on that browser: a tool call with a result saying the browser did not answer, was restarted, lost every tab and anything unsaved, and to navigate again and save as it goes on a long form; any other request with a JSON-RPC error carrying the same sentence. The server is then told to end: it closes the browser it launched, and a browser whose server is killed outright ends with its pipe (both measured in the image). A fresh server starts, the client's own `initialize` and `notifications/initialized` are replayed to it, calls sent meanwhile are held until its handshake is answered, and nothing a killed server still writes reaches the client. **(c)** A call the client cancels gets no answer from the server, however well its page is doing, so it cannot prove the page stuck by itself. Its deadline stays as a check: if the server has answered no tool call since it was sent and another call has itself waited 30 seconds behind it (the longest wait the server allows), the browser is restarted; a call sent a moment before the check proves nothing yet, so the check waits until it has; with nothing waiting it is forgotten, and the client gets no answer to it. A second review found the check counting a call sent a moment before it and restarting a browser that was fine. **(d)** Codex is told to wait longer than the supervisor (`tool_timeout_sec` = 120 on this one server): its default gave up first and said only "timed out", so the model never read that the browser had been restarted. **(e)** The browser section of the persona says the deadline before it bites, so a long script in a page is kept short and a long form is saved as it goes. An agent's own script (`browser_evaluate`, `browser_run_code_unsafe`) has no bound of its own in the server, so one that runs past the deadline is ended the same way. **(f)** The server ending by itself ends the supervisor with its code once its output is read (`close`, not `exit`), as the client saw before, and only after what the supervisor wrote has left its stdout: exiting at once cut a 2 MB answer at 128 KB for a client that read slowly. One that cannot be started ends it with 1. A deployment missing the supervisor refuses the mount by name, like one missing `@playwright/mcp`. Tests: `browser-supervisor.server.test.ts`, the real supervisor over a stand-in server process: a call answered in time passes through on one server; every request waiting on a stuck browser is answered, the stuck server ends, and the next call is answered by a fresh server that heard both halves of the handshake, with each request answered once; a cancelled call the browser never answered restarts it once another call has waited behind it, not for a call sent a moment before its deadline, and is forgotten when the browser answered since or nothing waits; a server's own ending keeps its code and its last words, and its own process passes a 2 MB last answer whole to a client that reads it a second late. Each canary, a line of the supervisor removed or bypassed (`settle`, the waiter's proof, the flush before exit among them), turns it red. `specialist-browser-mcp.server.test.ts` pins the supervisor and its deadline in front of the CLI, and `codex-runtime.server.test.ts` the browser's `tool_timeout_sec`. (`app/server/tasks/browser-supervisor.server.ts`, `app/server/tasks/browser-deadline.server.ts`, `app/server/tasks/specialist-browser-mcp.server.ts`, `app/server/runtimes/codex-runtime.server.ts`.)

555. **The deliverer is offered no verdict, and its reply is its delivery** (AWSC-3, 2026-09-28; extends rulings 313 and 388). The verdict channel was gated on the profile's grant, so a verdict-capable profile engaged as a task's deliverer got it on its delivering run. Live on AWSC-3 the Estimate Judge designed the benchmark samples (it delivers there) and ended its report "**Approved.**". Completion took that as a review verdict, filed the samples as the evidence for it, and never stamped `deliveredAt`. The task walked to Review with nothing delivered, a verdict bound to nothing ("Approval noted … no delivered revision"), a Review-entry note about a missing pull request, and the operator re-running the same agent into the same record. `requiredReviewers` has never counted a deliverer, so the deliverer's verdict was never one that gated anything: the deliverer mints and everyone else judges. Decided: **(a)** a delivering run, fresh or resumed, is dispatched with `collab.verdict` off, as ruling 313 withholds it per run: Claude's `report_outcome` has no verdict field and its prompt no "report `approve` or `request_changes`". Codex's envelope schema is one static schema that carries the field for every run (B-5), so there **(b)** decides. **(b)** Completion authorizes no verdict from a run dispatched to deliver (`verdictAuthorized` requires `!input.delivers`, the flag the delivery reconcile reads), so a verdict in its envelope or its prose is discarded. Its reply then carries its evidence and its files, and they stamp the delivery, which the review that follows binds to. The key is the run's dispatch, not the roster at completion: a review run whose profile was handed delivery while it worked still records the verdict it was asked for, and its saved files stamp the delivery only when it was dispatched to deliver (`stampNonCommitDelivery` takes the dispatch's `delivers`), so with no verdict to carry them its captures stay evidence (found in a second review). Tests: `agent-completion.server.test.ts` "ruling 555: a deliverer's reply is its delivery, whatever verdict it states" and "ruling 555: a review run whose profile was handed delivery while it worked keeps its verdict" and "ruling 555: that review run's captures never become the delivery, with no verdict to carry them", and `specialist-run.server.test.ts` "ruling 555: the deliverer is offered no verdict, whatever its profile grants" and "ruling 555: a RESUMED deliverer is offered no verdict either"; canaries, the dispatch term dropped from `verdictAuthorized` (or keyed on the roster again), `delivers` dropped from each collab gate, and the dispatch check dropped from `stampNonCommitDelivery`. The same suite's ruling 210 test now dispatches a real reviewer: it used to exercise the reviewer's contract on the deliverer. (`app/server/tasks/specialist-run.server.ts`, `app/server/tasks/task-actions.server.ts`.)

556. **The project's required reviewer cannot deliver, and no reviewer's verdict binds to its own work** (AWSC-3, 2026-09-28; extends rulings 178, 388 and 555). Ruling 178 lets a project require a reviewer at a stage on every task, and nothing stopped the same agent being made a task's deliverer. Live on AWSC-3 the operator did exactly that: the Estimate Judge delivered the benchmark design on a board whose rule is "Estimate Judge reviews at Review". Its verdict on its own delivery does not count (ruling 555), so the task could never pass Review. The gate kept saying "Run the review at Review", and each run it asked for was another delivering run. Worse, the gate let the move to Review file an acceptance card: the deliverer's files had never been stamped, so the task read as having delivered nothing, which ruling 385 does not hold. Accepting it would have recorded "completed with no changes" on a task that delivered files. And the way out an operator would take, handing delivery away and running the Judge as the reviewer, left the review subject the Judge's own files. Decided: **(a)** `assignSpecialist`, the one door to `delivers: true` (the dispatch's engage, its hand-off and a person's assignment all pass through it), refuses a profile any project rule requires as a reviewer: "<Agent> is this project's required reviewer at <Stage>, so it cannot deliver <KEY>: its verdict on its own delivery would not count, and <KEY> could never pass <Stage>. Have another agent deliver it and run <Agent>'s review on what that agent delivers, or change Settings → Required reviewers." **(b)** When nothing asks for delivery, such a reviewer is engaged to review, whatever its grants: the dispatch's derived posture and the operator's `resolveDeliversIntent` both read the rule, so the task page's Run control, the controller and the operator never walk it into (a)'s refusal, and the Run control says so before the click ("Runs as a reviewer: its verdict gates acceptance."; the task loader marks such an agent `requiredReviewer`, and only it, so no other agent's bytes grow). It had promised such an agent the branch. **(c)** The operator's explicit `delivers: true` hand-off to it is refused as a `noop` before any card or trace, because a card would strand a maintainer's Apply on (a)'s refusal. **(d)** On a task whose deliverer already is the required reviewer, engaged before this ruling, `requiredReviewerRefusals` says so before it asks whether anything was delivered: "Required reviewer <Agent> (project rule at <Stage>) is this task's deliverer, so its review cannot count. Hand delivery to another agent, have that agent deliver, and run <Agent>'s review, or an admin can force-accept." **(e)** A verdict never binds to the reviewer's own work. `reviewSubjectAuthor` names who made the subject: the active revision's `sourceProfileId`, or the agent whose event stamped `deliveredAt`. A verdict from that agent is recorded in words, "approved, but it made what is delivered, so its verdict does not count", and binds to nothing. **(f)** And the acceptance gates never ask for that review: delivery handed to another agent that has saved nothing yet leaves the reviewer's own work as the subject. `acceptanceBlockedReason` says "A required reviewer made the work delivered on this task, so its approval of it cannot count. Have another agent deliver its own work, then run the review, or an admin can force-accept." for an engaged one, and `requiredReviewerRefusals` names the project rule's reviewer the same way; both take the subject's author, which every caller reads from the timeline. They had asked for a review whose verdict could never bind (found in a second review). Tests: `required-reviewers.server.test.ts` "ruling 556: the project's required reviewer cannot deliver" (the engage refused with the sentence and the roster unchanged; the gate's sentence on a task the reviewer delivers, with its files delivered and with nothing recorded as delivered); `operator-actions.server.test.ts` "ruling 556: refuses a hand-off to the project's required reviewer before any card" and "ruling 556: offers the project's required reviewer as a reviewer, even when it could deliver"; `specialist-run.server.test.ts` "ruling 556: runs the project's required reviewer to review, even when it could deliver"; `agent-completion.server.test.ts` "ruling 556: a reviewer's verdict never binds to files it saved itself"; `required-reviewers.server.test.ts` "tells a task whose delivered work its required reviewer made that the review cannot count" (before it is engaged again, and once it is); and `task-detail-components.test.tsx` "names the posture the pick will take, BEFORE the run is spent". Canaries: the check dropped from `assignSpecialist`, the rule dropped from each derived posture, the deliverer branch moved below the "nothing delivered" return, the operator's pre-check dropped, `!ownWork` dropped from the binding, the author branch dropped from either gate, and the Run control's `requiredReviewer` term dropped. (`app/server/tasks/required-reviewers.server.ts`, `app/server/tasks/specialist-run.server.ts`, `app/server/tasks/operator-actions.server.ts`, `app/server/tasks/task-actions.server.ts`, `app/schemas/task-file.schema.ts`.)

557. **A task takes the files it works from** (AWSC-4 to AWSC-7, 2026-09-28; extends rulings 488 and 538). A relay pushes: `relay_to_task` runs on the task that holds the files, from its operator or its agents' outcomes. When AWSC-3 (the benchmark design) was accepted, its operator had relayed nothing, and a closed task's operator starts no run, so nothing could carry its inputs over. AWSC-4 to AWSC-7 each opened a packet asking the owner to attach its input by hand, the one thing the operator's doctrine says never to ask ("never ask for an attachment to be carried over"). One of them said why: it had no tool that copies a file from a closed task. Decided: the task that needs the files takes them. The operator's `take_from_task` (Claude tool and Codex plan action, the relay's `append-typed-events` grant) copies named attachments of another task of the project, open or Done, onto its own task. The files are claimed by the operator's comment under a relay's own header, "From <that task> (operator):", so completion credits no run on this task with them (ruling 538). The source task gets "Taken by <this task>: …", and the audit row is `task.files.taken {from, to, files}`. A person the optional line tags is notified, as by any comment (NEW-4). Every file passes the relay's checks, all or none: named, present on the source, no link (ruling 552), an upload's kinds and size, at most ten, never an overwrite (the next free name instead). Refused, writing nothing: this task, another project's task, a missing task, a missing file, a closed task to take onto, and an archived task to take from (its work was withdrawn, and its file takes no writes, the "Taken by" line included). The claim carries the relay's disclosure of a tag that reaches nobody (S5-G3). The audit row is written with the files; the source's line comes last and never fails the take, or a relay: a source whose file cannot be written (a hand-edited Done task's) must not turn files that landed into an error the operator acts on again, and the reply says whether the line was written. The Codex plan's `text` field names the take's line, which the executor passes on. The tool and the doctrine both say to take only what the task works from, never a file another task keeps from it, such as an answer key; the seeded operator definition and the app-expertise skill name the tool, their outgoing hashes recorded. Tests: `task-relay.server.test.ts` "ruling 557: a task takes the files it works from" (a Done source's named file lands claimed under a relay header and the answer key stays; the refusals, an archived source among them, write nothing; a tag that reaches nobody is said on the claim; a source that cannot take its line still gives its files, audited, and the reply says the line is missing; the tool is withheld with the comment grant), `operator-run.server.test.ts` "ruling 557: a Codex plan's take_from_task puts the other task's files on this one, with its line" and its all-denied fallback (14 tools, `take_from_task` among them), and `mention-notify.server.test.ts`'s writer table (the take's line fans its mention out, and the site inventory counts it); canaries, a closed source refused, the claim headed otherwise, the archived refusal dropped, the disclosure dropped, the source's line made fatal or reported as written, and the executor's case or its `text` dropped. (`app/server/tasks/task-relay.server.ts`, `app/server/tasks/operator-actions.server.ts`, `app/server/tasks/operator-toolkit.server.ts`, `app/server/runtimes/operator-run.server.ts`, `app/server/seed/assets/operator.definition.md`, `app/server/seed/assets/viberr-app-expertise.skill.md`.)

558. **A file still being put down for someone else is never a run's** (review of rulings 533 and 538, 2026-09-28). A completion credits its run with every file saved in the run's window except those a person's note or a relay's comment claims (rulings 533 and 538). Those writers, and the take (ruling 557), put the file down first and write the claim second. So a completion that listed the file between the two read a timeline with no claim on it, and took the file as the run's own; for a deliverer, as its delivery, stamping `deliveredAt` onto a person's input or a relayed sample. Reordering every writer to claim first would leave a claim naming a file that failed to land. Decided: `withAttachmentClaims` holds the names on the task, in memory (one process writes a data root), from before the files land until the claiming entry is on the timeline, and `attachTaskFile`, `relayToTask` and `takeFromTask` write inside it. A completion reads the held names after it lists the run's files and before it reads the timeline. A file it saw is then either still held, or already claimed on the timeline it reads next. Filing a task with its files needs no hold: no run exists yet. A file lands with its claim or not at all: the hold hands its writer the store's `put`, and when the claim cannot be written every file put is taken back up before the names are released, a new one removed and a replaced one put back (set aside by a rename, which moves the entry and never follows a link, ruling 552). A file nothing claims is the next completion's to credit, and a relay whose second file failed to land had left its first that way. A writer releases only its own entry: a relay of text alone holds no name, and when it dropped the task's entry on its way out it released a take's hold made after it (both found in review). Tests: `agent-completion.server.test.ts` "ruling 558: a file still being put down for someone else when the run completes is never the run's" (a deliverer's completion lands inside the hold), "ruling 558: a completion that lands while %s is claiming its file leaves the file to it" (a person's upload, a relay and a take, each stopped on the task's file lock between its file and its claim) and "ruling 558: %s whose claim cannot be written leaves no file behind"; `task-attachments.server.test.ts` "ruling 558: a file put down for someone else" (taken back, a replaced file restored; kept with nothing set aside left over; held for its writer when another finishes first). Canaries: the held names dropped from the completion's exclusion; a writer holding no name; a writer writing past `put`; the take-back, the keep and the entry check each dropped. (`app/server/files/task-attachments.server.ts`, `app/server/tasks/task-actions.server.ts`, `app/server/tasks/task-relay.server.ts`.)

559. **A resumed Claude run records its own spend after a restart too** (live, 2026-09-28: the first controller turn after deploy 3; completes ruling 542). Ruling 542 keeps the totals each Claude session last reported in the adapter's memory, and a restart empties it, so a resumed session's first run after every deploy recorded the whole session's spend again: the controller's turn was recorded at $3.36 where its own share was about $0.85. Decided: `startRun` reads, for a resumed Claude run, the newest `result` message the session's other runs logged (`lastSessionResultRaw`: a completion compaction's result is a line of the run it compacted, so it counts; a run stopped before its result is passed over for the one before it), and hands its totals to the adapter as `resumedSessionReported`. The adapter uses them only when its own memory of the session is empty. A session whose lines were pruned has nothing to read and is recorded as reported, as before. Tests: `run-service.server.test.ts` "ruling 559: a resumed Claude run is handed what its session last reported, read from the run log" and `claude-runtime.server.test.ts` "ruling 559: after a restart, a resumed run takes its share from the result its run log recalls" (the live figures); canaries, the lookup dropped and `recallReported` dropped. (`app/server/runtimes/run-store.server.ts`, `app/server/runtimes/run-service.server.ts`, `app/server/runtimes/claude-runtime.server.ts`, `app/server/runtimes/adapter.server.ts`.)

560. **An epic's history reads as a feed, and the epic page is one column on a phone** (owner, 2026-09-28, on a screenshot of the AWSC epic's History, eight "Arda (via the controller) made AWSC-N in this epic." lines under eight "10:41" stamps: "make this look better please, shadcn like and research"; extends ruling 503(e)). The History panel drew each entry as a grid row: an 8.5rem stamp column, which held "10:41" for today and "Yesterday · 18:02" before it, then the sentence. The tasks a sentence names were `RichText` links, and outside `.md-body` no rule styled them, so they took the browser's own link colours: lavender, and pink once visited, which is why AWSC-1 and AWSC-2 read differently from AWSC-3 in the screenshot. The references were the shadcn registries' timeline and activity-feed examples (ReUI's, on the Origin UI timeline): a thin rail with small markers, the event in a muted voice with its objects set apart, the time small at the side, days as quiet headers. They were read the way `design/html-app` is, per the ruling-166 boundary; nothing was installed. Decided: **(a)** *Days head the entries.* The newest eight entries (the preview is unchanged) are grouped by day, "Today", "Yesterday", "Sep 25". The walk keys on the absolute day, never on its year-less label, and its first pass is UTC like every hydrated stamp's. It is `daySections` (`app/shared/dates/day-sections.ts`), which the Notifications stream now calls for the same loop it held inline. **(b)** *An entry is a dot on one rail.* Each entry is a hollow dot on a hairline rail that runs on to the next entry's dot. The sentence is in the feeds' muted voice, and its clock ("10:41", tabular figures) sits at the right edge in a `<time>`. **(c)** *A task an entry names is a key chip.* `RichText`'s task links carry `.keybtn`, the chip the Activity and Notifications feeds link a task with, so the browser's colours are gone. Today the epic History is the only `RichText` that links tasks. **(d)** *"Show N more" and "Show less".* The toggle is the page's small ghost button, with a chevron and `aria-expanded`. It used to be the "Show all 11 entries" / "Show the latest only" link. **(e)** *The epic page is one column at 1100px and under.* The 1100px block's collapse of `.epic-layout` and `.epic-side` came earlier in the sheet than their base rules and had the same specificity, so it never applied. At 375px, About, Tasks and History were 0px wide beside the 340px Details column. The collapse now carries one class more (`.policy-wrap .epic-layout`, `.epic-layout .epic-side`), the precedent of ruling 99's `.ctl-wrap .ctl-layout`. Not changed: which entries there are, their words and order, the preview of eight, and what a history line says (the controller still writes one line per task it makes). Tests: `epic-page.test.tsx` "History shows the newest eight entries under their days, with Show more for the rest, and links the tasks it names" (the days, the preview, the task link, Show 2 more and Show less); `notifications-page.test.tsx` keeps the day walk's year-apart case through `daySections`; and `e2e/09-epics.spec.ts` "at 375px the epic page reads in one column" (on the old sheet the main column measured 0px wide at 375px in Chromium). Budgets (ruling 457): the stylesheet every route loads grew 156 B gzip (45,478 -> 45,634), and each budgeted closure by the same bytes, 150 to 164 B (root 182,349 -> 182,505, login 185,660 -> 185,816, Home 206,671 -> 206,821, board 254,540 -> 254,696, task 330,015 -> 330,179, Controller 279,222 -> 279,380, Profile 212,000 -> 212,158), each ceiling raised with its note. `daySections` is its own module (`app/shared/dates/day-sections.ts`), so it rides only the Notifications and epic pages: inside `format.ts` it added about 90 B more to every one of them. (`app/features/epics/epic-page.tsx`, `app/ui/rich-text.tsx`, `app/shared/dates/day-sections.ts`, `app/features/notifications/notifications-page.tsx`, `app/app.css`, `docs/domain/controller-and-epics.md` §7.4, `docs/ui/surfaces.md`, `test-support/perf-budgets/bundle.json`.)

561. **A press that takes the focus out of a label field lands on what it pressed: the field keeps its height until the press is over** (owner, 2026-09-28, starting the follow-up that ruling 548's PR named as a known issue: "One click on Save with the list open saves, in a real Chromium"; the case ruling 548's picker was built around). On a task's Details panel, with the Labels editor's list open under its field, one press on Save posted nothing and left the editor open; a second press saved, and Cancel lost its first press the same way. Measured in Chromium on VIB-151: the press took the focus from the field, so its blur and `useDismiss`'s outside press folded the list as the press began, and Save rose 128 px (67 px with a label half typed, which the blur commits) before the release. The release landed on no button, and a browser sends a click only where both halves of a press land. Decided: **(a)** *The field holds its height through the press.* While its list is shown or a label is half typed, `LabelInput` (`app/ui/label-input.tsx`) listens for a press outside it, on the window in the capture phase so before anything the press sets off, and holds the height it has until the press's click, which the browser aims at where the press began and ended before any listener runs, or the drop of a drag the press started. What the press does is unchanged: the list folds and a half-typed label is committed as the press begins, so Save still posts that label, and for the moment the press lasts the list's room stays empty under the chips. **(b)** *Not for a select.* A select opens its menu on the press and the menu takes the release, so a held field would let go under an open menu, or never; a press on one (the New-task dialog's Epic menu) folds the list at once, as before. A press with another button than the first holds nothing either. **(c)** *Every label field.* The hold is `LabelInput`'s, so the New-task dialog's field keeps it too, where the fields below it, or above it in a body scrolled to its end, moved with the list. **(d)** *The list still folds.* It is not kept open while the editor is, as ruling 548's picker keeps its own: a folded list is how the field shows the focus has left it, and a half-typed label moves the rows either way. **(e)** *Pinned in a browser.* `e2e/11-label-editor-press.spec.ts` presses Save once where it stood, after a pick and with a label half typed; without the hold both fail with the editor still open.

562. **An answer goes back to the agent that asked only when it can run now** (live, 2026-09-28, AWSC-6; narrows R15-14, completes ruling 447). An agent's question is answered back to it by resuming its session through the @mention door, and when that run does not start the answer falls back to the operator. Live on AWSC-6 the Cloud Solutions Architect asked its mapping question and the operator moved the task on to Estimate on the defaults it proposed; when Arda answered, the hand-back was posted first, "This is the decision you were blocked on. Continue from where you stopped", and the run was refused after it: the Architect does not work at Estimate, and a relayed answer writes no "Mention not started" note (F35-5). The record kept an instruction nobody read, under a decision that said "Operator re-engages the specialist with a summon note", and only the operator's own comment said the Architect would not run. Decided: `answerAskingAgent` asks the resume door's own gate (`assertResumeEligible`: the stage, the hold, the closure) before it posts anything. When the asker cannot run, nothing is posted to it, a note says "The answer went to the operator, not back to <agent>, who asked: <the gate's first sentence>", and the operator gets the answer as `packet-resolved`. And the record of an agent's question names the decision only, "**Decision:** <option>.": the events after it say who took the answer, which the fixed sentence could not know. Test: `agent-reply.server.test.ts` "ruling 562: the answer to an agent that cannot run at the task's stage now goes to the operator, and says so"; canaries, the eligibility check dropped from `answerAskingAgent` and the fixed sentence restored. (`app/server/tasks/task-actions.server.ts`.)

563. **An agent can read a timeline entry its prompt clipped** (live, 2026-09-28, AWSC-4; completes rulings 285 and 392). An agent's prompt carries the task's five newest timeline entries, each clipped at 220 characters, and no agent tool read one whole: ruling 285 gave the operator `read_timeline_entry`, and ruling 392 carried standing verdicts whole, but every other entry stopped at the clip. Live on AWSC-4 the Cloud Solutions Architect's run was cut off by the Codex usage limit while it worked from Arda's four-item answer, and the retry on Claude started with no directive; the answer reached it only as "1=Shared tenancy for the 16 ordinary EC2 VMs. > 2=RDS for SQL Server 2…". It looked for a tool to read the rest, found none, reconstructed items 3 and 4 from its own defaults, and raised a packet asking for the text again. Decided: a clipped entry in the prompt's recent timeline ends "(clipped; the whole entry is at `<occurredAt>`)", and a whole one carries no stamp. Claude agents get `read_timeline_entry`, which reads one entry of their own task whole by that stamp (`readTimelineEntry`, the operator's reader), behind `read_board`'s gate: this task only, read-only, nothing a member could not read on the task page. Tests: `canonical-anchor.server.test.ts` "ruling 563: a clipped timeline entry names the stamp that reads it whole, and a whole one does not"; `agent-toolkit.server.test.ts` "ruling 563: read_timeline_entry reads one entry of this task whole" and the mounted-tools list. Canaries: the stamp dropped, every entry stamped, the tool left unbuilt. (`app/server/tasks/task-actions.server.ts`, `app/server/tasks/agent-toolkit.server.ts`.)

564. **A run that posts files keeps its file tools, confined to where its posting goes** (live, 2026-09-28, AWSC-4..7; completes rulings 109 and 535 on Claude; narrows the parity ruling of 2026-08-31). Ruling 109 gives every run whose profile holds `attach-evidence-references` the task's attachments folder, and ruling 535 lets the agent that makes a result deliver it there without a repo-write grant. The write posture never met either: a withheld `execute-code-or-write-repo` removes `Edit`, `MultiEdit` and `Write` outright, so on Claude the agent a results board exists for could post files and had no tool to write one. Live on AWSC-4..7 every Claude run of the AWS calculator board called `Write` first, read "No such tool available: Write", and wrote its deliverable through a shell heredoc: the Cloud Solutions Architect's `mapping.md`, the Calculator Builder's `estimate-link.md`, `summary.md` and `assumptions.md`. The architect wrote every amount as "USD", because an unquoted heredoc expands a `$` away (`$766.63` reads `66.63`). Decided: a specialist or review run with an attachments folder whose grants deny the three keeps them, and a `PreToolUse` hook (matcher `Edit|MultiEdit|Write`) refuses a call whose `file_path` resolves outside the folder and the temp directory, with a sentence naming the withheld grant, the folder and the path. `NotebookEdit` stays denied, the operator and the controller never qualify, and the Bash hook still names a refusal from the grants' whole denylist. One derivation, `fileWriteRoots` (`file-tool-policy.server.ts`), feeds the adapter's hook and the run's disclosure: `tools.denied` drops the three and `tools.fileWriteRoots` lists the roots, which the console's tools row states. It is coverage, not containment, like the Bash hook beside it (ruling 101(e)): the run keeps Bash. Codex is unchanged, advisory since ruling 185. The persona's posting sentence now reads "write or copy it into that directory". Tests: `claude-runtime.server.test.ts` "the file tools of a run that posts files (ruling 564)" (kept and confined; writes the folder and the temp directory, a symlinked spelling of it included, and refuses the checkout, a `..` escape, a sibling prefix, the folder itself and a relative path; nothing changes without a folder, with repo-write granted or on an operator; `git commit` still names the grant); `specialist-run.server.test.ts` "ruling 564: a Claude run that posts files records its file tools as confined, not denied" (fresh and resumed, and Codex unconfined); `runs-helpers.test.ts` "ruling 564: a run whose file tools are confined says where they write". Canaries: hand the SDK the unfiltered denylist; answer `{}` from the file hook; drop the kind check (the operator's own `Write` deny is stripped); name Bash refusals from the filtered list; compare paths without `realpathSync`; drop `fileWriteRoots` from either disclosure path or the console clause.

565. **An answer to an agent still running waits for that run** (live, 2026-09-28, AWSC-5; completes rulings 203 and 562). An agent raises its question with `ask_human` and may keep working, so the answer can land while its run is still going. `answerAskingAgent` posted it through `commentToAgent`, whose single-flight guard refused the resume, and because a relayed answer writes no "Mention not started" note (F35-5), the refusal fell through as "not delivered" to the operator hand-off. That was the wrong reading of the one refusal viberr makes good on: the busy run's completion delivers every human comment addressed to the agent after it started (`deliverDeferredMention`, ruling 203). Live on AWSC-5 the Cloud Solutions Architect asked about three sizing choices and kept checking its tables; Arda's answer, which corrected the cart-mongo cluster to one writer and one reader, was refused, the operator was handed it with nothing on the record, and it wrote that the answer "went straight to" the architect's live run. The run never saw it until its own completion delivered the comment two minutes later. Decided: `commentToAgent` marks a refusal by its single-flight guard `deferred`, and `answerAskingAgent` treats a deferred relay as delivered: the answer stays on the record, a note says "The answer waits for <agent>, who asked: its run on this task is still going, and Viberr starts it on the answer as soon as that run finishes.", and the operator is not handed it; the run's completion starts the asker on it, and ruling 211(b)'s note covers a delivery that cannot start then. Test: `agent-reply.server.test.ts` "ruling 565: the answer to an agent still running on the task waits for that run, and says so" (the note, no operator hand-off, and the completion owes exactly that comment). Canaries: return `triggered !== null` alone; stop marking the guard's refusal `deferred`.

566. **An agent can look at the pages of a PDF** (live, 2026-09-28, AWSC-6 and AWSC-7; extends ruling 196). calculator.aws exports an estimate as a PDF, and the board's rulings ask the Calculator Builder to deliver every verified export and the Estimate Judge to check them. Neither could look at one: the image had no PDF renderer, and a run cannot install an operating-system package. Three of four result runs on the board reached for `pdftoppm` and read "pdftoppm is not installed"; the Estimate Judge approved AWSC-6 with "the PDF pages were not rendered because there is no PDF renderer here", and the AWSC-7 Builder, trying to decode the PDF's streams by hand instead, was killed when its command's output passed 5 GB. Decided: the image installs `poppler-utils` (`pdftoppm`, `pdftotext`, `pdfinfo`) in its own `apt-get` layer after chromium, so the addition re-fetches nothing; the layer measured 15.2 MB. It is not added to the shell inventory's fixed list (ruling 191): that list names the tools a run plans around when they are ABSENT, `pdftoppm` writes its version to stderr where the probe does not read, and the runs here reached for it unprompted. Verified by building the image (`pdftoppm version 25.03.0`) and rendering a one-page PDF to PNG inside it. Test: `toolchain.server.test.ts` "ruling 566: installs poppler-utils, in a layer after chromium" (the Dockerfile pin ruling 196 uses; canary: delete the install line).

567. **A run a restart cuts off keeps what it saved** (live, 2026-09-28, AWSC-7; completes rulings 177 and 388). A person's Stop and a failed run both reach the completion effects, which post the run's saved files under its name and record a deliverer's as the delivery (`stampNonCommitDelivery`). A restart reached none of it: `finalizeOrphanedRuns` marked the run interrupted, wrote the "Interrupted by a restart" note and re-invoked the operator. Live on AWSC-7 deploy 17 cut the Calculator Builder after it had saved every result file and before it reported. The files belonged to nobody and `deliveredAt` stayed null, so the required reviewer's gate read "nothing delivered" (ruling 161), the operator's move to Review filed "Recommendation: Accept completion and move AWSC-7 to Done" before the Estimate Judge had started, and the Judge's verdict, dispatched on no subject, could bind to nothing. Decided: before the note, each started specialist or review run the restart cut off gets the completion effects a person's Stop gets, replayed as `state: "interrupted"` (no deferred @mention redelivery, ruling 211(c); an interrupted run never reacts, so the operator re-invoke stays the only one). Its last words and saved files are posted under its name, and a deliverer's files become the delivery. The re-invokes now wait for the notes, so the operator reads the delivery the replay recorded; they also take the sweep's data root, as the notes do, and its `runOperator` is replaceable like every other operator hand-off's (`deps.runOperator`). Tests: `run-recovery.server.test.ts` "ruling 567: a deliverer the restart cut off keeps its saved files as the delivery, recorded before the operator runs again" (the files under the deliverer's name, `deliveredAt` on that event, the note after it, and `deliveredAt` already set when the operator is called) and "ruling 567: a reviewer the restart cut off has its files posted under its name, and they are not the delivery". Canaries: drop the replay (both fail); drop `await notes` from the re-invokes (the operator is called while `deliveredAt` is null). *(Narrowed 2026-09-28 by ruling 570: a cut-off deliverer's files are the delivery only when they are not all browser working files.)*

568. **A correction does not carry a knowledge base's text to agents it is not given** (live, 2026-09-28, AWSC-4; narrows ruling 498). Ruling 498 records every knowledge-base correction on the task that made it, with the passage before and after. A task's timeline is read by every agent that can be engaged on it (the prompt's recent entries, ruling 563; `read_timeline_entry`; the operator's snapshot), and a grant is the only thing deciding who reads a knowledge base. So correcting one granted to few agents copied its text to the rest. Live on AWSC-4 the Estimate Judge found that its own sample-01 golden-set entry asked for a configuration calculator.aws cannot price, and did not correct it: the entry would have put expected answers on a benchmark task in front of the agents under test. The operator then asked Arda to edit the file by hand. Decided: a correction's entry quotes the passages only for the project's rulings, which every run reads, or for a knowledge base every specialist deployed on the project is given. Otherwise it names the document and the correction's id, says which agents are not given the knowledge base, and points to the Controller page, which shows it whole. An undo's entry follows the same rule, and the tool's answer says the entry did not quote it. The operator is not counted: it holds no knowledge base on most projects, and counting it would leave no correction quoted outside the rulings. The specialist tool description and persona note say so, and the Codex note, whose correction rides the agent's report, now says to quote nothing from a knowledge base some agents are not given. Tests: `operator-actions.server.test.ts` "ruling 568: a correction to a knowledge base some deployed agents are not given quotes none of it, and neither does its undo" and "ruling 568: a correction to a knowledge base every deployed agent is given keeps its quote". Canaries: build the entry without the left-out agents; build the undo from the quote alone.

569. **A task can read how the tasks it waited on ended** (live, 2026-09-28, AWSC-8; extends rulings 281 and 282). A task that waits on others (`blockedBy`) is released when they finish, and its work is usually to use what they found. Its readers could learn only that they had finished: `read_board` with a key stopped at the goal, and `take_from_task` carries files. Live on AWSC-8, the research task that turns four benchmark scores into workflow changes, three operators had relayed their Judge's score and AWSC-7's had not. Its 90/100 for sample-04 lived only in AWSC-7's verdict, so the AWSC-8 operator told its researcher "neither you nor I can read that" and to ask Arda to paste it. Decided: `read_board` with a key carries the task's `outcome` once it has one: the completion summary when it describes what the task delivered (`currentCompletionPacket`), and each verdict bound to that delivery, with its agent, result and report. Each side is up to 8,000 characters, with an excerpt marker past that. A verdict on an earlier delivery is left out, and a task with neither carries no `outcome`. The operator and the specialists share the reader (ruling 281), and both tool descriptions name the field. Test: `operator-toolkit.server.test.ts` "ruling 569: read_board(taskKey) carries a finished task's outcome, and nothing stale". Canaries: drop `outcome` from the single-task read; stop filtering verdicts on the current subject. *(Amended 2026-09-28: a verdict stores the first 2,000 characters of its report and a line naming the timeline (ruling 292), which a reader on another task cannot open, so live on AWSC-8 the researcher read AWSC-7's verdict to character 2,000 of 5,382 and asked Arda to paste the rest. The report now comes whole from the agent's "Review verdict" comment (ruling 317), the newest at or before the verdict's stamp that opens with what the verdict stored, and the stored text stands when there is none. Test: "ruling 569: a verdict's report is read whole from its Review verdict comment, not the stored excerpt". Canaries: return the stored reason; drop the opening match.)*

570. **The browser's working files are never a delivery** (live, 2026-09-28, AWSC-8; narrows rulings 388 and 567). A deliverer's saved files become the task's delivery (`stampNonCommitDelivery`), and ruling 567 made a run a restart cuts off reach that stamp. Among its files can be the browser's working files: the `page-….yml` snapshots and `console-….log` dumps its tools write into the attachments folder. Ruling 105 calls them tool transport and prunes them from a finished run, and an interrupted one keeps them as its only diagnostics. So a deliverer cut off mid-browse had its snapshots recorded as the delivery. Live on AWSC-8 deploy 20 cut the Workflow Researcher while it reproduced a calculator form, and `deliveredAt` moved off its report, whose `improvements.md` it had saved at 21:34, onto twelve page snapshots and a console log. Decided: a run whose saved files are all browser working files (`isBrowserWorkingArtifact`: a machine-stamped name that is not visual evidence) does not move the delivery; the files are still posted under its name. A screenshot or a deliberately named file still counts. Test: `run-recovery.server.test.ts` "ruling 570: a deliverer cut off mid-browse has its working files posted under its name, and they are not the delivery". Canary: stamp on any attachment again.

571. **No string the server writes carries an em or en dash** (owner, 2026-09-28, on a screenshot of an Operator comment on a task timeline, "Started a Claude run for the Estimate Judge agent — streaming to the agent logs.": "why did operator put em dash in comments I thought we taught "humanizer" skill to block these kind of behaviour"; completes P21 and ruling 502). The comment was not the model's. `runDispatchLine` (`specialist-run.server.ts`, ruling 311) builds the dispatch sentence on the server and posts it under the Operator's name, so ruling 502's writing guide, which only the model reads, never reached it. P21 (2026-08-20) banned the dashes from rendered copy and the seed assets and left `app/server` ungated as prompt machinery, and the timeline sentences, errors, tool replies, prompts and log lines built there kept 632 string literals with one, in 95 files. Decided: **(a)** *Every string literal under `app/server`, `app/schemas`, `app/shared` and `app/lib` is free of them, prompts and log lines included.* An agent imitates its prompt and its tools' descriptions, and a log line is read by whoever runs the instance. Each literal was reworded with a comma, a period, a colon, a semicolon or parentheses, never a spaced hyphen. The dispatch sentence now reads "Started a Claude run for the Estimate Judge agent. It is streaming to the agent logs.", and a queued run's note "… got a slot and started.
